28:
He directs all the aforementioned fulfillment of giving (dāna) towards the welfare and happiness of the entire world, for his own indestructible liberation (vimutti), and for inexhaustible aspiration (chanda), inexhaustible energy (viriya), inexhaustible concentration (samādhi), inexhaustible intuition (paṭibhāna), inexhaustible meditative absorption (jhāna), and for inexhaustible supreme enlightenment (sammāsambodhi-ñāṇa). The Great Being (Bodhisatta) who fulfills this perfection of giving (dāna-pāramī) develops the perception of impermanence (anicca-saññā) regarding life. Likewise, he develops the perception of impermanence regarding wealth and possessions. He also reflects on the fact that these possessions are shared with many enemies. He constantly arouses great compassion (mahākaruṇā) toward beings. In this way, one who takes the essence from wealth and possessions is like a person who carries out all his belongings and himself from a burning house, leaving nothing behind, making no distinction in any place, but indeed relinquishing them without attachment. This is the sequence of the practice of the perfection of giving.

As for the sequence of the practice of the perfection of morality (sīla-pāramī): The Great Man (Mahāpurisa) who wishes to adorn beings with the ornaments of morality of an Omniscient Buddha must first purify his own morality. That morality is purified through four aspects: purity of disposition (āsaya), undertaking (samādāna), non-transgression (avitikkama), and restoration (paṭikamma) if a transgression occurs. Due to having a pure disposition, some individuals, making themselves the primary authority and having a nature of loathing evil, arouse the sense of shame (hiri) within themselves and become practitioners of extremely pure conduct. Similarly, in undertaking from others, some individuals, making the world the primary authority and being fearful of evil, arouse the dread of wrongdoing (ottappa) and become practitioners of extremely pure conduct. In both these ways, they establish themselves in morality through non-transgression. However, if at times, due to a lapse in mindfulness, a breach in morality occurs, because of being endowed with the aforementioned shame and dread, they quickly rise from that unwholesome state and restore it to its original condition.

That morality is of two kinds: morality of avoidance (vāritta-sīla) and morality of performance (cāritta-sīla). Therein, in the practice of the Bodhisatta's morality of avoidance: the Bodhisatta must have a heart of compassion such that even in dreams, no enmity arises toward any being. By not touching the belongings and wealth of others, he should not handle others' property as if it were a cobra. If he is a monk, he is one who practices far from ignoble sexual intercourse and avoids the seven types of sexual associations; it goes without saying that he avoids approaching the wives and daughters of others. If he is a layman, he never allows even a depraved thought to arise toward the wives and daughters of others. In speech, he speaks only words that are true, beneficial, endearing, and moderate, and he is one who speaks Dhamma at the appropriate time. In all matters...
230:
When asked, "Do you, who are joyful, understand the well-spoken and ill-spoken words of others?" and they reply, "No, Bhante," this is called the third round (tatiya-vāra). It is because it is extracted in the place of the third round according to the method already mentioned in the ground of dispraise (avaṇṇa-bhūmi). Although this third round does not directly appear in the teaching (desanā) at the time of delivery because there was no person to be enlightened by that round, it is indeed present in meaning because that meaning is possible. To show that third round in detail like the Kathāvatthu treatise, it is said starting with "Tatiya-vāro pana." By saying this, it shows that when making the commentary (saṃvaṇṇanā), that round should be brought in and explained for the sake of beings who can understand in that way. With the words "Yatheva hi" etc., the occurrence of that meaning is clarified. It should be connected as: "Just as an angry person does not know the meaning (attha)."

In the round showing the manner of practice refers to the fourth round, which is spoken based on the aforementioned third round. It should be connected from the words "Your teacher" up to the words "For this reason also, it is true." The words "That Blessed One" etc., are the explanation of that fourth round. Therein, "itipī" means "for this reason also." For details, see the Visuddhimagga. Although it is said, "There is no offense for a monk who reports the truth to another monk," it is appropriate to report only to monks of similar standing (sabhāga); therefore, it is said, "It should be acknowledged only to monks of similar standing." Only those monks desire his welfare and consider his words trustworthy; because of that, the meaning stated as "It serves to demonstrate the non-emptiness (amoghatā) of the Dispensation" can be fulfilled. "Evañhi" etc., are words showing the reason. Either "having low desires" is avoided, or that "low desire" should be connected as the agent (kattā). "Amoghatā" means the state of not being empty because it is the means of escape from saṃsāra. By the method already mentioned refers to the method stated in the words "Therein, you" as "In that praise, you" etc., and "The second term is a synonym (vevacana) of the first term, and the fourth of the third" etc.

## Commentary on the Small Morality (Cūḷasīla-vaṇṇanā)

The question "What is the sequence (anusandhi)?" is asked because the inquiry "Has not the teaching connected with the aforementioned dispraise and praise reached its conclusion with just this much?" is possible. (It is shown) by those two terms, "by praise and by dispraise." Those who consider the syllables say that just as there is an indication of meaning, there is also an indication of sound. Or else, it is said "by terms" because it is the cause of such speaking and because it is a portion. "By dispraise and by praise" is the manifestation of the actual nature by way of lack of virtue and presence of virtue, and by way of blame and praise. He desists...
231:
The teacher, the Elder Dhammapāla, stated that [the teaching] recedes because there is no root cause and because there is nothing to be answered. To elaborate on that statement, it ceases by the Buddha's intention not to teach because there is no person to be enlightened by the teaching; it should be understood just as the third cessation in the Vaṇṇabhūmi. Since the state of being answerable is known due to the presence of a person to be enlightened, [the teaching] indeed continues. In the phrase 'iti petaṃ bhūtaṃ', the word 'iti' has the meaning of 'beginning', because it continues even above that; therefore, the teacher will say 'idha pana', and so forth. By this sequence of words, he shows that 'this is the Vaṇṇānusandhi' (the connection of praise), and wishing to show the connection of praise for the youth Brahmadatta among those two types of praise, he said 'so pana', and so forth. Later, in the exposition of emptiness (suññatā), he will show the connection (anusandhi) with the words 'atthi bhikkhave', and so forth.

Having thus stated the collective meaning through the opening of questions and answers, he now shows the meaning of the parts with the words 'tattha', and so forth. It is called 'paritta' (limited) because it is cut off from all sides only to a small extent; therefore, he said that 'appamattaka' is a name for 'paritta'. 'Mattā' is said to be 'measure' (pamāṇa) because it is measured or compared. With the letter 'ka' at the end of the compound, it becomes 'appamattakaṃ', like the word 'bahuputtako'; it is the same in the word 'oramattaka'. For that very reason, he shows that the suffix 'ka' has meaning because there is no difference in sense, such as in 'virtue (sīla) which has a small measure is appamattaka'. Since the word 'mattaka' has no [additional] meaning, virtue itself is called 'sīlamattaka'. Having no meaning means existing only in its own sense, because it exists only in the sense of the preceding word. Teachers who contemplate phonetics (akkharacintaka) say that words do not exist without any meaning at all.

Is it not said that by the power of the Buddha's perfections (pāramī), not even a single meaningless letter reaches his noble mouth, and the entire Pariyatti Sāsana manifests the Four Noble Truths in every word? If so, how can it be possible for that word to be meaningless? It is true; that word [mattaka] also expresses the very meaning expressed by another word by way of qualifying it, but since that meaning can be known by that other word alone, it is said to be 'meaningless'. Have we not already said, 'Having no meaning means... because it exists [in the sense of the preceding word]'? Furthermore, the Buddha's teaching proceeds according to the inclinations of those to be disciplined (veneyya). Those to be disciplined are those whose minds have become accustomed only to worldly words in the beginningless saṃsāra. In the world, even when there is no understanding of a different meaning, the use of words is seen for the sake of linguistic smoothness, such as 'labbhati-palabbhati, khañjati-nikhañjati, āgacchati-paccāgacchati'. For those who are so accustomed, by such use of words...
232:
The use of meaningless words is stated to make the meaning easy to understand. It should be understood thus in all cases. There is a summary verse (gāthā) here:

'To specify the meaning expressed by another word,
And to make it known to those to be disciplined,
In such a manner, He speaks a meaningless word.'

Alternatively, in this word 'sīlamattakaṃ', the word 'matta' has the sense of excluding specifics, as in 'avitakkavicāramattā dhammā' and 'manomattā dhātu manodhātū', etc. The meaning expressed generally by the two words 'appamattakaṃ oramattakaṃ' is expressed specifically by the word 'sīlamattakaṃ'. Therefore, to show that the definition should be made as 'virtue itself is sīlamatta, and that sīlamatta itself is sīlamattakaṃ', it is said 'virtue itself is sīlamattakaṃ'.

This is a method outside of the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā-muttaka): In this word 'oramattakaṃ', 'ora' refers to 'this side', as in 'orato bhogaṃ' and 'oraṃ pāraṃ', etc. Alternatively, the word 'ora' has the meaning of 'lower part', as in 'those fetters (saṃyojana) that lead to the lower part are orambhāgiya', etc. Virtue (sīla), relative to concentration (samādhi) and wisdom (paññā), exists on 'this side' and in the 'lower part'. In both cases, the definition is 'virtue which has a measure existing on this side (or the lower part)'. In this word 'sīlamattakaṃ' also, the word 'matta' expresses a small amount, as in 'bhesajjamattā', etc.

Alternatively, this word 'matta' is used to include only a portion of virtue. For that reason, Indriya-saṃvara-sīla (virtue of sense restraint) and Paccaya-sannissita-sīla (virtue concerning requisites) are not included (not taught) in this Cūḷasīla. Why? Because those virtues are not as manifest in all worldlings (puthujjana) as Pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla and Ājīva-pārisuddhi-sīla. In this sense of excluding specifics, the word 'mattaṃ' is of the neuter gender. However, in the senses of 'measure' and 'small amount', 'mattaṃ' or 'mattā' can be both neuter and feminine.

He shows the collective meaning by connecting it with 'this is the intended meaning', and so forth. The connection is: 'the virtue by which one would speak, that is called sīlamattakaṃ'. The phrase 'even having made an effort to speak words of praise' is an explanation of 'speaking words of praise'. By this explanation, he shows that the suffix 'māna' has the sense of capability, as in 'Monks, a certain person, when arising in the world, arises...', and so forth. The statement 'making an effort' means that words ending in 'māna' and 'anta' suffixes, like words ending in Taddhita suffixes, are indeed dependent on the subsequent verb.
233:
The use of the word "Katvā" instead of "Kurumāno" is to show that words ending in the "māna" suffix, like those ending in "tvā" and other such suffixes, are also dependent on a subsequent action. By the words "Tattha siyā" and so forth, it shows that such an objection might arise for someone who, not knowing the intended meaning and taking only the literal sense, considers it to be in contradiction with other discourses. "Tattha" refers to the statement beginning with "Appamattakaṃ kho panetaṃ" (Dī. Ni. 1.7). One is called a "yogī" because they habitually strive in the development of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna-bhāvanā) through virtue (sīla); [this is the meaning] of that yogī.

Decoration is called "alaṅkāra," meaning the act of decorating. Alternatively, it is called "alaṅkāra" because one makes oneself beautiful with it, such as earrings and other ornaments. Adornment is called "maṇḍana," meaning the filling of what is deficient. Alternatively, it is called "maṇḍana" because one is adorned by it, referring to accessories that fill a deficiency such as face powder. In this context, however, virtue (sīla) itself is spoken of in that way, either through similar usage or by way of a derivative (taddhita). "Maṇḍana" means one has gone for the sake of adornment or because of the cause of the act of adornment. Alternatively, a "maṇḍana" is a man whose nature is to adorn himself through virtue. This word is used in the singular to refer to the class (jāti), even though it implies a plural. Some teachers desire the singular even in the sense of extraction (ubbāhana), but that is inappropriate because it does not appear in grammatical treatises and lacks logical consistency. How could performing extraction from what is indicated by the singular be appropriate, since in a single meaning there is no other meaning to be extracted? Therefore, this singular should be understood as representing the plural by way of grammatical substitution (vacanavippallāsa); the meaning is "in those whose nature is adornment." Indeed, this very decision was stated by the teacher, the Elder Dhammapāla (Dī. Ni. Ṭī. 1.7). "Aggataṃ" means [reaching] the state of excellence.

It should be connected as "Assaṃ bhavissāmīti ākaṅkheyya" (He should long for: 'I shall be...'). "Assa" means "bhaveyya" (should be). In the phrase "Paripūrakārī" and so forth, the word "iti" carries the meaning of "and so forth" or "in this manner"; by that word "iti," the entire Sīlathomanasutta is indicated.

In the phrase "Kikīva aṇḍaṃ" as well, by the word "iti" having that meaning—

"As a hen guards her egg,
As a yak guards its tail,
As a mother her beloved only son,
As a one-eyed man his eye;
So should you always guard your virtue,
Being well-behaved and ever respectful."
(Visuddhi. 1.19)—

This verse is included. Having said "Pupphagandho" (scent of flowers), the phrase "Na candanaṃ" and so forth is stated to show it by way of a part [of the flowers]. Sandalwood, tagara, and jasmine are mentioned because they are associated with that scent...
234:
It refers only to the scent of those [sandalwood, tagara, and jasmine]. "Pupphagandho" means the flower and the scent remaining from that flower. Alternatively, the scent remaining from the tagara and jasmine flowers is called "pupphagandho." In the phrase "Satañca gandho," virtue itself is called "scent" either by similar usage or by way of metaphor. Or, the sound of praise connected with virtue is intended as "scent" in the manner already mentioned. For virtue is the cause of fame. As it is said: "The good reputation of one possessed of virtue spreads upwards" (Dī. Ni. 2.150, etc.). A virtuous person wafts fragrance in various ways because they are comparable to a tree heavy with scent.

"Vassikī" refers to the jasmine flower (sumana); there is also a reading "vassikaṃ," which has the same meaning. "Gandhajāta" means scents or types of scents. "Yvāyaṃ" is connected as "This excellent scent wafts."

"Sammadaññā vimuttānaṃ" means [the scent] of those who are liberated from defilements by knowing rightly, or by knowing rightly through the Path of Arahatship. "Maggaṃ na vindati" means one does not find the cause, or does not know.

In the verse beginning with "Sīle patiṭṭhāya," a person called a bhikkhu, who possesses innate wisdom, who has effort that burns away defilements, and who is prudent with protective wisdom, being established in virtue, developing concentration (which is spoken of primarily as 'mind') and likewise developing insight-wisdom, would be able to untangle, would be able to resolve, this tangle known as the internal tangle and the external tangle. This is the summary of the meaning.

"Pathaviṃ nissāya" means just as one relies on the earth by way of taking nutrients, in the case of virtue, one should understand "relying" as being established by way of fulfillment.

Because it is a concept by comparison (upanidhā-paññatti) like "the far shore" and "the near shore" due to being small or large, it is said "by comparing with higher qualities" in order to explain that they are taught by comparing one with another. In the word "Sīlañhi," the word "hi" has a causal meaning; by it, this cause is shown: "Because virtue, although of great help to concentration by being its foundation, does not reach even a fraction when compared to the special qualities of concentration such as its power; likewise, concentration when compared to wisdom." Therefore, it says "Tasmā" and so forth. "Na pāpuṇāti" means it does not reach or equal in terms of parity of qualities. "Uparimaṃ" refers to concentration and wisdom. "Upanidhāya" means by providing support. For it is a support for such a concept. "Heṭṭhimaṃ" refers to the pair of virtue and concentration.
235: The word beginning with 'Kathaṃ' is a detailed explanation. Here, the mention of performing the miracle at the foot of the Kaṇḍamba mango tree should be understood as a well-known miracle and by way of illustration, because it is intended to establish the impossibility of [others'] virtue reaching [such] concentration. The words 'Abhi...pe... titthiyamaddanaṃ' are spoken to show the great fame of that Twin Miracle and to show its distinction from other miracles performed at the foot of the Bodhi tree and at the assembly of relatives. On the eighth day after His enlightenment, the Buddha created a jeweled walkway in the sky and performed a miracle while walking on it to dispel the doubts of the deities who wondered, 'Is He a Buddha or not?' Furthermore, in the second year, when He went to His home city of Kapilavatthu, He performed the Twin Miracle at the assembly of relatives in the Nigrodhārāma monastery to dispel their pride. In that context, 'Abhisambodhitō' means from the time of His enlightenment. 'Sāvatthinagaradvāre' means at the southern gate of the city of Sāvatthī. 'Kaṇḍambarukkhamūle' means at the foot of the mango tree named Kaṇḍamba because it was planted by the gardener of King Pasenadi named Kaṇḍa. When the thought arose in the Blessed One's mind to perform the Twin Miracle, some say that the celestial architect Vissakamma, ordered by Sakka, the king of devas, created a jeweled pavilion and other structures, thinking, 'A suitable place for that miracle is needed.' Others say the Blessed One Himself created it. However, in many commentaries, it is said, 'The pavilion was made by the celestial son Vissakamma, ordered by Sakka, the lord of devas, but the walkway was created by the Blessed One.' It should be understood that the deities held a divine white parasol, as this would not be possible for others. 'An assembly of twelve yojanas' refers to the human audience extending twelve yojanas in each of the four directions. At that time, deities and Brahmas from ten thousand world systems also gathered, filling the interior of the universe. The phrase 'attādānaparidīpanaṃ' is used because it is like a challenge: 'If anyone is able to perform such a miracle, let him come.' 'Attādāna' means taking up the opposing self (cause), and thus it is an exhortation (anuyoga). 'Titthiyamaddanaṃ' means the crushing of the sectarians (titthiyas) who had previously risen up with the intent to deceive, saying, 'We will perform a miracle.' This crushing is simply making them unable to perform such a miracle. These two terms should be connected with the term 'Yamaka Pāṭihāriya.' Everything from the occurrence of the sandalwood bowl of the Treasurer of Rājagaha onwards should be mentioned here.
236: In this matter of the miracle, everything from the occurrence of the sandalwood bowl of the Treasurer of Rājagaha (or from the striking of the sandalwood in the net) onwards should be mentioned. The words beginning with 'Uparimakāyato' show the method found in the Paṭisambhidāmagga Pali; therefore, it is briefly stated as 'proceeding in this way' and 'everything should be detailed.' In that Pali text, the following is the remaining portion: From the lower body, a mass of fire proceeds; from the upper body, a stream of water proceeds. From the front of the body, fire; from the back of the body, water. From the back of the body, fire; from the front of the body, water. From the right eye, fire; from the left eye, water. From the left eye, fire; from the right eye, water. From the right ear-hole, fire; from the left ear-hole, water. From the left ear-hole, fire; from the right ear-hole, water. From the right nostril, fire; from the left nostril, water. From the left nostril, fire; from the right nostril, water. From the right shoulder, fire; from the left shoulder, water. From the left shoulder, fire; from the right shoulder, water. From the right hand, fire; from the left hand, water. From the left hand, fire; from the right hand, water. From the right side, fire; from the left side, water. From the left side, fire; from the right side, water. From the right foot, fire; from the left foot, water. From the left foot, fire; from the right foot, water. From the fingers, fire; from the gaps between the fingers, water. From the gaps between the fingers, fire; from the fingers, water. From each single hair, fire; from each single hair, water. From every single pore, a mass of fire proceeds; from every single pore, a stream of water proceeds. In the Commentary, however, it appears only as 'from each single hair-pore' (ekekalomakūpato). In the phrase 'channaṃ vaṇṇānaṃ' (of six colors), the entire remaining Pali text—blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, and brilliant—is shown by the method of ellipsis (peyyāla) and by the word 'ādi'. In this phrase 'channaṃ vaṇṇānaṃ', it should be connected with the remaining text: 'the colors proceed in pairs, which are the emanations of the six colors.' Because of this connection, it will be said later, 'the rays are in pairs,' and so on. In that performance of the miracle, of those six rays...
237:
The separate occurrence of reflection (āvajjanā), preparation (parikamma), and resolution (adhiṭṭhāna), along with the manner of their occurrence in pairs, is shown. Some teachers, however, connect the phrase "channaṃ vaṇṇānaṃ" (of the six colors) with the preceding words "aggikkhandho udakadhārā" (mass of fire and stream of water). This is not appropriate, because the attainment of the fire kasina and the air kasina for the sake of the mass of fire and the stream of water will be mentioned later. Alternatively, "channaṃ vaṇṇānaṃ" should be connected by way of the agent (kattā), as in "the six colors occur," just as in the Pali passage: "ekassa cepi bhikkhuno na paṭibhāseyya taṃ bhikkhuniṃ apasādetuṃ." Indeed, grammarians desire the use of the genitive case (sāmivibhat) for the agent and the object even when used with a finite verb.

Having thus shown the Twin Miracle (Yamaka Pāṭihāriya) according to the method of the Pali, the author now wishes to explain it according to the method of the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā). To first explain the phrase "channaṃ vaṇṇānaṃ" by the method of proximity, he said the words beginning with "tassā." In that context, "tassā" means "of the Blessed One." The phrase "golden-colored rays" is said because of the predominance of those yellow-colored rays; it means it was like the time of being adorned with rays of six colors. Indeed, those rays, having risen from within the universe (cakkavāḷa), reached the Brahma realm, and then turning back, they took hold of the very rim of the universe's mouth. The interior of a single universe was illuminated all at once like a Bodhi-house with curved rafters.

"Dutiyā dutiyā rasmiyo" refers to the rays that emerged after the rays that emerged previously. Why is the word "viya" (like/as if) used by way of similar appearance? To answer this, he said the words beginning with "dvinnñca." There is no such thing as the occurrence of two thoughts in a single moment, by which those rays would occur in such a way. Nevertheless, it is meant that they appear in this very way due to these two reasons. "Bhavaṅgaparivāsassa" means saturation by way of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), or the saturation known as the life-continuum, meaning the falling into the life-continuum. "Āciṇṇavasitāya" means because of having mastery through practice in the five ways, such as reflection and attainment.

He removes the objection, "How can two rays occur from the occurrence of a single thought?" with the words beginning with "tassā tassā pana rasmiyā." Due to the diversity of mental cycles (cittavāra), the reflection thoughts and preparation thoughts occur separately; and due to the diversity of kasinas, the resolution mental cycles also occur separately. The impulsions (javana) that occur three times at the end of reflection are referred to here by the name "parikamma" (preparation).

To show how this is so, he said the words beginning with "nīlarasmiatthāya hi." The statement, "He attains the red kasina for the sake of the crimson ray, and the yellow kasina for the sake of the brilliant ray," is not mentioned separately because it is already established when the causes for the red and yellow rays were stated. Indeed, of those rays...
238:
The crimson rays and the brilliant rays are distinct varieties. The explanation of the words beginning with "uparimakāyato" is given by the words beginning with "aggikkhandhatthāya." The mass of fire and the mass of water also ascended as far as the Brahma realm without mixing with each other and remained at the rim of the universe. On that day, the Teacher taught the Dhamma and displayed the miracle according to the inclinations (ajjhāsaya) of whoever was inspired by whatever Dhamma or miracle. While the Dhamma was being taught and the miracle was being performed, the multitude of people attained the realization of the Dhamma (dhammābhisamaya).

In that assembly, not seeing anyone capable of understanding His mind and asking a question, He created a created Buddha (nimmita Buddha). The Teacher answered the questions asked by that created Buddha. That created Buddha also answered the questions asked by the Teacher. When the Teacher performed the walking meditation, the created Buddha adopted one of the other postures, such as standing. When the created Buddha performed the walking meditation, the Teacher adopted one of the other postures, such as standing. To show this meaning, the words beginning with "satthā caṅkamati" were said. By the phrase "sabbaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ," it is shown that while the Teacher stands, the created Buddha walks, sits, or lies down; thus, taking each of the four postures as a base, four rounds on the Teacher's side and four rounds on the created Buddha's side, all eight rounds should be explained in detail. Since virtue (sīla) serves only as the foundation for concentration (samādhi) and then subsides, and only concentration remains established there to perform all the aforementioned tasks of the miracle, it is said that "this miracle is solely the work of concentration" with the words beginning with "ekampi."

With the words beginning with "yaṃ pana," it is explained that concentration cannot reach the level of wisdom (paññā). That which is the penetration of knowledge is the function of wisdom. That function of wisdom is shown in sequence with the words beginning with "bhagavā." The phrase "four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons" is said starting from the initial aspiration (abhinīhāra) made at the feet of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara. It should be understood that even before that aspiration, He had accumulated a store of merit sufficient to attain the enlightenment of a disciple (sāvakabodhi) had He so desired in that life. For that very reason, among the eight conditions mentioned in the words beginning with "manussattaṃ liṅgasampatti," there was the fulfillment of the cause (hetu). Some teachers speak of the prior accumulation of merit by dividing the incalculables in many ways according to the mental aspiration and verbal aspiration. That is not appropriate because it is not stated that way in the Commentaries authorized by the Councils (Saṅgāyana). In those Commentaries, only the fulfillment of the cause prior to the initial aspiration is shown according to the aforementioned method. The phrase "leaving the world and ordaining at the age of twenty-nine" is the connection of the preceding and following events.
239:
Because of possessing the merit worthy of the Wheel-treasure, the Bodhisatta is endowed with the glory of a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti); therefore, the residence of that Bodhisatta is described as being "like the glorious residence of a Universal Monarch." *Bhavanā* refers to the mansions known as Ramma, Suramma, and Subha. *Padhānayoga* refers to the exertion of supreme energy for the sake of difficult practices (*dukkharacariyā*).

It is heard that in the Senānigama of Uruvelā, a young woman named Sujātā, the daughter of a householder, having reached maturity, made a prayer at the foot of a banyan tree on the bank of the Nerañjarā River: "If I go to a household of equal status and obtain a son in my first pregnancy, I shall make an offering to the deity with milk-rice." That prayer of Sujātā was fulfilled. She fed seven cows in a licorice forest, then fed the cows born from them in the same manner, and thus, taking the milk from the cows descended through seven generations of offspring, she began to cook the milk-rice. At that moment, Mahābrahmā held a white umbrella three leagues wide over it. Sakka, the king of gods, lit the fire. Deities infused it with all the flavors (*rasa*) existing in the world. The milk-rice cooked while circling to the right. Sujātā, after offering that milk-rice together with a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand to the Bodhisatta, departed. Then the Bodhisatta took that milk-rice to the landing place named Suppatiṭṭhita on the bank of the Nerañjarā River, made forty-nine morsels about the size of a palm fruit, and consumed them. With reference to that consumption, it is said: "On the full moon day of Visākhā (Kasone), in the village of Uruvelā, having consumed the honeyed milk-rice infused with divine essence offered by Sujātā."

In that passage, Sujātā refers to the wife of a merchant, the mother of the Venerable Yasa Thera, who later attained the title of foremost (*etadagga*) among those who take refuge. The essence of flavor that spreads through the major and minor limbs, providing strength and depending on the great elements, is specifically called *ojā* (nutritive essence). Because that essence originated in the celestial realm and was infused by the deities, it is called "infused with divine essence." Because it is both drinkable and eatable, it is called *pāyāsa* (milk-rice). It is a special kind of food suitable for drinking as a liquid and for eating as morsels. Being milk-rice poured over with honey, it is called *madhupāyāsa*.

Thereafter, because he spent the day in various meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) in the Great Sāla grove on the bank of the Nerañjarā River, it is said "in the evening time," and so forth. The details should be sought in the respective texts. The word "*dakkhiṇuttarena*" is said with reference to the path entering the Bodhi tree from the place of the day-rest. It means by a straight path running from south to north, decorated by the deities.
240:
This is the meaning. Some teachers also say: "*Dakkhiṇuttarena*" means by way of the south, west, and north directions. This is said because by taking the beginning and the end, the middle is also included, and also because such elided usage is seen. If this is the meaning, it agrees with the statement in the Jātaka-nidāna: "Having entered the Bodhimaṇḍa by way of the south, west, and north directions, he stands." Other teachers say it means entering by the northern direction which is to be reached from the southern direction.

However, some teachers say: "In this context, the word *uttara* refers to a path. If it referred to a direction, it would be said as *dakkhiṇuttarāya*." That statement is not appropriate. This is because the instrumental case ending in *-ena* associated with the word *uttara* is also seen to denote a direction, as in "To the north (*uttarena*) is the Sīdā River, deep and difficult to cross," and because the word *uttara* meaning 'path' is not found here. Alternatively, it is said thus with reference to the side of a direction. Indeed, the side of a direction is the direction itself.

Then, on the way, having taken the eight handfuls of kusa grass offered by the grass-cutter named Sotthiya, the Bodhisatta approached the Bodhimaṇḍa, which was like a mountain of black collyrium, a place of solace for all Bodhisattas, and the ornament of the Bodhi tree. Having circumambulated it three times to the right, he stood at the southern side. That spot shook like a drop of water on a lotus leaf. From there, even when the Great Being went and stood at the western and northern sides, they shook in the same way. Then the Great Being thought, "Not all of this place is capable of supporting my virtues," and went to the eastern side. There, the area the size of a throne remained firm and motionless. That very spot is literally called the Bodhimaṇḍa. The Great Being, deciding "This is the place for the destruction of defilements," stood facing the north-east and, holding those grasses by their tips, shook them over that motionless spot. Immediately, a throne fourteen cubits high appeared. Those grasses also appeared in a wonderful manner, like lines drawn with a brush.

That Great Being, having sat cross-legged in a triple-jointed posture on that throne, and having preceded it with the meditation on loving-kindness (*mettā-kammaṭṭhāna*) endowed with four factors, resolved upon the fourfold effort (*vīriya*) and sat down. Intending to show that meaning in brief, it is said: "Having entered the Bodhimaṇḍa," and so forth.

In that passage, *Bodhi* refers to the Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship and Omniscient Knowledge. Because that *Bodhi* is clarified or established here by reaching its full strength, it is called *Bodhimaṇḍa*. Literally, it refers to the aforementioned spot; figuratively, in this context, it refers to the Bodhi tree, the king of trees. Thus, it was said by the teacher Venerable Ānanda Thera: "The word *Bodhimaṇḍa* should be understood only as the place where the initial Enlightenment was attained, not as any place where a Bodhi tree happens to stand." It refers to that Bodhimaṇḍa.
241:
It is called *Assattha* because it comforts or pleases the Blessed One through the conquest of the five Maras and the attainment of omniscience. Indeed, teachers desire the word *assa* in the sense of instruction and in the sense of pleasing. That same *Assattha* (Bodhi tree) is also called in the world "*Caladalo*" and "*Kuñjarāsano*." Because of its great height, because it has reached the summit of the unconquerable earth, and because it grows in the place where all the qualities of omniscience are obtained, it is the king of trees, thus called "*Dumārājā*." Since that tree is both *Assattha* and *Dumārājā*, it is called "*Assatthadumārājā*." It is called "*Tisandhi*" because it has three joints—two joints of the thighs and knees, and one joint of the base of the thighs and the waist—or because it has three corners in shape. That very throne is called "*Tisandhipallaṅka*" because of the meaning of sitting with legs crossed from all sides, by changing the letter 'r' to 'l' and doubling it, or because it is a throne marked by three joints.

"*Ābhujitvā*" means binding or having placed both legs well-folded. The details will come in the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta Commentary*.

It is the meditation on loving-kindness (*mettā-kammaṭṭhāna*) endowed with four factors by way of extending it equally towards four types of persons: oneself, a friend, a neutral person, and an enemy. This term "*caturaṅgasamannāgata*" (endowed with four factors) should also be applied to the determination of energy (*vīriyādhiṭṭhāna*). That energy is also endowed with four factors according to the method stated: "Verily, let only skin, sinews, and bones remain; let the flesh and blood in the body dry up; as long as I have not attained what is attainable by manly strength, manly energy, and manly effort, I will not stop my energy."

It is called "*Cuddasahattha*" because it has a measurement of fourteen cubits in width. It is called "*Pallaṅka*" because it is marked or delimited from all sides; it is a word formed by changing the letter 'r' to 'l' and doubling it. Alternatively, because it is stated in the Commentaries, "This is the place for destroying defilements," it is called "*Pallaṅka*" because it performs the destruction of defilements in this place, either by the arrival of the *niggahīta* or by way of an *alutta-samāsa* (uncompounded compound). Because it is a throne fourteen cubits wide and is noble due to its exalted and desirable nature, it is called "*Cuddasahatthapallaṅkavara*." The Lord who is seated on that throne is also like that. Here, the measurement of fourteen cubits should be understood in terms of width.
242:
Only those grasses, through the power of immeasurable merit, became a throne fourteen cubits wide. It is not possible for those grasses, which were originally eight handfuls in size, to rise fourteen cubits upwards. Therefore, it is said in this text, "having spread the grass-mat," and in the *Dhammapada Commentary* etc., "having spread the grasses... having sat facing the east." In other texts, it is said, "on the grass-seat known as fourteen cubits." Some teachers, however, say that it is fourteen cubits only because of its rising upwards, according to their own imagination. That statement should not be accepted because it contradicts the aforementioned reasons and evidence. Although in the *Manorathapūraṇī*, the *Aṅguttara Commentary*, the text appears as: "having circled the Bodhi tree three times clockwise, having ascended the *Bodhimanda*, having spread the grass-mat in a place fourteen cubits in height (*ubbedha*), and having sat down after determining the fourfold energy," nevertheless, the word *ubbedha* there should be understood as meaning width or extent. This is like in the *Mahāpanāda Jātaka*: "sixteen *ubbedha* in width, and they say a thousandfold upwards." Indeed, in its commentary, it is said: "sixteen *ubbedha* in width means it was sixteen *kaṇḍapāta* wide in extent." Otherwise, if *ubbedha* is taken as height, it would mean the grass-mat was spread in the sky and not on the firm ground, which is not intended as it is not found in other texts.

"Like having the silver mountain behind" is how the words should be connected. "*Atthaṃ*" refers to the western mountain. "*Mārabalaṃ*" refers to Mara and his army, or the power of Mara. "*Pubbenivāsaṃ*" refers to the aggregates previously lived. "*Dibbacakkhu*" refers to the knowledge of the divine eye. Having directed the knowledge into Dependent Origination starting with aging and death, with the words "Alas, this world has fallen into suffering," etc. In the phrase "*Ānāpānacatutthajjhāna*" (the fourth Jhana of mindfulness of breathing), it should be connected by changing the inflection as "the practice of all Buddhas." Teachers say that the fourth Jhana of mindfulness of breathing is indeed the practice of the Buddhas. "*Pādakaṃ katvā*" means having made it the cause or the foundation. "Having developed insight (*vipassanā*)" means having developed insight by way of grasping the "Great Vajira Knowledge" (*Mahāvajirañāṇa*), also known as the knowledge of the destruction of taints (*āsavakkhayañāṇa*), through three million six hundred thousand *koti* modes. Indeed, the insight knowledge that proceeds through three million six hundred thousand *koti* modes because of contemplating the formations in many ways through the insight into successive phenomena (*anupadadhamma-vipassanā*) to attain omniscience is also called *Mahāvajirañāṇa*. The knowledge that occurs before and after the twenty-four million *koti* attainments (*samāpatti*) used daily is also called *Mahāvajirañāṇa*. However, in this context, only the Path Knowledge (*maggañāṇa*) is meant by *Mahāvajirañāṇa*. Specifically, the Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship is called *Mahāvajirañāṇa*, and thus its nature as the "insight-chamber" of the Path of Arahatship should be understood. "*Sabbabuddhaguṇe*" refers to the infinite qualities of the Buddha, such as omniscience. Based on that insight, concentration declines. Therefore, the author of the *Sangaha* says that the remainder of that insight is the function of wisdom. "*Assa*" means "of the Blessed One."
243:
The insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) developed by cultivating insight through the power of acquiring the 'Great Diamond Knowledge' (Mahāvajirañāṇa), which is called the knowledge of the destruction of taints (āsavakkhayañāṇa) based on three million six hundred thousand [units], is also called 'Mahāvajirañāṇa'. The knowledge that occurs before and after the twenty-four million attainments (samāpatti) used daily is also called 'Mahāvajirañāṇa'. In this context, however, only the Path Knowledge (maggañāṇa), specifically the Knowledge of the Path of Arahantship (arahattamaggañāṇa), is called 'Mahāvajirañāṇa'. Therefore, only this Knowledge of the Path of Arahantship should be understood as the womb of insight.

'Sabbabuddhaguṇe' refers to the qualities of the Buddha without remainder, such as Omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa). The statement that concentration (samādhi) recedes after making that insight its basis refers to this function of wisdom (paññākicca) of the Blessed One.

'Tattha yathā hatthe' etc., is an explanation through similes to make the meaning clear. 'Hatthe' means in the palm of the hand or in the hollow of the hands. 'Pātiyaṃ' means in a small bowl. 'Ghaṭe' means in a water-carrying pot. A vessel with a capacity of thirty-two doṇas is called a 'kolamba'. A pot larger than that is called a 'cāṭi'. A pot even larger than that is called a 'mahākumbhī'. 'Soṇḍī' refers to a small pond. A river cleft is called a 'kandara'. The ocean within the circular walls of the universe is called the 'Cakkavāḷamahāsamuddara'. The phrase 'sine-rupādake mahāsamudde' refers specifically to the Sīdantara ocean. The meaning is further clarified in another way starting with 'pātiyaṃ'. It should be connected as 'pari-ttaṃ hoti yathā' (as it is small). To show the quality of the commentary (aṭṭhakathā) written to clarify the meaning of a certain Pali text, the phrase 'tenāha' (therefore he said) etc., is used. This is the same in all places.

'Duve puthujjanā' etc., is stated only for the purpose of showing the divisions found among worldlings (puthujjana). It is not for the purpose of distinguishing specific worldlings as in the commentary to the Mūlapariyāya Sutta, because here all worldlings without remainder are intended. Indeed, every worldling is unable to clarify the higher qualities of the Blessed One. Let alone worldlings, the qualities of the Buddha are beyond the scope even of noble disciples (ariyasāvaka) and Paccekabuddhas. Thus, it will be said later, 'sotāpanno' etc. Because of the lineage connection, being a kinsman of the Sun deity (Ādicca), he is called 'Ādiccabandhu' (Kinsman of the Sun). Thus it is said in the Niddesa:

'The Sun is called Ādicca. The Sun is a Gotama by lineage; the Blessed One is also a Gotama by lineage. The Blessed One is a relative by lineage, a kinsman by lineage of the Sun; therefore, the Buddha is called Ādiccabandhu.'

Grammarians, however, prefer the reading 'buddhassādiccabandhunā'. This is because he has a kinsman known by lineage who is equal to the Gotama lineage, the kinsman of the Sun, and because he is both the Buddha and the kinsman of the Sun, he is called 'Ādiccabandhu'. Because through skill in the discourse on aggregates (khandhakathā) etc., there is great learning (bāhusacca) which is the cause for knowing the defilements (upakkilesa) and secondary defilements (anupakkilesa). In what manner does great learning occur...
244:
'Venerable Sir, to what extent is one truly a person of great learning (bahussuta)?' (he asked). 'Monk, when a monk is skilled in the aggregates (khandha), skilled in the elements (dhātu)... the bases (āyatana)... and skilled in dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda), to this extent, monk, is one truly a person of great learning.' (the Buddha replied).

Therefore, it is said (by the author of the summary), 'To whom in the aggregates, elements, bases, etc.' Here, the word 'ādi' (etc.) includes everything up to dependent origination. Among those (learning etc.), making it fluent by heart is called 'learning' (uggaha). Repeatedly questioning the meaning is called 'inquiry' (paripucchā). Making the meaning connected to the ear-door by means of the commentary is called 'hearing' (savana). Carrying the Dhamma by well-placing and well-bearing the words and meanings is called 'retaining' (dhāraṇa). Thinking about and repeatedly contemplating with the mind the Dhamma thus heard, retained, and practiced is called 'reflection' (paccavekkhaṇa).

Having thus shown the divisions, he also shows the word-meaning (vacanattha) with the words 'duvidho' etc. 'Puthūnaṃ' refers to the various and manifold defilements etc. It is connected as 'puthujjana' because of being thoroughly included within the multitude of people (puthujjanantogadhatta). 'Puthu cāyaṃ jano' means this group of people is counted as separate from others. Therefore, it is connected as 'puthujjana'. The meaning thus shown in brief by the composition of the verse is expanded by the commentator with 'so hi' etc. By the word 'nānappakārānaṃ', it is shown that the word 'puthu' here has the meaning of 'many'.

Desiring to show the meaning included by the word 'ādi' and the evidence for that meaning through the Mahāniddesa Pali using the method of 'Ambasecanagarusīnāna', he said 'yathāha' etc. Personality beliefs (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) not yet destroyed by the Path are many for them, thus they are called 'puthu-avihata-sakkāyadiṭṭhika'. By this, it shows the meaning that because they are not destroyed, they produce many personality beliefs, or they are produced by many personality beliefs. Or, the word 'jana' expresses only the meaning of 'not destroyed'; therefore, they produce many personality beliefs and do not destroy them. Or, it is also appropriate to say it shows the meaning that many personality beliefs exist for those who have not destroyed them. Here, the placement of the adjective (vissessana) at the end should be noted, as in 'ajyāhito'. By the phrase 'puthu satthārānaṃ mukhullokikā', the derivation is shown that many people are teachers for them. In the phrase 'puthu sabbagatīhi avuṭṭhitā', they are produced by kamma and defilements, or beings are born in these destinations (gati), therefore destinations are called 'jana'. The word-meaning is that all destinations are many for them. 'Puthu...'
245:
By the statement 'they perform various volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra),' and because beings are born (jāyanti) due to these meritorious volitional formations (puññābhisaṅkhāra) and so forth, these [formations] are called 'jana' (producers). For these [beings], there exist various and diverse formations called 'jana.' Alternatively, it means they produce or perform various volitional formations.

Furthermore, desiring to show three meanings such as 'they are carried away by various and diverse floods (ogha),' it is said that because beings are born due to these floods and so forth, the flood of sensuality (kāmogha) and so forth, the heat of passion (rāgasantāpa) and so forth, the fever of passion (rāgapariḷāha) and so forth, or all the fevers of defilements (kilesa), are called 'jana.' For these [beings], there exist those various and diverse floods and so forth. Alternatively, this is said to show the etymological definition (vacanattha) that through those states, they produce beings, carry them away, cause them to burn, and cause them to be consumed.

Terms such as 'rattā' (lustful) and 'giddhā' (greedy) are synonymous expressions. In another way, 'rattā' means they are lustful through desire and lust (chandarāga) which transforms the mind, like a cloth dyed with dye. 'Giddhā' means they are greedy through greed (abhigijjhana) which has the nature of desiring. 'Gathitā' means they are fettered to those sensual pleasures in a way that is difficult to release, as if tied in a knot. 'Mucchitā' means they have reached a state of delusion where there is no other concern, like one who has lost consciousness due to the oozing of defilements. 'Ajjhosannā' means they remain settled, having swallowed [the object] as if it were not shared with others. 'Laggā' means they are stuck like cattle on thorns, or they are submerged in a way that they cannot be extricated, like a man fallen into a great swamp and submerged up to the tip of his nose. 'Laggitā' means they are adhered through the power of the five senses, like a monkey stuck with monkey-glue. 'Palibuddhā' means they are bound, or 'upaddutā' means they are oppressed. This meaning is stated in the Aṅguttara-ṭīkā. By this, it means 'one is called jana because one is born,' and 'lust is greed (gedha),' and so forth. For them, there exist various and diverse lusts and so forth; or it shows the meaning that beings are lustful, greedy... bound in the many five cords of sensual pleasure.

Terms such as 'āvutā' (obstructed) are also merely synonymous expressions. Furthermore, it is stated in that same Aṅguttara-ṭīkā: 'āvutā means obstructed; nivutā means hindered; ophutā means enveloped or entwined; pihitā means closed; paṭicchannā means covered; paṭikujjitā means overturned (facing downwards).' Here too, because they are produced by these hindrances (nīvaraṇa), there exist hindrances called 'jana.' Because these people have various and diverse hindrances called 'jana,' they are called 'puthujjana' (worldlings). Alternatively, it shows the etymological definition that beings are obstructed... overturned by many hindrances. It shows the meaning by the words 'puthūnaṃ' (of the many) and so forth, because they are born among those of low conduct, or because the person is included within those of low conduct, or because they are many beings. By this, the third foot [of the verse] is explained or completed. By the words 'puthu vā' and so forth, the fourth foot is explained. The etymological definition here is that only a being who is not associated with the Noble Ones (Ariyas) is a 'puthujjana.'
246:
Because of which special qualities acting as the cause (nimitta) this designation 'Tathāgata' has arisen for the Blessed One, it is said: 'The Blessed One is the Tathāgata for eight reasons,' and so forth, in order to show that [designation]. Indeed, even a single word, depending on many causes for its occurrence, can express meanings in many ways. All the names and titles of the Blessed One are indeed caused by his many virtues. As it is said:

'The Great Seer (Mahesi), endowed with virtues, has innumerable names;
Though there be thousands of names, the wise declare the name according to his virtue.'

If there is an inquiry as to what those [names] are, he first points out the nature of that name in brief and then explains it with 'How?' and so forth. In the phrase 'Tathā āgata,' the word 'tathā' has the meaning of establishing a comparison by way of determining the manner (ākāra). Because it stands in a specific sense [even when] expressing a general sense, and because one who desires the specific must apply even a general word only to the specific meaning, the word 'āgata' should be understood as meaning 'come by way of practice (paṭipadā).' It does not mean 'arrived by knowledge' as in the passages like 'arrived at the true characteristic (tathalakkhaṇaṃ āgato),' nor does it mean 'physical coming' as in the passages like 'The Great Recluse has come (āgato) to Giribbaja of the Magadhans.'

In that phrase, the word 'tathā' has the meaning of establishing a comparison by determining a certain manner. Showing that manner generally by way of example through the practice of the coming of previous Buddhas, based on Great Compassion (mahākaruṇā) since he is foremost in compassion, he said 'As in the whole world' and so forth. Since the words 'yaṃ' and 'taṃ' are always connected, here, in showing the meaning of the word 'tathā,' the meaning is clarified by the word 'yathā.' He explains that same meaning in detail with 'Just as the Blessed One Vipassī' and so forth. It should be understood that he shows that practice by way of those six Buddhas, Vipassī and others, because they are very well-known through the frequent mentions in the Mahāpadāna Sutta and so forth, and because they are close [in time]. The connection should be made everywhere as: 'As he came, so (tathā) he has come (āgata).' 

He explains that same meaning again in detail with 'What is meant?' and so forth. In that explanation, 'by which aspiration (abhinīhāra)' refers to the noble aspiration endowed with the eight factors: being human, being male, having the supporting condition for Arahatship, seeing a living Teacher (Buddha), going forth as a monk, being endowed with the quality of Jhana and higher knowledge (abhiññā), having the merit of great service (adhikāra) performed even at the cost of life, and having a strong desire to become a Buddha.
247:
Also by way of the Great Aspiration (mahāpaṇidhāna) [He is called Tathāgata]. For the initial aspiration of all Buddhas is fulfilled only by this means of directing the mind towards Buddhahood (abhinīhāra). In this context, the term 'abhinīhāra' should be understood as a designation expressing the excellence of the original aspiration.

Having thus shown the meaning of the word 'Tathāgata' by way of the Great Resolve (mahābhinīhāra), he now says 'atha vā' (or else) and so forth to show it also by way of the fulfillment of the perfections (pāramī). In this regard, the Elder Dhammapāla stated a decisive discourse on the perfections, beginning with: 'Here, for the sake of generating skill in the practice leading to Great Enlightenment (mahābodhi) for those who follow the method of the Suttas, I shall speak this detailed discourse on the perfections.' If we were to state that decisive discourse here, it would seem to make the text excessively long. However, since this new sub-commentary (saṃvaṇṇanā) has arisen for the purpose of clearing away errors made by later negligent scribes and for the purpose of exhausting the remaining meanings, that discourse on the perfections must indeed be stated here. Therefore, drawing from that [old sub-commentary] and from the Cariyāpiṭaka Commentary, and adorning it with appropriate verses, I shall clarify the meanings and intentions. How?

What are these perfections? In what sense are they perfections? How many kinds are there?
What is their order? What are their characteristics and so forth in every way?
What is the cause, the defilement, the purification, and the opposite?
The analysis of practice, the summary, and the fulfillment likewise.
In how much time are they accomplished? What is the advantage, and what is the fruit?
Having answered these questions, the decision will be made.

The answer to those questions is as follows:
To the question, 'What are these perfections?':
Excluding craving, conceit, and so forth, that state which is grasped by wisdom skillful in means is explained as a perfection (pāramī).

Those actions consisting of virtues such as giving (dāna) and so forth, which are not oppressed by craving, conceit, and so forth, but are grasped by compassion and skill in means, are explained as 'perfections'.

To the question, 'In what sense are they perfections?':
Because of the sense of being supreme (parama), [the Bodhisatta] is called 'Parama'; that which belongs to this Supreme One is a 'pāramī'.
Likewise, by way of the senses of action (kamma) and state (bhāva), giving (dāna) and so forth should be understood in three ways according to the derivative (taddhita) method.
248:
He binds other beings to himself; he is exceedingly pure from the stains of defilements; he reaches the noble Nibbāna; likewise, he knows the other world distinctly; or else, he places the group of virtues such as morality (sīla) and so forth excessively within his own continuity; or else, he suppresses and destroys the group of thieves, the defilements, which are other than his Dhamma-body (dhammakāya) and are the opposite, doing harm to it. Therefore, he is called 'Parama' (the Supreme). He is pure in Nibbāna and purifies beings; or else, he binds and joins beings in Nibbāna; or else, he goes to that Nibbāna and causes beings to reach it; or else, he knows that Nibbāna as it really is; or else, he places beings in that Nibbāna; or else, he suppresses and destroys the enemy of defilements of beings in that Nibbāna. Therefore, that Great Being (Mahāsatta) is called 'Pāramī'. According to the aforementioned method, it should be understood as 'Pāramī' through the three types of derivative (taddhita) meanings. Because he is supreme among beings, being endowed with special virtues such as giving (dāna) and morality (sīla), the Great Bodhisatta (Mahābodhisatta) is called 'Parama'. The state or the action of that Supreme One is 'Pāramī'. It refers to actions such as giving and so forth. Alternatively, according to the etymological method (nirutti), he is called 'Parama' because he fulfills and protects virtues such as giving and so forth. This refers to the Bodhisatta who fulfills and protects virtues such as giving and so forth. The state or the action of that Supreme One is 'Pāramī'. Furthermore, he is called 'Parama' because he binds other beings to himself through special virtues; because he is exceedingly pure from the stains of defilements; because he goes especially to the noble Nibbāna; because he knows the other world through his special knowledge as if it were this world; because he places the group of virtues such as morality and so forth excessively within his own continuity; and because he suppresses the opposing enemies, the defilements, which are other than his Dhamma-body. The state of that Supreme One is 'Pāramī'. It is called 'Pāramī' because of being pure in Nibbāna, purifying beings, joining beings in Nibbāna, going to Nibbāna, causing others to reach it, seeing Nibbāna as it really is, placing beings in Nibbāna, and suppressing the defilement-enemies of beings in Nibbāna. In this way, the word-meaning (vacanattha) of the perfections should be understood. 

In brief, there are ten kinds of perfections. These have already appeared in their specific forms in the Buddhavaṃsa Pāli. As it is said: 'Searching, I then saw the first, the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramī),' and so forth. And as it is said: 'Venerable Sir, how many are the qualities that make one a Buddha?' 'Sāriputta, there are ten qualities that make one a Buddha. Which ten? Sāriputta, giving is a quality that makes one a Buddha; morality, renunciation, wisdom, energy, patience, truthfulness...'
249:
Resolution, loving-kindness, and equanimity are the qualities that make one a Buddha. Sāriputta, these ten are indeed the qualities that make one a Buddha. The Blessed One said this. Having spoken these words, the Sugata, the Teacher, said this further:

‘Generosity, morality, renunciation, wisdom, and fifthly energy;
patience, truthfulness, resolution, loving-kindness, and equanimity—these are the ten.’

Some teachers say that there are six such qualities that make one a Buddha. That statement is made by way of the inclusion of these perfections. That inclusion will become clear later.

What is the order of these perfections? In this context, 'order' refers to the order of teaching (desanākkama). That order of teaching is based on the initial undertaking. The undertaking is based on investigation. Thus, just as they were investigated and undertaken at the beginning, at the time of the first aspiration, so they were taught. As it is said: “While investigating then, I saw the first, the perfection of generosity,” and so on. Therefore, it is said:

‘This order is taught by way of the initial undertaking;
or else, because of the great assistance they provide to one another.’

In that order, generosity is of great assistance to morality and is easy to perform; therefore, it is mentioned first. Generosity embraced by morality is of great fruit and benefit; therefore, morality is mentioned immediately after generosity. Morality embraced by renunciation... renunciation embraced by wisdom... wisdom embraced by energy... energy embraced by patience... patience embraced by truthfulness... truthfulness embraced by resolution... resolution embraced by loving-kindness... loving-kindness embraced by equanimity is of great fruit and benefit; therefore, equanimity is mentioned immediately after loving-kindness. It should be understood that equanimity embraced by compassion, and compassion embraced by equanimity, are of great fruit and benefit.

How do Bodhisattas, who possess great compassion, remain equanimous toward beings? Some teachers say they are equanimous for a short time toward beings who deserve equanimity, but not toward all beings at all times. Others say they are not equanimous toward beings, but rather toward the misconduct committed by beings. This statement alone is appropriate here.

Another way:

‘Generosity is taught first because of reasons such as being common to all;
whereas the remaining perfections are taught with regard to the preceding ones.’
250: Giving (dāna) is mentioned at the beginning because it occurs among many people, is common to all beings, yields [comparatively] little fruit, and is easy to perform. Virtue (sīla) is mentioned immediately after giving because it purifies both the donor and the recipient, thereby showing favor to others; because after mentioning the practice of giving, [the Buddha] wished to mention the restraint from harming others; because after mentioning the active Dhamma (kiriyadhamma), he wished to mention the Dhamma of refraining (akiriyadhamma); and because after mentioning the cause of the attainment of wealth, he wished to mention the cause of the attainment of [favorable] existence.## Renunciation (nekkhamma) is mentioned immediately after virtue because the perfection of virtue is accomplished through renunciation; because after mentioning good conduct of body and speech, [the Buddha] wished to mention good conduct of mind; because one with pure virtue can easily attain meditative absorption (jhāna); because after mentioning purity through the abandonment of faults of action (kamma), he wished to mention purity of intention (āsaya) through the abandonment of faults of defilement; and because he wished to mention the abandonment of obsession (pariyuṭṭhāna) for one established in the abandonment of transgression (vītikkama).## Wisdom (paññā) is mentioned immediately after renunciation because the accomplishment and purification of renunciation are achieved through wisdom, and because he wished to mention that without meditative absorption, wisdom does not arise. Indeed, concentration (samādhi) is the proximate cause of wisdom, and wisdom is the manifestation of concentration. Furthermore, it is mentioned because after mentioning the sign of serenity (samatha-nimitta), he wished to mention the sign of equanimity (upekkhā-nimitta); and because after mentioning meditative absorption that benefits others, he wished to mention skill in means (upāya-kosalla) in performing what is beneficial for others.## Energy (viriya) is mentioned immediately after wisdom because the task of wisdom can be accomplished through the exertion of energy; because after mentioning the patience (khanti) that discerns the emptiness of beings, he wished to mention the wonderful nature of the effort for the welfare of beings; because after mentioning the sign of equanimity, he wished to mention the sign of exertion (paggaha-nimitta); and because after mentioning acting with circumspection, he wished to mention the arousal of energy. Indeed, the arousal of energy by one who acts with circumspection brings about a special result.## Patience (khanti) is mentioned immediately after energy because endurance (titikkhā) is accomplished through energy. Indeed, an energetic person, by virtue of their aroused energy, can live by overcoming the suffering brought about by beings and formations (saṅkhāra). Also, because patience is the ornament of energy; for the patience of an energetic person is truly beautiful. Furthermore, it is mentioned because after mentioning the sign of exertion, he wished to mention the sign of serenity; because he wished to mention the abandonment of the fault of restlessness (uddhacca) caused by excessive exertion; because the fault of restlessness is abandoned through the patience that discerns the Dhamma; because he wished to mention the constant application of the energetic person; because one who is abundant in patience is unagitated and constantly active; because he wished to mention that a heedful person, in undertaking the welfare of others, has no craving (taṇhā) for a reciprocal favor; because when there is discernment of the Dhamma as it really is, craving does not arise; and because he wished to mention the endurance of the suffering caused by others that arises excessively while striving for the welfare of others.## Truthfulness (sacca) is mentioned immediately after patience because patience can endure for a long time through truthfulness; because after mentioning patience toward those who do harm, he wished to mention non-deceptive speech in benefiting them; because he wished to mention that through patience, one does not abandon speaking the truth despite being unshaken by words of blame; and because after mentioning the patience that discerns the emptiness of beings, he wished to mention the truth of knowledge (ñāṇa-sacca) that develops that patience.## Determination (adhiṭṭhāna) is mentioned immediately after truthfulness because truthfulness is accomplished through determination. Indeed, for one with unshakable determination, abstinence [from wrong speech] (virati) is accomplished. Furthermore, it is mentioned because he wished to mention the state of being unshakable in speaking non-deceptive words; because a truthful person remains unshakable in what they have undertaken, such as giving and so on; because after mentioning the truth of knowledge, he wished to mention the completion of the foundations such as giving; because one with true knowledge, having resolved upon the requisites of enlightenment (bodhisambhāra), brings those requisites to completion; and because of the state of being unshakable by opposing states.
251:
Because [the Buddha] spoke of the state of being unshakable in that determination, and because one who is bound by truth remains unshakable in giving and so forth, according to what was promised, [determination is taught after truth]. Indeed, a person with true knowledge remains unshakable in giving and so forth according to their word. Because, having spoken of the truth of knowledge, he spoke of the completion of the practice in the requisites such as giving, [he taught determination]. Indeed, a person with true knowledge undertakes the requisites of enlightenment (bodhisambhāra) and completes those requisites. Determination is also taught after truth because of the state of being unshakable by opposing states.

Because the determination to undertake the welfare of others through loving-kindness is accomplished, and because, having taught determination, he taught the conferring of benefits, [loving-kindness is taught after determination]. Indeed, one who is firmly established in the requisites of enlightenment dwells in loving-kindness. Loving-kindness is also mentioned after determination because for one with unshakable determination, the undertaking exists clearly without being disturbed.

Because loving-kindness is purified by equanimity, and because, having taught the conferring of benefits to beings, he taught indifference toward those beings who offend, and because, having taught the development of loving-kindness, he taught the development that is its result, and because he taught the marvelous quality, "He can be indifferent even toward beings for whom he desires welfare," equanimity is mentioned after loving-kindness. Thus, the sequence of these perfections should be understood.

To the question, "What are those characteristics and so forth in every way?"—here, in a general sense without distinction:

Supporting others is called the characteristic (lakkhaṇa).
Benefiting and being unshakable are called the function (rasa).
Seeking welfare and Buddhahood are called the manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna).
Compassion and knowledge are called the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna).

However, the individual characteristics and so forth of those perfections should be understood by their distinctions. In fact, all perfections have the characteristic of supporting others, the function of benefiting others or the function of being unshakable, the manifestation of seeking welfare or the manifestation of Buddhahood, and the proximate cause of great compassion or the proximate cause of compassion and skill in means (upāya-kosalla).

Specifically:

The volition of relinquishing one's own belongings, embraced by compassion and skill in means, is called the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramī).

The volition and so forth of abstaining from misconduct that should not be done and performing conduct that should be done, in essence, embraced by compassion and skill in means, is the perfection of virtue (sīla-pāramī).

The arising of thought (cittuppāda) that emerges from the realm of desire and existence, preceded by the seeing of danger (ādīnava), embraced by compassion and skill in means, is the perfection of renunciation (nekkhamma-pāramī).

The penetration of the general and specific characteristics of phenomena (dhammas), embraced by compassion and skill in means, is the perfection of wisdom (paññā-pāramī).

The exertion for the benefit of others with body and mind, embraced by compassion and skill in means, is the perfection of energy (viriya-pāramī).

The arising of thought characterized by non-hatred, consisting of the endurance of offenses by beings and formations (saṅkhāra), embraced by compassion and skill in means, is the perfection of patience (khanti-pāramī).

The non-deceptive speech, consisting of the volition of abstinence and so forth, embraced by compassion and skill in means...
252: Sacca-pāramī. The arising of consciousness characterized by an unshakable undertaking, embraced by compassion and skill in means, and proceeding in that manner, is called Adhiṭṭhāna-pāramī. The state of non-ill will, embraced by compassion and skill in means, which brings about the welfare and happiness of the world, is called Mettā-pāramī. Equanimity towards beings and formations, whether pleasant or unpleasant, characterized by the destruction of affection and resentment, and embraced by compassion and skill in means, is called Upekkhā-pāramī. Therefore, Dāna (Giving) has the characteristic of relinquishing; its function is the destruction of greed for the objects of donation; its manifestation is non-attachment or the success of existence and prosperity; its proximate cause is the object to be relinquished. Sīla (Virtue) has the characteristic of properly composing or establishing physical and vocal actions; its function is the destruction of immorality or the state of faultlessness; its manifestation is purity; its proximate cause is moral shame (hiri) and moral dread (ottappa). Nekkhamma (Renunciation) has the characteristic of departing from sense-pleasures and existence; its function is the manifestation of the faults of those sense-pleasures; its manifestation is turning away from them; its proximate cause is a sense of urgency (saṃvega). Paññā (Wisdom) has the characteristic of penetrating the true nature of things, or penetrating without error just as an arrow shot by a skilled archer penetrates its mark; its function is illuminating the object like a lamp; its manifestation is non-delusion like a good guide in a forest; its proximate cause is concentration (samādhi) or the Four Noble Truths. Viriya (Energy) has the characteristic of striving; its function is supporting; its manifestation is non-collapse or non-retreat; its proximate cause is the grounds for initiating energy or a sense of urgency. Khanti (Patience) has the characteristic of endurance; its function is enduring the pleasant and the unpleasant; its manifestation is abiding in extreme patience or non-opposition; its proximate cause is seeing things as they truly are. Sacca (Truth) has the characteristic of non-deceptive speech; its function is revealing the truth; its manifestation is goodness; its proximate cause is gentleness (soracca). Adhiṭṭhāna (Resolution) has the characteristic of steadfastness in the requisites of enlightenment; its function is overcoming their opposites; its manifestation is unshakability in those requisites; its proximate cause is the requisites of enlightenment (bodhisambhāra). Mettā (Loving-kindness) has the characteristic of proceeding in the mode of welfare for beings; its function is providing welfare or removing resentment; its manifestation is a state of pleasantness; its proximate cause is seeing the lovableness of beings. Upekkhā (Equanimity) has the characteristic of proceeding in a neutral mode; its function is seeing with equality; its manifestation is the quieting of affection and resentment; its proximate cause is reflecting on the fact that beings have kamma as their own property. In explaining these characteristics and so forth, the fact of being embraced by compassion and skill in means is stated as a qualifier for the characteristics of relinquishing and so on in Dāna and the rest. This is because only when they are so embraced do they acquire the name of 'Perfections' (Pāramī). Apart from the aspiration for Supreme Enlightenment and so forth, Dāna and other deeds that are not embraced by compassion and skill in means and which lead to the round of rebirth do not acquire the name of 'Perfections'. To the question of what the cause (paccaya) is, it is shown thus: In those perfections, the preliminary resolve (abhinīhāra), compassion, and knowledge are the causes. Furthermore, effort, wisdom, resolution, and practicing for the welfare of beings and so forth are also causes.
253:
What is the cause?

For those perfections, the Great Resolve (abhinihāra) is a cause, as are compassion (dayā) and wisdom (ñāṇa). Likewise, exertion (ussāha), wisdom (ummanga), resolution (vatthāna), and the practice for welfare (hitācāra) and so forth are causes.

Firstly, the Great Resolve is the cause of all perfections without exception. That Great Resolve which arises when one is endowed with the eight factors such as "humanity, the male sex," etc., and which proceeds in the manner: "Having crossed [the round of rebirths], I will lead others across; having been liberated, I will liberate others; having known, I will make others know; having been purified, I will purify others; having been tamed, I will tame others; having been calmed, I will calm others; having found relief, I will give relief to others; having attained Nibbāna, I will lead others to Nibbāna," is the cause of all perfections without distinction. For it is only after its occurrence that the investigation, manifestation, undertaking, resolution, and accomplishment of the perfections occur for the Great Beings (Mahāpurisa). In essence, this Great Resolve is the arising of thought (cittuppāda) occurring in such a way in combination with the remaining eight factors, characterized by the aspiration: "O, may I truly realize the unsurpassed Supreme Enlightenment; may I truly accomplish the welfare and happiness of all beings." It should be understood as a special merit of immeasurable power, the most excellent and auspicious, being the root of all the Buddha-making factors (buddhakāra-dhamma) that arise by taking as its object the inconceivable state of a Buddha and the boundless welfare of the world.

Simultaneously with the arising of that Great Resolve, the Great Being is said to have entered the practice of the Great Vehicle to Enlightenment (Mahābodhiyāna), because of having attained the state of certainty and because of the nature of not turning back from it; he receives the designation "Bodhisatta" (Enlightenment-being). He possesses a mind properly attached to Supreme Enlightenment in every way, and the ability to train in the requisites of enlightenment (bodhisambhāra) is established in him. For, through the success of the aforementioned Great Resolve, the Great Beings, by means of the self-evolved knowledge (sayambhū-ñāṇa) which is the precursor to the attainment of the Knowledge of Omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), properly investigate all the perfections, undertake them, and fulfill them in due order. Just like the wise Sumedha who made the Great Resolve. As it was said by the Blessed One:

"Come now, I shall investigate the Buddha-making factors here and there, upwards, downwards, and in the ten directions, as far as the realm of phenomena (dhammadhātu). While investigating then, I saw the first, the Perfection of Giving (Dāna Pāramī)."

—and so on in detail. In terms of characteristics and so forth, this Great Resolve has the characteristic of properly aspiring for Supreme Enlightenment. Its function (rasa) is the aspiration: "O, may I truly penetrate the unsurpassed Supreme Enlightenment; may I truly accomplish the welfare and happiness of all beings." Its manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna) is appearing as the cause for the requisites of enlightenment. Its proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) is Great Compassion (Mahākaruṇā); or its proximate cause is the fulfillment of merit which is the powerful condition [for it].
254:
(That resolve) has the function (rasa) of aspiring, "May I be able to accomplish the welfare and happiness of all beings." It has the manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna) of being the cause for the requisites of enlightenment (bodhisambhāra). It has great compassion (mahākaruṇā) as its proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna), or it has the perfection of supporting conditions (upanissayasampatti—the fulfillment of merit which is a powerful cause for attaining the knowledge of the path of Arahatship) as its proximate cause.

The four supporting conditions (paccaya), the four generating causes (hetu), and the four powers (bala) of that resolve should be understood. Among these, what are the four supporting conditions for the great resolve (mahābhinihāra)?
