Here, a Great Being (mahāpurisa) sees the Tathāgata performing a wonderful and marvelous miracle through the great power of a Buddha. Relying on that miracle and taking it as an object, his mind becomes well-established in the Great Enlightenment (mahābodhi). He reflects: "Indeed, this Dhamma-element (the knowledge of omniscience) has great power; because of having well-penetrated this Dhamma-element, the Blessed One possesses such wonderful and marvelous qualities and inconceivable power." Relying on the sight of that great power and making it a condition, with a mind inclined toward supreme enlightenment, he fixes his mind upon it. This is the first supporting condition for the great resolve.

Even if he does not actually see the aforementioned great power of the Tathāgata, he hears, "The Blessed One is of such and such a nature." Relying on what he hears and making those virtues the cause, with a mind inclined toward supreme enlightenment, he fixes his mind upon it. This is the second supporting condition for the great resolve.

Even if he does not actually see the aforementioned great power of the Tathāgata, nor hears it from others, he hears the Dhamma connected with the Buddha's power, such as when the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma: "Monks, the Tathāgata is endowed with the ten powers (dasabala)." Relying on that Dhamma... (he fixes his mind). This is the third supporting condition for the great resolve.

Even if he does not actually see the aforementioned great power of the Tathāgata, nor hears it from others, nor hears the Dhamma of the Tathāgata, yet, being one of noble intention and good inclination, he thinks: "I shall preserve this lineage of the Buddhas, the tradition of the Buddhas, the succession of the Buddhas, and the nature of the Buddhas." Thus, showing great respect, esteem, reverence, veneration, and honor to the Dhamma alone, and relying on that lineage of the Buddhas, etc... (he fixes his mind). This is the fourth supporting condition for the great resolve.
255:
What are the four causes (hetu) for the great resolve? Here, a Great Being is naturally endowed with supporting conditions (upanissaya), having performed extraordinary merit in the presence of previous Buddhas. This is the first cause for the great resolve. Furthermore, a Great Being is naturally of a compassionate disposition, inclined toward compassion, desiring to remove the suffering of beings; indeed, he even sacrifices his own body and life. This is the second cause for the great resolve. Furthermore, a Great Being, for the sake of leading beings out of the entirety of the suffering of the round of rebirth and for their welfare, exerts effort and strives through difficult practices for a very long time without becoming weary or terrified until the desired goal is accomplished. This is the third cause for the great resolve. Furthermore, a Great Being relies on a good friend (kalyāṇamitta) who restrains him from what is harmful and establishes him in what is beneficial. This is the fourth cause for the great resolve.

In relation to that resolve, this is the Great Being's perfection of supporting conditions (upanissayasampadā). Just as the Great Being's intention is certainly bent, sloped, and inclined toward supreme enlightenment, so it is toward practicing for the welfare of beings. This is because he has made an aspiration for supreme enlightenment in the presence of previous Buddhas, both mentally and verbally: "May I too, having become a Perfectly Enlightened Buddha like this, properly accomplish the welfare and happiness of beings." For the Great Being thus endowed with supporting conditions, these signs and marks of the perfection of supporting conditions arise. In a Great Being endowed with these marks, a great distinction and vast difference from the Bodhisattas who will become disciples or Paccekabuddhas is known in terms of faculties (indriya), practice (paṭipatti), and skillfulness (kośalla). For here, a Great Being endowed with supporting conditions has such clear faculties and clear knowledge as others do not. He is one who practices for the welfare of others, not for his own welfare. For he practices for the benefit and happiness of the many, out of compassion for the world, for the good, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans, in a way that others do not. In that practice, he brings about skillfulness through ready wit (paṭibhāna) that arises on the spot and through skill in discerning what is a cause and what is not.

Likewise, a Great Being is naturally of a generous disposition, delighting in giving. When there is an object to be given, he certainly gives; he does not shrink from giving. He is one whose character is to share constantly and continuously. He gives with a joyful and respectful heart, not with an indifferent mind. Even after giving a great gift...
256:
Even if that Great Man (Mahāpurisa) gives a great gift, he is not satisfied with that gift, let alone giving a small gift (he is certainly not satisfied). He also inspires others to make an effort, speaks of the virtues of giving, and gives Dhamma discourses related to giving. Seeing others giving to others, he is delighted. In places of danger, he gives fearlessness (abhaya) to others. These and other such qualities are the signs of the Perfection of Giving (Dāna-pāramī) of the Great Man who is inclined toward giving.

Likewise, he has shame (hiri) and fear (ottappa) regarding evil deeds such as killing living beings. He has a nature of not harming beings. He is gentle in body and speech and has a habit of being pleasant. He is not crooked, not deceitful, and has an upright nature. He is easy to admonish and is endowed with qualities that make one easy to admonish. He has a soft nature, is not harsh, and does not have excessive pride. He does not take the property of others, starting from even a blade of grass or a piece of wood. Whether it be a debt placed in his hand or taken by him, he does not fail others. If another person is confused or forgetful regarding their own property, he informs them and acts so that the property does not fall into the hands of others. He is not frivolous and does not even allow an evil thought to arise regarding the property possessed by others. He avoids from afar the ruin caused by women and so forth. He is a speaker of truth, firm in truth, a reconciler of those who are divided, an encourager of those who are united, and a speaker of endearing words. Preceded by a smile, he is the first to greet. He speaks words of benefit and words related to the Dhamma. He is without covetousness and without a mind of ill-will. He has an undistorted view through the knowledge that beings are the owners of their actions (kammassakatā-ñāṇa) and through the insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) that is in accordance with the Four Noble Truths. He is grateful and appreciative of the favors done by others. He is respectful toward elders, has a very pure livelihood, and loves the Dhamma. He also establishes others in wholesome states, restrains beings from all deeds that should not be done, and establishes them in duties that should be performed. He himself also engages in those duties to be performed; or if he himself happens to do what should not be done, he quickly refrains from that deed. These and other such qualities are the signs of the Perfection of Morality (Sīla-pāramī) of the Great Man who is inclined toward morality.

Likewise, he has few defilements, few hindrances, an inclination toward seclusion, and much unwavering concentration. Evil thoughts do not follow and oppress the mind of that Great Man. The mind of that Great Man who has reached seclusion becomes concentrated quickly and without difficulty. Even toward enemies, a mind of loving-kindness (mettā) is quickly established, let alone toward others (friends). He is mindful and can well remember and repeatedly recall what was done or said long ago. He is a wise man endowed with wisdom born of the essence of the Dhamma. He is also prudent in various duties to be performed. He has energy (vīriya) exerted in performing the welfare of beings. He is endowed with the power of patience (khanti) and can endure all things. He has a firm determination (adhiṭṭhāna) that is unshakable. He is one who is very equanimous toward things that should be viewed with equanimity. These and other such qualities should be understood as the signs of the Perfection of Renunciation (Nekkhamma-pāramī) and so forth, by virtue of the Great Man's inclination toward renunciation and the like.
257:
Thus, regarding the statement made concerning the Great Man endowed with these signs of the requisites of enlightenment (bodhisambhāra), that "the reliance on a good friend (kalyāṇamitta) is the cause for the Great Aspiration (mahābhinīhāra)," this is the characteristic of a good friend in brief: In this world, a good friend is endowed with faith (saddhā), endowed with morality (sīla), endowed with learning (suta), and endowed with generosity (cāga), energy (vīriya), mindfulness (sati), concentration (samādhi), and wisdom (paññā). In being so endowed, through the fulfillment of faith, he believes in the enlightenment of the Tathāgata, in kamma, and in the result of kamma. Because of that belief, he does not abandon the desire for the welfare of beings, which is the cause for Perfect Enlightenment (sammāsambodhi). Through the fulfillment of morality, he is dear to beings, pleasing, respected, venerable, a counselor, a censurer of evil, a speaker, and one who endures the words of others. Through the fulfillment of learning, he is a speaker of deep Dhamma discourse that brings welfare and happiness to beings. Through the fulfillment of generosity, he has few wishes, is composed, easily contented, secluded, and not entangled with the cords of sensual pleasure. Through the fulfillment of energy, he possesses energy exerted for the practice of the welfare of beings. Through the fulfillment of mindfulness, he has established mindfulness in blameless states. Through the fulfillment of concentration, he is undistracted and has a concentrated mind. Through the fulfillment of wisdom, he knows things correctly and without distortion. That good friend, seeking the courses of wholesome states with mindfulness, knowing truly the benefit and harm of beings with wisdom, having a one-pointed mind therein with concentration, restrains beings from harm and urges them toward benefit with energy. Therefore, the Buddha said:

## He is dear, respected, and venerable, a speaker and one who endures words,
## He is a maker of deep discourse, and not one who urges in an improper place.

By relying on a good friend endowed with such qualities in this manner, the Great Man perfectly purifies his own fulfillment of supporting conditions. Having very pure inclination (āsaya) and effort (payoga), being endowed with the four powers, and before long combining the eight factors, when he makes the Great Aspiration, he stands in the state of a Bodhisatta, one of non-retreating nature, certain, and destined for enlightenment.

For that Great Man, there are these four powers. The internal power (ajjhattika-bala) is the inclination and desire that is solely directed toward Perfect Enlightenment, having great delight and reverence for the Dhamma by relying on oneself. By that inclination, the Great Man, relying on self-supremacy (attādhipati) and shame (hiri), and being endowed with the aspiration, fulfills the perfections and reaches Perfect Enlightenment. The external power (bāhira-bala) is the inclination and desire that is solely directed toward Perfect Enlightenment, having great delight by relying on others. By that inclination, the Great Man, relying on world-supremacy (lokādhipati) and fear of wrongdoing (ottappa), and being endowed with the aspiration...
258:
(The Great Man) fulfills the perfections (pāramīs) and attains Supreme Enlightenment (Sammāsambodhi). The power of strong support (upanissayabala) is the great delight and affection arising from the fulfillment of strong supporting conditions for Supreme Enlightenment, and the inclination that is exclusively directed toward Supreme Enlightenment. Due to this power of strong support, the Great Man (Mahāpurisa) becomes one with keen faculties, a pure nature, one who always relies on mindfulness, and one who is endowed with the great resolve (abhinīhāra); thus, he fulfills the perfections and attains Supreme Enlightenment. The power of effort (payogabala) is the fulfillment of effort appropriate for Supreme Enlightenment, acting with thoroughness and acting with constancy. Due to this power of effort, the Great Man becomes one with pure effort, one who acts continuously, and one who is endowed with the great resolve; thus, he fulfills the perfections and attains Supreme Enlightenment. In this way, this great resolve, which is the accomplishment of the combined four conditions, four causes, and four powers, and is achieved through the convergence of the eight factors, is the cause of the perfections because it is the root cause.

When that great resolve arises, four wonderful and marvelous qualities (acchariya abbhuta dhammā) are established in the Great Man. He embraces the entire assembly of beings with a heart of love, as if they were his own breast-born children. The mind of that Great Man is never again defiled by the power of defilements. He possesses the desire and effort to bring about the welfare and happiness of beings. The qualities that make one a Buddha (buddhakārakadhammā) also increase and mature progressively within him. From the time he makes that great resolve, the Great Man, because of the increase of the great flood of merit and the flood of wholesome deeds, and because of being endowed with the cause that brings happiness, becomes one worthy of offerings from beings, the highest object of reverence, and an incomparable field of merit for sowing the seeds of merit. Thus, the great resolve, which possesses many virtues and many benefits, should be understood as the cause of the perfections.

Just like the great resolve, great compassion (mahākaruṇā) and skill in means (upāyakosalla) are also (causes of the perfections). Among these two, skill in means is the wisdom (paññā) that is the cause for making giving (dāna) and other qualities the requisites of enlightenment (bodhisambhāra). Because of that great compassion and skill in means, the Great Man's disregard for his own happiness, his constant exertion in bringing about the happiness of others, his lack of discouragement in the extremely difficult practices of a Great Bodhisatta, and his becoming the cause for beings to obtain welfare and happiness even during moments of seeing, hearing, or recollecting with increasing faith, are all fulfilled. Indeed, through his wisdom, the attainment of Buddhahood is accomplished, and through his compassion, the work of a Buddha is accomplished. Through wisdom, he himself crosses over (the ocean of Saṃsāra); through compassion, he helps others to cross over. Through wisdom, he fully understands the suffering of others; through compassion, he exerts himself to remove the suffering of others. Through wisdom, he is weary of suffering; through compassion, he accepts suffering. Through wisdom, he is directed toward Nibbāna,
259:
through compassion, he does not reach that Nibbāna [prematurely]. Furthermore, through compassion, he is directed toward Saṃsāra; through wisdom, he does not delight in that Saṃsāra. Through wisdom, he is detached from all things of the round of rebirth; because he follows compassion, it is not that he does not act for the benefit of all beings (he indeed does). Through compassion, he has compassion for all beings; because he follows wisdom, it is not that he lacks a mind detached from all things (he indeed has such a mind). Through wisdom, there is the absence of 'I-making' and 'mine-making' (ahaṃkāra-mamaṃkāra); through compassion, there is the absence of the fault of indolence.

Likewise, through wisdom and compassion respectively, there is being one's own refuge and being the refuge of others, being wise and being courageous (or having steady posture), not tormenting oneself and not tormenting others, the accomplishment of one's own benefit and the benefit of others, being fearless oneself and the absence of fear in others, being governed by the Dhamma (dhammādhipati) and being governed by the world (lokādhipati), being grateful and being the first to do a favor, the removal of delusion and craving, the perfection of clear vision and conduct (vijjā-caraṇa), and the accomplishment of the powers and intrepidity (bala-vesārajja). In this way, because they are especially the means for all the fruits of the perfections, wisdom and compassion are the causes of the perfections. These two, wisdom and compassion, are causes for the great resolve (paṇidhāna) just as they are for the perfections.

Furthermore, zeal (ussāha), insight (ummanga), resolution (avatthāna), and beneficent conduct (hitacariyā) should also be understood as causes of the perfections. Those qualities such as zeal are called "Buddha-grounds" (buddhabhūmi) because they are the arising-place of Buddhahood. Among those Buddha-grounds, zeal (ussāha) is the energy (vīriya) of great exertion for the perfections which are the requisites of enlightenment. Insight (ummanga) is the wisdom (paññā) that is skillful in the means regarding the requisites of enlightenment. Resolution (avatthāna) is the unwavering determination (adhiṭṭhāna). Beneficent conduct (hitacariyā) is the cultivation of loving-kindness (mettā) and the cultivation of compassion (karuṇā). As it was said: "Venerable Sir, how many Buddha-grounds are there?" When asked, he replied: "Sāriputta, there are four Buddha-grounds. Which four? Zeal, which is energy; insight, which is the cultivation of wisdom; resolution, which is determination; and beneficent conduct, which is the cultivation of loving-kindness. Sāriputta, these four are the Buddha-grounds."

Furthermore, the six inclinations (ajjhāsaya) consisting of renunciation (nekkhamma), seclusion (paviveka), non-greed (alobha), non-hatred (adosa), non-delusion (amoha), and deliverance (nissaraṇa) are also (causes of the perfections). This was said: "Bodhisattas, having the inclination for renunciation, see the faults in sense pleasures and in the household life. Having the inclination for seclusion, they see the faults in socializing. Having the inclination for non-greed... in greed... non-hatred... in hatred... non-delusion... in delusion... having the inclination for deliverance, they see the faults in all states of existence."
260: Therefore, it should be understood that these six inclinations are also the conditions for the perfections. Indeed, without seeing the danger in greed and the like, and without the excellence of non-greed and the like, the perfections such as giving and so forth cannot arise. It should be known that due to the excellence of non-greed and the like, there is a state of mind inclined toward relinquishment and so forth, and the state of having an inclination toward non-greed and so forth. Just as these six inclinations are conditions for the perfections, so too are the inclinations toward giving and so forth. Regarding this, the Blessed One said: "Venerable Sir, how many are the inclinations of the Bodhisattas who are practicing for enlightenment?" (When asked by the Venerable Sāriputta), "Sāriputta, there are ten inclinations of the Bodhisattas who are practicing for enlightenment. What are the ten? Sāriputta, Bodhisattas have an inclination toward giving; they see the danger in stinginess (macchariya). They have an inclination toward virtue; they see the danger in non-restraint (asaṃvara). They have an inclination toward renunciation; they see the danger in sensual pleasures (kāma). They have an inclination toward knowledge of things as they are (yathābhūtañāṇa); they see the danger in doubt (vicikicchā). They have an inclination toward energy; they see the danger in laziness (kosajja). They have an inclination toward patience; they see the danger in impatience (akkhanti). They have an inclination toward truth; they see the danger in deception (visaṃvādana). They have an inclination toward determination; they see the danger in lack of determination (anadhiṭṭhāna). They have an inclination toward loving-kindness; they see the danger in ill-will (vyāpāda). They have an inclination toward equanimity; they see the danger in [attachment to] pleasure and pain (sukha-dukkha)." Indeed, the inclinations toward giving and so forth—characterized by a mind inclined toward giving and so forth, preceded by seeing the danger in stinginess, non-restraint, sensual pleasures, doubt, laziness, impatience, deception, lack of determination, ill-will, and pleasure and pain—are the conditions for the arising of the perfections such as giving. Furthermore, the reflection on the dangers and the benefits in non-relinquishment and relinquishment respectively are also conditions for the perfections such as giving. In that reflection, this is the method of reflection: To beings whose minds are particularly attached to the possession of fields, lands, gold, silver, cattle, buffaloes, female slaves, male slaves, children, and wives, such things as fields and so forth, being objects of sensual desire (vatthukāma), are much longed for; they are common to kings, thieves, and other [enemies]; they are the basis for disputes; they cause the increase of enemies; they are without essence; they are the cause of oppressing others in the process of acquisition and protection; they bring about various ruins such as sorrow because they are causes of destruction; and they are the cause of rebirth in the lower realms for beings whose minds are overwhelmed by the stain of stinginess rooted in attachment to those things. Thus, possessed objects bring about many disadvantages. Only the relinquishment of those objects is the sole state of safety; reflecting thus, one should practice diligence in relinquishment. Moreover, [one should reflect]: "The beggar, by revealing his own secret through begging, is my trusted friend." And: "He is my instructor because he advises me, saying: 'Take your own property and go to the next world, for you must go leaving [everything else] behind.'" And: "When the house..."
261: ...is burning, just as a friend who carries one's property out of a house in the world that is being consumed by the fire of death, he is a friend who carries [wealth] out because he carries my property away from the fire of death. And because he is the place of deposit for that property which has been carried out, where it cannot be burned. And because he is a companion in the meritorious action called giving. And because he is the cause for reaching the stage of Buddhahood (buddhabhūmi), which is the most noble of all attainments and extremely difficult to attain, he should be reflected upon as a supreme spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitta). Likewise, one should cultivate an inclination toward relinquishment by reflecting: 'This person has honored me in this noble meritorious deed; therefore, I should act so that this honor is not in vain.' And: 'Since life is certainly perishable, I should give even if not requested; how much more so when requested?' And: 'I should give even by searching with noble inclinations; now, however, he has come of his own accord due to my merit.' And: 'The beggar is actually favoring me by providing the occasion for giving.' And: 'Like myself, I should favor this entire world of beings.' And: 'If there were no beggars, how would my perfection of giving be fulfilled?' And: 'I have accumulated all this wealth only for the sake of beggars.' And: 'When will beggars take my property of their own accord even without asking me?' And: 'How can I become one who is dear and pleasing to beggars?' Or: 'How can they become dear and pleasing to me?' Or: 'How can I be one who is glad, delighted, and filled with joy and happiness while giving and even after having given?' Or: 'How may there be beggars for me, and how may there be a noble inclination toward giving?' Or: 'How can I give by knowing the heart's desire of beggars even without being asked?' And: 'While there is wealth and there are beggars, not to relinquish is a great deception of myself.' And: 'How shall I relinquish even my own limbs and life?' Furthermore, one should generate a mind free from attachment to wealth, thinking: 'This benefit (or wealth) follows the donor who is free from attachment, just as a caterpillar follows the one who casts it away.' If the beggar is a beloved person, one should generate joy, thinking: 'A beloved person is begging from me.' If he is a neutral person, one should generate joy, thinking: 'This beggar will surely become my friend through this relinquishment.' For indeed, a donor becomes dear to beggars. If an enemy begs, one should especially generate joy, thinking: 'An enemy is begging from me; this person, though an enemy, will surely become a dear friend through this relinquishment.'
262:
In this way, just as towards a beloved person, one should give only after establishing compassion preceded by loving-kindness towards neutral persons and enemies as well.

However, if greed regarding the objects to be given should arise in him due to greed being cultivated for a long time, that person who has made the vow of a Bodhisatta should reflect thus: "O good man, when you made the initial resolution for the sake of supreme enlightenment, did you not relinquish this body for the benefit of all beings? Is there not also the merit gained by relinquishing that body? While having relinquished even the body itself, the arising of intense attachment to external objects would be like washing an elephant (only for it to get dirty again). Therefore, you should not produce intense attachment to anything. For example, when a great medicinal tree exists, those who need the root take the root; those who need the sapwood, the bark, the trunk, the branches, the twigs, the leaves, the flowers, or the fruits take them. Just as that tree does not have the thought, 'These people are taking what belongs to me,' even so, I, who am striving for the benefit of the entire world, should not produce even a subtle wrong thought when this body—which is full of suffering, ungrateful, and constantly impure—is being utilized for the benefit of others. Indeed, what difference is there between the internal and external great elements (mahābhūta), which are by nature subject to breaking, scattering, and destruction? This is merely the play of delusion, namely the obsession that 'This is mine, this I am, this is my self.' Therefore, just as with external great elements, one should be without longing for internal parts such as hands, feet, eyes, and so forth, as well as flesh and so on, and should have a mind of relinquishment, thinking, 'Let those who need them take them.'" For him who reflects thus, whose mind is directed towards supreme enlightenment, and who is without longing for body and life, his bodily, verbal, and mental actions become very pure without much difficulty. Having such pure actions and pure livelihood, and standing in the right practice, being endowed with skill in the means of progress and decline, he is able to favor all beings by relinquishing gifts beyond measure, by the gift of fearlessness, and by the gift of the True Dhamma. This is the method of reflection in the perfection of generosity (dāna-pāramī).

In the perfection of virtue (sīla-pāramī), however, one should reflect thus: "This virtue is the water for washing away the stain of hatred, which cannot be cleansed by the waters of the Ganges and so forth. It removes the fever of passion (rāga) and so on, which cannot be removed by yellow sandalwood and so forth. It is the extraordinary ornament of the virtuous, unlike the common ornaments of people such as strings of pearls, diadems, and earrings. It is a fragrance that blows in all directions, bringing great fame..."
263: "This virtue is suitable for all times and has a fragrance of supreme scent. Because it brings about the state of being worthy of worship by monarchs such as the Khattiya-mahāsāla and by deities, it is like a supreme mantra of enchantment. It is a flight of stairs for ascending to the celestial worlds such as the Cātumahārājika. It is the means for attaining Jhana and Abhiññā. It is the path that leads to the great city of Nibbāna. It is the foundational ground for Sāvaka-bodhi, Pacceka-bodhi, and Sammā-sambodhi. Furthermore, because it is the means for the fulfillment of whatever is desired or prayed for, it surpasses even the wish-fulfilling gem (Cintāmaṇi) and the wish-fulfilling tree (Kapparukkha). For it was said by the Blessed One: 'Bhikkhus, the mental aspiration of a virtuous person succeeds because of its purity.' In another sutta, it is also said: 'Bhikkhus, if a bhikkhu should desire to be dear to his companions in the holy life, pleasing to them, respected and esteemed by them, he should be one who fulfills the virtues,' and so forth. Likewise, the qualities of virtue should be reflected upon by way of such suttas as: 'Ānanda, skillful virtues have non-remorse as their purpose,' and 'Householders, these five are the benefits for a virtuous person in his perfection of virtue.' Similarly, the dangers in the lack of virtue should be reflected upon by way of the Aggikkhandhopama Sutta and others. Furthermore, virtue should be reflected upon because it is the cause for the arising of joy and gladness; because of the absence of fear of self-reproach (attānuvāda), reproach by others (parānuvāda), punishment, and woeful states; because it is praised by the wise; because it is the cause of non-remorse; because it is the supreme place of safety; and because it surpasses the excellence of lineage, wealth, power, life, beauty, mansions, positions, relatives, and friends. For to a virtuous person, great joy and gladness arise because of his own perfection of virtue, thinking: 'Indeed, I have done what is skillful, I have done what is good, I have established the virtue that protects from fear.' Likewise, the virtuous person does not reproach himself, nor do the wise among others reproach him; there is no possibility of the fear of punishment or the fear of woeful states; and he receives the praise of the wise, who say: 'The virtuous person is of good character.' Furthermore, that remorse which arises in an immoral person, thinking: 'Indeed, I have done evil, I have done what is cruel, I have done what is sinful,' does not arise in a virtuous person. This virtue is the supreme place of safety because it is the foundation of heedfulness, because it achieves great benefit by way of avoiding the ruin of wealth and so forth, and because it is a blessing. Even if one is of low birth, if he is virtuous, he becomes one to be worshipped by monarchs such as the Khattiya-mahāsāla. Thus, the perfection of virtue surpasses the perfection of lineage. The words of the Sāmaññaphala Sutta, such as 'Great King, if there were a man here who was your slave and worker...' are the very evidence for this point."
264:
"Great King, suppose there were a man here, your slave, your worker..." (DN 1.183). This statement from the Sāmaññaphala Sutta, which will be mentioned later, is evidence here. Virtue (sīla) is superior to external wealth because it is not shared with thieves and others, it follows one to the next world, it yields great fruit, and it is the foundation for qualities such as tranquility (samatha). Virtue excels the sovereignty of kings and others because it is the basis for supreme mastery over the mind. Indeed, the sovereignty of beings in various classes of existence arises because of virtue. Virtue is more excellent than life because it is taught that even a single day of life for a virtuous person is superior to a long life of a hundred years, and because abandoning the training (sikkhā) while still alive is said to be death. Virtue excels physical beauty (rūpasampatti) because it brings delight even to enemies and cannot be overcome by old age, disease, or ruin. Virtue is superior because it is the basis for special happiness in various types of mansions such as palaces and hammiyas, and in special positions such as king, crown prince, or general. Virtue is superior because it brings absolute benefit even more than relatives and friends who are naturally affectionate and close, and because it follows one to the next world. The statement, "Neither mother nor father can do that [benefit]..." (Dhp 43) is evidence here. Likewise, virtue alone is more excellent as a protection for the helpless who are difficult to protect with armies of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, or with mantras, medicines, and efforts for well-being, because it is self-dependent, not dependent on others, and has a vast scope. Therefore, it was said, "The Dhamma indeed protects the Dhamma-practitioner" (Thag 303, Ja 1.10.102). For one who reflects on virtue as being endowed with such numerous qualities, the unfulfilled perfection of virtue reaches fulfillment, and the impure reaches purity.

If, due to long-standing habit, states contrary to virtue such as anger arise intermittently, that person who has made the vow of a Bodhisatta should reflect thus: "Did you not make a vow for Enlightenment (bodhi)? If it is not possible or easy to attain even worldly success through deficiency in virtue, what need is there to mention supramundane success?" Virtue, which is the foundation for the Supreme Self-Enlightenment (sammāsambodhi)—the pinnacle of all successes—must reach the highest excellence. Therefore, following the method stated as "Like the kikī bird protecting its egg" (DN-A 1.7, Vism 1.19), you must be one who loves virtue greatly, guarding it well.
265:
Furthermore, through the preaching of the Dhamma, you must lead beings into the three vehicles (yāna) and mature them. The words of one deficient in virtue are not to be trusted, just as one does not trust the treatment of a physician who habitually consumes unsuitable food. Therefore, one should think, "How shall I become trustworthy and be able to lead and mature beings?" and possess naturally pure virtue. Moreover, [one should think,] "Through association with special qualities such as the meditative absorptions (jhāna), I will be able to benefit beings. The fulfillment of the Perfection of Wisdom (paññā-pāramī) and qualities like the jhānas are not possible without the purity of virtue." Thus, virtue should be thoroughly purified.

Likewise, one should practice reflection on the Perfection of Renunciation (nekkhamma-pāramī) by first seeing the disadvantages in household life as "Household life is crowded, a path of dust," etc.; in sensual pleasures as "Sensual pleasures are like a skeleton," "Even a mother disputes with her son," etc.; and in sensual desire as "Just as a man might take a loan and invest it in business," etc. Conversely, one should reflect on the advantages in monkhood as "Going forth is like the open air," etc. This is a summary here; the details should be understood through the Dukkhandha Sutta, Āsīvisopama Sutta, etc.

Likewise, one should contemplate the qualities of wisdom (paññā), thinking, "Without wisdom, states such as giving (dāna) are not pure and are not capable of performing their respective functions." Just as a bodily machine without life does not look beautiful and is not capable of performing its actions, and just as the sense faculties like the eye are not able to perform their functions regarding their objects without consciousness (viññāṇa), so too the faculties like faith (saddhā) are incapable of performing their own functions without wisdom. Therefore, wisdom is the primary cause in practices such as giving. The Great Beings, the Bodhisattas, whose eye of wisdom is opened, give even their own limbs and organs without self-exaltation or disparaging others. Like medicinal trees that are useful without discrimination, they are filled with joy in all three times. Through the power of wisdom, giving associated with skill in means (upāyakosalla) reaches the state of the Perfection of Giving (dāna-pāramī) because it carries out the welfare of others. Giving for one's own benefit is like [mere] growth.
266:
Furthermore, due to the absence of wisdom, it is impossible to separate from defilements such as craving; thus, even the purification of virtue (sīla) cannot occur. How then could the state of being the foundation for qualities such as omniscience (sabbaññutaññāṇa) be possible? Only a wise person, clearly perceiving the faults in household life, in sensual pleasures, and in Saṃsāra, as well as the benefits in renunciation (pabbajjā), in meditative attainments (jhāna-samāpatti), and in Nibbāna, having renounced and attained meditative absorptions, becomes inclined toward Nibbāna and establishes others therein.

Effort (vīriya) devoid of wisdom does not achieve the desired goal because it is a wrong undertaking. Indeed, non-undertaking is better than a wrong undertaking. With effort accompanied by wisdom, however, there is nothing difficult to attain because of practice through skillful means (upāya). Moreover, only a wise person is of a nature to endure the wrongs and oppressions of others, not one of poor wisdom. For one devoid of wisdom, the wrongs committed by others only increase anger, which is the opposite of patience (khanti). For a wise person, however, those wrongs serve to increase the perfection of patience, leading to its firmness. Only a wise person, having known the three truths (the truth of speech, the truth of ultimate reality, and the truth of views) as they really are, along with their causes and opposing factors, becomes one who does not deceive others. Furthermore, supporting oneself through wisdom and being endowed with steadfastness, one becomes one whose determination (adhiṭṭhāna) is unshakable in all perfections (pāramīs). Only a wise person is skillful in bringing about the welfare of all beings without making distinctions between the beloved, the neutral, and the enemy. Moreover, by the power of wisdom, one remains neutral (equanimous) without being affected when encountering worldly conditions (lokadhamma) such as gain and loss. Thus, one should contemplate the attributes of wisdom, seeing that wisdom alone is the cause for the purification of all perfections.

In another way, without wisdom, the perfection of seeing the Four Noble Truths is not possible. Without the perfection of wisdom, the perfection of virtue is not possible. For one devoid of the perfection of virtue and wisdom, the perfection of concentration (samādhi) is not possible. If one who is not concentrated cannot even achieve one's own benefit, what need is there to mention the supreme benefit of others? The Bodhisatta should admonish himself: "Are you not, who are practicing for the benefit of others, to respectfully apply yourself to the purification of wisdom?" By the power of wisdom, the Great Being (Mahāsatta), established in the four foundations (Truth, Generosity, Peace, and Wisdom) and favoring the world with the four bases of sympathy (saṅgahavatthu), leads beings into the path of liberation and matures their faculties (indriya). Furthermore, by the power of wisdom, being frequent in investigation of the aggregates (khandhas), sense-bases (āyatanas), and so on, and knowing the arising and ceasing of Saṃsāra as they really are, one brings special qualities such as generosity (dāna) to the state of partaking in penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya) and fulfills the training of the Bodhisattas. In this way, having defined the attributes of wisdom in various ways, the perfection of wisdom should be cultivated.
267:
Furthermore, even worldly tasks whose other shore is visible cannot be reached with inferior effort. But for one with effort aroused without counting the fatigue, there is nothing called difficult to attain. Indeed, one with inferior effort is not even able to begin, thinking, "I will rescue all beings from the great flood of Saṃsāra." One with medium effort, having begun, reaches a standstill in the middle. But one with superior effort, without regard for one's own happiness, having begun, reaches the other shore of Nibbāna. Thus, the perfection of effort should be contemplated.

In another way, if even for a person striving to lift only himself out of the mire of Saṃsāra, the goal cannot be reached due to laxity of effort, what need is there to mention one who has made the resolution to rescue the world together with the devas? Because the group of defilements such as lust (rāga) are difficult to restrain like great elephants in rut; because the undertaking of unwholesome kamma based on that lust, etc., is like an executioner with a raised sword; because the miserable realms (duggati) caused by that lust, etc., are like a gateway always standing wide open; because the evil friends who urge one toward that unwholesome kamma are always near; and because as long as there is the state of a low worldling (puthujjana) who follows their advice, it is proper to escape from the suffering of Saṃsāra by oneself. Wrong thoughts (micchā-vitakka) are distanced by the power of effort. If the Supreme Enlightenment (sambodhi) can be attained by effort dependent on oneself, what is difficult in this? In this way, the attributes of effort should be contemplated.

Furthermore, this thing called patience (khanti), because it dispels anger which is the opponent of all remaining virtues, is like an irresistible weapon of the virtuous in accomplishing good qualities. It is like armor for those capable of enduring the oppression of others. It is the perfection of strength for recluses and brahmins. It is like a stream of water that extinguishes the fire of anger. It is the birthplace of the sound of good fame. It is like a mantra-medicine that pacifies the poison of the words of evil persons. It is the noble nature of the wise who stand in restraint (saṃvara). Because of the depth of its intention (āsaya), it is like the ocean. It is the shore of the great ocean of anger. It is the door-panel that closes the gate to the miserable realms. It is the stairway for ascending to the deva and brahma worlds. It is the foundation for all virtues. It is the supreme purification of body, speech, and mind. Thus should it be kept in mind. In another way, these beings suffer in this present world due to the absence of the perfection of patience, and they suffer in the future world due to the practice of unwholesome states that cause suffering. If suffering arises due to the wrongs and oppressions of others, I alone have prepared the physical body which is like the field for that suffering, and the unwholesome kamma which is like the seed. This suffering caused by the wrongs of others is the settling of the debt of unwholesome kamma I have committed. If there were no oppressor, how could the perfection of patience be possible for me? If now this person...
268:
One should develop the perfection of patience (khanti) by reflecting: 'Even though this person is an offender, he has done such and such a favor for me in the past'; or, 'The very act of offense is a benefit because it is the cause for patience'; or, 'All these beings are like my own children; what parent would get angry at the faults committed by their children?'; or, 'This person offends me because of the possession by the demon of anger; I should dispel only that possession by the demon of anger'; or, 'This suffering has arisen for me because of this offense; I myself am also a cause for that offense'; or, 'By whichever unwholesome states the offense was committed, and at whichever moment it was committed, all those states ceased at that very moment; now, who should be angry with whom?'; or, 'Since all phenomena are non-self (anatta), who offends whom?'

If, however, due to long-standing habit, anger caused by the offenses of others persists and overwhelms the mind, one should reflect as follows: 'This patience is the cause for returning a favor through practices opposite to the offense of others'; or, 'The offender, by causing me suffering, becomes a condition for faith (saddhā), which has suffering as its proximate cause, and for the perception of disenchantment with the whole world (sabbaloke anabhiratisaññā)'; or, 'Encountering agreeable and disagreeable objects is just the nature of the faculties (indriya); in such a case, how can it be obtained that "May I not encounter disagreeable objects"?'; or, 'A being under the power of anger is maddened and distracted by anger; what is the use of offending such a person in return?'; or, 'All these beings have been protected by the Fully Enlightened One like his own breast-born children; therefore, I should not harbor anger toward them'; or, 'If the offender possesses virtues, I should not be angry with one who is virtuous'; or, 'If he has no virtues, because of the absence of any virtue, one should especially feel compassion (karuṇā) for him'; or, 'Through anger, my virtues and reputation decline'; or, 'Due to anger, things desired by enemies, such as ugliness and sleeping in misery, come upon me'; or, 'This anger is a powerful enemy that causes all suffering and harm, and destroys all happiness and welfare'; or, 'When there is patience, there is no enemy at all'; or, 'The suffering that the offender will receive in the future because of the offense will not exist for me if I have patience'; or, 'By thinking resentfully and being angry, I am merely following the will of the enemy'; or, 'When anger is conquered by me through patience, the enemy who is a slave to anger is truly conquered'; or, 'It is not proper for me to abandon the virtue of patience because of anger'; or, 'If there is anger, which is a state hostile and contrary to virtue, how can my qualities such as virtue (sīla) reach fulfillment?'; or, 'And without those qualities like virtue, how can I, after having been of great benefit to beings, reach the supreme Omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) in accordance with my own vow?'; or, 'When there is patience, because there is no distraction toward external objects, for one who is composed, all conditioned things (saṅkhāra) [are seen] as impermanent (anicca), as suffering (dukkha)...'
269: One should reflect: 'If I possess patience, such suffering cannot affect me.' 'Whether through deliberation or through anger, I would only be following the enemy's will.' 'If I conquer anger with patience, I have truly conquered the enemy who is a slave to that anger.' 'It is improper for me to abandon the virtue of patience because of anger.' Furthermore, 'If the opposing anger, which destroys virtue, exists, how can my virtues such as morality (sīla) reach fulfillment?' 'If these virtues like morality are absent, by what means can I, as one who has vowed to be of great benefit to beings and to save them from Saṃsāra, reach the fulfillment of supreme Omniscience?' When there is patience, because there is no distraction toward external objects, for one who is concentrated, all conditioned things (saṅkhāra) are seen as impermanent (anicca) and suffering (dukkha); all phenomena (dhamma) are seen as non-self (anatta); and Nibbāna is seen as the unconditioned (asaṅkhata), the deathless (amata), the peaceful (santa), and the sublime (paṇīta). The teachings of the Buddha are also seen as having inconceivable and immeasurable power. Because of such vision, while established in conformatory patience (anulomika-khanti), one reflects: 'These phenomena are merely dhammas, devoid of "I" or "mine"; they arise and perish according to their respective causes; they do not come from anywhere, nor do they go anywhere; they do not stay anywhere; and herein there is no agency of anyone.' Thus, it is fitting to contemplate the absence of a basis for the notions of 'I' and 'mine'. Through such contemplation, the Bodhisatta becomes firm in Enlightenment and is of a nature that never turns back. In this way, the reflection on the Perfection of Patience (khanti-pāramī) should be understood. Similarly, the fulfillments of the Perfection of Truthfulness (sacca-pāramī) should be reflected upon: 'Without truth, virtues such as morality cannot arise'; 'There can be no practice in accordance with one's vow'; 'If one transgresses the truth, one becomes a gathering place for all evil states'; 'One who lacks truth is untrustworthy'; 'In the future, his words will not be accepted by others'; 'One who is endowed with truth is the foundation of all virtues'; 'Through the determination of truth, all the requisites of enlightenment (sambodhi-sambhāra) follow toward purity and fulfillment'; 'By not deviating from the nature of things, truth performs the function of all requisites of enlightenment'; and 'The practice of the Bodhisatta reaches its completion.' Similarly, the virtues of the Perfection of Determination (adhiṭṭhāna-pāramī) should be reflected upon: 'The firm undertaking of giving (dāna) and so forth'; 'The unwavering determination in them even when their opposites gather'; and 'Without the state of a steadfast hero in those virtues, the requisites of enlightenment such as giving, which are the causes of Bodhi, cannot arise.' Similarly, one should especially arouse the state of desiring the welfare of all beings: 'If even one who stays only for his own benefit cannot attain the successes of this world and the next without a mind of welfare toward beings, what need is there to say of one who wishes to establish all beings in the bliss of Nibbāna?' 'It is not fitting for one who desires the supramundane success of all beings in the future to desire worldly success now.' 'If I cannot now bring about the welfare and happiness of others even by mere intention, when will I be able to accomplish it through effort?' 'Those who are nurtured by me now through the bringing of welfare and happiness will later become my companions in the distribution of the Dhamma.' 'Without them, my requisites of enlightenment cannot arise; therefore, because they are the cause for the accomplishment of the splendor of all the Buddha's qualities, these beings are like a supreme field of merit for me to sow the seeds of merit, an incomparable basis for wholesome deeds, and a noble object of respect.'
270:
"It is the basis for supreme respect." Also, "One should establish the disposition of desiring the welfare of all beings specifically. Even through the basis of a small amount of compassion, loving-kindness (mettā) should be repeatedly cultivated towards all beings. For one who delights in bringing about the welfare and happiness of beings with a boundless mind, there arises a powerful and firmly rooted desire to remove the harm and suffering of those beings. Compassion (karuṇā) is the initial practice, the foundation, the root, the beginning, and the foremost of all the qualities that make one a Buddha (buddhakaraka-dhamma)." In this way and so forth, the virtues of loving-kindness should be reflected upon.

Likewise, "Without equanimity (upekkhā), the offensive actions committed by beings would cause agitation of the mind. If there is mental agitation, the requisites (sambhāra) such as giving (dāna) and so forth cannot even arise." Also, "When the mind is softened by the affection of loving-kindness, the purification of the requisites is not possible without equanimity." Also, "One who does not look on formations (saṅkhāra) with equanimity cannot direct the requisite of merit or its fruit for the welfare of beings." Also, "Without equanimity, one cannot give without making distinctions between the gift and the recipient." Also, "A Bodhisatta devoid of equanimity cannot purify virtue (sīla) without disregarding the requisites of life or the dangers to life."

Likewise, "Only for one who endures dissatisfaction and delight through the power of equanimity is there the fulfillment of the power of renunciation (nekkhamma-bala); because all tasks of the requisites are accomplished only through proper observation; because one with excessive energy (vīriya) cannot perform the main task of exertion if they do not remain equanimous; because only for one who is equanimous can patience and insight occur; because of non-deviation regarding beings and formations through the power of equanimity; because of the accomplishment of unshakable determination in the undertaken qualities by being equanimous towards the worldly conditions (lokadhamma); because the dwelling in loving-kindness is accomplished only by not attending to the harms done by others and so forth; the undertaking, determination, and fulfillment of all the requisites of enlightenment (sambodhi-sambhāra) are accomplished through the power of equanimity." In this way and so forth, the perfection of equanimity (upekkhā-pāramī) should be reflected upon.

Thus, the reflection on the faults and benefits in non-renunciation and renunciation, respectively, should be understood as the cause for the perfections such as giving (dāna) and so forth.

Likewise, the fifteen practices of conduct (caraṇa-dhamma) along with their appurtenances and the five higher powers (abhiññā) are also causes for the perfections such as giving and so forth. Among them, the practices of conduct are: restraint of virtue (sīla-saṃvara), guarding the doors of the senses, moderation in eating, devotion to wakefulness, the seven noble qualities (saddhamma), and the four jhānas. Among these practices of conduct, for the four starting with virtue, the thirteen ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) and qualities such as fewness of wishes (appicchatā) and so forth are the appurtenances.

Among the noble qualities, the appurtenances of faith (saddhā) are: the recollections of the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, virtue, generosity, the deities, and peace (buddhānussati, dhammānussati, saṅghānussati, sīlānussati, cāgānussati, devatānussati, upasamanussati), along with avoiding harsh persons, associating with refined persons, reflecting on inspiring teachings, and having a mind inclined towards that faith. The appurtenances of moral shame (hiri) and moral dread (ottappa) are: reflecting on the faults of unwholesome actions, reflecting on the dangers of the woeful states, reflecting on the support of wholesome qualities, avoiding persons devoid of shame and dread, associating with persons endowed with shame and dread, and being inclined towards those qualities. The appurtenances of great learning (bāhusacca) are: exertion in the preliminary stage of the path, inquiring and discussing the scriptures, great effort in the noble qualities, learning blameless arts and sciences, maturity of the faculties, distance from defilements, avoiding persons of little learning, associating with persons of great learning, and being inclined towards that learning. The appurtenances of energy (vīriya) are: reflecting on the fear of the woeful states...
271:
Reflection on the danger of the woeful states, reflection on the supportive nature of wholesome states, avoiding persons devoid of moral shame (hiri) and moral dread (ottappa), associating with persons endowed with moral shame and moral dread, and being inclined towards that moral shame and moral dread—these are the requisites (of hiri and ottappa). The requisites of great learning (bāhusacca) are: prior application, repeatedly discussing and questioning the Pali and meanings of the scriptures already learned, great exertion in the true Dhamma, practicing blameless arts and sciences, maturity of the faculties, being distant from defilements, avoiding persons of little learning, associating with persons of great learning, and being inclined towards that great learning. The requisites of energy (viriya) are: reflecting on the fear of the woeful states, reflecting on the path to be traveled, reflecting on the greatness of the Dhamma, dispelling sloth and torpor (thīna-middha), avoiding lazy persons, associating with energetic persons, reflecting on the four right efforts (sammappadhāna), and being inclined towards that energy. The requisites of mindfulness (sati) are: having mindfulness and clear comprehension (sati-sampajañña), avoiding unmindful persons, associating with mindful persons, and being inclined towards that mindfulness. The requisites of wisdom (paññā) are: repeated discussion and questioning, purifying internal and external objects, balancing the faculties, avoiding unwise persons, associating with wise persons, reflecting on the Suttas which are the domain of profound knowledge, reflecting on the greatness of the Dhamma, and being inclined towards that wisdom. The requisites of the four jhānas are: the four factors starting with virtue (sīla), the preliminary development of the thirty-eight meditation objects, and the mastery (vasībhāva) of adverting and so forth.

Among those factors of conduct (caraṇa), through the purity of application (payoga-suddhi) by means of virtue and so forth, one becomes capable of giving the gift of safety to beings; through the purity of intention (āsaya-suddhi), one becomes capable of giving material gifts such as alms-food; through the purity of both, one becomes capable of giving the gift of Dhamma. In this way, the causal status of conduct (caraṇa) and so forth as the requisites for giving (dāna) and so forth should be determined accordingly. For fear of being too lengthy, we shall not elaborate further. Likewise, the wheels of prosperity (sampatti-cakka) and so forth should be understood as causes for giving and so forth.

Regarding the question, 'What is defilement (saṃkilesa)?': In general, being touched by craving and so forth is the defilement of the perfections. Specifically, it is the discrimination according to what is appropriate.

Generally, being touched by craving and so forth is the cause of defilement for the perfections. Specifically, however, discrimination regarding the gift and the recipient is the defilement of the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramī). Discrimination regarding beings and time is the defilement of the perfection of virtue (sīla-pāramī). Discrimination of delight and non-delight in the sensual realm and its cessation is the defilement of the perfection of renunciation (nekkhamma-pāramī). Discrimination of 'I' and 'mine' is the defilement of the perfection of wisdom (paññā-pāramī). Discrimination of sluggishness and restlessness is the defilement of the perfection of energy (viriya-pāramī). Discrimination of self and others is the defilement of the perfection of patience (khanti-pāramī). Discrimination of seeing and so forth in what is not seen and so forth is the defilement of the perfection of truthfulness (sacca-pāramī). Discrimination of faults and virtues in the requisites of enlightenment and their opposites is the defilement of the perfection of resolution (adhiṭṭhāna-pāramī). Discrimination of those who are beneficial and those who are not is the defilement of the perfection of loving-kindness (mettā-pāramī). Discrimination of agreeable and disagreeable objects is the defilement of the perfection of equanimity (upekkhā-pāramī) should be understood.
272: ## What is Purification (Vodāna)? – The state of not being oppressed by craving and so forth, and the state of being free from conceptual differentiations (vikappa), is to be understood as the purification (vodāna) of all those perfections. Indeed, the perfections such as giving (dāna), being unpressed by the defilements such as craving (taṇhā), conceit (māna), wrong view (diṭṭhi), anger (kodha), enmity (upanāha), depreciation (makkha), rivalry (palāsa), envy (issā), stinginess (macchariya), deceit (māyā), treachery (sāṭheyya), obstinacy (thambha), impetuosity (sārambha), pride (mada), and negligence (pamāda), and being free from conceptual differentiations regarding the gift and the recipient, become utterly pure and resplendent. ## What is the Opposite (Paṭipakkha)? – In general, unwholesome states and defilements are the opposites. Specifically, however, stinginess (macchariya) and so forth, which were mentioned previously, are the opposites. In general, all unwholesome states and all defilements are the opposites of these perfections. Specifically, stinginess and so forth, mentioned earlier, should be understood as the opposites. In another way, giving (dāna) is the opposite of greed, hatred, and delusion because of its association with the qualities of non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion regarding the gift, the recipient, and the fruit of the gift. Virtue (sīla) is the opposite of greed and so forth because of its departure from the crookedness that is the triad of faults of the body and so forth. Renunciation (nekkhamma) is the opposite of the triad of hatred because of the avoidance of sensual pleasure, the harming of others, and self-mortification. Wisdom (paññā) is the opposite of greed and so forth because it causes the blinding of greed and so forth, and because it causes the non-blinding of knowledge. Energy (viriya) is the opposite of greed and so forth by way of making a proper effort that is neither sluggish nor agitated. Patience (khanti) is the opposite of greed and so forth because of the endurance of the voidness of the desirable and the undesirable. Truthfulness (sacca) is the opposite of greed and so forth because of the occurrence of things as they really are, even when there is benefit or harm from others. Determination (adhiṭṭhāna) is the opposite of greed and so forth because of being unshakable in the foundations such as giving that have been undertaken, after overcoming the worldly conditions (lokadhamma). Loving-kindness (mettā) is the opposite of greed and so forth because of seclusion from the hindrances (nīvaraṇa). Equanimity (upekkhā) should be understood as the opposite of greed and so forth because of the destruction of attraction and repulsion toward the desirable and the undesirable, and because of its even occurrence. ## What is the Practice (Paṭipatti)? – In the sequence of fulfilling the perfections, the modes of giving and so forth, which are produced in many ways by the Bodhisatta, are to be understood as the practice (paṭipatti). In the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramī), the practice consists of benefiting beings in many ways through the sacrifice of fine requisites, the body, and life, through the removal of fear, and through the instruction of the Dhamma.
273:
Among those types of giving (dāna), there are three kinds based on the nature of the object to be given: the giving of material things (āmisa-dāna), the giving of fearlessness (abhaya-dāna), and the giving of the Dhamma (dhamma-dāna). Among these, the objects to be given by a Bodhisatta are of two kinds: internal objects (ajjhattika-vatthu) and external objects (bāhira-vatthu). Among these two, external objects are of ten kinds: food, drink, clothing, vehicles, flowers, perfumes, ointments, bedding, dwellings, and lamps. Food and other items are also of many varieties when classified as hard food, soft food, and so on. Furthermore, there are six kinds based on the sense objects, from visual objects to mental objects. Visual objects and others are also of many varieties when classified by colors such as blue and so forth. Moreover, there are many varieties based on various items and utensils such as gems, gold, silver, pearls, coral, etc.; landed property such as fields and orchards; and servants, maids, oxen, buffaloes, and so on.

In fulfilling this perfection of giving (dāna-pāramī), when the Great Being (Mahāpurisa), the Bodhisatta, gives external objects, he gives to a person exactly what that person needs. In giving to that person, he gives even without being asked, knowing by himself, "This person is in need." If he is asked, what more need be said? He gives with a mind of liberal generosity (mutta-cāga), not with a mind that is not liberal. He gives by making it complete or according to his capability; he does not give incompletely or beyond his capability. Even when he has the objects to give, he does not give with the expectation of receiving a favor in return. Even when he lacks the objects to give or the capability, he distributes what is worthy of being shared. He does not give things that bring harm to others, such as weapons, poison, or intoxicants. He also does not give objects that are for mere play, associated with harm, or that lead to heedlessness. He does not give unsuitable drinks or food to a sick recipient, nor does he give in an immoderate amount; rather, he gives only what is suitable and in moderate measure.

Furthermore, when asked, he gives to laypeople what is suitable for laypeople, and to monks what is suitable for monks. He gives without causing distress to anyone among his parents, relatives, friends, wife and children, servants, or employees. He does not give an inferior object after having promised a superior one. He does not give based on gain, honor, or fame. He does not give based on receiving a favor in return. He does not give with an expectation of worldly results, except for the sake of Supreme Enlightenment (Sammāsambodhi). When asked, he does not give with a mind of disgust toward the object to be given. He does not give disrespectfully, as if discarding something, even to recipients who are unrestrained, or who abuse and threaten him; on the contrary, he gives only with a clear mind, out of compassion and with respect. He does not give out of belief in superstitious omens (kotūhala-maṅgalika); rather, he gives believing only in Kamma and its results. He does not give by making the recipients weary through requirements such as constant attendance; on the contrary, he gives without causing weariness. He does not give with the intention of deceiving others or with the intention of causing division; he gives only with an undefiled mind. He does not give with harsh speech or with a frowning face; on the contrary, he gives being one who speaks kindly, who is the first to speak, and who has a smiling countenance. In whatever object of giving there is a superior quality of delightfulness...
274:
...or if greed is very strong due to long habit or a naturally lustful disposition, the wise Bodhisatta, recognizing this, quickly dispels that greed and gives the object even by seeking out a recipient. Even if the object to be given is small, and even if the recipient is present before him, he does not disregard that smallness but exerts himself to give, honoring the recipient with respect, just like the wise Akitti (Akitti-paṇḍita). Furthermore, the Great Being does not give his wife, children, servants, or employees to recipients when they have not been persuaded and are in a state of distress. He gives only when they have been well persuaded and are in a state of joy. In giving, he does not knowingly give to ogres (yakkhas), demons (rakkhasas), or pisācas, nor to humans of cruel deeds. Likewise, he does not give the kingdom to such people who would practice what is detrimental, painful, and useless for the world. He gives the kingdom only to the righteous who protect the world according to the Dhamma. Thus should the practice regarding the giving of external objects be understood.

The giving of internal objects (ajjhattika-dāna) should also be understood in two ways. How? Just as a man might surrender himself to another and enter into slavery for the sake of food and clothing, in the same way, the Great Being, for the sake of Enlightenment, with a mind free from attachment to material things and desiring the unsurpassed welfare and happiness of beings, surrenders himself to others, wishing to fulfill his perfection of giving. He places himself in a position where he can be dealt with according to the recipient's wish. He gives his major and minor limbs, such as hands, feet, and eyes, to those who need them, without trembling or shrinking. He has no attachment to those limbs, just as he has no attachment to external objects, and he does not fall into hesitation. Indeed, the Great Being relinquishes external objects in two ways: either for the recipients to use as they please, or to fulfill their wishes while mastering his own will (vasībhāva). In such relinquishment, the Bodhisatta, who is entirely liberal in his giving, says, "Through this state of non-attachment, I shall reach Supreme Enlightenment." Thus should it be understood regarding internal objects as well.

In the giving of those internal objects, he gives whatever internal object, when given, will definitely lead to the benefit of the recipient; he does not give otherwise. The Great Being does not knowingly give his body or his major and minor limbs to Māra or to deities of Māra’s retinue who have the intention to harm. He thinks, "Let there be no harm to them." Just as he does not give to those of Māra’s retinue, he also does not give to those possessed by them, nor to the insane. However, when asked by others, he gives immediately, because such a request is rare and such a gift is difficult to perform.
275:
Abhayadāna (the gift of freedom from fear) refers to the gift given by way of providing protection to beings when they are faced with dangers arising from kings, thieves, fire, water, enemies, predatory animals such as lions and tigers, or from nāgas, yakkhas, rakkhasas, pisācas, and so forth.

Dhammadāna (the gift of the Dhamma) refers to the preaching of the undistorted Dhamma with a mind free from defilement. In such preaching, it is the guidance provided according to the benefits of this world, the world beyond, and the ultimate goal, whereby those who have not yet entered the Sāsana are made to enter, and those who have already entered are brought to maturity. In this regard, the method is as follows: briefly, it is the preaching of the discourse on giving (dānakathā), the discourse on virtue (sīlakathā), the discourse on heaven (saggakathā), the danger, corruption, and vileness of sensual pleasures, and the benefits of renunciation (nekkhamma). In detail, for those whose minds are inclined toward Sāvakabodhi (the enlightenment of a disciple), it involves establishing and purifying them in their respective levels by praising the virtues of: taking refuge (saraṇagamana), restraint in virtue (sīlasaṃvara), guarding the sense doors, moderation in eating, devotion to wakefulness, the seven noble qualities (saddhamma), the practice of tranquility (samatha) by means of meditative work on the thirty-eight objects, the practice of insight (vipassanā) by way of appropriate application to the fields of insight such as the material aggregate (rūpakkhandha), and furthermore, the attainment of the Path, Fruit, and Nibbāna through the path of purity, the three knowledges (vijjā), the six supernormal powers (abhiññā), the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā), and Sāvakabodhi. Similarly, for those whose minds are inclined toward Paccekabodhi and Sammāsambodhi, it involves establishing and purifying them in the two vehicles (Abhiññā and Caraṇa) by praising the nature, function, and characteristics of the perfections (pāramī) such as giving, and by manifesting the great majesty of those Buddhas in their three stages. In this way, the Mahāpurisa (Great Being) gives the gift of the Dhamma to beings.

Furthermore, when the Mahāpurisa gives āmisadāna (the gift of material things), he gives food with the thought: 'By this gift, may I bring about for beings the attainment of long life, beauty, happiness, strength, and wisdom, as well as the attainment of the delightful and supreme Fruit (Arahatship).' He gives drink to quench the thirst of the defilements of sensual desire in beings. He gives garments to bring about a golden complexion and the ornament of moral shame and moral dread (hiri-ottappa). He gives vehicles to bring about the various psychic powers (iddhividha) and the bliss of Nibbāna. He gives scents to bring about the scent of virtue (sīla). He gives flowers and unguents to bring about the beauty of the Buddha's qualities. He gives seats to bring about the seat of the Bodhi-throne (or the foundation of Omniscience). He gives bedding to bring about the Tathāgata's rest. He gives dwellings to bring about the state of being a refuge. He gives lamps to obtain the five eyes. He gives visual objects (rūpa) to bring about the fathom-wide radiance (byāmappabhā). He gives sounds to bring about the Brahma-voice. He gives tastes to obtain the affection of all the world. He gives touch to bring about the delicacy of a Buddha (or the subtle Omniscient Knowledge)...
276:
...He gives the gift of touch (phoṭṭhabba) to become delicate as a Buddha or to obtain the extremely subtle Omniscient Knowledge. He gives the gift of medicine to reach the state of being ageless and deathless. He gives the gift of freedom to slaves to liberate them from the slavery of defilements. He gives the gift of blameless amusement to cause great delight in the True Dhamma. He gives the gift of his sons to bring all beings to the state of being his own sons in the noble birth. He gives the gift of his wife to reach the state of being the lord of the entire world. He gives gold, gems, pearls, coral, and so forth, to be endowed with the excellence of beautiful marks. He gives various kinds of ornaments to be endowed with the minor marks (anubyañjana). He gives the gift of treasuries of wealth to attain the treasury of the True Dhamma. He gives his kingdom (sovereignty) to reach the state of a King of Dhamma. He gives parks, gardens, and forests to be endowed with the excellence of giving and other virtues. He gives his feet so that he may approach the Bodhi-throne with feet marked by the wheel-sign. He gives his hands to provide the hand of the True Dhamma to beings in crossing over the four floods (ogha). He gives his ears, nose, and so forth, to obtain the faculty of faith (saddhindriya) and other faculties. He gives his eyes to obtain the all-seeing eye (samantacakkhu) of Omniscience. He gives his flesh, blood, and so forth, with the thought: 'May my body at all times be a source of welfare and happiness for all beings in their seeing, hearing, remembering, and serving, and may it be a support for the whole world.' He gives the gift of his head, the supreme limb, with the prayer: 'May I be the supreme one in all the world.'

In giving thus, he does not give through wrong livelihood, nor by harming others, nor out of fear, nor out of shame, nor by provoking the recipient. He does not give coarse things when fine things are available. He does not give by exalting himself or by disparaging others. He does not give out of desire for worldly fruits, nor out of disgust for the beggar, nor without respect. On the contrary, he gives respectfully; he gives with his own hands; he gives at the proper time; he gives with due consideration; he gives without discrimination; and he gives with a joyful heart in all three times (before, during, and after giving). Because he gives joyfully in all three times, he has no subsequent regret after giving. He does not show pride or disrespect toward the recipient. He is one who speaks endearingly to recipients, who easily understands the needs of beggars, who gives according to what is requested, and who gives with accompaniments. Indeed, when giving food, he gives it along with clothes and other items, thinking, 'I shall give this together with its accompaniments.' Likewise, when giving clothes, he gives them along with food and other items, thinking, 'I shall give this together with its accompaniments.' The same method applies to the gift of drinks and so forth. Similarly, when giving a visual object (rūpa), he gives it making the other sense objects its accompaniments. The same should be understood for the remaining gifts.

Among those gifts, what is called Rūpadāna (the gift of visual objects) is the act of obtaining any one of the colored objects such as blue, yellow, red, or white flowers, cloths, and so forth, and then, focusing on it as a visual object and thinking, 'I shall give a gift of a visual object; this is my gift of a visual object,' one establishes that gift in a suitable recipient. This is called Rūpadāna.
277:
The gift of sound (sadda-dāna) should be understood through the power of the sound of large drums and so forth. In that gift, one is not able to give sound by uprooting it like tubers and roots, nor by placing it in the hand like a bunch of blue lotuses. In fact, only when it is done together with a physical object is it called giving the gift of sound. Therefore, thinking, "I will give the gift of sound," one personally performs or causes others to perform the offering to the Triple Gem with any musical instrument such as a large drum or a muraja drum; or with the thought, "I will give the gift of sound, may the gift of sound be mine," one offers large drums and so forth; or one gives medicine, oil, molasses, etc., to Dhamma preachers to make their voices clear; or one announces the invitation to listen to the Dhamma, chants in the Sarabhañña style, preaches the Dhamma, gives a discourse to those seated nearby, and personally performs or causes others to perform the Anumodanā discourse—this is called the gift of sound.

Similarly, having obtained any pleasant fragrant object among roots, scents, and so forth, or any ground perfume powder, and reflecting on it by way of its scent, one performs or causes others to perform the offering to the Buddha Gem and so forth, thinking, "I will give the gift of scent (gandha-dāna), may the gift of scent be mine"; or one relinquishes and offers fragrant objects such as aloe wood and sandalwood for the purpose of worshipping with scent—this is called the gift of scent (gandha-dāna).

Similarly, having obtained any pleasant object of taste among the tastes of roots and so forth, and reflecting on it by way of its taste, one gives it to those worthy of offerings, thinking, "I will give the gift of taste (rasa-dāna), may the gift of taste be mine"; or one relinquishes and offers the food which is the basis of taste, or other things such as cows and buffaloes—this is called the gift of taste (rasa-dāna).

Similarly, the gift of touch (phoṭṭhabba-dāna) should be understood through the power of couches, chairs, and so forth, and through the power of floor coverings, robes, and so forth. For when one has obtained a blameless object of touch (phoṭṭhabba) that is pleasant to the touch, such as a couch, a chair, a mattress, a pillow, or a waist-cloth, a robe, and so forth, and reflecting on it by way of its tactile quality, one gives it to those worthy of offerings, thinking, "I will give the gift of touch, may the gift of touch be mine"; or one relinquishes and offers the aforementioned objects of touch—this is called the gift of touch (phoṭṭhabba-dāna).

The gift of Dhamma (dhamma-dāna), however, because it is intended as the object of the mind (dhammārammaṇa), should be understood through the power of nutrients (ojā), drinks (pāna), and life (jīvita). For having obtained any pleasant Dhamma-object among nutrients and so forth, and reflecting on it by way of its being a Dhamma-object, one gives the gift of nutrients such as ghee and fresh butter, thinking, "I will give the gift of Dhamma, may the gift of Dhamma be mine"; or one gives the eight kinds of drinks such as mango juice; or reflecting, "This is the gift of life," one gives ticket-food (salāka-bhatta), fortnightly food (pakkhika-bhatta), and so forth.
