One provides a physician for those oppressed by illness and disease, causes nets to be torn, causes fishing hooks to be destroyed, causes bird cages to be destroyed, effects the release of beings bound by fetters, causes the drum of non-killing (māghāta-bheri) to be sounded, and personally performs or causes others to perform such deeds for the protection of the lives of other beings—this is called the gift of Dhamma.
278: All this aforementioned fulfillment of giving, he dedicates for the welfare and happiness of the entire world, for his own unshakable liberation (akuppa-vimutti), and for the sake of inexhaustible desire, inexhaustible energy, inexhaustible concentration, inexhaustible perspicuity (paṭibhāna), inexhaustible jhāna, and for the sake of inexhaustible Supreme Enlightenment (Sammāsambodhi). The Great Being (Mahāsatta) who practices this perfection of giving should establish the perception of impermanence (anicca-saññā) in life. Likewise, in wealth and pleasures, he should also establish the perception of impermanence; he should also reflect on their being common to many enemies such as kings and thieves. He should constantly and continuously establish great compassion (mahākaruṇā) toward beings. Thus, when taking the essence from wealth, just as a person taking all his property and himself out of a burning house leaves nothing behind, so too, in taking the essence from wealth, he leaves nothing behind, makes no division in any wealth, but indeed gives it away without any lingering attachment. This is the sequence of practice for the perfection of giving. ## The Sequence of Practice for the Perfection of Virtue - Because the Great Being (Mahāpurisa) who wishes to adorn beings with the ornaments of virtue of the All-Knowing One must first purify his own virtue. In purifying that virtue, virtue is purified by four aspects: purity of intention (ajjhāsaya), undertaking (samādāna), non-transgression (avītikkamana), and restoration (paṭipākatika) if a transgression occurs. Indeed, because of the purity of intention, some people, making themselves the dominant factor (attādhipati) and having a nature that loathes evil, establish the quality of shame (hiri) within themselves and become those of extremely pure conduct. Likewise, when there is an undertaking from others, some people, making the world the dominant factor (lokādhipati) and being afraid of evil, establish the quality of fear of wrongdoing (ottappa) and become those of extremely pure conduct. Thus, in both ways, they stand in virtue through non-transgression. However, if at any time there should be a breach in virtue due to a lapse of mindfulness, they quickly restore that broken virtue to its original state through the aforementioned fulfillment of shame and fear of wrongdoing, by rising from the unwholesome state. That virtue is of two kinds: virtue of avoidance (vāritta-sīla) and virtue of performance (cāritta-sīla). Among these, the sequence of practice in the Bodhisatta's virtue of avoidance is as follows: That Bodhisatta should be one with a heart moved by compassion toward all beings, such that even in a dream, no thought of harming would arise. Because of abstaining from taking what belongs to others, he should not touch another's property as if it were a cobra. If he is a monk, he is one who lives far from the ignoble practice of sexual intercourse, abstaining from the sevenfold sexual bond, not to mention sexual relations with another's wife. If he is a householder, he does not even produce an evil thought toward the wives of others at any time. In speaking, he is one who speaks the truth, what is beneficial, what is endearing, and only in measured amounts; at the proper time, he is one who speaks words associated with the Dhamma. In all matters...
279:
One who is non-covetous, possesses a mind associated with loving-kindness, has an undistorted vision, and is endowed with the knowledge of the ownership of deeds (kammassakatā-ñāṇa). He possesses established faith and established affection for those who are harmonious and of good conduct.

In this way, by abstaining from the unwholesome courses of action (akusala-kammapatha) and unwholesome states which are the causes of the suffering of the round of rebirth in the four woeful planes, and by being established in the wholesome courses of action (kusala-kammapatha) and wholesome states which are the causes of the heavens, the paths, the fruits, and Nibbāna, the desires of the Great Being (Mahāpurisa) that are associated with the welfare and happiness of beings are swiftly fulfilled due to his pure intentions and efforts; his perfections (pāramīs) also become fulfilled. Such a Great Being, by desisting from harming others, gives the gift of fearlessness to all beings, fulfills the meditation on loving-kindness (mettā-bhāvanā) without difficulty, attains the eleven benefits of loving-kindness, is free from illness and affliction, lives a long life, abounds in happiness, attains special marks, and eradicates the habitual tendency (vāsanā) of anger.

Likewise, by abstaining from taking what is not given (adinnādāna), he acquires wealth that is not shared with thieves and others; he is one who is not suspected by others, is dear, pleasing, and trustworthy; his mind is unattached to the worldly attainments of life, he is habitually generous, and he eradicates the habitual tendency of greed. By abstaining from unchastity (abrahmacariya), he becomes free from greed, possesses a peaceful body and mind, is dear to beings, pleasing, and not suspected; his good reputation spreads far and wide; his mind is unattached to women, his intentions are without lust, he is abundant in renunciation (nekkhamma), attains special marks, and eradicates the habitual tendency of greed.

By abstaining from false speech (musāvāda), he becomes a standard for beings to rely upon, one whose word is trustworthy, firm, and acceptable; he is dear and pleasing to the devas, has a fragrant mouth, and has bodily and verbal conduct protected from unwholesome states; he attains special marks and eradicates the habitual tendency of defilements. By abstaining from slander (pesuñña), he has a body that cannot be divided by the efforts of others, has an inseparable retinue, has unwavering faith in the True Dhamma, has firm friends, is truly dear to beings he was acquainted with in other lives, and is largely free from defilements. By abstaining from harsh speech (pharusavācā), he is dear and pleasing to beings, has a happy disposition, speaks sweet words, is worthy of honor, and is born with a voice endowed with eight qualities. By abstaining from frivolous talk (samphappalāpa), he is dear and pleasing to beings, is respected and honored, has words that are acceptable, speaks in a measured way, and possesses great influence.
280:
He possesses great majesty. With wisdom that arises on the spot, he is skilled and proficient in answering various questions. Upon reaching Buddhahood, he is capable of answering the numerous questions of beings of many languages with just a single word.

Due to his non-covetousness (anabhijjhā), he acquires gains and offerings without difficulty. He finds delight in noble wealth. He is honored by those such as the Khattiya Mahāsālas. He cannot be oppressed or overcome by enemies. He does not suffer from deficiencies in the sense faculties such as the eyes. He becomes a peerless person. Due to his lack of ill-will (abyāpāda), he is seen as dear and beloved by beings. He is worthy of honor. Being one who delights in the welfare of others, he can inspire faith in beings without difficulty. He is not of a harsh nature and habitually dwells in loving-kindness. He possesses great power and great majesty. Due to the absence of wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi), he acquires good spiritual friends (kalyāṇamittas). Even when facing the danger of decapitation, he does not commit evil. Because of seeing that only kamma is one's own property (kammassakatā), he does not believe in superstitious omens (diṭṭha-suta-maṅgala) that cause a stir. For that Bodhisatta, faith rooted in the True Dhamma is well-established. He also believes in the Enlightenment (bodhi) of the Buddhas. Just as a royal swan does not delight in a heap of dung, he does not delight in other doctrines. He is skilled in perceiving the three characteristics (tilakkhaṇa). In his final life, he attains the unobstructed knowledge (anāvaraṇa-ñāṇa). As long as he has not yet attained Enlightenment, he is the most supreme among various groups of beings and attains grand and noble prosperity.

"This virtue (sīla) is the foundation of all attainments; it is the source of all the qualities of the Buddhas; it is the initial practice, the root cause, the beginning, and the foremost of the factors that make one a Buddha." Having generated great reverence in this way, one should be heedful through the power of mindfulness and clear comprehension (sati-sampajañña) in the restraint of body and speech, the taming of the sense faculties, the purity of livelihood, and the use of the four requisites. Regarding gains, offerings, and fame as an enemy with an uplifted sword, one should respectfully fulfill virtue in the manner stated, such as "as a kiki bird protects its egg," and so forth. This is the sequence of practice in the virtue of avoidance (vāritta-sīla).

As for the practice in the virtue of performance (cāritta-sīla), it should be understood thus: In this Dispensation, the Bodhisatta habitually performs acts of salutation, rising to greet, saluting with joined palms, and showing proper respect to spiritual friends (kalyāṇamittas) who are worthy of honor at the appropriate times. Likewise, he serves and attends to them at the appropriate times. He performs physical service (veyyāvacca) for the sick and inquires after them verbally. When he hears well-spoken words, he utters words of appreciation (sādhukāra).
281:
The Bodhisatta is one who praises the virtues of those who possess virtue, endures the wrongs (harms) committed by others, repeatedly recollects favors received, rejoices in meritorious deeds, and directs his own merits toward Supreme Enlightenment (Sammāsambodhi). He dwells with diligence in wholesome states at all times. If there is a fault, he sees it as a fault and reveals it truthfully to fellow practitioners of such nature; he also perfectly fulfills the higher right practice.

Likewise, in matters associated with the welfare of beings suitable to him, he takes the lead, thinking 'this should be done,' and approaches them as a companion without laziness. When beings suffer from diseases and so forth, he is one who arranges appropriate remedies; he dispels the sorrow of those who have met with the destruction of relatives, wealth, and so on. Remaining established in the nature of lifting beings out of the round of rebirths, he rightfully restrains those who deserve restraint in order to raise them from the unwholesome and establish them in the wholesome, and he rightfully encourages those who deserve encouragement. There are those practices of the former Great Bodhisattas which are most noble, extremely difficult to perform, of inconceivable power, and which bring about the absolute welfare and happiness of beings. By those practices, their requisites of enlightenment (bodhisambhāra) reached full maturity. Upon hearing of those practices, without being startled or terrified, he thinks: 'Those Great Beings (Mahāpurisa) were also just human beings; however, by gradually fulfilling and developing the training, they reached the pinnacle of the perfections (pāramī) as requisites of enlightenment, endowed with such most noble attainment of power. Therefore, I too should practice well in the trainings such as virtue (sīla) just as those former Bodhisattas did. By which practice, having gradually fulfilled the training, I shall certainly reach the state of Nibbāna.' Thus, with faith as his precursor and without abandoning energy, he is one who perfectly fulfills the virtues.

Furthermore, he is one who conceals his own goodness and reveals his faults; he is of few wishes, contented, secluded, not gregarious, patient with suffering, of a nature to see things as they truly are, not restless, not arrogant, not frivolous, not harsh-tongued, not a scatter-talker, with restrained senses, of a peaceful mind, free from wrong livelihood such as scheming (kuhana), and endowed with proper conduct and resort. Seeing danger even in the slightest faults, he undertakes and trains in the training rules. Possessing exerted energy and a resolute mind, he is indifferent to body and life; he does not tolerate even a slight attachment to body or life but abandons and dispels it, let alone an excessive attachment. He abandons and dispels all defilements and secondary defilements such as anger and malice, which are causes for immorality. He is not satisfied with a mere slight attainment of distinction; without shrinking back, he strives for higher and higher attainments of distinction.
282:
He exerts that energy so that the prosperity and happiness obtained through energy do not become partaking of decline or merely partaking of stability. Moreover, the future Great Being (Mahāpurisa) acts as a guide for the blind and shows them the way. He gives signs by hand gestures to the deaf and makes them understand the meaning; likewise for the mute. He gives a stool (pīṭha) to those who crawl on their bellies, or he carries them. He strives for the acquisition of faith in those without faith, for the arousal of effort in the lazy, and for the application of mindfulness in the forgetful.

He strives for the attainment of concentration in those with distracted minds and for the acquisition of wisdom in those with little wisdom. He strives to dispel sensual desire in those overwhelmed by sensual desire. He strives to dispel doubt in those overwhelmed by ill-will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt. He strives to dispel wrong thoughts such as sensual thoughts in those oppressed by sensual thoughts and so forth. Based on his gratitude toward beings who have previously done him favors, he is the first to greet, speaks endearingly, and is helpful. He is one who honors them by returning favors equally or even more greatly.

In times of danger, he follows and carries out the affairs of his companions. Having discerned the behavior and nature of various beings, he associates with them in the manner that is appropriate for association. He conducts himself toward them in the manner that is appropriate for conduct. Such conduct is only for the purpose of raising them from the unwholesome and establishing them in the wholesome, and not otherwise. Indeed, the Bodhisattas' protection of others' minds is only for the growth of wholesome states. Thus, even while desiring their welfare, one should not mock others, should not argue, should not cause them to be dejected, should not cause remorse in others, should not accuse others in a place where they are being restrained, and should not place oneself in a very high position in front of one who conducts himself very humbly. One should not live without associating with others at all, nor should one associate excessively, nor should one associate at the wrong time.

He associates with suitable beings according to the place and time. He does not disparage a loved one in front of others, nor does he praise an unloved one. He is not excessively intimate. He does not reject a righteous invitation. He does not follow worldly conventions. He does not accept more than what is appropriate. He gladdens those endowed with faith with talk on the benefits of faith. He gladdens those endowed with virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom with talk on the benefits of wisdom. If the Bodhisatta has attained the power of supernormal knowledge (abhiññā), he inspires spiritual urgency (saṃvega) in negligent beings by showing them hell and so forth as appropriate through the power of supernormal knowledge, and establishes those without faith in faith and so on; he makes them enter the Dispensation (Sāsana) and brings to maturity those endowed with qualities such as faith. Thus, it should be understood that for this Great Being, the immeasurable flow of merit and the flow of wholesome states, which constitute his conduct, increase higher and higher.
283:
Furthermore, having raised questions such as "What is virtue? In what sense is it virtue?" and so on, the detailed discourse on virtue in its various aspects—such as "Virtue consists of the states of volition and so on of one who abstains from killing and so forth, or of one who fulfills the duties of practice"—has been stated in the Visuddhimagga. All those explanations should be brought forward and stated here as well. However, in the Visuddhimagga, the discourse on virtue is presented from the perspective of a Disciple Bodhisatta (Sāvaka-bodhisatta), whereas in this work, it should be stated from the perspective of a Great Bodhisatta (Mahā-bodhisatta), preceded by compassion and skill in means. This is the only distinction. For this reason, the Great Being (Mahāpurisa) does not direct this virtue toward liberation from the afflictions of his own rebirth in states of misery, nor toward the attainment of sovereignty in states of happiness, such as the status of a Universal Monarch, a Deva, Sakka, Māra, or Brahma. Likewise, he does not direct it toward his own attainment of the threefold knowledge, the six higher knowledges, the four analytical knowledges, nor toward the enlightenment of a disciple or the enlightenment of a private Buddha. Rather, he directs it solely for the purpose of accomplishing the peerless ornament of virtue for all sentient beings through his omniscience. This is the sequence of practice for the Perfection of Virtue.

Similarly, the arising of wholesome consciousness that is embraced by compassion and skill in means, preceded by the perception of danger, and which proceeds by way of renouncing both sensual pleasures and existences, is called the Perfection of Renunciation (Nekkhamma-pāramī). Therefore, the household life (gharāvāsa) is a place without opportunity for the happiness of renunciation and so forth, because it is the dwelling place of all defilements, because it is extremely crowded with children, wife, and so on, and because it is cluttered with the undertaking of various tasks such as farming and commerce. Sensual pleasures (kāma) are like "a drop of honey clinging to the edge of a sword" or "like a banana tree," having little sweetness when licked but followed by great harm. They are obtained only for a brief moment, like a dance seen by a flash of lightning. They are experienced with a perverted perception, like the ornaments of a madman. They are loathsome, like a face covered with excrement. They are unsatisfying, like drinking essence-less water with a finger dipped in it. They are accompanied by oppressive illness, like the food of a starving person. They are the cause of falling into ruin, like bait attached to a fishhook. They are the cause of suffering in all three periods of time, like the heat of a fire. They are the cause of bondage, like a monkey-trap of sticky resin. They conceal harm, like a cocoon that hides the fault of death. They are a place of danger, like living in a village of enemies. They are the bait for the Mara of defilements and so forth, like one who nurtures an enemy. They involve the suffering of change, like the fulfillment of festivals. They burn within, like fire in a hollow tree. They have many disadvantages, like a honeycomb hanging in an old well. They are the cause of thirst, like drinking salt water. Like liquor...
284:
...being resorted to by low people, and being like a skeleton because of having little gratification—having thus noted the disadvantages and seeing the benefits in renunciation (nekkhamma) as the opposite, one should practice the Perfection of Renunciation with a mind that is bent, sloped, and inclined toward the happiness of renunciation, seclusion, and peace.

Since renunciation is rooted in the "going forth" (pabbajjā), one should first strive to attain the state of a monk. A Great Being (Mahāsatta) striving for the going forth should, in the absence of a Buddha's arising, go forth in the lineage of ascetics and wanderers who teach the doctrine of kamma and the doctrine of action. However, when the Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas have arisen, one should go forth only in their Dispensation (Sāsana). Having gone forth and being established in the aforementioned virtue, one should undertake the ascetic qualities (dhutanga) for the purpose of purifying that very Perfection of Virtue. For Great Beings who have undertaken the ascetic practices, while properly maintaining them, have the stains of defilements washed away by the water of such qualities as fewness of wishes, contentment, effacement, seclusion, non-association, arousal of energy, and being easy to support. Having pure conduct through the qualities of blameless virtue and vows, and being established in the three ancient Noble Lineages (Ariyavaṃsa), they reach the fourth Noble Lineage known as delight in meditation. They dwell having attained the access and absorption concentrations among the forty meditation subjects as appropriate. In this way, his Perfection of Renunciation reaches proper fulfillment.

In this context, the thirteen ascetic practices, along with the forty subjects of serenity meditation—namely, the ten kasinas, the ten foulness subjects, the ten recollections, the four divine abodes, the four formless states, the one perception, and the one defining—and the method of developing meditation should be stated in detail. However, since all of this has been stated in detail in all its aspects in the Visuddhimagga, it should be understood exactly as stated in that work. The only distinction is that while it is stated there from the perspective of a Disciple Bodhisatta, here it should be stated from the perspective of a Great Bodhisatta, preceded by compassion and skill in means. Thus should the sequence of practice in this Perfection of Renunciation be understood.

Likewise, a Bodhisatta who wishes to fulfill the Perfection of Wisdom (Paññā-pāramī) should first avoid the causes of delusion (moha), because wisdom does not coexist with delusion, just as light does not coexist with darkness. These causes of delusion are: discontent (arati), drowsiness (tandī), yawning, laziness, delight in company, excessive sleep, indecisiveness, lack of desire for knowledge, false pride, lack of inquiry, not taking proper care of the body, and lack of concentration of mind.
285:
Associating with the unwise, not attending to the wise, self-contempt, wrong thoughts, improper attention, excessive pampering of the body, lack of spiritual urgency (saṃvega), the five hindrances (nīvaraṇa), and in brief, the repeated cultivation of unwholesome states—for one who does so, unarisen wisdom does not arise, and arisen wisdom declines and perishes. Thus, these are the causes of delusion (moha). Avoiding these causes of delusion, a Bodhisatta should exert effort in great learning (bāhusacca) and in meditative absorptions (jhāna) and so forth.

The scope of that great learning (bāhusacca) consists of: the five aggregates (khandha), the twelve sense bases (āyatana), the eighteen elements (dhātu), the four truths (sacca), the twenty-two faculties (indriya), the twelve-linked dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda), as well as the various wholesome states such as the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), blameless worldly sciences, and the specific treatises on grammar (byākaraṇa) which are the means for providing the welfare and happiness of beings. Having thoroughly penetrated this entire range of learning through learning, hearing, memorizing, practicing, and inquiring, guided by wisdom, mindfulness, and energy characterized by skill in means, one should generate wisdom based on learning (sūtamayā paññā) by establishing others in that learning. Likewise, wisdom that arises spontaneously in the affairs of beings, intuitive wisdom (paṭibhāna), and wisdom skilled in the means of achieving welfare and avoiding harm should be exercised appropriately in various matters based on the desire for welfare. Furthermore, wisdom based on reflection (cintāmayā paññā) should be generated by means of reflecting on the nature of the aggregates and so forth, and by accepting the investigation through knowledge.

By generating worldly full understanding (lokiya-pariññā) through the comprehension of the individual and general characteristics of the aggregates and so forth, one should perfect the wisdom of development (bhāvanā-paññā) belonging to the preliminary stage of the path. Thus, discerning without distinction between internal and external phenomena as: 'This is merely mind and matter (nāmarūpa); it arises and ceases according to its respective causes; there is no doer or instigator here; it is impermanent (anicca) in the sense of non-existence after having been; it is suffering (dukkha) in the sense of being oppressed by rise and fall; it is non-self (anattā) in the sense of being uncontrollable'—one abandons attachment to them and causes others to abandon it. Out of pure compassion, as long as the qualities of a Buddha have not yet come into one's hand, one establishes beings in the three vehicles (yāna) by introducing and maturing them, and attains the pinnacle of wisdom by achieving worldly mastery over the meditative absorptions (jhāna), liberations (vimokkha), concentrations (samādhi), attainments (samāpatti), and direct knowledges (abhiññā).

Among those wisdoms of development, there is the wisdom of development known as the five worldly direct knowledges (abhiññā) together with their accessories, namely: the knowledge of the modes of supernormal power (iddhividha-ñāṇa), the knowledge of the divine ear-element (dibbasota-dhātu-ñāṇa), the knowledge of penetrating the minds of others (cetopariya-ñāṇa), the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇa), the knowledge of the divine eye (dibbacakkhu-ñāṇa), the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings according to their kamma (yathākammūpaga-ñāṇa), and the knowledge of the future (anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa)...
286:
...and in the states belonging to the four planes categorized as aggregates, sense bases, elements, faculties, truths, dependent origination, and so forth. Having cultivated the accumulation of knowledge through learning and inquiry, and being established in these two basic purifications—purification of virtue (sīlavisuddhi) and purification of mind (cittavisuddhi)—one should develop the wisdom of development, both worldly and supramundane, by perfecting these five purifications which are like the body: purification of view (diṭṭhivisuddhi), purification by overcoming doubt (kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhi), purification by knowledge and vision of what is and is not the path (maggāmaggañāṇadassanavisuddhi), purification by knowledge and vision of the way (paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhi), and purification by knowledge and vision (ñāṇadassanavisuddhi). The method for perfecting them is explained in detail in all its aspects in the Visuddhimagga, along with the analysis of objects and subjects, in such passages as: 'There, a beginner yogi who wishes to perform supernormal transformations such as "being one, he becomes many"...' and 'Aggregates means the five aggregates: the aggregate of matter, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness.' Therefore, it should be understood according to the method stated there. However, in that work, wisdom is presented from the perspective of a Disciple Bodhisatta (Sāvaka-bodhisatta); here, it should be spoken of from the perspective of a Great Bodhisatta (Mahābodhisatta), preceded by compassion and skill in means. The specific difference is that insight (vipassanā) should be maintained only within the purification by knowledge and vision of the way (paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhi) without reaching the purification by knowledge and vision (ñāṇadassanavisuddhi). Thus, the sequence of practice for the perfection of wisdom (paññā-pāramī) should be understood.

Furthermore, since a Great Being (Mahāsatta) who has made the resolution for supreme enlightenment (sammā-sambodhi) must always be diligently engaged and prepared for the fulfillment of the perfections (pāramī), he should exert effort for the welfare of beings, reflecting every day: 'What accumulation of merit or accumulation of knowledge have I gathered today? Or what benefit have I done for others?' For the sake of all beings, he should relinquish his possessions, body, and life with a mind free from attachment. Whatever action he performs by body or speech, it should all be done with a mind directed only toward enlightenment (sambodhi); it should be dedicated to enlightenment. He should possess a mind that has turned away from both grand and trivial sensual pleasures. In all duties to be performed, he should practice by bringing to the fore skill in means (upāyakosalla).

Being thus energetic in the welfare of beings, he should be one who is undeviating, enduring all things such as the desirable and the undesirable. He should pervade all beings without exception with loving-kindness (mettā) and compassion (karuṇā). Should any suffering arise for beings, he should wish for all that suffering to be upon himself alone. He should greatly rejoice in the merit of all beings. And the greatness of the Buddhas...
287:
One should constantly reflect upon the greatness and the vast power and majesty of the Buddhas. Whatever wholesome deed one performs, whether by body or by speech, it should be preceded by the bodhicitta (the mind directed toward omniscience). In this way, for the Great Being, the Bodhisatta, who is intensely devoted to wholesome deeds such as giving (dāna), who is endowed with capability, and who possesses firm persistence, the immeasurable accumulation of merit (puñña-sambhāra) and the accumulation of knowledge (ñāṇa-sambhāra) increase day by day.

Furthermore, for the sake of the enjoyment and protection of beings, having sacrificed one's own body and life, one should seek and bring about the remedy for the suffering caused by hunger, thirst, cold, heat, wind, sun, and so forth. Whatever happiness one obtains for oneself through such remedies for suffering; and furthermore, whatever happiness one obtains for oneself through being cooled and free from the fever of body and mind in delightful parks, gardens, mansions, and ponds, or in forest dwellings; and whatever words one hears such as, "The Buddhas, the enlightened followers, the Paccekabuddhas, and the Great Bodhisattas stand firm in the practice of renunciation (nekkhamma)," and "They enjoy such happiness of meditative attainments (jhāna-samāpatti), which is a pleasant dwelling in this very life"—all such happiness one should direct (share) toward all beings without limitation. This is the method for a Bodhisatta established on the plane of the unconcentrated (asamāhita-bhūmi).

However, a Bodhisatta established on the plane of concentration (samāhita-bhūmi) directs and dedicates to beings the rapture (pīti), tranquility (passaddhi), happiness (sukha), concentration (samādhi), and knowledge of things as they really are (yathābhūta-ñāṇa) that have arisen from his own experience of attaining distinction. Furthermore, seeing the multitude of beings submerged in the great suffering of saṃsāra and in the suffering of defilements and volitional formations (kilesa-abhisaṅkhāra) which is its cause; and seeing the beings in hell who continuously and for a long time experience intense, harsh, and bitter painful feelings born of being devoured, cut, split, steamed, crushed, tormented, and scorched by fire, and so forth; and the animals who experience great suffering through mutual anger, intimidation, persecution, torment, and being subject to the will of others; and the hungry ghosts (petas), such as the nijjhāmatanhika (those consumed by thirst), who experience great suffering, having bodies troubled by blazing flames, being scorched and dried up by hunger, thirst, wind, and sun, having only vomit and saliva for food, and wailing with upraised arms; and the human beings who meet with great ruin and disaster on account of seeking food, who undergo the cutting off of hands and feet, who are afflicted with ugliness, unsightly appearance, poverty, hunger, and disease, and who experience suffering no different from the suffering of the lower realms—even exceeding that of hell-beings, ghosts, and animals—due to being oppressed by the powerful, bearing the burdens of others, and being subject to the will of others; likewise, those whose minds are distracted by the enjoyment of sensual objects and are thus scorched by the fevers of lust and so forth, existing with the unappeased heat of defilements like a heap of dry wood ablaze with flames fanned by the force of the wind...
288:
The Bodhisatta, seeing with the eye of wisdom the celestial beings of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara-deva) who are burning with the unquenched heat of defilements and are dependent on others due to the lack of peace; and the celestial beings of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) and the immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara) who—like birds flying into the far distance of the sky with great effort, or like arrows shot far by the hand of a strong man—though they exist for a long time, end in impermanence, finish in falling away, and have not transcended birth, aging, and death; seeing them, he should arouse a great sense of urgency (saṃvega) and pervade all beings without limit with loving-kindness (mettā) and compassion (karuṇā). In this manner, the Bodhisatta, who continuously accumulates the requisites of enlightenment (bodhisambhāra) through body, speech, and mind, should exert effort with respect, constancy, and without shrinking in order to fulfill the perfections (pāramīs); thus, the perfection of energy (vīriya-pāramī) should be fulfilled.

Furthermore, the energy (vīriya) that is worthy of joy and exertion for the sake of attaining Buddhahood—which is the source of a mass of inconceivable, immeasurable, vast, noble, pure, incomparable, and stainless qualities—is indeed of inconceivable power. Most people are unable even to hear about such energy, let alone practice it. To elaborate on this: the three kinds of arising of the thought of aspiration (abhinīhāra-cittuppāda), the four grounds of Buddhahood (buddhabhūmi), the four bases of sympathy (saṅgahavatthu), being of the sole flavor of compassion, having a special cause through the realization of the Buddha-dhamma, patience in reflecting on the Dhamma (nijjhānakkhanti), being unstained by all worldly things, the perception of all beings as one's own dear son, being untiring despite the sufferings of saṃsāra, the renunciation of all things to be given and the resulting freedom from pride, the undertaking of higher virtue (adhisīla) etc. and being unshakable therein, joy and gladness in performing wholesome deeds, a mind inclined toward seclusion (viveka), devotion to meditative absorption (jhāna), being insatiable in blameless wholesome states, firmness in the effort to teach the Dhamma as heard with the intention for the welfare of others, the state of being firm and heroic, being unperturbed by the blame and harm of others, the resolution on truth (saccādhiṭṭhāna), mastery in meditative attainments (samāpatti), reaching power in direct knowledges (abhiññā), the penetration of the three characteristics, the accumulation of the requisites for the supramundane path through devotion to the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) etc., and the entry into the nine supramundane states—all such practices of the requisites of enlightenment are accomplished only through the power of energy (vīriya). 

Therefore, from the initial aspiration until the Great Enlightenment, one should fulfill energy with respect and continuity, without giving up, so that it brings about successive higher distinctions. When the aforementioned energy is accomplished, all other requisites of enlightenment such as patience (khanti), truth (sacca), and resolution (adhiṭṭhāna), as well as generosity (dāna) and virtue (sīla), are also accomplished because they are dependent on that energy. The practice regarding the perfection of patience (khanti-pāramī) and so on should be understood in this same way. Favoring beings in many ways by renouncing material things (āmisa) that cause their happiness is the practice of generosity (dāna). Protecting the lives, property, and spouses of those beings, speaking words that are endearing, beneficial, and not divisive, and practicing non-harming is the practice of virtue (sīla). Accepting material gifts such as alms-food and giving the gift of Dhamma, thus practicing for the welfare of beings in many ways, is the practice of renunciation (nekkhamma). Skill in the means of working for the welfare of beings is the practice of wisdom (paññā).
289:
Thus, the practice (paṭipatti) through giving (dāna) is the act of providing support in many ways by relinquishing material things that are causes for the happiness of beings. Through virtue (sīla), there is the protection of the lives, property, and families of those beings, the speaking of words that are endearing, beneficial, and conducive to harmony, and the non-infliction of harm, and so forth. Through renunciation (nekkhamma), there is the practice of welfare in various ways, such as by receiving material offerings and giving the gift of Dhamma. Through wisdom (paññā), there is skill in the means of accomplishing the welfare of those beings. Through energy (vīriya), there are acts performed without wavering by initiating great effort in those matters of welfare for beings. Through patience (khanti), there is the enduring of wrongs committed by those beings. Through truthfulness (sacca), there is the non-deception of those beings, the firm undertaking of acts of assistance, and the non-violation of one's word, and so forth. Through determination (adhiṭṭhāna), there is unwavering steadiness even when faced with misfortune while providing assistance to those beings. Through loving-kindness (mettā), there is the constant reflection on the welfare and happiness of those beings. Through equanimity (upekkhā), there is the absence of mental fluctuation regarding the benefits or harms [received from] those beings. Thus, the accumulation of the immeasurable requisites of merit and knowledge (puṇya-ñāṇa-sambhāra), which is not shared with worldlings (puthujjanas) and belongs to the Bodhisatta who has compassion for all beings by taking immeasurable beings as his object, should be understood here as the practice (paṭipatti). Furthermore, the respectful fulfillment of whatever cause has been mentioned for these [perfections] should also be understood as the practice (paṭipatti).

## How is the classification [of these perfections] made?

These perfections are ten in terms of general classification;
By way of further division, each becomes three,
Making thirty in total.

Indeed, there are thirty perfections: ten perfections (pāramī), ten intermediate perfections (upapāramī), and ten ultimate perfections (paramattha-pāramī). Among them, some teachers say: "For a Bodhisatta who has made the formal resolution (abhinīhāra) and whose intention and effort are inclined toward the welfare of others, the wholesome states mixed with dark states (kaṇha-dhamma) are the perfections (pāramīs); those wholesome states unmixed with them are the intermediate perfections (upapāramīs); and those states that are neither dark nor bright (akaṇha-asukka) are the ultimate perfections (paramattha-pāramīs)." Others say: "The perfections fulfilled during the times of accumulation are the pāramīs; those perfected at the stage of a Bodhisatta (bodhisatta-bhūmi) are the upapāramīs; and those fully perfected in every aspect at the stage of a Buddha (buddha-bhūmi) are the paramattha-pāramīs. Or, they are called pāramīs because of performing the welfare of others at the stage of a Bodhisatta, upapāramīs because of performing one's own welfare, and paramattha-pāramīs because of fulfilling both types of welfare through the attainment of the Powers and the Intrepidities (vesārajja) at the stage of a Buddha. Thus, their classification exists in the beginning, middle, and end, [corresponding to] the resolution, the undertaking, and the completion." Others say: "The classification of these perfections is based on the different accumulations of merit by Bodhisattvas who are compassionate by nature, calming faults, and who have reached the happiness of existence, the happiness of fruition, and the supreme happiness [of Nibbāna]."

Some teachers say: "The aforementioned classification exists because of the attainment of the three types of Bodhi—by the Disciples (anubuddha), the Paccekabuddhas, and the Sammāsambuddhas—through the pāramīs, upapāramīs, and paramattha-pāramīs, [respectively], by those who rely on shame (lajjā), mindfulness (sati), and pride (māna), who take the supramundane Dhamma as their authority, who honor virtue, concentration, and wisdom, and who have crossed over, are crossing over, and will cause others to cross over." "The requisites (sambhāra) that occur from the mental resolution until the verbal resolution are called the pāramīs..."
290: Other teachers say that the merits arising from the mental resolve (manopaṇidhi) up to the verbal resolve (vacīpaṇidhi) are called Pāramīs; those from the verbal resolve up to the physical resolve (kāyapaṇidhi) are called Upapāramīs; and those from the physical resolve onwards are called Paramattha-pāramīs. Still other teachers say that the accumulation of merits arising by way of rejoicing in the merits of others are Pāramīs; those arising by way of causing others to perform merits are Upapāramīs; and those arising by way of performing them oneself are Paramattha-pāramīs. Similarly, some teachers say that the accumulation of merit and knowledge that brings about happiness in existence is Pāramī; that which brings about one's own happiness of Nibbāna is Upapāramī; and that which brings about both of those for others is Paramattha-pāramī. The relinquishing of external requisites such as children, wife, and wealth is Dāna-pāramī; the relinquishing of one's own limbs is Dāna-upapāramī; and the relinquishing of one's own life is Dāna-paramattha-pāramī. Likewise, the three types of Sīla-pāramī arise by way of non-transgression of precepts for the sake of those three objects (children, wife, and wealth). The three types of Nekkhamma-pāramī arise by way of renouncing and cutting off attachment to those three objects. The three types of Paññā-pāramī arise by way of discerning the benefit and harm of beings after removing the craving for requisites, limbs, and life. The three types of Viriya-pāramī arise by way of striving for the aforementioned types of relinquishing and so forth. The three types of Khanti-pāramī arise by way of enduring those who cause harm to one's requisites, limbs, and life. The three types of Sacca-pāramī arise by way of not abandoning the truth for the sake of requisites, limbs, and life. Since perfections such as Dāna are fulfilled only by way of unshakable resolution, the three types of Adhiṭṭhāna-pāramī arise by way of unshakable resolution even when requisites and so forth are destroyed. The three types of Mettā-pāramī arise by way of not abandoning loving-kindness even toward beings who destroy one's requisites and so forth. The three types of Upekkhā-pāramī arise by way of attaining neutrality toward beings and formations, whether they are benefactors or wrongdoers, in relation to the three aforementioned objects. In this manner, the classification of these perfections should be understood. ## To the question of how they are grouped - Although there are thirty divisions by way of classification, there are ten by way of summary; among these perfections, there are only six types, which are accomplished through pairs such as Dāna and Sīla. In detail, just as those perfections are thirtyfold by classification but tenfold by way of being Dāna-pāramī and so forth, they are likewise sixfold by the nature of Dāna, Sīla, Khanti, Viriya, Jhāna, and Paññā. Among these ten perfections, Nekkhamma-pāramī is included in Sīla-pāramī in the sense of monkhood. In the sense of seclusion from the hindrances, it is included in Jhāna-pāramī. In the sense of being a wholesome state, it is included in all six perfections such as Dāna. Sacca-pāramī is included only as a part of Sīla-pāramī in the aspects of verbal truth and abstinence truth.
291:
Specifically, in the aspect of the truth of knowledge (*ñāṇa-sacca*), it is subsumed under the perfection of wisdom. The perfection of loving-kindness is subsumed under the perfection of meditative absorption alone. The perfection of equanimity is subsumed under the perfections of meditative absorption and wisdom. The perfection of determination is subsumed under all the perfections.

Furthermore, the fifteen pairs (*yugala*) and so on of these six qualities such as giving, which are mutually connected, bring about fifteen pairs of accomplishments. They are as follows: Through the pair of giving and virtue, the pair of doing what is beneficial for others and not doing what is harmful is accomplished. Through the pair of giving and patience, the pair of non-greed and non-hatred is accomplished. Through the pair of giving and energy, the pair of relinquishment and learning is accomplished. Through the pair of giving and meditative absorption, the pair of abandoning sensual desire and hatred is accomplished. Through the pair of giving and wisdom, the pair of the burden of the noble vehicle is accomplished. Through the two of virtue and patience, the two of purity of means (*payoga*) and purity of intention (*āsaya*) are accomplished. Through the two of virtue and energy, the two types of mental development (*bhāvanā*—tranquillity and insight) are accomplished. Through the two of virtue and meditative absorption, the two of abandoning immorality and abandoning obsession (*pariyuṭṭhāna*) are accomplished. Through the two of virtue and wisdom, the two types of giving (material and Dhamma) are accomplished. Through the two of patience and energy, the two of endurance and power (*khamā* and *teja*) are accomplished. Through the two of patience and meditative absorption, the two of abandoning conflict and compliance are accomplished. Through the two of patience and wisdom, the two of the patience of emptiness and penetration are accomplished. Through the two of energy and meditative absorption, the two of exertion and non-distraction are accomplished. Through the two of energy and wisdom, the two of refuge are accomplished. Through the two of meditative absorption and wisdom, the two vehicles (the vehicle of tranquillity and the vehicle of insight) are accomplished.

Through the triad of giving, virtue, and patience, the triad of abandoning greed, hatred, and delusion is accomplished. Through the triad of giving, virtue, and energy, the triad of taking the essence from wealth, life, and the body is accomplished. Through the triad of giving, virtue, and meditative absorption, the triad of the bases of meritorious action is accomplished. Through the triad of giving, virtue, and wisdom, the triad of the gift of material things, the gift of fearlessness, and the gift of the Dhamma is accomplished. In this way, the triads, tetrads, and so on should be combined as appropriate with the remaining triads, tetrads, and so forth.

In this way, the subsumption of these perfections, though sixfold, should be understood through the four determinations (*adhiṭṭhāna*). When all perfections are subsumed as a group, there are four determinations. They are: the determination of truth (*sacca-adhiṭṭhāna*), the determination of relinquishment (*cāga-adhiṭṭhāna*), the determination of peace (*upasama-adhiṭṭhāna*), and the determination of wisdom (*paññā-adhiṭṭhāna*). Among these, it is called 'determination' because one determinedly stands by this quality, or one stands determinedly in this quality, or it is simply the act of determination. It is the determination of truth because it is both truth and determination, or because it is the determination of truth, or because truth is its determination. The same method of verbal definition applies to the remaining determinations such as relinquishment.

Among those four determinations, speaking generally without distinction: it is called the determination of truth because of the encompassing of all perfections in accordance with the promise of the Great Being (*Mahāsatta*) who, having first made the aspiration for Buddhahood, has compassion for all beings. It is called the determination of relinquishment because of the relinquishing of the opposites of those perfections. It is called the determination of peace because of the subsiding of defilements through the qualities of all the perfections. It is called the determination of wisdom because of the skill in means regarding the welfare of others through those same qualities of the perfections.

Specifically, however, it is so called because of the promise, "I shall give to those who come to beg without failing them," and because of giving without failing the promise, and because of not failing the gift...
292:
Giving (Dāna) is a wholesome state that has the four determinations as its proximate cause, because of rejoicing, because of the relinquishment of opposing states such as stinginess, because of the subsiding of greed, hatred, delusion, and fear regarding the gift, the recipient, the act of giving, and the exhaustion of the gift, because of giving systematically at the proper time and in the proper way, and because of the predominance of wisdom. Likewise, Virtue (Sīla) has the four determinations as its proximate cause, because of not transgressing the restraint (saṃvara) undertaken, because of the relinquishment of immorality, because of the subsiding of misconduct, and because of the predominance of wisdom. Patience (Khanti) has the four determinations as its proximate cause, because of enduring in accordance with one's promise, because of the relinquishment of specific thoughts of offense committed, because of the subsiding of the obsession of anger, and because of the predominance of wisdom. Energy (Viriya) has the four determinations as its proximate cause, because of performing the welfare of others in accordance with one's promise, because of the relinquishment of [sensual] objects, because of the subsiding of unwholesome states, and because of the predominance of wisdom. Jhana has the four determinations as its proximate cause, because of repeatedly reflecting on the welfare of the world in accordance with one's promise, because of the relinquishment of the hindrances (nīvaraṇa), because of the subsiding of the mind, and because of the predominance of wisdom. Wisdom (Paññā) has the four determinations as its proximate cause, because of skill in means for the welfare of others in accordance with one's promise, because of the relinquishment of performing what is not a cause, because of the subsiding of the fever born of delusion, and because of the attainment of omniscience.

Among those four determinations, the Determination of Truth (Saccādhiṭṭhāna) occurs through the arrangement of things to be known in accordance with one's promise. The Determination of Relinquishment (Cāgādhiṭṭhāna) occurs through the relinquishment of the objects of desire (vatthu-kāma) and the defilements of desire (kilesa-kāma). The Determination of Peace (Upasamādhiṭṭhāna) occurs through the subsiding of hatred and suffering. The Determination of Wisdom (Paññādhiṭṭhāna) occurs through appropriate knowledge and penetrative knowledge. There is the Determination of Truth, embraced by the threefold truth, which is opposed to the three faults; the Determination of Relinquishment, embraced by the threefold relinquishment, which is opposed to the three faults; the Determination of Peace, embraced by the threefold peace, which is opposed to the three faults; and the Determination of Wisdom, embraced by the threefold knowledge, which is opposed to the three faults. The determinations of relinquishment, peace, and wisdom are embraced by the determination of truth because of non-deviation and because of arrangement in accordance with one's promise. The determinations of truth, peace, and wisdom are embraced by the determination of relinquishment because of the relinquishment of opposing states and because of being the fruit of total relinquishment. The determinations of truth, relinquishment, and wisdom are embraced by the determination of peace because of the subsiding of the fever of defilements and the fever of kamma. The determinations of truth, relinquishment, and peace are embraced by the determination of wisdom because of being preceded by knowledge and because of following after knowledge. In this way, all the perfections (pāramīs) are produced by the determination of truth, manifested by the determination of relinquishment, augmented by the determination of peace, and purified by the determination of wisdom. For truth is the generating cause of these perfections; relinquishment is the cause for the recipient; peace is the cause for growth; and wisdom is the cause for purity. Likewise, in the beginning, there is the determination of truth because of the promise made through truth. In the middle, there is the determination of relinquishment because of the relinquishment of oneself for the welfare of others after having made the resolution. In the end, there is the determination of peace because of culminating in the subsiding of all defilements. In the beginning, middle, and end, there is the determination of wisdom because it [the other determinations] can arise when wisdom is present, cannot arise when it is absent, and arises in accordance with one's promise.
293:
Among these four resolutions, Great Beings (Bodhisattas) always benefit themselves and others by being worthy of respect and affection. Through the resolutions of Truth (Sacca) and Relinquishment (Cāga), while living as householders, they support others with material gifts (āmisa-dāna). Similarly, through the resolutions of Peace (Upasama) and Wisdom (Paññā), while living as monastics, they support others with the gift of Dhamma (dhamma-dāna).

Regarding the fulfillment of these four resolutions, some teachers say that they are fulfilled in the Bodhisatta's final birth. Indeed, for a Bodhisatta who has fulfilled the four resolutions, the final birth occurs. In that final birth, through the perfection of the resolution of Wisdom, he is mindful and clearly comprehending during the descent into the womb and at birth. Through the perfection of the resolution of Truth, immediately after birth, facing north, he takes seven steps, surveys all directions, and with words consistent with truth, he utters the bold 'Lion's Roar' three times:
"I am the foremost in the world,
I am the eldest in the world,
I am the greatest in the world."
Through the perfection of the resolution of Peace, after seeing the omens of the old, the sick, the dead, and the monk, the Bodhisatta—who is skilled in pointing out the fourfold Dhamma—finds the calming of the intoxication of youth, health, and life. Through the perfection of the resolution of Relinquishment, he renounces without attachment his vast circle of relatives and the status of a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) that was within his reach.

Some teachers say the four resolutions are fulfilled at the second stage, the Great Enlightenment (Abhisambodhi) at the foot of the Bodhi tree. At that time, through the perfection of the resolution of Truth as pledged, there is the penetration of the Four Noble Truths. Because of this penetration, the resolution of Truth is fulfilled. Through the perfection of the resolution of Relinquishment, there is the relinquishing of all defilements and secondary defilements (kilesa and upakkilesa). Because of this relinquishing, the resolution of Relinquishment is fulfilled. Through the perfection of the resolution of Peace, he attains the supreme peace. Because of this attainment, the resolution of Peace is fulfilled. Through the perfection of the resolution of Wisdom, he gains the Unobstructed Knowledge (anāvaraṇa-ñāṇa). Because of this gain, the resolution of Wisdom is fulfilled. However, this statement is not fully established because even the Great Enlightenment is a means to the ultimate goal.

Others say the four resolutions are fulfilled at the third stage, the preaching of the first sermon, the Dhammacakkappavattana. At that time, for the Blessed One who has perfected the resolution of Truth, the resolution of Truth is fulfilled by teaching the Noble Truths in twelve modes. For the Blessed One who has perfected the resolution of Relinquishment, the resolution of Relinquishment is fulfilled by making the great sacrifice of the True Dhamma. For the Blessed One who has perfected the resolution of Peace, having attained peace himself, the resolution of Peace is fulfilled by bringing peace to others. For the Blessed One who has perfected the resolution of Wisdom, the resolution of Wisdom is fulfilled by fully discerning the inclinations (āsaya) and so forth of those to be tamed. This statement is also not fully established because the Buddha's work was not yet completed.
294:
Other teachers say the four resolutions are fulfilled at the fourth stage, the Final Passing (Parinibbāna). This is because at the time of the Final Passing, having attained the ultimate truth, the resolution of Truth is fulfilled; by the relinquishing of all acquisitions (upadhi), the resolution of Relinquishment is fulfilled; by the stilling of all formations (saṅkhāra), the resolution of Peace is fulfilled; and by the Final Passing which is the purpose of wisdom, the resolution of Wisdom is fulfilled.

Among these four resolutions, the fulfillment of the resolution of Truth is particularly evident in the noble birth, which is the field of loving-kindness (mettā-khetta). The fulfillment of the resolution of Wisdom is particularly evident at the Great Enlightenment, which is the field of compassion (karuṇā-khetta). The fulfillment of the resolution of Relinquishment is particularly evident in the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, which is the field of appreciative joy (muditā-khetta). The fulfillment of the resolution of Peace is particularly evident at the Final Passing, which is the field of equanimity (upekkhā-khetta).

Furthermore, the virtue (sīla) of a Bodhisatta who has perfected the resolution of Truth is to be known through living together. The purity (soceyya) of a Bodhisatta who has perfected the resolution of Relinquishment is to be known through dealings. The strength (thāma) of a Bodhisatta who has perfected the resolution of Peace is to be known in times of adversity. The wisdom (paññā) of a Bodhisatta who has perfected the resolution of Wisdom is to be known through discussion. Thus, the purification of virtue, the purification of livelihood, the purification of mind, and the purification of view (sīla-, ājīva-, citta-, diṭṭhi-visuddhi) are to be known. Moreover, due to the perfection of the resolution of Truth, because he is not deceptive, he does not go to the wrong path of hatred (dosa-agati). Due to the perfection of the resolution of Relinquishment, because he is not attached by greed and craving, he does not go to the wrong path of desire (chanda-agati). Due to the perfection of the resolution of Peace, because he does not conflict through anger, he does not go to the wrong path of fear (bhaya-agati). Due to the perfection of the resolution of Wisdom, because he penetrates things as they really are, he does not go to the wrong path of delusion (moha-agati).

Furthermore, with the first, the resolution of Truth, he endures without malice. With the second, the resolution of Relinquishment, he makes use of requisites without greed. With the third, the resolution of Peace, he avoids evil without fear. With the fourth, the resolution of Wisdom, he dispels delusion without confusion. Through the first resolution, the happiness of renunciation (nekkhamma-sukha) arises. Through the others, the happiness of seclusion (paviveka), peace (upasama), and enlightenment (sambodhi) arise. Likewise, the happiness of joy born of seclusion, the happiness of joy born of concentration, the bodily happiness born of the absence of joy, and the happiness of equanimity born of the purity of mindfulness arise respectively through these four. In this way, the collection of all perfections (pāramī) should be understood as being encompassed by the four resolutions, which are associated with many virtues. Just as all perfections are encompassed by the four resolutions, they should also be seen as encompassed by compassion (karuṇā) and wisdom (paññā). Indeed, the entire equipment for enlightenment (bodhi-sambhāra) is encompassed by compassion and wisdom. For qualities such as giving (dāna) and so forth, when embraced by compassion and wisdom, become the great equipment for enlightenment that culminates in the attainment of Buddhahood. Thus, their inclusion should be understood.
295:
## The Means of Accomplishment (Sampādanūpāya)

What is the means of accomplishment?

In the accomplishment of all the perfections, factors such as non-deficiency and the dedication of oneself should be understood as the means.

Indeed, it is the fulfillment of all the requisites of merit (puññasambhāra) without omission, aiming for supreme enlightenment, through the practice of non-deficiency (avekallakāritā); performing them respectfully with devotion and high regard (sakkaccakāritā); persevering continuously (sātaccakāritā); and practicing for a long duration without giving up in the middle (cirakālādiyoga). The duration of the Bodhisatta's [endeavor] will be made clear later. Thus, the engagement with these four factors is the means of accomplishing these perfections.

Likewise, the Great Being (Mahāsatta) practicing for enlightenment must first dedicate himself to the Buddhas for the sake of supreme enlightenment, saying: "I offer this person (attabhāva) to the Buddhas." Even before obtaining various possessions, he should first renounce them for the sake of giving, thinking: "Whatever requisites for life may arise for me, I shall give them all if there is a solicitor; only after giving to them shall I enjoy what remains."

When the Bodhisatta, whose mind is thus well-prepared for renunciation, obtains possessions, whether animate or inanimate, four fetters of giving (dānavinibandha) may arise: (1) lack of previous habituation in giving, (2) the smallness of the object to be given, (3) the excellence of the object to be given, and (4) concern over the exhaustion of wealth. Among these four, if there is an object to be given and a solicitor present, but the mind does not incline toward giving, he should conclude: "Surely, because I have not practiced giving in the past, the desire to give does not remain steady in my mind now." He reflects: "In the future, my mind will delight in giving. Let me give from now on. Have I not already renounced this object to solicitors beforehand?" Thus, with hands washed, delighting in renunciation, he gives. In this way, the Great Being's first fetter of giving is destroyed.

Likewise, when the object to be given is small and resources are deficient, the Great Being reflects: "Because I did not have the habit of giving in previous lives, I am now deficient in resources. Therefore, now, whether it be small or inferior, I should give whatever object is obtained, even by pressing myself. Through this gift, I shall bring the perfection of giving to its culmination in the future." That Great Bodhisatta gives whatever object is obtained. He is one who renounces freely without attachment to possessions, with hands washed to give to whoever comes, delighting in renunciation, devoted to giving, and delighting in sharing. In this way, the Great Being's second fetter of giving is destroyed.

Likewise, if a mind unwilling to give arises because the object is very excellent and he is stingy, the Great Being reflects: "O good man, you have aspired for the supreme enlightenment which is most excellent and superior to all..."
296:
He reflects: "I should give even by pressing myself with whatever object is obtained; through this gift, I shall bring the perfection of giving to its culmination in the future." That Great Bodhisatta gives with whatever object is obtained, renouncing freely without attachment, with hands washed to give to whoever comes, delighting in renunciation, devoted to giving, and delighting in sharing. In this way, the Great Being's second danger to giving (dānavinibandha) is killed, destroyed, and utterly uprooted.

Likewise, when a mind unwilling to give arises because the object to be given is excellent and pleasing, the Great Being reflects: "O good man, did you not aspire for supreme enlightenment, which is especially superior to all noble things and superior to all dhammas? Therefore, for the sake of that supreme enlightenment, it is fitting for you to give only those objects that are excellent and pleasing." That Bodhisatta gives the excellent and pleasing gift, renouncing freely without attachment, with hands washed to give to whoever comes, delighting in renunciation, devoted to giving, and delighting in sharing. In this way, the Great Man's third danger to giving is killed, destroyed, and utterly uprooted.

Likewise, when the Great Being sees the exhaustion of objects while giving, he reflects: "This nature of exhaustion and decay is the very nature of wealth. Indeed, it is because I did not perform such giving in previous lives that I now see the exhaustion of wealth. Now, whether it be little or much, I shall give only the gift with whatever object is obtained. Through this gift, I shall reach the culmination of the perfection of giving in the future." That Bodhisatta gives with whatever object is obtained, renouncing freely without attachment, with hands washed to give to whoever comes, delighting in renunciation, devoted to giving, and delighting in sharing. In this way, the Great Being's fourth danger to giving is killed, destroyed, and utterly uprooted. Thus, whatever disadvantages there are that act as dangers to the perfection of giving, removing them by reflecting appropriately is called the means (upāya). As it is noted for the perfection of giving, so should it be noted for the perfection of virtue and the others.

Alternatively, the Great Being's dedication of himself to the Buddhas is the means for the fulfillment of all perfections. The Great Man who stands having dedicated himself to the Buddhas, while striving in various lives for the fulfillment of the requisites of enlightenment (bodhisambhāra), reflects in the face of difficult tasks that cut off the body and comforts, which are unbearable and hard to accomplish, and in the face of sharp and life-threatening disadvantages brought about by beings and formations: "I have already surrendered this person to the Buddhas; let whatever happens to this body happen." For that reason, he is unshaken, unmoved, and without even the slightest deviation, truly [striving] in the practice of merit...
297:
"Let it be as it will"—because of this act of determination, he does not tremble, does not shake, does not undergo even the slightest change, and in the undertaking of wholesome deeds, he is always of unshakable determination. This surrendering of oneself (to the Buddhas) is also a means for the fulfillment of these perfections.

Furthermore, in brief, for a Great Bodhisatta who has made the aspiration, the exhaustion of attachment to oneself and the increase of love for others is the means for fulfilling these perfections. For the Great Being who has made the great resolve to attain Supreme Enlightenment (Sammāsambodhi), through the thorough comprehension of all phenomena without being tainted by them, attachment to self comes to an end and is exhausted. However, through the practice of Great Compassion (Mahākaruṇā), looking upon all beings as his own dear children, the affection of loving-kindness and compassion for those beings increases. Because of the growth of such loving-kindness and compassion, according to the respective circumstances, by removing greed, hatred, and delusion in the continuums of himself and others, the Great Man (Mahāpurisa), having far removed the obstacles to the requisites of enlightenment (bodhisambhāra) such as stinginess and so forth, through the four bases of sympathy (sangahavatthu)—namely, giving (dāna), pleasant speech (piyavacana), beneficial conduct (atthacariyā), and impartiality (samānattatā)—and by following the four determinations (adhiṭṭhāna), truly benefits the multitude of beings, causing them to enter the three higher vehicles and bringing their wisdom to maturity.

The Great Compassion and Great Wisdom of the Great Bodhisattas are adorned by giving (dāna). Giving is adorned by pleasant speech; pleasant speech by beneficial conduct; and beneficial conduct by impartiality; and they are thus integrated. For those Bodhisattas who practice the requisites of enlightenment by making all beings no different from themselves, impartiality (samānattatā) is accomplished because of having equal happiness and suffering in all circumstances. Even when they become Buddhas, the task of disciplining beings is accomplished by constantly benefiting them through those four bases of sympathy and the four determinations, which have been fully perfected and realized. Giving is fully perfected and realized by the determination of relinquishment (cāgādhiṭṭhāna) of the Fully Enlightened Buddhas. Pleasant speech is perfected by the determination of truth (saccādhiṭṭhāna); beneficial conduct by the determination of wisdom (paññādhiṭṭhāna); and impartiality by the determination of stillness (upasamādhiṭṭhāna). The Tathāgatas have the same result as all Disciples (Sāvakas) and Private Buddhas (Paccekabuddhas) in the attainment of Parinibbāna. In that Parinibbāna, there is no distinction among them; they are one. Therefore, it was said: "There is no diversity in liberation (vimutti)." In this regard, there are these summary verses:

One who is truthful, generous, tranquil, wise, and compassionate, who has accumulated all the requisites—what benefit could such a Great Man not achieve?
298:
"The Teacher of Great Compassion, the seeker of welfare, yet equanimous; detached in all things—oh, how wonderful is the Conqueror!

Dispassionate towards all phenomena, equanimous towards beings, yet always devoted to the welfare of beings—oh, how wonderful is the Conqueror!

Always striving for the benefit and happiness of all beings, without weariness—oh, how wonderful is the Conqueror!" (Thus stated in the Cariyāpiṭaka Commentary, Miscellaneous Discussion).

Regarding the question "In how much time are they fulfilled?":

The time is known to be of three kinds according to the three types of Bodhisattas, such as those with predominant wisdom (paññādhika), and those who are 'one who understands quickly' (ugghāṭitaññū), etc.

At the minimum, it is four incalculables (asankheyyas) and a hundred thousand great aeons (mahākappas); at the medium, eight incalculables and a hundred thousand great aeons; and at the maximum, sixteen incalculables and a hundred thousand great aeons. These divisions should be understood respectively according to the predominance of wisdom (paññādhika), faith (saddhādhika), and energy (vīriyādhika). For wisdom-predominant Bodhisattas, faith is weak and wisdom is sharp. For faith-predominant Bodhisattas, wisdom is medium. For energy-predominant Bodhisattas, wisdom is weak. Nevertheless, it is stated in the Commentary that Supreme Enlightenment is to be attained through the power of wisdom.

Other teachers, however, say that this division of time for Bodhisattas is due to the sharpness, mediumness, or dullness of energy (vīriya). Specifically, they say that the requisites of enlightenment (bodhisambhāra) reach fulfillment for those Bodhisattas according to the aforementioned time divisions because of the sharpness, mediumness, or dullness of the factors that mature liberation (vimuttipāpacanīya dhamma); thus, all three time divisions are appropriate.

In this way, at the moment of making the aspiration for Buddhahood, Bodhisattas are of three types: Ugghāṭitaññū, Vipañcitaññū, and Neyya. Among them, the Ugghāṭitaññū Bodhisatta is one who, while listening to a four-line verse in the presence of a Buddha, would have the supporting condition (upanissaya) to attain Arahatship together with the six higher powers (abhiññā) and the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) even before the third line of the verse is finished, if he were inclined toward the enlightenment of a disciple (sāvakabodhi).

The second type, the Vipañcitaññū Bodhisatta, is one who, while listening to a four-line verse in the presence of the Blessed One, would have the supporting condition to attain Arahatship together with the six higher powers even before the fourth line of the verse is finished, if he were inclined toward the enlightenment of a disciple.
299:
Furthermore, the Bodhisatta who is a person to be led (neyya), upon hearing a four-line verse in the presence of the Blessed One, possesses the supporting condition (upanissaya) to attain Arahantship along with the six higher powers (abhiññā) at the conclusion of the verse (if he were to incline towards the enlightenment of a disciple).

All these three types of Bodhisattas have made their initial resolution (abhinīhāra) without a specific time limit. Having received the prophecy in the presence of the Buddhas, they fulfill the perfections (pāramīs) in succession and reach Right Self-Enlightenment (Sammāsambodhi) according to the specified time periods mentioned earlier. As long as those respective time periods are not yet complete, even if those Great Beings (Mahāsattas) give great gifts daily like the gift of King Vessantara, or cultivate all the perfections such as virtue (sīla) suitable for that Sammāsambodhi, or make the five great sacrifices (mahāpariccāga), or carry out the conduct for the benefit of relatives (ñātattha-cariya), the conduct for the benefit of the world (lokattha-cariya), and the conduct for the benefit of Buddhahood (buddhattha-cariya) to the highest degree, it is impossible for them to become a Perfectly Enlightened Buddha (Sammāsambuddha) in the interim. Why is that? Because their knowledge (ñāṇa) is not yet mature and the factors for making a Buddha (buddhakāraka-dhamma) are not yet completed. Just as grain ripens only at its designated time, Sammāsambodhi can only be accomplished through the specified duration of aeons. It cannot be attained in the interim even by striving with all one's effort. Therefore, it should be understood that the fulfillment of the perfections is achieved only through the specified time periods mentioned.

What are the benefits?
For those Bodhisattas who have made their initial resolution:

Thus, those men who are endowed with the eight factors and are certain of enlightenment,
Though they wander in saṃsāra for a long time, even for hundreds of millions of aeons,
They are not reborn in the Avīci hell, nor likewise in the Lokantarika hells,
They do not become hungry ghosts consumed by craving, nor those suffering from hunger and thirst, nor Kālakañjika asuras.
Even if they are reborn in a state of woe, they do not become very small animals,
When born among humans, they are not blind from birth.
They have no deafness, nor are they mute or crippled,
They do not become female, nor do they become hermaphrodites or eunuchs.
Those men certain of enlightenment are not included among those [of low lineage],
They are free from the five heinous crimes (ānantariya-kamma) and have a pure sphere of activity in all places.
300:
Bodhisattas do not follow wrong views because they see kamma and its results. Even when living in the heavenly realms, they are not reborn in the realm of non-percipient beings (asaññasatta). The cause for being born in the Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa), [namely the fruit of Non-returning], does not exist for them. Those virtuous ones have minds inclined towards renunciation (nekkhamma); without being attached to various states of existence, they fulfill all the perfections while acting for the welfare of the world. It should be understood that all these praised benefits, as well as the sixteen kinds of wonderful and marvelous phenomena (acchariya-abbhuta-dhamma) such as 'Ānanda, the Bodhisatta, mindful and clearly comprehending, passes away from the Tusita heaven and enters his mother's womb,' and the thirty-two kinds of omens (pubbanimitta) such as 'the cold disappears and the heat is subsided' and 'Sāriputta, when the Bodhisatta is born, this ten-thousandfold world-system shakes, trembles, and quakes,' and other various benefits shown in the Jātakas, Buddhavamsa, etc., such as the fulfillment of the Bodhisattas' aspirations and their mastery over kamma and so forth—all these are the benefits of these perfections. Furthermore, the pairs of qualities such as non-greed (alobha) and non-hatred (adosa) in the manner already shown are also benefits.

In another way, from the time the Bodhisatta makes his resolution for Buddhahood, he is like a father to all beings because he seeks the welfare of all beings. Because he is endowed with special qualities, he is worthy of offerings, worthy of respect, worthy of praise, and is a supreme field of merit (puññakkhetta). Generally, he is beloved by humans and beloved by non-humans. He is protected by deities. Because his mental continuum is permeated with loving-kindness (mettā) and compassion (karuṇā), he cannot be overcome by wild beasts and so forth. In whatever class of beings he is reborn, because he is endowed with special merit in those respective lives, he surpasses other beings with magnificent appearance, magnificent fame, magnificent happiness, magnificent strength, and magnificent sovereignty.

He has little illness and little affliction. The faith (saddhā) of that Bodhisatta is extremely pure and clear. His energy (viriya) is extremely pure. His mindfulness (sati), concentration (samādhi), and wisdom (paññā) are extremely clear. He has few defilements (kilesas), few distresses, and few fevers of passion. Precisely because of the fewness of his defilements, he is easy to admonish and accepts instruction respectfully. He is patient, delights in good conduct (soracca), is gentle in speech, and is skilled in hospitality (paṭisanthāra). He is free from anger.
301:
He is skillful in hospitality (paṭisanthāra). He is free from anger, free from malice, free from detraction, free from domineering, free from envy, free from stinginess, free from deceit, free from craftiness, free from stubbornness, free from pride, free from agitation, and free from heedlessness. He is able to endure the oppression of others and does not himself oppress others. In whatever village or field he resides, dangers and calamities for beings there generally do not arise; if they do arise, they are appeased. Even if he is born in the lower realms, he is not excessively oppressed by suffering like the majority of beings, but rather experiences an abundance of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) and fear.
