Therefore, for the Great Man-to-be (Mahāpurisa), these special qualities obtained in various existences—such as having a father-like mind toward beings and being worthy of offerings—should be understood as the benefits of the perfections (pāramīs).

Likewise, longevity (āyu-sampadā), beauty (rūpa-sampadā), noble birth (kula-sampadā), sovereignty (issariya-sampadā), credible speech (ādeyyavacanatā), and great majesty (mahānubhāvatā) should also be understood as the benefits of the Great Man's perfections. Among these benefits, longevity (āyu-sampadā) means long life and enduring stability in each rebirth. Through that longevity, he can bring to completion the wholesome undertakings he has begun and accumulate much merit. Beauty (rūpa-sampadā) means being handsome, pleasant to look at, and inspiring. Through that beauty, he inspires faith in beings who measure by appearance and becomes one worthy of respect. Noble birth (kula-sampadā) means being born into noble families. Because of that noble birth, he is approachable and worthy of being attended even by those intoxicated with pride of birth. By attending him, they perform acts free from pride. Sovereignty (issariya-sampadā) means having great wealth, great power, and a large retinue. Through these, he is capable of supporting those worthy of support through the four bases of sympathy (saṅgahavatthu) and restraining those worthy of restraint in accordance with the Dhamma. Credible speech (ādeyyavacanatā) means being trustworthy and reliable. Due to this quality, he becomes a standard for beings, and his authority is inviolable. Great majesty (mahānubhāvatā) means having great power. Because of that power, he is not oppressed by others; rather, he himself overcomes others through the Dhamma, through righteousness, and through genuine qualities. Thus, these qualities like longevity are the benefits of the Great Man's perfections. They are the cause for the increase of his own immeasurable accumulation of merit and the cause for leading and ripening beings in the three vehicles (yānatthaya).
302:
What is the fruit? In brief, the fruit of those perfections should be known as the state of a Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddhata). In detail, the infinite and immeasurable mass of qualities are considered the fruit of those perfections. In brief, first, the state of a Perfectly Enlightened One is their fruit. In detail, it is the splendor of the Dhamma-body (dhammakāya), adorned with an infinite and immeasurable collection of qualities, such as the ten powers (dasabala), the four intrepidities (vesārajja), the six uncommon knowledges (asādhāraṇañāṇa), and the eighteen unique Buddha-qualities (āveṇikabuddhadhamma), based on the perfection of the physical body (rūpakāya) which shines with many groups of qualities like the thirty-two marks of a great man, the eighty minor marks, and the fathom-wide aura. As many as the Buddha's qualities are, even a Perfectly Enlightened One himself could not finish describing them with words over many aeons; this indeed is the fruit of those perfections. Regarding this, the Blessed One said: “Even if a Buddha were to speak the praises of another Buddha, speaking of nothing else for an entire aeon, the long and extended aeon would come to an end, but the praise of the Tathāgata would not reach an end.” Thus, the miscellaneous discussion (pakiṇṇakakathā) on these perfections should be understood.

With reference to the fulfillment of the perfections of the aforementioned types through the aforementioned practice, it is said: “Having fulfilled the thirty perfections.” Although the five great sacrifices (mahāpariccāga) exist within the nature of the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramī), they are taken separately to show the distinction of sacrifice, to show them as a special accumulation (sambhāra), and to show the extreme difficulty of performing them. For that very reason, the sacrifice of the eyes is taken separately from the sacrifice of limbs; and although they are similar in being the sacrifice of possessions, the sacrifice of children and wife is taken separately from the sacrifice of wealth and kingdom. In the same way, the Elder Dhammapāla stated. The Elder Sāriputta also said the same in the Aṅguttara Commentary (Ṭīkā). In some places, however, they speak of the five great sacrifices by taking the sacrifice of children and wife separately, the sacrifice of eyes elsewhere, or by including the sacrifice of life, and placing the sacrifice of the kingdom elsewhere.
303:
The completion of higher knowledge and attainments (abhiññā-samāpatti) along with the practice preceding the Path, known as the duty of going and returning (gatapaccāgatikavatta), is called preliminary exertion (pubbayoga). The completion of extraordinary practice specifically in giving (dāna) and so forth is called preliminary conduct (pubbacariyā). Alternatively, the conduct included in the Cariyāpiṭaka text is called preliminary conduct (pubbacariyā). However, some teachers say: "Aspiration (abhinīhāra) is preliminary exertion (pubbayoga); the practice of giving and so forth, or solitary conduct by way of physical seclusion (kāyaviveka), is preliminary conduct (pubbacariyā)."

Proclaiming the Dhamma (dhammākkhāna) is the discourse that occurs by way of explaining the faults and benefits of saṃsāra and nibbāna regarding giving and so forth, and fewness of wishes and so forth, and by way of establishing and maturing beings in the three types of enlightenment (bodhi). Conduct for the benefit of relatives is called ñātatthecariyā, and that ñātatthecariyā also occurs solely by way of compassion. By the word "ādi" (and so forth), conduct for the benefit of the world (lokatthecariyā) and others are included.

The range of knowledge occurring by way of the knowledge of the ownership of kamma (kammassakatā-ñāṇa), by way of familiarity with blameless occupations, crafts, and branches of science, by way of familiarity with the aggregates (khandha) and bases (āyatana) etc., and by way of investigating the three characteristics, is called the conduct of wisdom (buddhicariyā). In essence, this buddhicariyā is the perfection of wisdom (paññā-pāramī) itself, but it is taken separately to show the accumulation of knowledge (ñāṇasambhāra). The word "koṭi" means the end or the excellence. In the phrase "In the same way, our Blessed One came," it should also be connected with "having fulfilled the perfection of giving" and so forth.

Having thus shown the meaning of the word "Tathāgata" by way of fulfilling the perfections, he now says "the four foundations of mindfulness" and so forth, wishing to show it by way of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyadhamma). There, by taking the foundations of mindfulness and so forth, he shows the practice leading to the goal by bringing it to the summit. This is because only the states belonging to the Path and Fruit should be taken. Alternatively, the foundations of mindfulness and so forth should be regarded as states included in insight (vipassanā) because they are taken as the practice preceding the Path. "Bhāvetvā" means having produced, and "brūhetvā" means having developed. Here too, by "yena abhinīhārena" and so forth, he shows the beginning of the practice leading to the goal; by "dāna-pāramiṃ pūretvā" (having fulfilled the perfection of giving) and so forth, the middle; and by "cattāro satipaṭṭhāne" (the four foundations of mindfulness) and so forth, the end. Therefore, it should be understood that the distinction between the three methods is simply the showing of the specific practice which is the cause of the "coming" (āgata). Now, to show the first cause, which is established by the three aforementioned methods of interpretation, by way of a verse, he said "yatheva" and so forth.

Just as in this world, the Sages such as Vipassī reached the state of Omniscience through the three aforementioned causes,
So too, this Sakyamuni, the One with Vision, who is endowed with the five eyes, reached the state of Omniscience through that same cause;
For that reason, this Blessed One is called "Tathāgata."
Thus should the connection (yojanā) be understood.
304:
"Sampatijāta" refers to one who is born just a moment ago, having been released from the hands of humans. It does not mean just having emerged from the mother's womb. When the Great Being (Mahāsatta) had just emerged from the mother's womb, first the Brahmas received him with a golden net. From the hands of those Brahmas, the four Great Kings received him with a rug of black antelope skin. From the hands of those Great Kings, humans received him with a roll of fine cloth. It will be said (in the Dīgha Nikāya Commentary): "Having been released from the hands of humans, he stood on the earth." The words "kathañca" and so forth are for showing the details, just as the Blessed One taught in the Mahāpadāna discourse.

"Under the white parasol" means the divine white parasol. "While it was being held" means while it was being carried. At present, there is also the reading "anudhāriyamāne." In this context, by the mention of the parasol alone, the five royal regalia (kakudhabhaṇḍa) such as the sword should also be understood as included. This is because the sword, the palmyra fan, the peacock-tail fan, the yak-tail fly-whisk, and the diadem were also present along with the parasol at that time. "At that time, only the regalia such as the parasol were visible, but those who held the parasol and so forth were not visible," said the Teacher Dhammapāla Thera. The Teacher Sāriputta Thera also said the same in the Aṅguttara-ṭīkā. If that is so, the palmyra fan and so forth also receive the designation of royal regalia. Alternatively, it was said with the intention that the royal regalia such as the sword, and others such as the palmyra fan, were present at that time.

"All directions" means the ten directions. "He surveys" means that when the miracle of the opening of the world occurred through the power of merit, he surveyed the ten-thousandfold world system that became visible, using his physical eye (mamsacakkhu). This surveying of all directions did not happen after taking the seven steps, but was the very first surveying. This is because as soon as the Great Being was released from the hands of humans, he surveyed the eastern direction. There, gods and humans, worshipping him with scents and garlands and so forth, said: "O Great Man, in this place there is no one even equal to you, let alone superior." In this way, having surveyed all directions—the four cardinal directions, the four intermediate directions, the downward direction, and the upward direction—and seeing no one equal to himself anywhere, he went seven steps towards the north, saying "This is the northern direction." This was stated by the Teacher Dhammapāla Thera and the Teacher Sāriputta Thera. It is also described in this same way in the Mahāpadāna Sutta Commentary. Therefore, it should be understood that he first surveyed all directions before taking the seven steps, and then, having walked the seven steps, he uttered the bold lion's roar (āsabhivācā) at the end of those seven steps. In this Brahmajāla Sutta Commentary and in other commentaries...
305: From the moment he stood with level feet until he uttered the bold words (āsabhī vācā), explaining the sequence of precursors (pubbanimitta), it is said: "Standing upon the seventh step and looking towards all directions is the precursor for the attainment of the unhindered knowledge of Omniscience," and so forth. In this regard, the meaning should be taken in a way that is not contradictory. The reading "standing upon the seventh step" is a later occurrence due to the negligence of scribes, as such a sequence of words is not found in the Mahāpadāna Commentary (Mahāpadāna-aṭṭhakathā). "Āsabhi" means noble, or unshakable, or fearless. It is called "āsabha" because it belongs to a bull (usabha), possessing the nature of courage. Because it is endowed with that courage, this speech is called "āsabhī". "Aggo" means being the foremost of all. "Jeṭṭho" and "seṭṭho" are synonyms of that same word "agga". In terms of literal meaning, "agga" means the principal among all due to virtues. "Jeṭṭho" means the most senior among all by way of virtue, the eldest in terms of qualities. "Seṭṭho" means the most excellent among all by way of virtue. The genitive case in "lokassa" is used in the sense of the ablative (nissakkattha) to indicate a limit. By the words "This is the last birth, now there is no further rebirth," he declared (vyākaroti) the Arahantship to be attained in this very existence, because by the power of that Arahantship, there is no more rebirth. Now, wishing to praise that manner of walking, he said "Tañcassa" and so forth. Because it is a precursor, it should be connected with the meaning of being true and unerring. "Visesādhigamānaṃ" means the attainment of specific distinctions of virtue. He explains that meaning in detail with "Yañhi" and so forth. There, the word "yaṃ" refers to the action; therefore, it refers to the action of standing (patiṭṭhāna) contained in the word "patiṭṭhahi". "Idamassa" means this standing is of that Blessed One. This "assa" is a genitive of possession (sāmi) or an agent (kattu) in relation to the word "paṭilābha". "Pubbanimittaṃ" means the primary cause for recognizing the future benefit known as the attainment of those distinctions. For the Blessed One, when attaining such wonderful and marvelous distinctions of virtue, these signs appear just like the five great dreams (mahāsupina), just as in the world, signs appear to those with merit when they are about to attain the special fruits of their merit. "Sabba-lokuttara-bhāvassa" means the state of being supreme over all worlds, or the state of transcending all worlds. Seven steps are called "sattapada"; the specific taking of those steps is "sattapada-vītihāra", meaning the setting down of seven steps. In that even walking, the distance between the two feet is said to be about the size of a fist (muṭṭhi-ratana).
306: "The devas held in the sky an umbrella with many branches and more than a thousand circles. Golden-handled yak-tail whisks (cāmara) were fanning to and fro, but the devas holding the whisks and the umbrella were not seen." (Sutta Nipāta, 693). With reference to the introductory verse uttered by the Venerable Ānanda Thera in the Nālaka Sutta of the Sutta Nipāta, it is said: "In this place, golden-handled yak-tail whisks were fanning to and fro." "In this place" means in this verse. Since the raising of the yak-tail whisks is not mentioned in the Mahāpadāna Sutta, it should be understood in that way (as per the Nālaka Sutta). Following what is mentioned there, this commentary speaks of it as a precursor. The "camara" is a specific kind of animal. From the tail of that animal, the yak-tail whisk (vālabījanī), which is a royal regalia, is made. The tail of that animal is called "cāmarī". The raising of that whisk is "cāmarukkhepa". The raising of the aforementioned whisk is "vutta-cāmarukkhepa". "Arahatta-vimutti-vara-vimala-setacchatta-paṭilābhassa" means the precursor for the attainment of the noble, stainless white umbrella known as the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship. In the phrase "sattama-padūpari", the word "pada" refers to a footprint or the act of treading. Therefore, it means "above the seventh footprint". Omniscience itself is called "unhindered" (anāvaraṇa) because of its unhindered movement in all objects; thus it is said: "for the attainment of the unhindered knowledge of Omniscience". Likewise, in the passage "This Blessed One... is the state of being a precursor," the words "Yañhi" etc. are not repeated because they are already governed by the context and are clearly understood. By this, it is shown that the special qualities arising by way of natural law (dhammatā) at birth are common to all Bodhisattas. For these are the results of the perfections (pāramitā). "Porāṇā" refers to the teachers of the Commentaries. Just as a bull (usabha), because it carries treasures, touches the earth called "vasundharā" with level feet, so too the Bodhisatta Gotama, having been released from the hands of humans immediately after birth, touched the earth with level feet. "Vikkamī" means he walked. "Satta padāni" means up to the place of the seventh footprint. Here, the accusative case is used in the sense of continuous duration (accanta-saṃyoga). Or, it should be understood as the instrumental sense "by means of seven steps" (sattapada-vārehi) with the deletion of the latter word. "Marū" refers to the devas, who are so called because they have the nature of death within their own limits. "Samā" means they were similar because of the equality of looking. For the Great Being looked towards one direction, and in the same way towards the remaining directions; there was no obstruction to his looking anywhere. Or, "samā" means they were suitable to be looked at. This is because at that time, there were no deformed, loathsome, or uneven sights in the directions that were unsuitable for the Bodhisatta to look at.
307:
When looking at those directions, the Bodhisatta did not see any unsuitable, distorted, unpleasant, or uneven forms in those directions. He uttered a speech endowed with eight factors, characterized by purity, pleasantness, and ease of understanding, and roared a fearless and brave lion's roar, like a lion standing on a mountain peak. This is the meaning.

Having thus indicated the name 'Tathāgata' by the word 'gata' in the sense of physical going, he now says 'atha vā' (or else) etc., to indicate it by the word 'gata' in the sense of going by knowledge. In that context, in the passages such as 'yathā vipassī bhagavā' (as the Blessed One Vipassī), it should be connected as 'having abandoned sensual desire through renunciation (nekkhamma),' and so on. Renunciation (nekkhamma) here refers to the arising of wholesome consciousness characterized by non-greed. In this context, all wholesome states are called renunciation because they are the opposite of sensual desire; it does not refer only to going forth (pabbajjā) and so on. Some teachers say 'through the first jhāna,' but that is inappropriate because here only the preliminary practice (pubbabhāgapatipadā) of the first jhāna is intended. 'Pahāya' means having abandoned. 'Gato' means having reached a distinguished excellence through the 'going' of knowledge.

Alternatively, 'pahāya' means because of abandoning or when there is abandoning. This suffix '-tvā' is used in the sense of cause (hetu) or characteristic (lakkhaṇa), as in 'having become Sakka, he was reborn' and so on. In this word 'gato,' which has the abandoning of sensual desire etc. as its cause, 'going' refers to either the going known as penetration (avabodha) or the going known as practice (patipatti). That going is characterized by the abandoning of sensual desire and so on; this method should also be understood in 'padāletvā' (having broken through) and so on. 'Through non-ill will' means through loving-kindness (mettā). 'Through the perception of light' means through the knowledge of light that appears by making it clear in the mind. 'Through non-distraction' means through concentration (samādhi). 'Through the definition of phenomena (dhammavavatthāna)' means through the correct determination of wholesome and other states; some teachers also say it means through the defining of mind and matter along with their causes.

Having thus shown the Tathāgata-state, which is distinguished by the Buddha's going by knowledge through the preliminary practice of the first jhāna—described as 'having abandoned covetousness in the world' etc. by abandoning the hindrances such as sensual desire—he now says 'ñāṇena' (by knowledge) etc., to show that [Tathāgata-state] together with the means, by way of the eight attainments and the eighteen principal insights. For, to one established in the full understanding of the known (ñātapariññā) by removing delusion (moha), which is a fetter to the discernment of mind-and-matter and the overcoming of doubt, the perception of impermanence and so on are accomplished. Therefore, the breaking through of ignorance (avijjā) is the means for insight (vipassanā). Likewise, in the meditative attainments, one attains the jhānas etc. because one can dispel dissatisfaction in those jhānas through the joy (pāmojja) that is the cause for delight in the meditative attainments. Therefore, dispelling dissatisfaction with the attainments is the means. Although the sequence of attainments and insight should be indicated according to the method to be explained later, the non-sequential description (uppatipāṭiniddeso) should be understood here to show the inclusion of the hindrances shown by way of sensual desire etc. even under ignorance (avijjā), which is of the nature of a hindrance.
308:
Because they prevent entry into the dwelling of meditative attainments, the hindrances are like door-panels; thus he said, 'having opened the door-panel of the hindrances.' Just as in the passage in the Vammika Sutta of the Mūlapaṇṇāsaka in the Majjhima Nikāya, 'having reflected and pondered at night, he applies himself to work by day,' the stilling of initial and sustained thought is intended; with this in mind, he said 'having stilled the smoke of initial and sustained thought,' meaning having stilled the smoke known as initial and sustained thought. Although the current reading is 'vitakkavicāraṃ,' that is not the ancient reading. This is because the Elders Dhammapāla and Sāriputta cited only the aforementioned reading 'vitakkavicāradhūmaṃ.' 'Virājetvā' means having become disgusted or having well transcended. It has both meanings of disgust and transcending, as in the passages 'pītiyā ca virāgā' (with the fading away of rapture) and so on. In reality, pain is abandoned at the access (upacāra) to the first jhāna, and pleasure is abandoned at the access to the fourth jhāna. However, referring to the total abandonment, he said 'having abandoned pleasure and pain through the fourth jhāna.'

'Perception of form' (rūpasaññā) refers to the fine-material sphere jhānas and their objects, with 'perception' (saññā) as the heading. For the fine-material sphere jhāna is also called 'form' (rūpa) by dropping the latter word, as in 'one who has form sees forms' (rūpī rūpāni passati) etc. Its object, the kasina-form, is also called 'form' by dropping the preceding word, as in 'he sees external forms, beautiful and ugly' (bahiddhā rūpāni passati suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇāni) etc. Therefore, here, the perception associated with the fine-material jhāna in the fine-material sphere is called 'perception of form' (rūpasaññā); thus the fine-material sphere jhānas are mentioned with perception as the heading. 'Rūpasaññaṃ' means one who has the perception of form, meaning one endowed with the perception of form. Thus, it should be understood that this name 'perception of form' is a designation for the objects of those fine-material sphere jhānas, such as the earth-kasina.

'Perception of sensory impact' (patighasaññā) is the perception associated with the twofold fivefold consciousness, which arises from the impact or striking together of the bases such as the eye and the objects such as forms, through the meeting of the subject and the object. 'Perception of diversity' (nānattasaññā) is a designation for these forty-four perceptions: 8 wholesome sense-sphere perceptions, 12 unwholesome perceptions, 11 wholesome resultant sense-sphere perceptions, 2 unwholesome resultant perceptions, and 11 functional sense-sphere perceptions. These are called 'perceptions of diversity' because they proceed in diverse objects of different natures such as forms and sounds, and because they are diverse and of different natures, being dissimilar to one another.

The repeated contemplation of conditioned phenomena as impermanent, or as 'impermanence,' is called 'contemplation of impermanence' (aniccānupassanā). This is the name for insight that proceeds by taking the impermanent nature of the states belonging to the three planes. 'Perception of permanence' (niccasaññā) is [the perception] in conditioned states...
309:
"Permanent, eternal" refers to the wrong perception (micchā-saññā) that arises. Here, with perception as the head, it should be understood that [wrong] view and consciousness are also included. This method applies to subsequent terms as well. Nibbidānupassanā (contemplation of disenchantment) is the repeated contemplation that occurs by way of being weary of formations (saṅkhāra). Nandi (delight) is craving (taṇhā) accompanied by joy (pīti). Virāgānupassanā (contemplation of dispassion) is the repeated contemplation that occurs by way of fading away of lust for formations. Nirodhānupassanā (contemplation of cessation) is the repeated contemplation of the cessation of formations. Alternatively, it is the contemplation: "These formations indeed cease; they do not arise in the future by way of origination." Therefore, it is said: "One causes cessation through the contemplation of cessation, not origination." When this muñcitukamyatā-ñāṇa (knowledge of desire for deliverance) reaches its peak, [it is called nirodhānupassanā].

The repeated contemplation that occurs by way of relinquishment is called paṭinissaggānupassanā (contemplation of relinquishment). This is established at the end of paṭisaṅkhānupassanā (contemplation of reflection). Ādāna (grasping) is the adherence by way of permanence, etc. Ghana-saññā (perception of compactness) is the perception of oneness by way of continuity, group, function, and object. Āyūhana (accumulation) is the act of conditioning and striving. Vipariṇāma (change) is the reaching of a specific state of alteration. Dhuva-saññā (perception of stability) is the perception that grasps the nature of firmness. Nimitta (sign) is the appearance of formations as having a body/form because they are delimited by their own functions through the power of compactness such as a group. Paṇidhi (aspiration) is the longing such as lust. In essence, it is the inclination towards formations by the power of craving.

Abhinivesa (adherence) is the view that clings to a self (attānudiṭṭhi). Adhipaññā-dhamma-vipassanā (insight into phenomena through higher wisdom) is the investigation and reflection on all phenomena by way of impermanence, etc. Sārādānābhinivesa (adherence to taking the essence) is the perverted adherence that takes what is essence-less as having essence. "The world has arisen by the power of creation by Ishvara, Vishnu, etc."—such adherence is called sammohābhinivesa (adherence to delusion). Some teachers, however, say that reaching doubt such as "Was I in the past?" is sammohābhinivesa. Ālayābhinivesa (adherence to attachment) is the grasping of formations as a shelter or refuge. According to the words, "They delight in attachment (ālaya), they rejoice in attachment," craving is called ālaya. Some say it is ālayābhinivesa because that same craving occurs by way of adherence to the eye, etc., and to forms, etc. Paṭisaṅkhānupassanā (contemplation of reflection) is the knowledge that arises as: "Such formations should be relinquished." Nibbāna is called vivaṭṭa (turning away) because it is free from the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa). Gotrabhū-ñāṇa (change-of-lineage knowledge) is called vivaṭṭānupassanā because it occurs through contemplation characterized by making that Nibbāna the object. Saṃyogābhinivesa (adherence to conjunction) is the adherence to formations by way of being joined. Diṭṭhekaṭṭha (sharing the same ground as view) means being the same in terms of co-arising with [wrong] view and in terms of being abandoned. The word oḷārika (gross) is spoken with reference to the defilements to be abandoned by the higher paths. Otherwise, the defilements to be abandoned by dassana (the Path of Stream-entry) and those to be abandoned by the second path are also gross, and thus they could also be called oḷārika. Aṇusahagata (accompanied by the subtle) refers to defilements that have a subtle nature. Here, the word sahagata means occurring in that subtle state. This statement is made with reference to the defilements to be abandoned by the lower paths.
310:
"All defilements" (sabba-kilesa) refers to all the remaining defilements. This is because defilements already abandoned by the lower paths, such as the first path, are not abandoned again. Here, the word "all" (sabba) is used in the sense of having a remainder, as in "All tremble at the rod," etc.

Hardness is the state of being rigid (kakkhaḷatta). Flowing is the state of being liquid (paggharaṇa). Like a leather bag filled with worldly wind, the inflation of various groups of matter (rūpa-kalāpa) or the state of being propped up and stiff is vitthambhana (distension). Even though the great elements (mahābhūta) existing in each group of matter touch one another, the delimitation of matter, which is the state of being void of those respective elements, is ākāsa (space). When there is a delimitation of those forms, it is simply untouched by them. Otherwise, the elements would not have the nature of delimitation due to the consequence of being pervasive and mixed. In whichever group of matter there is a delimitation of elements, the state of not being touched by those elements is the characteristic of being untouched (asamphuṭṭha-lakkhaṇa). Therefore, the Blessed One said in the description of the space element (ākāsa-dhātu-niddesa): "Untouched by the four great elements."

Ruppana (being molested/deformed) is the arising of something dissimilar to the previous form when a meeting of opposing conditions occurs. Because volition (cetanā) is primary among the phenomena of the aggregate of formations (saṅkhārakkhandha), it is said by way of volition: "The characteristic of formations is conditioning/striving." Accordingly, in the Suttanta-bhājanīya of the Saṅkhārakkhandha-vibhaṅga, only volition is analyzed, such as "volition born of eye-contact," etc. And volition has the characteristic of conditioning (abhisaṅkhāra-lakkhaṇa). As it was said: "Therein, what is the formation of merit (puṇṇābhisaṅkhāra)? It is wholesome volition," etc. Placing or establishing associated phenomena on an object is abhiniropana (application). Following or repeatedly stroking the objects is anubandhana (anumajjana). The state of having pervasiveness is pharaṇa (suffusion). Faith is adhimokkha (decision/conviction). The word "assaddhiye" (in faithlessness) is due to the cause of faithlessness and is in the locative case (sattamī-vibhatti) in the sense of a sign (nimitta). This method should also be understood for words like kosajja (laziness), etc. The calming of the fever of body and mind is the characteristic of appeasement (vūpasama-lakkhaṇa). When the higher mind (adhicitta) that is free from sluggishness and agitation is occurring, equanimity (ajjhupekkhanā) without concern in uplifting, restraining, or gladdening is called paṭisaṅkhāna (reflection) because it cuts off partiality.

Since false speech (musāvāda), etc., have the function of deceiving and are harsh and non-embracing by nature, their opposite, Right Speech (sammā-vācā), has the nature of embracing. Because Right Speech is smooth and pleasant, it embraces the associated phenomena, the well-spoken words based on Right Speech, and the person who listens; thus, it has the characteristic of embracing (pariggaha). Bodily action causes some task to be performed, and since it is itself the origination (samuṭṭhāna) and striving (ghaṭana), the abstinence (virati) known as Right Action (sammā-kammanta) should be understood as having the characteristic of origination. Or, the uplifting (ukkhipana) of associated phenomena...
311:
Origination (samuṭṭhāna) is like lifting a burden by one's own physical action. The occurrence of the life faculty (jīvitindriya) of a living being or of associated states, or the purity of livelihood itself, is called purification (vodāna).

"Formations" (saṅkhāra) here refers to volition (cetanā). It does not refer to the fifty mental factors as in the phrases "formations, the aggregate of formations," etc.; therefore, it is said to have the "characteristic of volition of formations." Indeed, due to ignorance, only volitions such as meritorious formations (puññābhisaṅkhāra) and so on arise. Inclining towards an object is called "bending" (namana). Bringing into existence is called "base" (āyatana). This is because the occurrence of mind and mental factors is by way of the six bases. Regarding the "causal characteristic of craving," the state of being the cause that generates the round of rebirths is the causal characteristic of craving. The state of the Path, which will be mentioned later, leading to Nibbāna (is the causal characteristic of the Path). This is the distinction between craving and the Path. Grasping the object is the characteristic (of clinging). Striving for future arising is the characteristic (of existence). Being empty of a being or a soul is the characteristic of emptiness (suññata). Striving is called padahana. Accomplishment is called ijjhana. Leading out from the round of rebirths is called niyyāna. The state of being non-perverted is the characteristic of truth (tatha). Not occurring by surpassing one another is "single flavor" (ekarasa), which is simply the state of being neither deficient nor excessive.

Tranquility and insight are called "yoked together" (yuganaddha) because they should be joined as a pair through mutual assistance. "Faith and wisdom, and energy (paggaha) and concentration (avikkhepa)" are also called (yoked together). Purification of mind (citta-visuddhi) is concentration. Purification of view (diṭṭhi-visuddhi) is wisdom. Destruction (khaya) is the Path, and the characteristic (of destruction) is the total cutting off by the knowledge known as right view occurring in that Path. Non-arising (anuppāda) is the Fruit, because it is the finality of the non-arising of defilements. The calming of defilements is called tranquillity (passaddhi).

The state of being the standing point for the desire to act is the root characteristic (mūla-lakkhaṇa). The state of being the cause for the arising of associated states because of accomplishing the object is the characteristic of causing to arise (samuṭṭhāpana). The manner of being grasped through the meeting of objects and so on is called combination (samodhāna). This is the same thing called "conjunction" (saṅgati) in such phrases as "the conjunction of the three is contact." Because associated states are united evenly or rightly by this contact, contact is also called samodhāna. That state of uniting is the characteristic of combination. Because they converge or meet here in this feeling, feeling is called convergence (samosaraṇa). It is said thus because associated states, which cannot occur without that feeling, are as if converged for the sake of experiencing the feeling. That state of converging is the characteristic of convergence.

Being the chief of associated states, like the pinnacle of rafters in a palace and so on, is the characteristic of being foremost (pamukha). Because mindfulness accomplishes all benefits, the state of being the lord of associated states is the characteristic of predominance (ādhipateyya). Being the principal over those associated states or above those associated states is the characteristic of surpassing that (tatuttariya). Indeed, wholesome states have wisdom as their supreme. Liberation (vimutti) refers to the Fruit, because one has been liberated from defilements.
312:
That Fruit is called the essence (sāra) because of its state of supreme excellence among the essences of virtues such as morality (sīla) and so on. Nibbāna is called the end (pariyosāna) because there is no state superior to that Nibbāna. It should be understood that this classification of characteristics is stated according to the method found in the ancient commentaries, following the respective Sutta terms by way of the six elements, five factors of absorption, and so on. Indeed, even if a state has been mentioned before, it is shown again for the purpose of explaining it through another method (pariyāya). For that very reason, based on these Sutta terms: "All states have desire as their root, attention as their origination, contact as their combination, and feeling as their convergence"; "Wholesome states have wisdom as their supreme"; "This holy life has liberation (the fruit of Arahatship) as its essence"; and "Friend, the holy life plunges into Nibbāna, and has Nibbāna as its end"—the "root characteristic of desire" and so on are stated. The phrase beginning with "Thus" (evaṃ) shows the meaning that he has arrived at the true and unerring characteristic of those respective states. That "going" (gamana) is here stated as "going by knowledge" (ñāṇa-gamana); hence the term "path of knowledge" (ñāṇa-gati). Although the word gata has the meaning of penetration (avabodhana), it is not stated as penetration because it is already accomplished by the sense of going by knowledge. In this word "arrived" (āgata), the prefix "ā" merely follows the word gata. Therefore, it is said, "He has reached, he has repeatedly reached."

Because they have a non-perverted nature, it is said, "The four Noble Truths are called true states (tatha-dhamma)." They are "true" (tatha) because of their non-perverted nature. They are "not-untrue" (avitatha) because of their unerring nature. They are "not-otherwise" (anaññathā) because they are devoid of any other mode. Referring to the complete discussion of the four truths found in the Sacca-saṃyutta and so on, it is said, "Thus is the detailed explanation." Having said "Therefore" (tasmā), he shows the very meaning for which that word "therefore" is used by this statement: "Because of having perfectly realized the true states." In such matters, it should be understood according to this method.

Having thus shown the fourth reason by way of the Truths, now, wishing to show it also by way of the factors of Dependent Origination which are real (tatha-bhūta) because of their non-perverted nature as cause and result, he says the phrase beginning with "Moreover" (api ca). In that passage, "the sense of being produced and fully come forth through the condition of birth" (jāti-paccaya-sambhūta-samudāgataṭṭha) means the nature of repeatedly arising (anupavattaṭṭha) in higher and higher stages, having been produced due to the condition of birth, in accordance with its own condition. Alternatively, "the sense of being produced" (sambhūtaṭṭha) and "the sense of being fully come forth" (samudāgataṭṭha) are combined as sambhūta-samudāgataṭṭha by the method of eliding the subsequent word in the preceding compound (uttarapada-lopa). Even in a collective compound (samāhāra-dvanda), grammarians desire the masculine gender. And here, it is not that aging and death do not occur because of birth, nor do they occur from any other cause excluding birth; therefore, it is called "produced through the condition of birth." In this very way, because it fully comes forth from birth, it is called "fully come forth through the condition of birth." This is what is meant: whatever birth, in whatever manner...
313:
The cause exists; the nature that appears in accordance with that cause is the effect. On the side of the cause, in the context of "Ignorance is the cause of volitional formations," it is not that ignorance is not the cause of formations, nor do formations arise without ignorance. Whichever ignorance is the cause for whichever formations in whatever manner, this ignorance is the causal meaning, the causal nature of formations.

"Tathānaṃ dhammānaṃ" refers to [the meaning] of the phenomena of Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda). Just as in words like "Sugato," the root "gamu" is intended in the sense of "knowing," so it is said "Abhisambuddhattā" (because of having fully realized), not intending the sense of "going" by knowledge. For words meaning "going" and "knowing" are synonyms of each other. Therefore, in this context, the word "gata" should be understood as having the meaning of "abhisambuddha" (fully realized); or, because it is easily understood, it is not explicitly used.

Whatever is called a visible object (rūpārammaṇa) exists; it should be connected as "the Blessed One knows it, sees it." The location "among the generation... together with devas" should be connected to the word "exists." Furthermore, the phrase "in the infinite world systems" is said either with regard to the beings living in those world systems or with regard to the appearance of objects [to the senses]. Therefore, it should be construed that the visible base (rūpāyatana) as analyzed by the Blessed One is exactly as it is. The reason for its being true and unerring is stated by the words "knowing thus, seeing thus." Because it is known and seen in every aspect, these two words are terms that include the cause within them.

In the phrase "by way of desirable (iṭṭha), undesirable (aniṭṭha), etc.," the word "etc." (ādi) includes the neutral (majjhatta). Likewise, it also includes the divisions such as past, future, present, limited (paritta), internal (ajjhatta), external (bahiddhā), and both. "By way of the terms obtained" means that because of the words, "The visible base is seen, the sound base is heard, the odor base, flavor base, and tangible base are sensed, all matter is known by the mind," the terms "seen" (diṭṭha) and "known" (viññāta) are obtained in the visible object.

A visible object is [called] by many names such as desirable, undesirable, neutral, limited, past, future, present, internal, external, seen, known, matter (rūpa), visible base (rūpāyatana), visible element (rūpadhātu), color-radiance, visible matter, resistant matter, blue, yellow, and so on. By the words "by way of desirable, undesirable, etc.," the fact of having many names is shown in its own form. "By thirteen cycles" refers to the thirteen cycles of exposition (niddesavāra) that appear in the Section on Matter (Rūpakaṇḍa) of the Dhammasaṅgaṇī. In this context, in each cycle, by way of the four methods of determination, it is said "by fifty-two methods." "Exactly as it is" means it is true because it is a teaching that cannot be refuted by others through the aforementioned knowing, and because it is an unerring vision through the aforementioned seeing. To establish that meaning by the Kāḷakārāma Sutta of the Catukkanipāta, Aṅguttara Nikāya, the words beginning with "And it is said thus" are stated. Here, the word "ca" (and) is an indicator of strengthening.
314:
By that [word "ca"], it shows the strengthening of the aforementioned meaning. Or else, [the word "ca"] has the meaning of a conjunction joined with a word that is not the primary subject. It means: "Not only did I say it, but indeed the Blessed One also said it." "Anuvicaritaṃ" means pondered (paricaritaṃ). By showing the occurrence of knowledge in the present and past through "Jānāmi abhaññāsiṃ" (I know, I have fully known), the occurrence of knowledge in the future is also shown by way of method.

The word "vidita" (known), however, has no specific time assigned and is common to the three periods of time; as in "seen, heard, sensed," it means known by making it clear. By this [word "vidita"], it is shown: "Others merely know, but I have known by making it clear." Indeed, by these words, the Blessed One described the ground of omniscience (sabbaññubhūmi). "Na upaṭṭhāsi" (did not appear) means that the Tathāgata does not approach or go towards the object occurring at the six doors by way of craving or view as "self" or "belonging to self." By this term, the ground of the one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsavabhūmi) is described. Because he knows, sees, and understands those phenomena such as visible objects according to their true nature and their true manner, he is called "Tathāgata"; with this meaning in mind, it is said "in the sense of Tathadassī (one who sees the truth)." Roots and words have many meanings. Some teachers, however, by way of grammatical derivation or by inclusion in the Pisodarādi group, explain the formation of the word "Tathāgata" by dropping the word "dassī" and adding the word "āgata" as an augment. That is improper, because it involves discarding an existing word and taking a non-existent word. And it is said in the Commentary on the Buddhavaṃsa:

"Because he knows and observes phenomena in their true manner (tathākārena), the Fully Enlightened One is called Tathadassī, and therefore he is called Tathāgata."

In this verse, after stating the meaning of the word "āgata" by the word "anupassati" (observes), the word "jānāti" (knows) is said to show that such seeing is only seeing by knowledge. To clarify the meaning obtained by the word "jānāti," the word "Tathadassī" is also said.

"Yaṃ rattiṃ" means in which night. Or else, this accusative case is used in the sense of continuous duration (accantasaṃyoga) because of the continuous connection with the moment of awakening (abhisambujjhana) which is a part of the night. Or else, this entire night should be understood as being in continuous duration in a figurative sense, as it was the time of striving for awakening. Because he reached the summit of the supreme ground, beautiful on the surface of the earth, he was not defeated by others there, thus he is "Aparājita" (Unconquered). That very seat (pallaṅka) is the "Aparājita-pallaṅka" (Unconquered Throne). On that throne, "tiṇṇam mārānaṃ" refers to Kilesamāra (Mara of defilements), Abhisaṅkhāramāra (Mara of volitional formations), and Devaputtamāra (Mara as a deity). This is said in the direct sense (nippariyāya). In the figurative sense (pariyāya), as mentioned below, the five Maras...
315:
It should be understood as the crushing of the five Māras. 'Matthaka' refers to the summit (head), which is called prowess. 'In this interval' (etthantare) means between the two nights. By the words 'In the first enlightenment also' and so forth, the period of forty-five years is specifically distinguished by being included within it. Among those periods, the period defined as twenty years is called the 'First Enlightenment' (pathamabodhi) in the Vinaya-gaṇṭhipada. This statement is also made in that very Vinaya Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), saying, 'For the Blessed One, during the twenty-year interval of the First Enlightenment, there was no regular attendant monk' (Pārājika Aṭṭhakathā 1.16); thus, the First Enlightenment is taken as twenty years. However, the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla stated, 'Of the forty-five years, the first fifteen years are the First Enlightenment.' If it is so, the middle fifteen years would be the Middle Enlightenment (majjhimabodhi), and the final fifteen years would be the Final Enlightenment (pacchimabodhi), making the three enlightenments equal in duration. This statement is also appropriate, as forty-five years are completed by three periods of fifteen years. In the Commentary, however, it can also be understood that because the First Enlightenment of fifteen years is included within the twenty years, it was said, 'within the twenty years of the First Enlightenment.' The connection should be made with 'Which Sutta' and so forth.

Because it is faultless, it is irreproachable (anupavajja). Because there is nothing to be added, it is not deficient (anūna). Because there is nothing to be removed, it is not excessive (anadhika). Because it is endowed with the perfection of meaning and phrasing, it is complete in every way. Because it is the cause of subduing, it is called 'nimmadana'. 'Even as much as the tip of a hair' means even the measure of the tip of a tail-hair. 'Avakkhalita' means a deviation or speaking a falsehood. 'By a single seal' (ekamuddikāya) means by a single royal seal. 'By a single measure' (ekanāḷiyā) means by a single nāḷī or a single tumbu. 'By a single scale' (ekatulāya) means by a single weighing. By the phrase 'just so' (tathameva), it shows specifically that only the aforementioned meaning is intended and not otherwise. Therefore, for whatever purpose it was spoken, because it certainly accomplishes that purpose, just as the Blessed One spoke, so it is; thus, it shows the state of the teaching being unerring. By the word 'gadattho', it shows the definition that because He speaks (gadati) the truth (tatha), He is the 'Tathāgata', by changing the letter 'da' to 'ta' and adding the vowel 'ā' according to the method of linguistics (nirutti), or by the vowel 'ā' following the verbal root.

Thus, after showing the linguistic derivation by considering the formation from the verbal root as in the words 'Sugata' and so forth (Pārājika 1), the phrase 'Furthermore' (api ca) and so forth is said to show it by way of an exocentric compound (bāhirattha-samāsa). 'Agadana' means speaking intensely because it accomplishes all benefits; or the word 'ā' simply denotes that state.
316:
Because that Blessed One has the state of being in such a manner, He is called 'Tathāgata'. Or else, just as the occurrence of His speech is, so is the occurrence of His body; or just as the occurrence of His body is, so is the occurrence of His speech; therefore, He is the 'Tathāgata'.

To show that very definition, he said 'Of the Blessed One' (bhagavato) and so forth. In that passage, by the words 'gato pavatto' (gone, occurred) and 'gatā pavattā', it shows that the occurrence of bodily and verbal actions is intended here by the word 'gata', in the sense of their mutual conformity. By the words 'of one who has become such' (evaṃbhūtassa) and so forth, he shows the exocentric compound (bāhirattha-samāsa). By the words 'as... so...' (yathā tathā), because of the invariable connection between the words 'yaṃ' and 'taṃ', as soon as 'tathā' is said, the meaning of 'yathā' becomes manifest; thus he shows the meaning of the word 'tathā'. By the words 'speaker, doer' (vādī kārī), he shows the nature of the occurrence. By the words 'For the Blessed One' (bhagavato hi), he shows the reason such as being one who acts as He speaks.

'Of one who has become such' (evaṃbhūtassa) means one who exists in such a manner as acting as He speaks, or one who has reached such a state. By the word 'iti', he indicates the aforementioned manner. Since the word 'gata' here also shows the occurrence of speech, the meaning 'Tathāgata' because of speaking according to the truth is also certainly established. However, since that meaning was already shown in another way previously, by the method of residue (pārisesa-naya), he said 'He is the Tathāgata because of acting in such a manner' to show only the meaning of acting accordingly. And it is said:

'As the speech of Him has gone,
So the body has gone;
As the body, so the speech,
Therefore the Teacher is the Tathāgata.'

'Making the pinnacle of existence (bhavagga) the limit' is how it should be connected. As for what some teachers say, 'There are infinite world-systems above and below, just as there are horizontally,' it should be understood that this was said to refute the words of those teachers. 'By liberation' (vimuttiyā) means by the Fruition. 'By the knowledge and vision of liberation' (vimutti-ñāṇadassanena) means by the vision known as reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa). 'Tulo' means one who is equal. 'Pamāṇaṃ' means the cause of measuring. He is 'Abhibhū' because He overcomes others by His attributes, or because He is superior by overwhelming them. He is 'Anabhibhūto' because He is not overcome or overwhelmed by others. The word 'Aññadatthu' is an indeclinable (nipāta) used in the sense of certainty. He is 'Daso' by way of seeing; the meaning is that He sees all. He is 'Vasavattī' because He makes others follow His own will.

This definition 'Tathāgata because of the sense of overcoming' cannot be obtained directly from the word itself; however, to show that it can be obtained linguistically in this way, he said 'In that very way' (tatrevaṃ) and so forth. In that passage, 'agado' means divine medicine. It is called 'agado' because it cuts (dāti) or destroys the mountain (aga) of disease, or because there is no disease (gado) because of it.
317:
It is said 'like medicine' (agado viya) because of the meaning similar to divine medicine, and because in this Dispensation, the splendor of the teaching and the accumulation of merit can dispel afflictions like medicine. The Dhamma-element by which the teaching reaches splendor is called the splendor of the teaching (desanāvilāsa). The Dhamma-element is indeed the Omniscient Knowledge (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). Through that knowledge, having known the various modes of phenomena, He determines the teaching accordingly. Just as it is said 'consisting of giving' (dānamaya) or 'consisting of virtue' (sīlamaya), the splendor of the teaching itself is 'consisting of the splendor of teaching' (desanāvilāsamaya). However, at present, the word 'maya' is not found in many palm-leaf manuscripts. Accumulation of merit (puññussaya) means abundance or the superior merit which is the constituent of knowledge and so on. With the words 'By that' (tena) etc., the comparison is completed. It should be connected as: 'By both that splendor of teaching and the accumulation of merit, the Blessed One overcomes.' With 'iti' etc., the exocentric compound (bahiratthasamāsa) is shown. It means He is 'Tatha' (True) because of overcoming the entire world, and not otherwise.

The phrase 'Tathāya gato' is said with reference to the first three Truths. The phrase 'Tathaṃ gato', however, refers to the final Truth. Here, the four meanings of the word 'gata' are stated according to the sequence of the Four Noble Truths. Because of their proximity to the expressive word, prefixes (upasagga) and particles (nipāta) exist as illuminators of that meaning; thus, even the word 'gata' without a prefix expresses the meanings of 'understood' and 'transcended', as shown by the words 'avagato atīto'.

The words 'Therein' (tattha) etc., are an explanation of that. 'World' (loka) refers to the world of the aggregates which is the Truth of Suffering. It should be construed as 'tathāya tīraṇapariññāya' (by the true full understanding of investigation). 'The practice leading to the cessation of the world' (loka-nirodhagāminī paṭipadā) refers to the Noble Path, not merely the act of awakening. To show that the duties to be performed regarding those Four Truths have also been completed, the second aspect is stated for all four Truths with 'Tathāgata is disjoined from the world' (lokasmā tathāgato visaṃyutto) etc. Or, by these words, He shows the cause of awakening. For it is because of those that He has awakened to those Truths. 'Bhikkhus, whatever in the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, in this generation with its recluses and brahmins, its devas and humans, is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, and pondered over by the mind—all that has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata; therefore He is called the Tathāgata.' This Pali passage from the Book of Fours in the Aṅguttara Nikāya is shown by way of ellipsis (peyyāla). This is shown only because of the connection in meaning, not to prove this specific meaning. For that Pali passage indicated by ellipsis proves the meaning of 'Tatha-dassitā' (seeing the truth). With the words 'Its meaning should be understood thus' (tassapi evaṃ attho veditabbo), he makes a comparison between what is to be proven (sādhya) and the proof (sādhaka). With the words 'And this also' (idampi ca) etc., he shows the extensiveness of the term 'Tathāgata' and provides a mere illustration of the eightfold reasons. In that statement, 'idaṃ' refers to the eightfold reasons stated in a very broad sense. The word 'api' is used in the sense of praise (sambhāvana). Therefore, these eight meanings are also just a brief indication.
318:
With the words 'And this also' (idampi ca) etc., he shows the extensiveness of the term 'Tathāgata' and provides a mere illustration of the eightfold reasons already mentioned. In that sentence 'idampi ca' etc., 'idaṃ' refers to the eightfold reasons stated in a very broad sense. The word 'pi' or 'api' is used in the sense of praise (sambhāvana). It should be understood as: 'Even these eight meanings are just a mere introduction; how much more could be said in other ways besides these eight reasons?'

'Tathāgatabhāvadīpane' means in illustrating the name 'Tathāgata'. The Blessed One is called 'Tathāgata' by virtue of His qualities, and the word 'Tathāgata' applies to the Blessed One as a name. For it is said: 'The names of the Great Sage are immeasurable, according to His qualities.' To show that the term 'Tathāgata' encompasses all the qualities of a Buddha, just as the term 'appamāda' (heedfulness) encompasses the practice of all wholesome dhammas, he said 'In every way' (sabbākārena) etc.

The word 'vaṇṇeyya' (would praise) is a hypothetical term (parikappa) expressing reflection. It should be understood as: 'He might praise, or He might not praise.' And it is said:
'Even if a Buddha were to speak the praises of another Buddha,
And were to speak of nothing else for an entire aeon,
The aeon would come to an end after a very long time,
But the praise of the Tathāgata would not be exhausted.'

Some teachers also say that the word 'vaṇṇeyya' is used in the sense of capability (samatthana), as in the Pali passages such as 'He would disentangle this tangle' (so imaṃ vijaṭaye jaṭaṃ).

The method here which is outside the Commentaries (aṭṭhakathāmuttaka) is as follows: From the initial aspiration (abhinīhāra) until the Great Awakening (sammāsambodhi), because there was no decline, stagnation, defilement, or regression in the practice of the Great Enlightenment Vehicle (mahābodhiyāna) during this interval, He is 'Tathāgata' because He practiced according to His resolution (yathāpaṇidhānaṃ tathā gato). Alternatively, because of His great psychic power, His attainment of the excellence of the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), and His possession of unobstructed knowledge (anāvaraṇa-ñāṇa), there is no resistance anywhere; thus, the movements (gatāni) and activities of His body, speech, and mind proceed according to His wish—therefore He is 'Tathāgata'.

Furthermore, another method: Since in the world, the words 'vidha', 'yutta', 'gata', and 'pakāra' are seen to have the same meaning; therefore, just as the Blessed Ones such as Vipassī are of such a kind (tathā-vidha) due to being endowed with all the qualities of omniscience, this Blessed One is also of such a kind—thus He is 'Tathāgata'. And just as those Blessed Ones were endowed (yutta) in the manner described, this Blessed One is also endowed in that way—thus He is 'Tathāgata'.

Another method: Since the names 'Sacca' (Truth), 'Taccha' (Reality), and 'Tatha' (Fact) are synonyms for knowledge, He is 'Tathāgata' because He has come (āgata) by means of true (tatha) knowledge.
319:
Just as the Exalted Buddhas such as Vipassī, having abandoned the stains of defilements like sensual desire through concentration and wisdom, have gone, so too has this Sakyan Sage, the bearer of the light of wisdom, gone; therefore, he is known as the 'Tathāgata'.

Alternatively, because he has well-discerned and realized through his self-enlightened knowledge (sayambhū-ñāṇa) the characteristics of the elements (dhātu), sense bases (āyatana), and so forth, which are true and unerring, by way of their individual and general characteristics, the Exalted One, the most excellent among the Sakyans, is called the 'Tathāgata'.

Because he has clearly realized the four true Noble Truths and the unerring principles of specific conditionality (idappaccayatā) in all their aspects through his universal eye (samantacakkhu), which cannot be led by others, the Exalted One is called 'Tathāgata' in the sense of being truly as it is.

In the numerous world-systems, he has the true vision of the diverse objects such as the base of visible forms (rūpāyatana). Therefore, the Exalted One, who possesses the universal eye, is called 'Tathāgata'.

Furthermore, because he speaks only the true Dhamma, acts in accordance with his words, and exists having overcome the world of beings with his virtues, the Exalted One, the Leader of the World (lokanāyaka) who leads the three types of beings to Nibbāna, is called 'Tathāgata'.

Moreover, because he possesses the body, speech, and mind as he desired according to his original aspiration for Buddhahood, just as the former Great Sages were of such a nature, this Exalted One is also of such a nature; therefore, he is called 'Tathāgata'.

Alternatively, just as the former Buddhas (Sugatas) were endowed with such qualities, this Exalted One is likewise endowed with those very qualities. Therefore, the Exalted One who possesses the universal eye is called 'Tathāgata'. In another way, because he has well-gone with the knowledge that sees truly and unerringly, the Exalted One, the most excellent among the Sakyans, is called 'Tathāgata'.

## Summary Verses (Saṅgaha-gāthā)
320:
Regarding the question, "Monks, what is that virtue?", one might ask whose question this is; therefore, the teacher said "Yena" and so forth. Having thus shown that the question pertains to the mere virtue mentioned in a general sense, the commentator now, in order to make known the specific nature of the question, presents all the questions found in the Mahāniddesa by way of extracting their meanings, starting with "Tattha pucchā nāma". In that passage, "Tattha" refers to the general questioning word used in the phrase "Taṃ katamaṃ pucchati"; it means "in that question: Taṃ katamaṃ".

"Pakatiyā" means by its own nature, or automatically. "Lakkhaṇā" refers to the nature that one wishes to know without distinction. "Aññātaṃ" refers to a nature that is not known either by knowledge associated with specific distinctions like seeing, or by any other general knowledge. Indeed, seeing (dassana), weighing (tulana), and deciding (tīraṇa) by knowledge are distinct by their stages. "Adiṭṭhaṃ" means a nature not seen as if before one's eyes by the knowledge that constitutes seeing. "Atulitaṃ" means a nature not weighed by the knowledge that constitutes weighing, as in "this is just this much". "Atīritaṃ" means a nature that has not yet reached the function of knowledge (not yet decided) by the knowledge that constitutes deciding, as in "this nature is just like this". "Avibhūtaṃ" means a nature that has become unmanifest to knowledge. "Avibhāvitaṃ" means a nature not made manifest by knowledge.

"Tassa" refers to the meaning of the aforementioned characteristic. Through this question, an unknown and unseen characteristic is revealed; therefore, that question is called "Adiṭṭhajotanā" (Illuminating the unseen). "Saṃsandanatthāya" means for the purpose of making a decision through discussion. Indeed, "comparison" (saṃsandana) is the act of making a decision through discussion. Through this question, a characteristic that has already been seen and known is compared; therefore, that question is called "Diṭṭhasaṃsandanā" (Comparing the seen).

In terms like "Saṃsayapakkhanda", the firmly embedded doubt is called "Saṃsaya". The mere failure of wisdom that is not excessively doubtful is called "Vimati". Even smaller than that vimati is "Dveḷhaka", which is the occurrence of two ways of thinking, such as "Is it thus, or is it not thus?". Indeed, the mind wavers or trembles in two ways because of this state; therefore, with the suffix "ha" and the suffix "ka" used in the sense of the word itself, it is called "Dveḷhaka". One who is born of that two-fold wavering of the mind, or one who has that two-fold wavering of the mind, is called "Dveḷhakajāta". Through this question, doubt and perplexity are cut off; therefore, that question is called "Vimaticchedanā" (Cutting off doubt).

Referring to the questions related to the five aggregates found in the Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta and others, the teacher said, "All should be stated". A question asked for the sake of consent is called "Anumatipucchā" (Question for consent). Indeed, by a question such as "Monks, what do you think of that?", the consent is asked, as in "What is your opinion?". "Kathetukamyatā" is due to the state of desiring to explain. Indeed, as in "Aññāṇatā āpajjati" and so forth, it should be noted that the letter "ya" is elided in this term. Or, the nominative case is used in the sense of the instrumental. Or, a question asked because of the desire to explain is called "Kathetukamyatāpucchā". In terms of meaning, however, every question is a speech occurring in such a manner of inquiry, or it should be understood as the arising of consciousness (cittuppāda) that produces that question.
321:
This method of the *Mahāniddesa* is presented for the purpose of making known the specific nature of these questions; thus the commentator said "Among these" (*imāsu*), and so forth. Attention (*samannāhāra*) is the advertence of the mind. Doubt (*kaṅkhā*) that trembles intensely and all around is called *āsappanā* and *parisappanā*. All doubts are severed by the Path of Arahantship (*arahattamagga*), which has Omniscient Knowledge (*sabbaññutañāṇa*) as its proximate cause, because of its total eradication. It is said, "The remaining two types of questions belong to the Buddhas," because Dhamma teaching arises through the consent of others and the desire to speak, and because it is seen thus in various teachings. As for the many other types of questions mentioned in the *Niddesa* text, such as questions based on beings (*sattādhiṭṭhāna-pucchā*), questions based on dhammas (*dhammādhiṭṭhāna-pucchā*), questions based on one thing (*ekādhiṭṭhāna-pucchā*), and questions based on many things (*anekādhiṭṭhāna-pucchā*), the reason they are not analyzed here in this commentary is that it is understood that "this much is sufficient for knowledge; those who desire it should extract and analyze them using this method," thus completing the task of providing the method.

Since a question is only appropriate when there is an answer, the commentator said "Now" (*idāni*), and so forth. *Atipāta* means striking down excessively or striking down quickly. In this term *atipāta*, the word *ati* has the sense of "excess" (*atireka*). Speed itself is "excess." Therefore, it means striking down excessively in the interval of the natural falling away from the life-faculty, striking down quickly without allowing it to fall slowly. Alternatively, it has the sense of overwhelming; it means striking down by overwhelming with weapons and so forth. *Atipāta* is merely a conventional term. In terms of meaning (ultimate sense), it means the killing of a living being (*pāṇavadha*, *pāṇaghāta*), as understood according to the context. "By way of convention" means by way of designation (*paññatti*). A "being" (*satta*) is just the continuity of the aggregates (*khandha-santāna*). The designation "being" exists only in that continuity of aggregates. It is said:
"Just as the word 'chariot' exists due to the assembly of parts, so when the aggregates exist, the convention 'being' arises."

The life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) refers to both the physical life-faculty and the mental life-faculty. When the physical life-faculty is destroyed, the other (mental) also perishes because of its connection to the physical. Why is the singular used here as "the striking down of a living being" (*pāṇassa atipāta*) and "a living being (*pāṇo*) is a being by way of convention"? Is it not the case that what is intended here is the abstinence from killing all living beings without exception? Indeed, it will be stated later in the plural as "compassionate for the welfare of all living beings" (*sabba-pāṇabhūta-hitānukampī*). This is true. However, the singular is used here to denote the general state of being a living being. In that other place (where the plural is used), because it is associated with the word "all" (*sabba*), the plurality is easily understood; therefore, instead of a general designation, the plural is used with the intent to show the variety. Furthermore, there is a slight explanation: restraint (*saṃvara*) arises generally, and from the specifics of that restraint, the variety of restraint arises. Therefore, to make known this specific restraint, this distinction between singular and plural is made.
322:
Because the plurality is easily understood due to the proximity of the word "all" (*sabba*), the plural designation is used with the intent to show the variety, rather than a general designation. Furthermore, it should be understood that this distinction in expression (singular and plural) is made to make known this specific point: the undertaking of restraint is general, while the variety of restraint is specific. The expression "striking down of a living being" (*pāṇassa atipāta*) shows the variety of restraint, whereas "all living beings" (*sabba-pāṇabhūte*) shows the undertaking of restraint. However, experts in grammar say that in such places, it is merely a difference in expression regarding genus (*jāti*) and substance (*dabba*), and they are identical in meaning.

Regarding those two types of living beings mentioned, "perceiving a living being" (*pāṇasaññino*) refers to a person endowed with the perception of a living being. The volition (*cetana*) that originates the effort (*payoga*) such that, due to the effort made upon the great elements (*mahābhūta*) which are the support of the life-faculty, the great elements that would have arisen based on those great elements do not arise—that volition is called "killing" (*pāṇātipāta*). Thus it is said: "originating the effort that cuts off the life-faculty" (*jīvitindriyupacchedaka-upakkama-samuṭṭhāpikā*). This means it originates the bodily or vocal effort that cuts off the life-faculty in the great elements that are its support. For the elements that have been affected by the effort are not as clear as the previous elements; therefore, they cannot be the cause for elements of a similar kind. When effort is made upon them, if there is no obstacle, the elements that would have arisen subsequently and the life-faculty dependent on them are cut off. By the words "of the bodily and vocal doors" (*kāyavacīdvārānaṃ*), the view of the sophists (*vitaṇḍavādī*) that killing occurs by the mere murderous volition occurring in the mind-door is rejected.

The gravity of the offense (*mahāsāvajjatā*) through the greatness of the effort (*payoga*) and the object (*vatthu*), etc., should be understood by the strength of the volition arising from those causes. The greatness of the effort is known by the decisive volition (*sanniṭṭhāpakacetana*) which has gained repetition (*āsevana*) through many impulsions (*javana*) that accomplish the task, or by the forceful completion of a single effort. Even if the effort is sometimes equal for both small and large beings, the volition of one who kills a large being arises more intensely; thus the greatness of the object is known. Both of these occur through the strength of the volition. Even if the effort and the object are not great, if the being to be killed is great in virtue, the volition that causes harm there—like the volition that provides benefit to a person of great virtue—is strong and arises more intensely due to the specific field (of merit); thus its gravity should be noted.
323:
The gravity of that volition (cetanā) should be noted. Therefore, the teacher stated "guṇavantesu" and so forth. Furthermore, by "kilesānaṃ" and so forth, it is shown that even if the qualities of the object of the effort are not great, the degree of offensiveness—whether slight or great—should be understood according to the weakness or strength of the volition, due to the mildness or intensity of the defiled efforts.

Because they arise together with those factors, those factors are called sambhāra (constituents). Among those five factors, the perception of a living being and the mind intent on killing may also occur in the preliminary stage. However, the effort arising from the volition to kill occurs only together with that volition. The volition of killing (pāṇātipāta-cetanā) is endowed with the five factors; therefore, that volition should be understood as being distinct from the five factors. This same method applies to taking what is not given (adinnādāna) and so forth.

Regarding this killing, an objector says: Among the formations (saṅkhāra) which have the nature of perishing moment by moment, what kills, or what is killed? If the continuity of mind and mental factors kills, then it is not capable of destroying by means of causing appropriate torment, cutting, or breaking, nor is it something that can be destroyed. If the material continuity is killed, then because it is insentient, it is like a log or a piece of wood. Therefore, the act of killing cannot be found in that material continuity through cutting and so forth, just as it cannot be found in a corpse. The effort of killing, such as striking, must occur in past, future, or present formations. Among these three, it is not possible in past or future formations because they do not exist. In present formations, since formations last only for a moment and have the nature of perishing by their own essence, any effort directed at formations that are already heading toward destruction would be useless. Since destruction is without a cause, death cannot be caused by efforts such as striking. Since formations are without exertion, whose effort would that be? Because they perish at the same time as the intention to kill due to their momentariness, and because they do not persist at the time the act of killing is completed, to whom would the bond of the kamma of killing belong?

I shall state the answer: The collection of formations called a 'being' (satta), accompanied by the volition to kill, is what kills. Due to the cause of the effort of killing initiated by that collection of formations, the group of mental and material phenomena—which is characterized by the cessation of heat (kammaja-tejo-dhātu), resultant consciousness (vipāka-viññāṇa), and the life faculty (jīvitindriya), and which is associated with the conventional term 'dead,' and which would have arisen had the said effort of killing not been made—is what is killed. Or, the entire continuity of mind and mental factors is killed. Although that mental continuity is not the direct object of the effort of killing, because it exists dependent on the material continuity in the five-constituent realm (pañcavokāra-bhava), when someone else makes an effort that cuts off the life faculty, causing the material continuity to perish and preventing the arising of similar matter, that mental continuity also ceases. Therefore, it is not that killing is impossible; it indeed occurs. Killing is not without a cause, nor is the effort useless. Because of the effort made upon present formations, the group of formations that would have arisen immediately thereafter is unable to arise.
324:
Because the momentary death (khaṇika-maraṇa) of momentary formations is not intended here as 'death,' and because the death of continuity (santati-maraṇa) occurs with a cause according to the aforementioned method, death is not without a cause. Nor is the effort of killing devoid of an agent. Even in formations that lack exertion, the conventional term 'agent' is established because causes, by their mere presence, are helpful and certain to produce their respective appropriate results, just as it is said, "The lamp illuminates" or "The moon, the night-maker, illuminates." Nor is killing desired as merely the collection of mind and mental factors occurring simultaneously with the intention to kill, for it is acknowledged only by way of continuity. Since the accomplishment of one's own action is seen in lamps and so forth that proceed by way of continuity, there is indeed the bond of kamma through killing. This analysis should also be made clear, as applicable, in the case of taking what is not given and so forth.

Sāhattika (by one's own hand) means striking with one's own body or with something connected to the body while killing personally. Āṇattika (by command) means commanding another, saying, "Kill by stabbing or striking in this way." Nissaggiya (by missiles) means discharging arrows, machines, stones, etc., with the body or something connected to the body, desiring to kill someone at a distance. Thāvara (stationary) means desiring to kill with a non-movable device, such as throwing someone into a pit, placing a weapon near a trap-door, or preparing poison. Vijjāmaya (by science/magic) means reciting mantras to cause death, like those skilled in Atharvana lore. Those skilled in Atharvana lore, when a city is besieged or a battle is imminent, use Atharvana arts against the opposing army and enemies to cause calamities, accidents, diseases, fevers, piercing pains, cholera (visūcikā), and dysentery. Masters of magic (vijjādhara) also recite magic mantras when a city is besieged, etc., to cause dysentery. Iddhimaya (by psychic power) means power resulting from the fruition of kamma, such as the snapping of fangs. It is said that the death of the householder Cūḷasumana occurred due to the snapping of fangs by King Pitu, the father of the King of Sihala. By the words "In this sense, however" and so forth, the author avoids the heaviness of the text, and by the words "by those who desire" and so forth, he ensures the completeness of the work. Although not explicitly stated here, this meaning is complete and perfect, as if stated through extensive indication.

The state of one who lacks virtue is called immorality (dussīlya); it is the aforementioned volition itself. In the word "pahāya" (having abandoned), the suffix "tvā" indicates a preceding time, thus it is said "starting from the time it was abandoned." Or, it is said thus with reference to the causal sense. By this, he shows the abstinence by eradication (samuccheda-virati) intended here, which has abandonment as its cause. For, by the knowledge of the destruction of kamma...
325:
Because the lack of virtue known as killing (pāṇātipāta) has been abandoned, it is said that the Blessed One is absolutely and perpetually abstinent from it. This is because the abandonment (pahāna) and abstinence (virati) are intended in the sense of total eradication (samuccheda). Even if there is no temporal distinction between 'abandoning' and 'abstaining' as expressed by the words 'having abandoned, he abstains,' when considering the relationship of cause and effect between the Path factors such as Right View (the cause) and Right Speech etc. (the effect), the grasping of these co-nascent states as cause and effect is like a sequence of before and after. Indeed, the causal state exists first by its causal power, and following that, the resultant state arises depending on that causal power. Therefore, by way of the mode of grasping and occurrence, the term for the prior time applies to the act of abandoning in states like Right View, which are co-nascent causes and factors that abandon. The term for the subsequent time applies to the act of abstaining in the abstinences (virati) that arise from those causes. Thus, the meaning in the Pali should be understood as: 'Having abandoned killing through Right View etc., he abstains from killing through Right Speech etc.'

Here is a method not directly mentioned in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā-muttaka): Abandoning should be linked with eradication (samuccheda), and abstaining with tranquility (paṭippassaddhi). Thus, the meaning is: Having abandoned killing by the Path, he abstains from killing by the Fruition.
