Alternatively, it is called 'pāṇātipāta' because by this [group of states], beings are caused to fall excessively (killed). Pāṇātipāta is the collection of states that cause the killing of beings. What is this collection? It refers to defilements such as lack of shame (ahirika), lack of moral dread (anottappa), hatred (dosa), delusion (moha), and cruelty (vihiṃsā). The Blessed One, having abandoned and uprooted these defilements by the Noble Path, is absolutely abstinent from the lack of virtue of killing. This is because, once the defilements are abandoned, the kamma rooted in them does not arise. Therefore, the meaning is: Having abandoned the aforementioned defilements called 'pāṇātipāta' by the Path, he abstains from the volition of lack of virtue in killing by that same Path. This method also applies to 'having abandoned taking what is not given' (adinnādānaṃ pahāya), etc.

'Orato' and 'virato' are synonymous terms. Or, they are stated thus because the prefixes 'pati' and 'vi' are to be applied individually. 'Orato' means 'avarato' (abstaining) or 'abhimukhaṃ rato' (delighting in facing away [from evil]); by this, it shows the excellence of direct abstinence. This is the definition of 'paṭirata' (paṭivirato). 'Virato' means 'visesena rato' (specially abstaining); by this, it shows the state of abstinence along with the latent tendencies (vāsana). By both together, the state of eradication-abstinence (samuccheda-virati) is clarified. The word 'eva' is used to show the limitlessness of that abstinence in terms of time, etc. That 'eva' should be applied to both. Unlike others who, though having undertaken abstinence, break their undertaking due to an unsteady mind or for the sake of gain or livelihood, the Blessed One is not like that.
326:
Because he has abandoned killing in every way, the Blessed One is indeed absolutely abstinent. The word 'eva' in the passage beginning with 'natthi tassa' confirms the aforementioned meaning by way of the sense of negation. In that passage, the states that would arise as 'I will transgress' are connected with the rest of the text. These are weak, blameworthy states that arise occasionally, interspersed with blameless states. Since a wise person can know, 'Defilements have arisen in this person upon perceiving bodily or vocal expression,' these states are called 'cognizable by eye and ear' by this figurative method (pariyāya), not because they are the direct objects of eye-consciousness or ear-consciousness. Therefore, in the 'Discourse on the Components' (Sambhāra-kathā), the meaning should be understood as: having perceived bodily and vocal expressions through the eye and ear, or through the consciousnesses dependent on them, they are cognizable by mind-consciousness. 'Kāyika' refers to powerful unwholesome states that accomplish killing etc., performed by the body. In the Sub-commentary (Ṭီကာ), there is also a reading 'kāဠကာ' (kāḷakā), meaning powerful unwholesome states belonging to the dark side. The method is given starting with 'imināva,' and this method is applied to phrases such as 'having abandoned taking what is not given, he is one who abstains from taking what is not given.'

He is called 'Samaṇa' because he calms (sameti) evil (pāpa). This refers to the Blessed One by the name 'Gautama' (Gotama), and because it is connected to that lineage, the meaning 'Gotama' is intended in the passage 'The Blessed One is a Samaṇa.' It is a term acquired by way of lineage. Because this teaching proceeded in connection with the praise spoken by the youth Brahmadatta, and because he also spoke of the virtues of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha, the virtues of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha should also be taught according to the method mentioned. However, they were not taught. To remove the doubt, 'Does this abstinence from killing not exist in the Bhikkhu Saṅgha?', he said 'na kevalañca' etc. If so, why was it not taught? He answers this further inquiry with 'desanā pana' etc. 'Evaṃ' means 'just so.'

The intended meaning here is: The Blessed One, wishing to expand the teaching further regarding the unique qualities of a Buddha (not shared with others) starting with 'Monks, there are other states...', began the teaching from the start by way of the Buddha's qualities, saying 'One speaking the praise of the Tathāgata would speak...', and not by way of the virtues of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha. Indeed, it is the nature of the Blessed One's teaching that even when it is possible to show the teaching with a single flavor, certain things are not included. For instance, in the 'Section on Matter' (Rūpa-kaṇḍa), in the dyads etc. and their explanations, the heart-base (hadaya-vatthu) is not included. Why is it not included? Because the heart-base has a different mode of occurrence from other bases like the eye, it would cause a break in the teaching. For example—
327:
Eye-consciousness and others invariably depend on the eye-base and so forth. However, mind-consciousness does not invariably depend on the heart-base, because that [heart-base] does not exist in the immaterial realm (arūpabhūmi). Based on the relationship of the support (nissaya) and the supported (nissita), the teaching on the dyad of bases (vatthu-duka) and so forth proceeds as: 'There is matter that is the base of eye-consciousness; there is matter that is not the base of eye-consciousness,' and so on. Even though mind-consciousness invariably has the heart-base as its support, and it is taught in the dyads and so forth as 'There is matter that is the base of mind-consciousness,' the corresponding dyads of objects (ārammaṇa-duka) and so forth are not possible. It is not possible to say, 'There is matter that is the object of mind-consciousness; there is matter that is not the object of mind-consciousness,' because there is no matter that is not an object of mind-consciousness. Therefore, the dyad of bases and the dyad of objects would have different scopes; if so, the teaching would not be uniform (eka-rasa). Thus, the heart-base was not mentioned. Similarly, in the Nikkhepakaṇḍa section of the Cittuppāda analysis, because it is not mentioned separately, in answering the term 'without initial thought and without sustained thought' (avitakka-avicāra), it is not possible to say 'and sustained thought.' Therefore, although initial thought (vitakka) is obtained in answering the term 'without initial thought and only sustained thought' (avitakka-vicāramatta), it is not explicitly raised. Otherwise, it should have been said 'and initial thought.' In the same way, the virtue of the Saṅgha of monks is not taught here. Although it is not taught in words, it should be shown by way of showing the connection (anusandhi) to the praise spoken by Brahmadatta; thus it is said, 'But the meaning...' and so on.

In this regard, the explanation is: 'Having abandoned the taking of life, the community of disciples of the ascetic Gotama abstains from taking life; they have laid down the rod, laid down the weapon'—this should be expanded. Was not the praise of the Dhamma also spoken by Brahmadatta? True, it was spoken. However, because the Dhamma originates from the Fully Enlightened One, because the Noble Saṅgha is its support, and because their [attainments] are accomplished through the power of the Dhamma, it is already shown by showing the praise of both [the Buddha and the Saṅgha]; thus it is not separately raised. Indeed, it is only through the power of the True Dhamma (Saddhamma) that the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of monks are able to abandon the taking of life and so forth. To show the state of avoiding the harming of others by implication (atthāpatti), the statement about laying down the rod and weapon is made; thus it is said, 'for the purpose of harming others' and so forth. 'Not turning' (avattanato) means not proceeding or not moving. One who has laid down the rod is 'one who has laid down the rod' (nikkhitta-daṇḍa). Similarly, 'one who has laid down the weapon' (nikkhitta-sattha). Here, 'rod' (daṇḍa) refers to a stick four cubits long for an average man. Other things such as clubs (muggara) and swords (khagga) are 'weapons' (sattha); thus it is said, 'And here...' and so forth. It is called 'because of the nature of harming' (viheṭhanabhāvato) because it signifies injuring. By this, it shows the meaning that 'it is called a weapon (sattha) because one injures or kills with it.' It is said 'for the purpose of harming others' and so forth.
328:
To clarify the meaning of reaching an offense, 'But what...' and so forth is said. One who is old is 'katara'; the rod held by that old person is a 'walking stick' (kattara-daṇḍa). A piece of wood suitable for cleaning the teeth is a 'tooth-stick' (dantakaṭṭha); it should not be called 'wood for cleaning teeth.' There is also a reading 'dantakaṭṭhavāsiṃ vā,' which means a small knife for cutting tooth-sticks. A small knife used for tasks such as cutting nails is called 'pipphalika.' This statement pertains to the Saṅgha of monks. Since it was said 'it should also be shown by way of the Saṅgha of monks,' it is said for the purpose of showing a part of that Saṅgha.

The word lajjā (shame) has the meaning of hiri (moral shame); thus it is said, 'having the characteristic of loathing evil.' Because of the Buddhas' respect for the Dhamma and because the Dhamma is dependent on oneself, only lajjā (shame) which is self-governed (attādhipati) is mentioned, not ottappa (moral dread) which is world-governed (lokādhipati). Furthermore, by the lajjā mentioned in the term 'shameful' (lajjī), ottappa is also mentioned. Therefore, lajjā should be understood as a designation for both hiri and ottappa. Indeed, loathing evil is not without the fear of evil, nor is there such a thing as fear of evil without shame. Why is it said, 'has reached the state of a mind of loving-kindness'? Does not the word dayā in terms like 'dayāpanno' (attained to sympathy) also apply to compassion (karuṇā)? That is true. However, when this word dayā is used including the sense of protection, it applies to both loving-kindness (mettā) and compassion (karuṇā). In this context, since compassion will be mentioned later, the word dayā is used only in the sense of loving-kindness. It is called mettā because it loves (midati). A mind that has that mettā is called 'mettā.' A person who has such a mind of loving-kindness is called 'mettā-citta.' Or, it can be said as a person whose mind is associated with loving-kindness. The state of that person is 'mettā-cittatā.' Mettā itself is the root cause, and through that sign of mettā, knowledge and the word 'mettā-citta' arise in the person.

'Pāṇabhūte' means 'pāṇajāte' (living beings). With this meaning, the derivation is: those who have life (pāṇa) are 'pāṇabhūta.' Alternatively, it refers to all beings called 'bhūta' because they possess the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) and thus are called 'pāṇa,' and they proceed according to their respective kamma. 'Anukampaka' means one who is compassionate (karuṇāyanaka). Since loving-kindness is a specific condition for compassion, the meaning of the preceding term, which is loving-kindness itself, is stated as the condition: 'because of reaching the state of sympathy (dayā) through that very loving-kindness.' When compassion is taken by this term, the possession of those qualities—shame, loving-kindness, and compassion—by which abstinence from taking life is perfected, is shown in order by the three terms. Since the desire to remove the suffering of others is also the same as compassion for their welfare (hitānukampanā), this meaning must certainly be accepted. Through this Pali text and the commentary, it shows the limitlessness of that abstinence toward all beings.
329:
In the word "viharati," the prefix "vi" is used in the sense of cutting, and the root "hara" is used in the sense of carrying. Here, carrying means causing to occur, sustaining, or protecting; therefore, it is said: "iriyati yapeti yāpeti pāleti" (he moves, he sustains, he maintains, he protects). The words "yapeti" and "yāpeti" are synonymous terms. Therefore, it should be understood that, being of the aforementioned nature, he carries on or proceeds by cutting the suffering arising in one posture with another posture, or that he sustains and protects the individual existence (attabhāva).

In the phrase "iti vā hi," the particle "hi" is merely for the sake of euphony (smoothness of speech), as there is no specific meaning illuminated by that "hi" particle. Therefore, it is said: "evaṃ vā bhikkhave" (or thus, O monks). The term "vikappattha" (the sense of various options) is obtained only in meanings that have many divisions. Since many divided meanings will be spoken of above, it is said: "upari adinnā...pe... apekkhitvā" (having expected... above... not given). The expression beginning with "evaṃ" is for the purpose of avoiding the heaviness of the text or for providing a method.

Now, showing the combined meaning, he says "ayaṃ panettha" and so on. In that sentence, "na hanati" means not harming. "Na ghāteti" means not killing. "Tattha" refers to the taking of life (pāṇātipāta). "Samanuñño" means being pleased or satisfied. "Aho vata re" means "O sirs, it is truly wonderful." "Ācārasīlamattakaṃ" means merely the conduct of virtuous people. Here, the word "matta" has the sense of excluding anything special. By that word "matta," it shows that even with qualities such as sense restraint (indriyasaṃvara), a worldly worldling (puthujjana) is unable to speak of the Tathāgata's virtues. This is because the virtue of sense restraint and the virtue regarding the use of requisites are not classified and shown here in this Small Morality (Cūḷasīla). The word "eva" is a mere filler of the verse, or it defines the aforementioned meaning with the word "matta." It is a conclusion that one can only speak of the conduct and virtue by the word "eva." In such cases, it should be understood thus. By the power of the statement "iti vā hi bhikkhave puthujzano tathāgatassa vaṇṇaṃ vadamāno vadeyya," one will not be able to speak of virtues beyond that. Because that meaning is reached by saying "taṃ vo upari vakkhāmi" (I will tell you that above), the phrase "upari asādhāraṇabhāvaṃ" and so on is stated to show such a meaning. By the distinction of persons in "na kevalañca" and so on, it is shown that this word "puthujzano" is merely an illustration. With "ito paraṃ" and so on, he avoids the heaviness of the text. A word previously mentioned is called a "pubbapada" (previous word). If it is not so, or if it is a word that is not previous (a new word), it is the same.

Because roots express special meanings when combined with other words, it should be understood that this word "ādānaṃ" obtains the meaning of taking. Therefore, he says "haraṇaṃ" and so on. "Parassa" means the property of another that is distinct from one's own property, or one who is other than oneself...
330:
That person is called "another" (para); it is also appropriate to call his property "para." There is also a reading "parasaṃharaṇa"; here the word "saṃ" has the meaning of wealth, so it means taking the wealth of another. A thief is called "thena"; his state is "theyya" (theft). "Corikā" is the action of a thief. He explains that meaning with the word "Tattha," etc.

"Tattha" refers to the term "adinnādāna." In this term "adinnādāna," only property possessed by others is called "adinna" (not given). It does not mean one's own property that has not yet been formally accepted, as in the training rule regarding the tooth-stick (dantapoṇa). The phrase "Yattha paro," etc., is connected in both places by the method of repetition (āvutti), etc. Therefore, it should be construed as "it is called property possessed by another" and "in that property possessed by another." Because he acts as he wishes, he is called "yathākāmakārī"; his state is "yathākāmakaritā." It means reaching the state of acting according to one's desire. Because it is one's own property, one is not liable to punishment by way of fines or royal punishment. Nor is there blame by way of accusation or reproach.

Because one takes that property possessed by another through this effort, that effort is called "tadādāyaka." The intention that originates that effort is called "tadādāyaka-upakkama-samuṭṭhāpikā." The intention to steal itself is "theyyacetanā." There is an offense in an inferior (hīna) object by way of smallness or low value, and in a superior (paṇီta) object by way of largeness or high value. Why? It is not stated because it is obvious that it is due to the inferiority of the object. In an inferior object or in the property of one with inferior qualities, the intention is weak. In a superior object or in the property of one with superior qualities, the intention is strong. Therefore, as mentioned below, the state of being a minor offense or a major offense should be understood through those reasons.

However, the teachers, taking "small" and "large" separately from "inferior" and "superior," say: "In this taking of what is not given, there is a minor offense in a small object belonging to another, and a major offense in a large object. Why? Because of the greatness of the effort (payoga). If the qualities of the object are equal, it is a minor offense if the defilements and effort are weak, and a major offense if they are intense." This method should also be applied.

In the term "sāhatthikādayo," taking another's property with one's own hand is "sāhatthika." Taking by commanding others is "āဏattika." Taking by causing an object to fall outside a customs zone while staying inside is "nissaggiya." Taking by a command that achieves the purpose, such as "Steal such-and-such an item when you are able," or by sometimes damaging another's property by putting pieces of cloth or leather into jars of ghee or oil, etc., is "thāvara." Taking by reciting mantras is "vijjāmaya." Pulling another's property by means of such psychic power through bodily or vocal effort without mantras is "iddhimaya."
331:
In truth, theft by psychic power occurs only when there is bodily or vocal effort; it does not occur in their absence. Therefore, it was said (in the Pārājika Pāḷi): "Monks, there is no offense for one with psychic power in the range of psychic power." It should be understood in connection that those efforts also arise as appropriate. Because all those efforts cannot occur in every instance of theft, the term "as appropriate" (yathānurūpaṃ) is used.

Theft by stealth (theyyāvahāra) refers to stealing by making a breach in a wall and so on, or by making oneself invisible, or by deceiving with false weights and counterfeit coins. Theft by force (pasahyāvahāra) refers to stealing by overpowering with strength, by threatening, or by showing danger. Theft by concealment (paṭicchannāvahāra) refers to stealing by hiding another's property. Theft by premeditation (parikappāvahāra) refers to stealing by planning based on the location of the goods. Theft by moving markers (kusāvahāra) refers to stealing by shifting a lot or marker. In this context, by the word "iti," it should be understood that the other four sets of five are also included, either in the sense of "and so on" or by way of illustration. All twenty-five modes of theft, which are the combination of the five sets of five, are indeed the taking of what is not given (adinnādāna). The meaning is that property obtained without the owner's knowledge or through blameless communication (requesting) is indeed "given" (dinna). The phrase "taker of what is given" (dinnādāyī) shows purity in terms of effort, while the phrase "expecting only what is given" (dinnapāṭikaṅkhī) shows purity in terms of intention. Therefore, it was said beginning with "with a mind" (cittena).

In the word "atheṇena," the syllable "a" is the result of the word "na," or it is a particle (nipāta) having the meaning of "na"; to show this, it is said "na theṇena" (not as a thief). This is a demonstration of a compound (samāsa) together with the formation of a pseudo-analysis (viggaha) ending in the instrumental case as seen in the Pāḷi sentence. When analyzing the meaning obtained through the context, purity is understood here specifically from not stealing, because this is the section on the taking of what is not given. Thus, it is said, "pure specifically because of not being a thief," showing that this is an ornament of reason (hetālaṅkāra). The self or the individual existence (attabhāva) is called "attā" because the conceit of "I" is placed (clung to) in this body. However, for the Blessed One, the use of the term "attā" is merely a conventional designation (ruḷhī), just as the term "being" (satta) is used for Arahants who are free from desire and lust. Alternatively, it is called "attā" because it experiences the suffering of saṃsāra; therefore, it is said "by the self" (attabhāvena). To indicate that the instrumental case (third case) in all three words carries the sense of a characteristic state (itthambhūtalakkhaṇa), it is said "having made... atheṇam... etc." The meaning should also be understood as: he dwells as one who is not a thief by means of his non-thieving self, and as one who is pure by means of his pure self.
332:
The remaining words such as "having abandoned, he abstains" are to be understood in the same manner as previously explained. Although in this Brahmajāla Sutta, abstinence (virati) is not referred to by the term "training rule" (sikkhāpada), yet because abstinence and volition (cetanā) are the basis for the higher virtue (adhisīla) and are a part of those training categories as taught in other Suttas, the Vinaya, and the Abhidhamma, they should indeed be called "training rules." Therefore, it is said, "in the first training rule." In this training rule against taking what is not given, although it is not explicitly said "possessing shame and being compassionate," it should be understood that it is indeed stated by way of context and meaning. Just as shame and so on are the specific causes for abandoning the taking of life, they are likewise the specific causes for abandoning the taking of what is not given. This method should be understood for the subsequent training rules as well. Alternatively, because the possession of shame (hiri) and dread (ottappa) and the abandoning of shamelessness and so on are already expressed by the word "being pure," the phrase "possessing shame and being compassionate" is not separately preached.

In this context of the training rule of unchastity (abrahmacariya), the word "brahma" denotes "excellent." The conduct of those who are not excellent, who are base, is "abrahmacariya" (un-excellent conduct); it is sexual intercourse (methunadhamma). "Brahmacariya" (excellent conduct) is abstinence from sexual intercourse. One who does not practice that sexual intercourse is an "anācārī," meaning one who is devoid of that conduct; therefore, it is said, "one who dwells far from unchastity." The conduct known as sexual intercourse is "far"; that far conduct is absent in him, thus he is "dūracārī" (one who dwells far). Alternatively, he is "dūracārī" because he dwells far from sexual intercourse and practices abstinence from it; such a derivation is also appropriate. By the phrase "by the arousal of lust," the teacher shows that "methuna" (sexual union) is the property of a pair, a man and a woman, who are similar in their arousal of lust and enter into it together. Because it is the conduct of those who are not virtuous (asataṃ), it is called "asaddhamma" (the practice of the non-virtuous). By the word "gāma" (village), the people living in the village are taken by way of non-differentiation; thus it is said "gāmavāsīnaṃ" (of the villagers). The derivation "the practice of those dwelling in the village" is also suitable. This is understood because of the word "dūracārī" in this training rule, and because in the Pāḷi it is not only called "methuna" but also "gāmadhamma" (village dharma).

"Brahmin, here a certain recluse or brahmin, while rightly claiming to be a practitioner of the noble life, does not actually engage in sexual union with a woman. However, he consents to a woman's rubbing, massaging, bathing, and kneading. He enjoys that, desires that, and finds satisfaction in it. Brahmin, this too is a breach, a hole, a blot, and a mottle in the noble life of virtue. Brahmin, this person is said to practice an impure noble life, being fettered by the bond of sexual union. He is not liberated from birth, aging, and death..."
333:
“I say that he is not released from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; he is not released from suffering.

Furthermore... although he does not consent to a woman's anointing, massaging, bathing, and rubbing, yet he laughs, plays, and amuses himself with a woman. ... Although he does not laugh, play, and amuse himself with a woman, yet he gazes and stares into a woman's eyes. ... Although he does not gaze and stare into a woman's eyes, yet he listens to the sound of a woman laughing, talking, singing, or weeping through a wall or through an enclosure. ... Although he does not listen to the sound of a woman, yet he repeatedly recollects the laughing, talking, and playing he had with a woman in the past. ... Although he does not repeatedly recollect the laughing, talking, and playing he had with a woman in the past, yet he sees a householder or a householder's son provided and endowed with the five cords of sensual pleasure, enjoying himself. ... Although he does not see a householder or a householder's son, yet he leads the holy life with the aspiration for a certain company of devas, thinking, 'By this virtue, or practice, or austerity, or holy life, I shall become a deva or one among the devas.' He relishes that, longs for it, and finds satisfaction in it.

Brahmin, this too is a breach, a hole, a stain, and a mottle in the holy life. Brahmin, this person is said to practice an impure holy life, being bound by the bond of sexual union. I say that he is not released from birth, aging, and death; from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; he is not released from suffering.” (Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.50)

It should be understood that the avoidance of the seven types of sexual bonds mentioned in the Jāṇusoṇi Sutta of the Sattaka Nipāta, Aṅguttara Nikāya, is also shown here. In this Abrahmacariya-sikkhāpada as well, the unwholesome intention (cetanā) that arises at the body-door with the desire to indulge in the practice of the ignoble, which brings about the union of the organs (maggena magga paṭipatti)...
334:
...is Abrahmacariya. In the sequence of the five precepts, however, the intention to transgress against forbidden persons (agamanīya-ṭṭhāna) should be understood as 'Kāmesu micchācāra' (sexual misconduct), as previously stated.

In that context of sexual misconduct, for men, the forbidden persons (agamanīya-ṭṭhāna) consist of twenty types of women: the ten types beginning with those protected by their mother (māturakkhitā), and the ten types beginning with those bought with wealth (dhanakkītā). For women, however, the forbidden persons are other men besides their own husbands, specifically regarding the ten types beginning with those bought with wealth, as well as those protected by a guardian (sārakkhā) and those under the threat of punishment (sapari-daṇḍā), totaling twelve types. Some teachers say, 'Sexual misconduct in sensual pleasures is fourfold: wrong time (akāla), wrong place (adesa), wrong organ (anaṅga), and wrongful force (adhamma).' These teachers speak by imagining based on mere perversion of conduct. This is because perversion occurring with a person one is permitted to go to cannot be called sexual misconduct. Such perversion, in both cases, is of minor blame if the person is devoid of virtue, and of great blame if the person is endowed with virtue. Even with one devoid of virtue, perversion by force is of great blame; if there is mutual consent, it is of minor blame. Even with mutual consent, it should be understood that if the defilements and efforts are weak, it is of minor blame, and if they are intense, it is of great blame.

The factors (sambhāra) of that Abrahmacariya are two: the desire to indulge and the union of the organs (maggena magga paṭipatti). For sexual misconduct (micchācāra), however, there are four factors: a forbidden person (agamanīya-vatthu), the thought of indulging in that person, the effort to indulge, and the consent to the union of the organs. Thus, because it is stated in the Commentaries as 'four factors,' some teachers say, 'In a transgression by force, even if there is consent to the union of the organs, since there was no prior desire to indulge or effort, it does not constitute sexual misconduct for the one being forced.' However, the absence of effort when there is a desire to indulge is not a standard, because for women, there is generally no effort to indulge; the effort to indulge is generally only for men. If that were the case, the fault would arise that a woman who sits [or lies] down having first established a desire to indulge would not be guilty of sexual misconduct. Therefore, the 'four factors' are stated in the Commentaries primarily with respect to men. Otherwise, some say that when a woman performs the role of a man, the man would not be guilty of sexual misconduct because he lacks the effort to indulge.

The conclusion here is: In sexual misconduct performed by one's own choice, there are three factors—a forbidden person, the effort to indulge, and the consent to the union of the organs—since the desire to indulge is established by the very effort to indulge. In sexual misconduct performed by force, since there is no prior desire to indulge or effort, there is the forbidden person, and in that person...
335:
There are three factors: the mind desiring to indulge, and the delighted acceptance of transferring from one path to another. Some say there are four factors according to the method mentioned by taking them without remainder. It is stated in the Abhidhamma-anuṭīkā that this statement should be accepted after careful investigation. As for the effort (payoga), there is only one type: sāhattika-payoga (action by one's own hand).

The word 'musā' is an indeclinable (nipāta) ending in the third or second case, a synonym for 'micchā' (falsehood). Since it primarily denotes the action, it is said to be 'preceded by the desire to deceive' and so forth. Doing something first is called purekkhāra. One who first performs the act of speaking deceptively is called visambādana-purekkhāra. To show only the false speech that has reached the course of action (kammapatha), it is said to be 'destroying the benefit'. It means one who destroys the welfare of others. False speech (musāvāda) occurs either due to not wanting to give one's own property or due to the desire to joke. The action characterized by verbal effort is called vacī-payoga. Similarly, the action performed by the body is called kāya-payoga. The intention to deceive exists in the preceding moment before speaking, as well as at the moment of speaking. It is taught: 'Beforehand, he has the thought, "I will speak a lie"; while speaking, he has the thought, "I am speaking a lie."' Only these two are the factors. The statement 'After speaking, he has the thought, "I have spoken a lie"' is not a factor of musāvāda, whether it serves as a cause or not. 'Of him' (assa) refers to the deceiver and is connected with the word 'intention' (cetanā). Because one deceives by this bodily or verbal effort, that effort is called visambādana. Because it originates that deceptive bodily or verbal effort, that intention is called visambādana-samuṭṭhāpikā. It is called musāvāda because one makes others know by this bodily or verbal effort known as musā, or because one originates the bodily or verbal effort known as musā by that intention; this is the meaning. When the word 'vāda' is mentioned, the three characteristics—the mind desiring to deceive, the corresponding effort, and the other person's understanding of that meaning—are already made clear.

However, the characteristic of 'untrue matter' (atatha vatthu) is not yet clearly shown because the word musā denotes the action called effort (payoga). Therefore, in this method, because the characteristic is not all-encompassing and because the word musā can denote the meaning to be deceived, 'another method' etc., is stated to complete the definition of musāvāda. 'By characteristic' means by nature. 'Tathā' means because it originates bodily and verbal intimations (viññatti) in that true manner, it is called viññatti-samuṭṭhāpikā. In this second method, the derivative definition (vacanattha) should be understood as: it is called musāvāda because an untrue matter is spoken by means of this dhamma. By the words 'He, whatever benefit...' etc., the state of being slightly blameworthy or greatly blameworthy is stated according to the object of the musāvāda that has reached the course of action. If the person whose benefit is destroyed is low in virtues such as morality (sīla), the blame is slight.
336:
Just as in the case of adinnādāna (taking what is not given), the degree of blame should be applied according to the quality of the person. Due to the greatness of the qualities, the blame is great; due to the smallness of the qualities, the blame is slight. The state of being slightly or greatly blameworthy is also obtained through the mildness or intensity of the defilements (kilesa).

By the word 'apica' (moreover) and so forth, the state of being slightly or greatly blameworthy of general musāvāda is also shown. Speaking because of not wanting to give one's own property or because of the desire to joke is called general musāvāda. In both cases of general musāvāda, it becomes musāvāda only when preceded by the intention to deceive; it does not become musāvāda merely by the words spoken. In that general musāvāda, it is said to be slightly blameworthy because the intention (cetanā) is not strong. 'Nadī maññe' means 'like a river'. A speech that proceeds by way of filling in a meaning that is deficient due to smallness is called pūraṇakathā; it means a speech spoken in the sense of being excessive.

Because it is produced in that manner, it is called 'tajja'; it means the meaning that is appropriate to that deception. By the word 'vāyāma' (effort), the effort (payoga) is mentioned, taking 'effort' as the head. Here, bodily and verbal actions where energy (vīriya) is predominant are intended, not mere effort. Even if the effort is made with the intention to deceive, if the other person does not understand that meaning, the deception is not successful; therefore, the other person's understanding of that meaning is also mentioned as one factor (sambhāra). Some teachers, however, state three factors: 'untrue speech, the mind desiring to deceive, and the other person's understanding of that meaning.' To prevent someone from thinking that only bodily action is sāhattika (personal action), the words 'He, by body or...' etc., are stated. The statement that the other person understands that meaning by that action is said with reference to understanding at that moment or later after reflecting due to dullness of intellect. 'Ayaṃ' refers to the deceiver. 'Only at the moment of the intention that originates the action' means only at the moment of the occurrence of the intention that originates the bodily or verbal action. 'Is bound by the kamma of musāvāda' means he is connected with or attached to the kamma of musāvāda known as the intention to deceive. Even if the other person understands that meaning only after a long time by reflecting due to dullness, it is said that he is bound at that very moment because it was produced by the decisive intention (sanniṭṭhāpaka-cetanā).

The statement 'There is only one type of effort, sāhattika (personal action)' is said according to the method found in the ancient commentaries (porāṇa-aṭṭhakathā). Therefore, in this Sangaha-aṭṭhakathā, to show the difference of opinion of the author of the Sangaha, the words 'yasmā pana' etc., are stated. In that statement, by the words 'yathā... pe... tathā', āṇattika (command) and so forth should also be taken just like sāhattika. There is no reason for not taking them, as they are similar to it in the sense of deceiving another.
337:
The reason for including the one who commands (āṇattika) is shown by the words, “Let this be for this person... even the one who commands.” The reason for including the effort of relinquishing (nissaggiya) is shown by the words, “The one who... even the one who releases the leaf.” The reason for including the permanent effort (thāvara) is shown by the words, “This meaning... even the one who places.” Because he deceives, this connection should be applied to all terms.

“Writing on a leaf” means writing with letters on leaves such as palm leaves. Or, the word “paṇṇaṃ” is a word with an accusative ending used in the sense of the locative. Therefore, when the teacher says “on walls, etc.,” it means writing letters on a leaf with a stylus. “Should be accepted after investigation”—this is said without self-exaltation because one’s own opinion (attano-mati) is weaker than all the Suttas, Suttānuloma, and Ācariyavāda. In truth, since this has already been investigated by oneself, what reason is there for further investigation?

“Saccaṃ” means truthfulness in speech (vacī-sacca). “Saccena saccaṃ” means the former truthfulness of speech and the subsequent truthfulness of speech. The word “sandahati” (unites) is used with reference to the dropping of a part of the root through the power of the suffix. Scholars of grammar, however, recite the root dhā in the sense of uniting: “The root dhā with the prefix vi is in the sense of performing; with abhi, it is in the sense of speaking; with ni, ā, and saṃ, it is in the sense of depositing, placing upon, and uniting, as appropriate.” Therefore, it should be understood that “sandahati” is also said by way of a synonym. That meaning is shown by “not in between,” etc. The phrase “For he who...” is an explanation of that meaning. “Antaritattā” means because of being separated in between. “Na tādiso” means not having such a nature of lying. Even for the sake of life (he does not lie), let alone for other reasons; thus the word “api” has the sense of commendation (sambhāvana).

As in the words “by truth, by firmness” (saccato thetato), etc., the word “theta” is a synonym for “thira” (firm). Since it concerns the state of being a speaker of truth (saccavāditā), the state of being firm should be understood by way of speech; thus it is said, “it means one of firm speech (thira-katho).” The state of one who is firm is “theta,” meaning firmness; because he is endowed with that firmness, the person here is called “theta.” “Haliddī” is a specific small plant (turmeric) produced from a gold-colored bulb. “Thusa” refers to grain husks and stalks. “Kumbhaṇḍa” is a specific creeper (pumpkin/gourd) with large fruit used for making soup. “Indakhīla” is a threshold pillar firmly planted deep in the ground. Just as clothes dyed with turmeric, etc., do not last because of their unstable nature, so too, this person does not have unstable speech; therefore, he is called “naṭhita-katho” (one who does not have unstable speech). Just as inscriptions on stone, etc., last because of their stable nature, so too, this person has stable speech; therefore, he is called “ṭhita-katho” (one who has stable speech). Thus the word-definition should be understood. Turmeric dyeing, etc...
338:
“Ṭhita-katho” (in the Dīgha Nikāya Commentary, it is “thira-katho”). Just as turmeric dye, etc., are metaphors for speech, so should it be applied here. For these—turmeric dye, etc.—are metaphors for speech.

Because faith, known as “patti,” occurs in this person, he is called “paccayiko” (trustworthy). Therefore, he is called “pattiyāyitabbako” (one whose words are to be believed). With the addition of the letter ‘y’, “pattiyāyitabbā” refers to speech that causes belief. Because this person has such speech, he is called “pattiyāyitabbako.” Therefore, he is called “saddhāyitabbako” (one who is to be trusted). To show that meaning by way of exclusion (vyatireka) and inclusion (anvaya), the phrase “For a certain person...” is said. One becomes blameworthy due to deception. On the other hand, one becomes praiseworthy because of not failing (in truth); this is the meaning. By the word “lokaṃ,” it is shown that the genitive case in “lokassa” is used in the sense of the accusative (object).

Even though there are separate sequences of text in other Abhidhamma commentaries, etc., the phrase “by which speech...” is said to explain all three terms as having a single meaning according to the sequence of commentary. “He performs by which speech” is the connection. “Parassa” means of the person whom he speaks to in order to divide. The word “ca” is used in an unusual place, but it should be applied to both objects to indicate an internal conjunctive (dvanda) compound. “Suññabhāvaṃ” means the state of being empty/void due to separation from loved ones. “Sā” refers to the speech having the nature of sound mentioned before. Thus, because it makes one void of love, it is called “pisuṇā” (slander) according to the etymological method (nirutti). Or, it is called “pisuṇā” because it causes harmonious beings to become divided into groups. “Pharusā” (harsh) means speech that is rough due to the absence of affection. “Sayampi pharusā” means it is inherently rough because it arises from displeasure (domanassa). Because of its harsh nature, it is not pleasant to the ear. Because it destroys benefit, it does not reach the heart. Here, in the first method, the use of the word “pharusa” for speech should be understood either by the word-definition “it makes harsh” or by metonymy of the effect (phalūpacāra). In the second method, because it occurs by way of cutting the vitals and is absolutely cruel, the use of the word “pharusa” for speech should be understood either by way of conventional usage (ruḷhī) or by metonymy of the cause (kāraṇūpacāra). “Yena” means by that useless speech called “palāpa” (prattle). “Samphaṃ” is the name given to anything that is not beneficial to oneself or others, in the sense that it destroys the happiness and welfare called “sa.” Therefore, it is called “niratthakaṃ” (useless). By this, the word-definition of “samphappalāpa” is shown as “one prattles uselessly by which speech.”
339:
By the word "tesaṃ" and so forth, the occurrence of terms such as 'slander' (pisuṇā) is stated by way of metaphorical designation for the result of volition (cetanā). By the phrase "sā eva" and so forth, the reason for the conceptualization of the occurrence of that volition is explained. In that context, because it stands in proximity to the word "pahāya" (abandoning) and so forth, it is intended that logically, it is that very volition which should be abandoned. This is the meaning.

"Tattha" means among those actions such as slanderous speech. "Saṅkiliṭṭhacittassa" means of a person whose mind is oppressed, tormented, or corrupted by greed or hatred; this is connected with the word "cetanā." It means that when one speaks to cause a rift between others, it is due to the desire for oneself to be loved by them. Volition is called 'slanderous speech' (pisuṇā vācā) because slander is spoken by means of it. It should be noted that in the context of a compound (samāsa), the primary meaning (mukhya) should be taken, whereas in the context of a sentence (vākya), it should be taken by way of metaphorical usage (upacāra). In the act of causing a rift between one person and another, if they are not yet divided, the fault is small; if they are divided, the fault is great. Likewise, the specific degree of fault should be applied according to the mildness or intensity of the defilements (kilesa).

When slanderous speech is conveyed to someone, whether that person is divided or not, the mere making of that person understand the meaning of that speech is the standard, as stated by the phrase "tassa tadatthavijānanaṃ." There are four possibilities by including each side of the desire to cause a rift and the desire to be loved. However, the attainment of the 'course of action' (kammapatha) occurs only when they are actually divided. The word "imesaṃ" is used because of its indefinite nature, intending to refer to those who are absent but are present in one's own mind; to show this, the word "yesaṃ" and so forth is stated. "Ito" should be understood in connection as 'heard from those who are mentioned in this place.'

"Dvinnaṃ" (of two) is a word used as an illustration, as it can also apply to many. The phrase "mittānaṃ" and so forth is the object (kamma) in the word "sandhānaṃ" (uniting). By that, it shows the objective status of the word "bhinnānaṃ" in the Pāḷi. Since uniting means doing what is appropriate for them, it is called "anukattā" (one who acts accordingly). "Anuppadātā" means one who gives fresh strength or one who gives by way of following along. If it is asked, 'To whom does one give strength or follow along?', it is known to be the act of uniting because it is preached as "sahitānaṃ"; therefore, it is called "sandhānanuppadātā." Because the giving, receiving, protecting, or strengthening of the union occurs through giving strength and following along, it is called "daḷhīkammaṃ kattā" (one who makes it firm).

It is called "ārāma" because they delight in this place. The word "samaggo" (harmonious), which refers to a place of delight, is stated as an adjective of "ārāma" based on those who dwell there. Although some read it as "samagge," that is inappropriate because it contradicts the word "yattha" and so forth. Since this meaning can be obtained even without the manner, it is stated that "this alone is the meaning here." "Samaggesu" means among the groups of people who are in harmony; therefore, "te pahāya" and so forth is stated. The meaning of being harmonious is also an agentive (kattu) meaning.
340:
This meaning is shown by the word "nandati." With that meaning of harmony, the phrase "disvāpi sutvāpi" (having seen or heard) is well-established. Because one makes those who are harmonious stay harmonious by that speech, it is called "samaggakaraṇī." That speech itself makes them harmonious; the meaning that one speaks such speech is stated by "yā vācā" and so forth. Uniting by that speech is stated as "sāmaggīguṇaparidīpikameva" (merely illustrating the virtues of concord), because the benefits of concord are shown by Pāḷi passages such as "Happy is the concord of the Saṅgha; happy is the practice of those in concord" (Dhp. 194). "Itaraṃ" refers to the other kind of speech that causes division.

"Mammāni" refers to bad or sensitive wounds. Because they are similar to such wounds, the bases of abuse (akkosavatthu) are called "mammāni" here. Just as the mind reaches extreme suffering when a sensitive wound is touched by any object, so too the mind reaches extreme suffering by the mere touch of harsh speech upon those ten bases of abuse such as birth and so forth. Therefore, it is said "mammāni viya mammāni." The bases of abuse such as birth, which cause extreme suffering when touched like a sensitive wound, are called 'mamma'. Others say: just as a part of the body where one feels intense pain when struck by a weapon is called 'mamma', here, the mind where intense pain known as distress (domanassa) arises due to harsh speech is called 'mamma' because it is like a vital spot.

That bodily or vocal effort by which those vital spots are cut or broken is called "mammacchedaka." The volition that produces such a 'vital-spot-cutting' bodily or vocal effort is likewise called "mammacchedaka-samuṭṭhāpikā."

Strictly speaking, because one speaks harsh words with a cruel volition, it is called "pharusā vācā" (harsh speech). Instead of saying merely "pharusacetanā," the phrase "ekantapharusacetanā" (exclusively harsh volition) is used to make it known that a harsh volition is intended only when the mind is corrupted by anger, and not merely because the words are harsh to the ear. "Tassā" refers to that exclusively harsh volition. "Āvibhāvatthaṃ" is for the purpose of making the nature of harsh speech clear. Alternatively, "tassā" refers to the harsh speech of that exclusively harsh volition.

"Tatheva" means that it [the buffalo] came out to follow exactly in the manner spoken by the mother. "Saccakiriyaṃ" (act of truth) means that although she said with her mouth, "May that fierce buffalo follow you," that speech was not in the mother's heart. Therefore, she thought in her mind the reason: "May that not happen; may not even a lotus leaf fall upon me." Since that alone was in the mother's heart, the making of the truth is "May that alone happen," or it refers to the truth that should be made. "Tattheva" means at the very place of rising. "Baddhā viya" means as if bound by a rope or such. In this context of "mammacchedaka," the state of cutting the vital spots should be understood merely by the harshness of what is heard by the ear.
341:
"Payoga" refers to vocal effort (vacīpayoga). In the phrase "due to the softness of the mind," it specifically means the absence of harsh intention (cetanā). Because the intention is not harsh, such speech does not constitute harsh speech (pharusavācā) that reaches the path of action (kammapatha). However, it should be understood that its nature as an action (kamma) cannot be denied. This meaning is supported by the passage beginning with "Parents..." (For example, even if a mother buffalo, Mahiṃsī, says to her young calf, "May this harsh buffalo follow you," while in her mind she thinks, "May not even a lotus leaf fall upon my son.")

Having thus established the absence of harsh speech through the method of exclusion (vyatireka) when the intention is not harsh, the text now states "Yathā" etc., to establish it through the method of inclusion (anvaya). The meaning is that it is not that it is not harsh speech; it is indeed harsh speech. "Sā" refers to that harsh speech, and "yaṃ" refers to that person.

In this context as well, harsh speech that does not reach the path of action (kammapatha) is of little blame, while that which reaches the path of action is of great blame. Similarly, it should be understood by connecting it with the distinctions of the mildness or intensity of the defilements (kilesa). Some teachers say, "Harsh speech reaches the path of action only in the presence of the person it is directed towards." Others say, "Harsh speech occurs even in their absence."

Between these two views, this perspective seems appropriate: when spoken in someone's presence, the intention may be stronger due to the intensity of disrespect, etc., and the other person can understand the meaning of those words. This is not the same in their absence. However, just as an apology made at a cemetery after the death of the person who was reviled can prevent the danger of reproach, it can be known that harsh speech used in someone's absence is also indeed harsh speech. Therefore, it should be noted that harsh speech can occur both in someone's presence and in their absence. Indeed, the commentaries mention only three factors (sambhāra) of harsh speech, excluding the other person's understanding of the meaning. The term "angry mind" is used only with the intention to revile, not with the intention to kill. If there is an angry mind with the intention to kill, whether the purpose is achieved or not, it results in killing (pāṇātipāta) and ill-will (byāpāda) as appropriate.

Anger is called "ela" because the mind or the person trembles because of this fault (dosa). In this verse—

"The chariot rolls, with the wheel of the fruit of Arahantship,
With the white canopy of the fruit of Arahantship,
And the spoke of mindfulness.
Behold the one approaching, free from suffering,
With the stream of craving cut, and free from bonds."

In this context, virtue (sīla) is called "nela" because it is faultless. For this very reason, when Citta the householder was questioned by the Venerable Kāmabhū in the Saḷāyatana Vagga of the Saṃyutta Nikāya, he replied, "Venerable sir, 'nelanga' is a designation for the virtues (sīla)." Speech (vācā) by nature consists of sound and is connected to various meanings. Because it is like a sweet taste, the phrasing (vyañjana) is sweet, and the meaning is also like that. Referring to that meaning, it is called "sweetness of phrasing" (vyañjana-madhuratā) and "sweetness of meaning" (attha-madhuratā). In common usage, the qualifier (vissessana) is often placed at the end. Alternatively, considering the parts, it is said, "The phrasing of which speech is sweet," and so on.
342:
It is also said as 'byañjana-madhuratā' and 'attha-madhuratā.' In the world, the placement of the adjective at the end is seen in words like 'ajyāhito.' Alternatively, when considering the components, it should be stated as 'that whose sound is sweet,' etc. 'Sukhā' means that which produces happiness or is the cause of happiness. 'Kaṇṇasūlaṃ' means an ear-spike. Here, the word 'ear' (kaṇṇa) includes the cognitive series (vīthi) that follow and are connected to ear-consciousness. This Suttanta teaching is conventional discourse (vohārakathā), and its explanation is also conventional. Therefore, it is said, 'anger or love in the whole body.' In reality, anger and love, which depend on the heart-base (hadayavatthu), do not occur in the whole body. In such matters, it should be understood in this way. 'Enters the mind happily' means it enters easily due to the two reasons mentioned above. This is an alutta-samāsa (un-elided compound) like 'amataṅgato.'

'Pure' refers to the perfection of qualities; hence it is said 'because of the state of being full of qualities.' Speech is called 'porī' (urbane) like a woman raised in a city (pure), as explained by the words beginning with 'pure.' 'Sukumārā' means very tender. In the context of the thing compared, sukumāra-ness is simply the state of being soft and not harsh. In the word 'purassa,' the word 'pura' refers to the inhabitants of the city by way of association (sahacaraṇa), just as in the phrase 'the village has come.' Therefore, it is said 'of the city-dwellers.' 'Esā' is the speech indicated in connection with them. 'Evarūpī kathā' is speech manifested through three types of meaning. 'Kantā' means desired or pleasing, like the word 'pakkanto.' Or it is the suffix -māna changed to -anta, meaning 'being desired.' It is like the phrase 'anāpatti asamanubhāsantassa.' It is called 'manāpā' because it increases (vaḍḍheti) the mind (manaṃ); therefore it is said 'mind-expanding.' It means having the nature of acting in that way. In the phrase 'bahuno janassa,' the genitive case is used in the sense of possession (sambandha), not in the sense of the agent (kattar) as in the previous word.

Although the meaning they intend to convey may indeed be possible, because that meaning is fruitless, it is not even called 'meaning' in the sense of the stated meaning; therefore it is called 'anatthaviññāpikā' (communicating what is unbeneficial). Alternatively, because it lacks a purposeful meaning (payojanattha), it is unbeneficial speech, and it is also appropriate to call it speech that makes such unbeneficial things known. Unwholesome intention is called frivolous talk (samphappalāpa) because one prattles (palapanti) useless things (samphaṃ) with this intention. Āsevanā means cultivation, development, and frequent practice. If the person intended to be influenced does not accept it, the blame is small; if they accept it, the blame is great. The smallness or greatness of the blame should also be connected with the weakness or intensity of the defilements. Examples include the stories of the war between the two brother kings named Bharata, the story of the abduction of the queen named Sītā by the demon Dasagiri, and the story of King Rāma...
343:
Tales such as the story of King Rama bringing back (Sītā Devi), and the ancient Rama Jātaka and Bharata Jātaka composed in the Sanskrit language currently studied by those outside the Dispensation, are called frivolous talk (samphappalāpa). Therefore, it was said, "Bharata... purekkhāratā."

The passage beginning with "Kālavādī" (speaking at the right time) shows the practice of one who abstains from frivolous talk. For example, the passage beginning with "pāṇātipātā paṭivirato" shows the practice of abandoning the taking of life. When it is said, "He lives having abandoned the taking of life," the expectation (question) may arise, "How is the taking of life abandoned?" Therefore, it is said, "He is one who abstains from the taking of life." If asked how that abstinence is, it is said, "He has laid down the stick, he has laid down the weapon." If asked how he has laid down the stick and weapon, it is said, "He is conscientious (lajjī)," and so on. In this way, each subsequent statement shows the means (method) of the preceding one. The same should be applied as appropriate to the taking of what is not given (adinnādāna), and so forth. Thus it is said, "The passage beginning with Kālavādī shows the practice of one who abstains from frivolous talk."

Even speech connected with benefit may not bring benefit if spoken at an improper time, but may lead to the understanding of what is not beneficial. Therefore, to show that one who gives up frivolous talk should avoid speaking at the wrong time, it is said, "Kālavādī." Even when speaking at the proper time, one should avoid what is not true because it cannot fulfill the benefit of both parties; thus it is said, "Bhūtavādī" (speaking the truth). Even when speaking what is true, one should only speak that which accomplishes the welfare of this world and the world hereafter; thus it is said, "Atthavādī" (speaking what is beneficial). Even when speaking what is beneficial, one should not speak only that which is based on mundane things, but also that which is based on the supramundane; thus it is said, "Dhammavādī" (speaking according to the Dhamma). To show how benefit is based on the supramundane Dhamma, it is said, "Vinayavādī" (speaking according to the Discipline).

The meaning expressed through the five types of restraint-discipline (saṃvara-vinaya)—namely, restraint by the Pātimokkha, restraint by mindfulness, restraint by knowledge, restraint by patience, and restraint by energy—and through the five types of abandonment-discipline (pahāna-vinaya)—namely, abandonment by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga), abandonment by suppression (vikkhambhana), abandonment by eradication (samuccheda), abandonment by tranquilization (paṭippassaddhi), and abandonment by escape (nissaraṇa)—is based on the supramundane Dhamma because it is the cause for the attainment of Nibbāna. To show that speaking an attha (meaning/benefit) endowed with such special qualities is beautiful and effective only when there is skill in teaching (desanā-kosalla), and not otherwise, it is said, "One who speaks words worth treasuring (nidhānavatiṃ vācaṃ)."

Now, to clarify that very skill in teaching, the text says "Kālena" etc. When entering the domain of teaching by the power of the listener's disposition (ajjhāsaya), the occurrence of circumstances, and questions, one should note the analytical divisions such as categorical explanation (ekāṃsa-byākaraṇa), and then apply the thesis (ṭhapanā), the reason (hetu), the illustration (udāharaṇa), and the comparison (saṃsandana)...
344:
...explaining them according to the respective times. By means of a teaching that is limited and defined in form, yet deep in delivery and encompassing a vast range of meanings in detail, one establishes others in the achievement of the ultimate goal according to their inclinations; thus, one is called "skilled in teaching" (desanā-kusala). In this way, the connection of the meaning here should also be understood.

"The appropriate time for what should be said" (vattabbayutta-kāla) means the time suitable for the words to be spoken, or the time in which those words should be employed. Because it is true by the power of the nature of things, it was said, "only the nature" (sabhāvam-eva). One is an "atthavādī" because one speaks of benefit. With the intention that speaking of benefit is simply the speaking of words connected to that benefit, it was said, "making it connected only with the benefit of the present life and the future life." The same method should be understood for the terms beginning with "dhammavādī."

It is called "nidhāna" (a treasure/store) because one stores or places [speech] therein. It refers to a place of storage or the heart. When it is said "ṭhānavatī," the meaning that it is suitable to be placed in that location is also possible; therefore, it was said, "in the heart," and so on. Even speech worth treasuring (nidhānavatī) only brings benefit when it is timely. Therefore, the word "at the right time" (kālena) is shown to be a word that expects (refers to) the phrase "speaks speech worth treasuring" by the passage beginning with "of such a nature."

It is called "apadesa" because it is pointed out for the sake of accomplishing the desired meaning, or because the desired meaning is pointed out by it. It refers to causes such as similes, reasons (hetu), and examples (udāharaṇa). Because it is accompanied by such reasons, the speech is called "sāpadesā." Therefore, it was said, "the meaning is: accompanied by similes and accompanied by reasons." "Having shown the definition" means having shown the limit as far as the conclusion can be reached. Therefore, it was said, "speaks... in such a way." Indeed, speech that has not reached its climax (sikhā) is not called beneficial.

In the term "connected with benefit" (atthasaṃhita), the word "attha" is a synonym for the meaning of what is spoken; this was said in the passage beginning with "by many methods also." The "meaning of what is spoken" refers to all meanings understood according to the sequence of words, such as the meaning of the root (paka-tyattha), the meaning of the suffix (paccayattha), and the meaning of the state (bhāvattha). For this very reason, the word of the Blessed One, even if it is just a single verse, brings about a meaning that cannot be exhausted because it is capable of being extracted by many methods, such as the methods of brevity and detail, unity and diversity, and the Nandiyāvatta method. Having thus commented by way of the general meaning, the passage beginning with "or which" was stated to comment by way of the specific desired meaning. For here, only the meaning that the speaker (the atthavādī) intends to say is taken.

Is it not the case that everyone's speech is accompanied by their own intended meaning? What then is there to be said here? This latent objection is cleared by the passage beginning with "not another meaning." He does not first set forth one meaning and then later speak another meaning without any connection (anusandhi). The intention is that he speaks, concluding only according to the connection that was first set forth.
345:
## 
In this way, after analyzing the seven root training rules in order, although the abandoning of covetousness and so forth is included in the virtue of restraint (saṃvara-sīla), because it involves incorporating higher qualities and because it is not the domain of worldly worldlings (lokiya-puthujjana), the Blessed One, wishing to analyze only the virtue of conduct (ācāra-sīla) which is well-known to the general public, set aside that [higher] virtue to be included in the higher teaching and spoke the words beginning with "bījagāma-bhūtagāma-samārambhā." This connection should be stated in the Pali.

In that Pali, they grow and increase by means of these seeds; therefore, they are called seeds (bīja). It is a name for fruits with kernels and so forth that are capable of growing because they are the special cause for the arising of a similar fruit when other conditions are met. They are currently becoming and have already become; therefore, they are called "bhūta." It means they are growing, increasing, and have already increased. It is the sequential name for trees, shrubs, and so forth that are currently growing or have already grown and are standing. Indeed, young trees and shrubs that have taken root and attained a green color are said to be "growing and increasing." Large trees and shrubs that have grown and are standing are said to have "grown and increased." "Gāma" means a group or collection. That collection is a mere mass of the eightfold material groups (suddhaṭṭhaka-dhamma). It is a collection of the eightfold material groups of the seeds and the grown trees which have received such names. Alternatively, those seeds and trees themselves are called a collection (gāma). Since there is no whole apart from its parts, by both meanings, only those grasses, trees, creepers, and so forth are taken.

In another way, deities take possession of trees, shrubs, and so forth that stand on the ground and have attained a green color. Therefore, teachers also call them "bhūtagāma" because they are the dwelling place (gāma) of those deities (bhūta). To show those bījagāma and bhūtagāma by their specific forms, the Buddha spoke the words beginning with "mūla-bīja" (root-seed). Because the root itself is a seed, it is called "mūla-bīja." This method should be understood for the remaining terms as well. "Phalu-bīja" means joint-seed (node-seed). The word "bīja" is established for fruits with kernels capable of growing because they are the special cause for the arising of a similar result when other conditions are met. For the sake of accomplishing that result, it also occurs in some parts like roots and so forth. Therefore, to distinguish it from roots and so forth, it is specified with a single word "bīja" and called "bīja-bīja" (seed-seed). It is like saying "rūpaṃ-rūpaṃ" or "dukkha-dukkhaṃ." "Nīla-tiṇa-rukkha-ādikassa" means of green grass and green trees and so forth. By the word "ādi," medicinal plants, shrubs, creepers, and so forth should be understood. Here, "samārambha" means destruction. Since that destruction is only by means of cutting and so forth, it is said to be "by way of cutting, breaking, cooking, and so forth."

One might object: Are trees and so forth not without life (jīva) because they lack consciousness (citta)? That they lack consciousness is known because they have no movement, because they regrow even when cut, because they belong to a different class [than sentient beings], and because they are not included in the four modes of birth (yoni). Growth, however, exists even in coral, stones, salt, and so forth. Therefore, growth is not a reason for the existence of life in those trees. Their perception of objects is a mere imagination, like the sleeping of tamarind trees and so forth, or like the cravings (dohaḷa) for spicy or sour things. If that is so, why...
346:
## 
...is the abstinence from damaging seeds and plants (bījagāma-bhūtagāma) desired? It is desired because it is suitable for recluses (samaṇa-sāruppa) and because of compassion for the beings dependent on those plants. Therefore, the Blessed One said regarding the matter of the Āḷavī monks cutting trees: "These foolish men, people perceive life in a tree," and so forth. Eating only one meal is "ekabhatta." One who has that practice of eating only once a day is called "ekabhattika." Regarding the question of when that one meal should be eaten, it is said "pātarāsa-bhatta" and so forth. Between the two meals of morning and evening, it refers to the morning meal; this is the meaning. Rice to be eaten in the morning is "pātarāsa." Rice to be eaten in the evening is "sāyamāsa." That sāyamāsa itself is the meal (bhatta). In this term "ekabhattika," the word "eka" is used to define the period until noon, not as the number of times [of eating] within that period; this is shown by the words beginning with "tasmā."

Eating at night is expressed by the word "ratti" (night) through the omission of the latter term. Or, because that meaning is possible through the power of the derivative (taddhita), it is expressed as "rattiyā" and so forth. The period from dawn until noon is the time for eating practiced and habitually followed by the Noble Ones, such as the Buddha and others. Any time other than that is called the "wrong time" (vikāla). Since eating at night is already excluded by the second term, to show the meaning of the third term that only the afternoon is the wrong time (vikāla) here, the words beginning with "atikkante majjhanhike" (when noon has passed) are spoken. Here, the word "bhojana" is a verbal noun (bhāva-sādhana) expressing the meaning of swallowing; this is shown by the phrase "eating until the sun sets." If it is asked, "What is being swallowed?", it is understood as the swallowing of time-limited food (yāvakālika) because period-limited foods (yāmakālika) and others are permitted, and because the term "vikāla-bhojana" is established only for the swallowing of time-limited food (yāvakālika).

In this matter, the method of the teachers other than the Commentaries is: it is called "bhojana" because it is to be eaten; it refers to all time-limited (yāvakālika) things such as gruel, rice, and so forth. Just as in the term "rattūparato," eating at night is expressed by the word "ratti," so here also, the swallowing of food is expressed by the word "bhojana." Eating at the wrong time is "vikāla-bhojana." The meaning is [abstaining] from the swallowing of time-limited food (yāvakālika) at the wrong time. That such splendor of virtue existed not only during the Buddha's time is shown by the words beginning with "on the banks of the Anomā River." The sequence of connection in the Pali is: when it is said "ekabhattika" because of eating only once a day, eating at night might also be possible.
347:
Because eating at night is possible, he said 'rattūparato' (one who abstains from eating at night) to prevent it. If this were the case, one who eats in the evening might also be an 'ekabhattiko' (one-meal eater); to dispel such doubt, he said 'vikālabhojanā virato' (one who abstains from eating at the wrong time).

In brief, the Buddha's Dispensation (Sāsana), which arose through methods such as 'sabbapāpassa akaraṇaṃ' (not doing any evil) and so on, is not consistent with watching dancing and so on, which occur with desire and lust (chandarāga); therefore, it is said 'because it is inconsistent with the Dispensation'. Because it pierces the Dispensation by being inconsistent, it is called 'visūka' (a thorn/spike), which means an opposing thing. In this regard, an illustration is shown with the word 'paṭāṇībhūtaṃ', meaning it has become like a stake known as paṭāṇī. Teachers also say that the meaning of the word 'visūka' is 'paṭāṇībhūtaṃ' (becoming like a stake). Both dancing oneself and making others dance are included in the Pali by the single word 'nacca' through the method of general designation (sāmaññaniddesa) or the method of ellipsis (ekasesa), due to the common nature of dancing. Similarly, with the words 'gīta' and 'vādita', singing oneself, making others sing, playing music oneself, and making others play music are included; thus it is said 'by way of dancing, making dance, etc.' This is because these words can express both the simple agent (suddhakattu) and the causative agent (hetukattu). Watching dancing, singing, music, and things that are like thorns (visūka) is called 'naccagītavādita-visūkadassanaṃ', and here it is treated as a singular compound by way of a collective compound (samāhārasamāsa). In the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), however, to show it as a conjunctive compound (samuccayasamāsa) along with the word at the end of the sentence as it appears in the text, it is stated as 'naccā ca' and so on. It should be understood this way in all such places. (Regarding watching, by rejecting the dancing of peacocks etc., it should be understood that making others dance is also rejected). The phrase 'naccādīni hi' etc. supports the aforementioned meaning. Here, by the word 'watching' (dassana), 'hearing' (savana) is also included by the method of ellipsis of different forms (virūpekasesa). Alternatively, because it has the nature of reflecting on an object, the act of hearing by the five consciousnesses can also be included in the category of watching (dassana); therefore, it is said only as 'dassanā'. That is why it is said in the Commentary: 'With the five consciousnesses, one perceives no phenomenon other than the mere falling upon the object'.

By this phrase 'visūkabhūtā dassanā ca', it is shown that listening to a song that is not a thorn (avisūka) is sometimes permissible. Thus, in the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddakapāṭha, it is said: 'Even a song associated with the Dhamma is not permissible here in this Dispensation; however, Dhamma associated with the sound of a song is permissible.' In some versions, the letter 'na' appears transposed. In any case, the intention should be understood as: if it is a song, even if associated with a meaning consistent with the Dhamma, it is not permissible; if it is Dhamma, even if associated with the sound of a song, it is permissible. 'Monks...'
348:
## Cūḷasīlavaṇṇanā

'Monks, the Dhamma should not be sung with a musical tone; should any monk sing it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkhaṭa)'—by this teaching, only the preaching (in that manner) is prohibited, not the listening. Because this training rule is prescribed separately, it is understood that 'even if preached with a musical tone, the Dhamma is not called a song'. In the Commentary on the Sakkapañhasutta, when distinguishing between sounds to be cultivated and not to be cultivated, it is said: 'If, while listening even to the song of a potter's maidservant which is based on the meaning and based on the Dhamma, devotion arises or weariness (with saṃsāra) is established, such a sound should be cultivated.' This statement is made by way of a figure of speech (pariyāya) regarding what is to be cultivated only for a person who has not undertaken the training rule. For a person who has undertaken the training rule, however, it should be understood that if they listen to such a sound, their restraint of the training rule (saṃvara) is broken because it is the sound of a song. Accordingly, it is said in the Vinaya Commentaries: 'Song (gīta) means either the song of actors and so on, or the sādhukīḷana song associated with the virtues of the Triple Gem at the time of the Parinibbāna of Noble Ones, or the song of preaching Dhamma by unrestrained monks, or even at the minimum, the whistling sound (dantagīta) made beforehand with the thought "I will sing"—all this is called song'.

Although in the world the word 'mālā' refers to tied flowers, in the Dispensation, by usage (ruḷhī), it also applies to untied flowers. Therefore, since all flowers, whether tied or untied, should be regarded as 'mālā', he said 'any flower'. In the phrase 'any scent' (gandha), it refers to any kind of scent other than the application of perfumes, such as scented powder, incense, and so on. For, like the meaning already mentioned, a word can express a specific meaning even without the meaning about to be mentioned. 'Chavirāgakaraṇa' refers to any scented powder prepared by grinding to dye the skin through application. 'Piḷandhana' means wearing flowers (dhāraṇa). 'Ūnaṭṭhānapūraṇa' (filling up deficient places) means beautification (maṇḍana). Enjoying through the power of scent or through the power of dyeing the skin is called 'vibhūsana' (adornment). He clarifies that very meaning by way of personal attribution (puggalādhiṭṭhāna) with 'there, the person wearing flowers' and so on. The same is said in the Majjhima Commentary. In the Paramatthajotikā, the Khuddakapāṭha Commentary, however, only this much is said: 'In the case of garlands and so on, wearing and so on should be applied respectively.' There too, when applying them, they should be applied only according to the method already mentioned. What is the reason for this? He said 'which' and so on. The intention of immorality (dussīlyacetanā) with which one acts is the cause here. The phrase 'abstains from that' should be connected to both terms. By this phrase 'which intention of immorality', he also shows the meaning of the compound: 'the basis for garlands... adornment' or 'garlands... adornment themselves are the basis'.
349:
Indeed, the mental state such as intention (cetanā) that occurs in the form of wearing flowers and so forth is itself the action of wearing flowers and so forth. In those actions like wearing flowers, the cause of the mental factors associated with intention is due to their assistance as conascent conditions (sahajāta-paccaya) and their primary role. For it is said: "Having intended, one performs an action by body, speech, or mind." Only the intention that arises as the act of wearing flowers and so forth is called the "basis" (ṭhāna). Since the word ṭhāna is heard after a dvanda compound, it should be applied to each member.

Regarding the word "uccā" (high), the teacher said "exceeding the measure" because it is another word ending in "ā" that has the same meaning as the word "ucca" ending in "a", signifying something very high. Because one sleeps on it, such as a couch, it is called "sayana" (bed/sleeping place). To show that "mahāsayana" (large bed) intended in this mahāsayana-sikkhāpada refers to "unallowable coverings" because they are unsuitable for monks and are regarded as superior by laypeople, it is said "unallowable coverings". Here, sitting should be understood as being included within sleeping. The reason is that when the support, such as a couch, is prohibited, the action of staying on that support is also prohibited; therefore, it is only said "uccāsayanamahāsayana". In terms of meaning, however, it should be understood that abstinence from sitting and lying down, which constitutes the use of those high and large beds, is shown. Alternatively, this designation "uccāsayanamahāsayana" is made by the method of ekasesa (omission of similar terms), like the text "nāmarūpapaccayā saḷāyatanaṃ". In that method too, since the action of sleeping is preceded by sitting, by taking "sleeping", "sitting" is also taken. It is also stated in the Vinaya-ṭīkā that this is a designation where the subsequent word is omitted because the words āsana (sitting) and sayana (sleeping), which signify the actions, are elided.

Gold is called "jātarūpa" because its color is just as it is born and does not change; it possesses a color similar to the color of the Teacher (the Buddha). Silver is called "rajata" because it is pleasing due to its white color, or because beings delight in it, similar to the term "nesaṃ padakkantaṃ". A "kahāpaṇa" is a blue kahāpaṇa (alloyed coin) worth twenty māsakas, or a coin such as a dudradāmaka produced in various regions, or a coin made according to the local usage of various regions, based on the definition: "Four grains of rice are one guñjā, two guñjās are one māsaka." A coin made of copper and so forth is called "lohamāsaka" and so forth. The phrase "ye vohāraṃ gacchanti" (those which enter into commerce) is a comprehensive statement. "Vohāra" (commerce) refers to all designations by way of buying and selling. Since the meaning of "acceptance" is also found in causing others to receive and in consenting to what is placed nearby, it is said: "He does not cause [it] to be taken, nor does he consent to what is placed nearby." Alternatively, acceptance is of three kinds: by body, by speech, or by mind. Among these three, acceptance by body is called uggahaṇa (taking oneself).
