Acceptance by speech is called uggahāpana (causing to take). Acceptance by mind is called sādiyana (consenting). These three kinds of acceptance are referred to as "paṭiggahaṇa" (acceptance) by taking them either through the method of general designation (sāmañña-niddesa) or the method of ekasesa.
350:
The teacher said, "He does not take it himself," and so forth. This same method should be understood in the training rules such as the acceptance of raw grain (āmakadhañña-paṭiggahaṇa).

Since secondary grains such as nīvāra (wild rice) are included within the seven types of original grains such as sāli (rice), it is said "of the seven types as well." There is a special kind of sāli rice that ripens in sixty days and is called sāli because it is praised (salīyate). In the medical treatise Dabbaguṇa-pakāsa:
"Grain is of three types: sāli, saṭṭhika, and vīhi.
Among them, the sāli (rice) varieties are produced in the winter,
the saṭṭhika varieties are produced in the summer,
and the vīhi (paddy) varieties are said to be produced in the rainy season starting from the month of Āsāḷha."
It is called vīhi (paddy) because it carries or increases the life of beings. It is called yava (barley) because it should be mixed (yuvitabba). Because it is very coarse, that barley is consumed by mixing it with other things. It is called godhūma (wheat) because it envelops or oppresses; it is also called "milakkhabhojana" (food of the barbarians). A special, very fine grain that reaches a desirable state because of its beauty is called kaṅgu (millet). It is called varaka (beans/pulses) because it is avoided (vārīyati) due to its extreme coarseness, or because it is resorted to for removing hunger. It is called kudrūsaka (rye/kodo millet) because it spoils the blood (koraṃ rudhiraṃ dūsati); by the transposition of letters, it is also called "govaḍḍhana". All those seven types of grain are called "dhañña" (grain) because they are good for storing and for nourishing.

By the phrase "na kevalañca" and so forth, it is shown that "acceptance" and "handling" are intended here by the word "paṭiggahaṇa" (acceptance). In such matters, it should be understood in this way. Because it is said, "Monks, I allow these five kinds of medicinal fats: bear's fat, fish's fat, crocodile's fat, pig's fat, and donkey's fat," these five kinds of medicine are specifically authorized. However, since it is said of those medicines, "accepted at the proper time," acceptance is allowable. Therefore, it is said, "except for the medicines specifically authorized."

By the word "maṃsa" (meat), the flesh of fish is also included; to show this, it is said "āmaka-maṃsa-macchānaṃ" (raw meat and fish). Considering the example showing that fish and meat purified in three ways—not seen, not heard, and not suspected—are allowed, it should be understood that the method of virūpa-ekasesa is shown here.

Although worldly teachers say:
"An eight-year-old is called Gorī,
a ten-year-old is called Kaññā,
and when she reaches twelve years,
she is called Kumārī,"
but...
351:
Teachers say: In this context, however, the distinction between a woman and a maiden should be understood by means of having gone or not gone to another man; therefore, he said "Itthīti purisantara-gatā" and so forth. A girl of eight years is called Gaurī. A girl of ten years is called Kanyā. When she reaches twelve years, she is called Kumārī.

"Dāsidāsavasena-eva" means this is said only by way of the designation of female and male slaves. It is spoken with such allowable (kappiya) speech. Referring to the decision found in the Vinaya commentaries, it is said "Vinayavasena." That decision should be taken from the commentary on the Kuṭikāra Sikkhāpada and so forth.

It is called a field (khetta) because seeds are cast there, or because it protects the seeds that have been cast. To define a field, he said, "In which pubbaṇṇa grows." Food that exists before pulses is called pubbaṇṇa (cereals/pre-grain). By changing the letter 'n' to 'ṇ', it is called pubbaṇṇa, referring to Sāli rice and so forth. Because pulses are established in this place, that place is called vatthu (site/upland). He showed this meaning with "Vatthu nāma" and so forth. Food that exists after pubbaṇṇa is called aparaṇṇa (pulses/post-grain). Having shown the meaning according to the method of the commentaries, now, wishing to show the meaning according to the method of the Vinaya Pali, "A field is a place where either pubbaṇṇa or aparaṇṇa grows," he said "Yattha vā" and so forth. "Tadatthāya" means for the sake of the field. "Akatabhūmibhāga" refers to an unprepared portion of land intended for that field. By saying "Khettavatthu sīsena" and so forth, he shows that this is merely an illustration. By the word "ādi" (and so forth), ponds, wells, etc., are included.

It is called the work of a messenger (dūteyya) because it belongs to a messenger or because it is what a messenger ought to do. "Paṇṇa" refers to a written message. "Sāsana" refers to an oral message. "Gharā gharaṃ" means from one house to another. "Khuddakagamana" should be understood as traveling less than the travel of a messenger, not a long distance, a short journey. Since engaging in these two tasks is called anuyoga, he said "Tadubhayakaraṇaṃ." It is because of engaging in those two tasks.

Buying is called kaya. It is taking in succession and giving one's own property. Grammarians recite the root 'ki' in the sense of exchanging goods (buying and selling). Selling is called vikkaya. Teachers say it is first giving one's own property to another. In the Sāratthadīpanī Ṭīkā and others, however, it is said that kaya is taking another's goods, and vikkaya is giving one's own goods. This statement agrees with the words of the Vinaya commentary: "It is called 'bought' by bringing another's goods into one's own hand, and 'sold' by bringing one's own goods into another's hand." Deception is called vañcana (fraud). It means taking another's property by means of cleverness in stratagem to make another believe. It is called tulā (scales) because it is used for comparing and weighing.
352:
Fraud with those scales is called "tulākūṭa" (cheating by scales). One who commits tulākūṭa does so by means of the appearance (rūpākāra), the parts (aṅgākāra), the manner of holding (gahaṇākāra), and the concealed shape (paṭicchannasaṇṭhāna); thus it is said to be of four kinds. The teacher said "Gaṇhanto pacchābhāge" and so forth, meaning they weigh by placing the goods they take in the back part and the goods they give to others in the front part. Akkamati means pressing, and it is connected as "pressing in the front part." "Mūle rajjuṃ" refers to the cord attached at the base (root) of the scales. Likewise, it refers to the cord attached at the tip. "Taṃ" refers to iron powder.

It is called kaṃsa because it shines with color; these are eating and drinking vessels made of gold, silver, etc. Here, however, because it refers to a drinking vessel made of gold, it is called "suvaṇṇapātī." "Tāya vañcanaṃ" means deception by means of fraud. In the Kaṇha Jātaka commentary and others, the distinction between nikati and vañcana is stated: "Taking another's property by showing a counterfeit is called nikati; making another believe through one's own ingenuity is called vañcana due to skill in stratagem." In this commentary, however, both are called simply "vañcana." By the words "Kathaṃ" and so forth, he clearly shows only the taking of another's property by showing a counterfeit. "Samagghataraṃ" refers to the equalized special value of those golden bowls among themselves. "Pāsāṇe" refers to the touchstone that makes known whether it is gold or not. Since the nature of gold can be known only by rubbing (striking), it is said simply "ghamsitvā."

"Hadaya" is the interior of measuring vessels such as a nāḷi, and making a hole in that interior is called "hadayabheda" (breaking the heart). When measuring sesame and so forth with a nāḷi etc., the peak rising above is called "sikhā" (crest); reducing that peak is called "sikhābheda" (breaking the crest).

Making things uneven with a cord is called "rajjubheda" (breaking the cord). "Tāni" refers to ghee, oil, and so forth. "Antobhājane" refers to the vessel in which they were first placed. "Ussāpetvā" means causing to rise or making a heap on top. "Chindanto" means removing (discarding).

Overturning or subverting beyond the proper duty is called "ukkoṭana" (perverting justice). It refers to the taking of bribes by judges who act dishonestly; it does not mean merely harassing to start a new case, which is why the teacher said "Assāmike...pe... ggahaṇaṃ." "Upāyehi" means by false reasons or pretenses. In that deception, by saying "ekaṃ vatthu" (one story) instead of just "vatthu," he shows that there are many other stories as well. Other stories such as the Sasa-vatthu (Hare Story) and so forth are also mentioned in various commentaries. "Migaṃ" refers to a large deer. "Tena hi" is an exhortation to catch the deer, or it means "for that reason" because he said, "Give me the deer."
353:
The word "hi" is merely a particle. "Yogavasena" means by the power of effort such as the application of arts/sciences, chanting of mantras, and so on. "Māyāvasena" means by the power of illusion that confuses the eyes, making an unreal object appear as a real one without the chanting of mantras. Through such illusion, even things that are not jewels are seen in the form of jewels and the like. "Pāmanga" is a specific type of ornament consistent with family custom, which is called "yaññopavitta" (sacred thread) in the world. In the Vakkali Thera Apadāna, it is also said: "Behold this youth, wearing smooth yellow garments, with a golden sacred thread on his body, captivating the eyes and minds of people." In the commentary on that Apadāna, "pītamaṭṭhanivāsana" means wearing smooth, gold-colored cloth. "Hemayaññopavittanga" means having a body adorned with a golden pāmanga. "Savana, saṭhana, sāvi" mean lack of uprightness (crookedness). Therefore, it is called "kuṭilayoga" (association with crookedness), meaning association with dishonesty. By the words "etesamyeva" and so on, co-referentiality (tulyādhikaraṇa) is shown. The words "tasmā" and so on show the quality obtained. The doctrine of those teachers who speak of the four terms having different referents (bhinnādhikaraṇa) is stated by the words "keci" and so on. There, "keci" refers to the teachers who authored the Sārasamāsa and the residents of the Uttara Vihāra; it is shown by the words "taṃ pana" and so on that their view is inappropriate because "sāviyoga," which is already included in "vañcana" (deception), is taken again.

"Māraṇa" is said with reference to harming and oppressing by means of punching with the fist, hitting with a rod, and so on, but it does not mean killing (pāṇātipāta). Indeed, the word "vadha" is seen in the sense of harming in such passages as "one should cry, beating (vadhitvā) oneself repeatedly." It should be understood that here too, the word "māraṇa" occurs only in the sense of harming. Some teachers, however, say that in passages such as "having abandoned killing (pāṇātipāta) previously," it refers to doing it oneself (sayankāra), whereas here it refers to making others do it (parankāra). That cannot be said so, because it is stated: "the intention that originates bodily and vocal effort, and the six methods (payoga)." For example, although there is a general state of not being accepted, specific objects that should not be accepted by those who have gone forth, such as women, girls, female slaves, and male slaves, are mentioned separately to show their specific nature. And just as although there is a general state of taking what is not given because it is the taking of another's property, false scales and so on are mentioned separately to show the specific types of taking what is not given; in the same way, there is no purpose in taking the word "vadha," which is a synonym for killing (pāṇātipāta), again, as there is nothing to be so distinguished. Therefore, the meaning already stated (harming) is indeed better.
354:
"Viparāmosa" means causing confusion intensely and thoroughly from all sides, or it means stealing. Theft (theyya), robbery (corikā), and plundering (mosa) are synonyms. Since that "mosa" is of two kinds according to the cause, he said "gāmaviparāmosa" and so on. "Musanti" means they steal, or they plunder, or they cause confusion; it means that after causing confusion, they take their property. The word "yaṃ" is the object of that action (musanti). The phrase "maggappaṭipannaṃ janaṃ" (people on the road) also has application (adhikāra) to the other side, village-plundering (gāmaviparāmosa). "Ālopana," "vilumpana," and "ālopa" mean looting. "Sahasākaraṇa" and "sahasākāra" mean committing violence. The action that is performed with violence is "sāhasikā"; the action itself is so called.

By this much (ettāvatā), from the words "having abandoned killing" to the end "abstaining from violence," by this extent of the text. This morality (sīla), which is a collection of twenty-six training rules (sikkhāpada) as they appear directly in the Pali without taking internal divisions, is called "Cūḷasīla" (Minor Morality) because the training rules are mostly not analyzed. For here, the states of Minor (Cūḷa), Middle (Majjhima), etc., should be understood by way of the teaching (desanā), not by way of the nature of the Dhamma. Thus, the teaching of Middle Morality (Majjhimasīla) proceeds by way of analyzing the training rules that were mentioned briefly and unanalyzed here; therefore, he said, "explaining the Middle Morality in detail." The explanation of Minor Morality (Cūḷasīla-vaṇṇanā) is finished.

## Majjhimasīla-vaṇṇanā

The connection (sambandha) of the teaching beginning with "Yathā vā paneke bhonto" is stated by the words "idāni" and so on. In that Pali, this following method is a method outside the commentary (aṭṭhakathāmuttakanaya). The word "yathā" is a particle in the sense of a comparison. The word "vā" is a particle in the sense of an alternative (vikappa); by that word "vā" in the sense of an alternative, he makes an alternative of this meaning: "A worldling, even when making an effort to speak my praise, would speak only of mere morality of conduct (ācārasīla) in every way, such as 'Having abandoned killing, he abstains from killing,' by way of referring to others, but he would not speak of anything beyond that." Or: "Some honorable recluses and brahmins, while claiming to be recluses and brahmins, and being so regarded by others, do not succeed [in their practice] because they do not know or are unable to perform the practice suitable for that; this is not so with him. But this recluse Gotama has indeed fulfilled the practice suitable for a recluse in every way"—thus, by way of referring to others, he would speak only of mere morality of conduct in every way, but not of anything beyond that.
355:
The word 'pana' serves as a verbal ornament (vaca-alaṅkāra) and also functions in the sense of an alternative (vikappa) to fulfill meanings such as examples. 'Eke' refers to others. Some also say 'Ekacce'. 'Bhonto' is a pleasant mode of address used by the virtuous. Indeed, the virtuous properly address others as 'Bhonto' (Sirs/Gentlemen), 'Devānaṃ piya' (Dear to the gods), or 'Āyasmanto' (Venerable ones). 'Samaṇabrāhmaṇa' means they are 'Samaṇas' (ascetics) because they have entered some form of renunciation, and they are 'Brāhmaṇas' (brahmins) by birth alone.

In this context, 'saddhā' (faith) arises in four bases; thus, 'kammañca' and so forth are stated. Faith in this world and the next should be understood through the connection between kamma and the fruit of kamma, as in: 'In this matter, kamma bears fruit, and the fruit of kamma must be experienced.' To make this meaning known by way of exclusion (vyatireka), it is stated as 'ayaṃ me' and so forth. 'Paṭikariissati' means he will perform a return favor (reciprocate). To support that very act of reciprocation, 'evaṃ dinnāni hi' and so forth are stated. This is because it is shown by making the peak of the teaching the primary focus. By such demonstration, the four requisites are indicated, as stated in 'atthato pana' and so forth.

The word 'seyyathidaṃ' is a single particle or a collection of particles meaning 'What is that?'. Through that particle, in the phrase 'bījagāma-bhūtagāma-samārambha', although 'bījagāma' and 'bhūtagāma' are secondary according to the word order, they are pointed out as if they were primary in the context of analysis. Since the word order is one thing and the order of meaning is another, it is asked: 'What is that bījagāma-bhūtagāma?'. When that bījagāma-bhūtagāma is analyzed, the exertion (samārambha) regarding them is also analyzed. To show this meaning, it is said: 'yassa samārambhaṃ anuyuttā viharanti'. For this reason, in the Pali, it is indicated by 'mūlabīja' and so forth.

'Mūlabīja' has two meanings here: the root itself is the seed, or the root exists as a seed. The same logic applies to the remaining terms. Therefore, one should not question: 'Why is only bījagāma analyzed after asking about bījagāma and bhūtagāma?'. Among those two meanings, 'bījagāma' is indicated by the first meaning, and 'bhūtagāma' is indicated by the second meaning. Alternatively, it should be understood that both are indicated by a general reference or by the method of 'ekasesa' (single-remainder), as in 'mūlabīja and mūlabīja are mūlabīja'. For this reason, 'sabbañhetaṃ' and so forth will be said later.

'Ativisa' or 'Ativisā' is so called because it is extremely useful in medicinal preparations; it is also called 'Mahosadha'. 'Kacchaka' refers to the 'Kāḷakacchaka' tree, which some also call 'Pilakkha'. 'Kapitthana' is a white tree with sour shoots and fruit (the wood-apple tree). It is called 'Kapitthana' with the suffix 'thana' because it shakes (kampati), or 'kapi' means monkey.
356:
It is called 'Kapitthana' (wood-apple) because its fruit is like a monkey's teat. In the Visuddhimagga-ṭīkā, it is stated: 'Kapitthana is the silk-cotton tree (pippali-rukkha)'. 'Phalubīja' means joint-seed (pabbabīja). 'Ajjaka' is white basil (setapaṇṇāsa). 'Phaṇijjaka' is basil (samīraṇa). 'Hirivera' is the fragrant root (vāra). The word 'bīja' (seed) is established in the 'sāra-phala' (kernel-fruit) which is capable of germinating, as it is the specific cause for producing a similar fruit when a combination of other conditions is met; this is shown by the phrase 'only the fruit capable of germinating'. Other fruits fall into the category of non-seeds; these are fruits that have been separated from the tree. However, a fruit not separated from the tree, whether it is capable of germinating or not, is called 'bhūtagāma' according to the second meaning mentioned earlier. The distinction between them according to the Vinaya is shown by 'tattha' and so forth. What should be said here has already been stated below.

Storing up is called 'sannidhi'; requisites such as food and drink made by that storing are 'sannidhikāra'. Thus, referring to the objective sense of the word 'kāra', it is called 'sannidhikāra-paribhoga'. This is another method: Just as 'ācayaṃ gāmino' is expressed as 'ācayagāmino' by eliding the nasal (niggahīta), here too, 'sannidhikāraṃ paribhogaṃ' is expressed as 'sannidhikāra-paribhoga' by eliding the nasal; it means 'consumption after storing up'. 'Vinaya-vasena' means by the power of the conduct (ācāra) found in the Vinaya. The conduct found in the Vinaya is called 'Vinaya' by eliding the latter part (gatācāra), or Vinaya means the discipline of body and speech. Since the practice of the Suttanta method is taken separately, here only the Vinaya practice is applicable. In the term 'sallekha' (effacement), because it well-erodes the defilements, and because Vinaya practice is taken separately, only the Suttanta practice should be taken here. 'Paṭiggahita' means received by the body or by something connected to the body. 'Aparajju' means on the next day. 'Datvā' means having given by way of exchange. 'Ṭhapāpetvā' means having caused to be kept as one's own property. It is allowable to use their property through taking on trust (vissāsaggāha) and so forth. By the Suttanta method, it does not even constitute 'sallekha'.

In the phrase 'yāni ca tesaṃ anulomāni', excluding the allowable grain-juice, madhuka-flower juice, and cooked vegetable juice, all other fruit juices, flower juices, and leaf juices are to be understood as 'anuloma-pāna' (allowable drinks). 'Yathāparicchedakālaṃ' means not determined (anadhiṭṭhita) or not assigned (avikappita) for the duration of the specified time.
357:
It is called 'sannidhi' (storing up) because it is stored; it refers to the robe itself. Practicing in accordance with allowable speech is called 'pariyāya' (indirect way); speaking such an indirect hint is 'pariyāyakathā'. The opposite of that, practicing by way of contentment without resorting to thoughts of what is allowable [through hinting], is called 'nippariyāya' (direct way). Alternatively, the word 'pariyāya' occurs in the sense of 'cause'; therefore, speech spoken by way of an allowable cause is 'pariyāyakathā'. Speech spoken by way of contentment without saying such indirect words is 'nippariyāya'. The words beginning with 'Sace' (If...) show the manner of giving to another intensely. 'Uddesa' means pointing out the Pali text. 'Paripucchana' means questioning the meaning. By the words 'it is not proper not to give,' it shows the destruction of 'sallekha' (effacement) in not giving. 'Appahonte' means when one is unable to perform the action. 'Paccāsāya' means due to the desire to obtain robes. 'Anuññātakāle' (at the permitted time) refers to: if the kaṭhina is not spread, the one month of Pacchimakattika; if the kaṭhina is spread, the four months of winter including Pacchimakattika; or any one month outside the robe-season, etc., as permitted in the third Kaṭhina-sikkhāpada and others. 'Suttaṃ' refers to the thread for sewing robes. 'Vinayakammaṃ katvā' (having performed a Vinaya act) means: determining the original robe as a 'utility cloth' (parikkhāracola) and keeping the expected robe (paccāsā-cīvara) as the original robe. That robe then receives another month of protection. In this way, as long as one wishes, one can keep exchanging them as the original robe. Or, it means performing a Vinaya act by way of 'vikappanā' (assignment). To the question 'Why is it not allowable?', he said: 'Because it becomes a storage (sannidhi) and it destroys effacement (sallekha).'

A vehicle covered with a wooden roof like a pavilion or a fully enclosed carriage is called a 'vayha'. A carriage fitted with rafters made of gold, silver, etc., on both sides, constructed in the manner of a vulture's wings, is called a 'sandamānitā'. A platform-vehicle made of planks, etc., is a 'sivikā' (palanquin). A cloth litter known as an 'antolikā' is a 'pāṭaṅkī'. The words beginning with 'Ekabhikkhussa hi' support the meaning that such footwear is considered a vehicle for monks. 'Araññatthāya' means for the purpose of going to the forest. 'Dhotapādakatthāya' means for the purpose of protecting washed feet. They are called 'saṅghāṭā' because they are bound or tied. Sandals themselves are called 'saṅghāṭā' because they are bound; it means a pair of sandals. The gift should be understood here in the same manner as mentioned regarding robes for the phrase 'aññassa dātabbā' (should be given to another).

'Mañca' (bed) is merely an illustration. In fact, all items suitable for sitting or reclining, such as benches (pīṭha) and bolsters (bhisi), should be included, as one should practice regarding them in the same way as with a bed.

He shows that perfumes to be used by oneself are allowable only due to the cause of illness, with the words 'when there is an illness such as itch, scabies, skin disease, etc.' It has been stated below that 'when there is a mark (lakkhaṇa), the sense of cause (hetu) may also occur in some places.' Among those terms, 'kaṇḍu' is a dry itch, 'kacchu' is scabies, and 'chavidosa' refers to skin diseases such as ringworm, vitiligo, or freckles. It is also allowable to request (make a viññatti) medicinal requisites for a sick monk by having them brought in some way, whether from relatives, those who have given an invitation, or through alms-round. The Teacher of the Commentary said this because the Buddha taught: 'Monks, I allow one to take perfume and make a five-finger mark (pañcaṅgulika) on the door-leaf. I allow one to take flowers and place them in a suitable spot in the monastery.' Scenting the monastery with flowers and perfumes is called 'gharadhūpana'. Alternatively, scenting the shrine-room (cetiyaghara) with flowers and perfumes is called 'gharadhūpana'. By the word 'ādi' (etc.), the honoring of the cetiya and the Buddha-image is included.

It is called 'āmisa' (material things/bait) because it is handled by the defilements. To prevent viewing things like alms-food and drinks as 'āmisa' since they are indeed obtainable substances fit for use, the Commentator said, 'the remainder should be noted.' According to the pārisesa method (method of remainder), it means all usable items remaining after the aforementioned alms-food, etc., should be noted as 'āmisa'. What are those remaining items? He mentions 'seyyathidaṃ' (as follows), etc. 'Tathārūpe kāle' means for the purpose of entering the village...
358:
Kaṇḍu refers to scabies. Kacchu refers to an itch. Chavidosa refers to skin diseases such as ringworm, vitiligo, and melasma. Āharāpetvā means having it brought or procured from relatives or those who have offered an invitation, or through the practice of alms-round, or by any other means. For a sick monk, making a request (viññatti) for medicinal requisites is also allowable. Because it was said, "Monks, I allow you to take perfume and make five-finger marks on the door-panels, and to take flowers and place them in a suitable spot in the monastery" (Cullavagga), the phrase "at the door" (dvāre) and so on is mentioned. Gharadhūpana means perfuming the monastery or the stupa-house. By the word "ādi" (etc.), offerings to stupas and Buddha images should be included.

It is called āmisa (material things) because it is something to be touched by the defilements; it refers to any object suitable for use. Therefore, to prevent the misconception that āmisa refers only to the previously mentioned alms-food, drinks, etc., it is said, "The remaining objects should also be understood." Since it is taken by the method of residue (pārisesa-naya), the meaning is that all usable items remaining from what was previously mentioned should be understood as āmisa. What is this residue? It is stated starting with "seyyathidaṃ" (as follows). Tathārūpe kāle refers to a time when it is difficult to enter a village. Vallūra refers to dried meat. The word bhājana (vessel) should be connected with the words for ghee, oil, and molasses, because these things cannot exist without a container. Kālassēva means early in the morning. Udakakaddame means in water and in mud. Here, the locative case (sattamī) expresses the sense of cause (nimitta) or a characteristic state (bhāvalakkhaṇa). Acchatha means "sit down." Bhuñjantassēva means "for the monk who is eating"; it is the genitive case used in the sense of dative (sampadāna) or disregard (anādara). Here, the sense of disregard arises from interrupting the act of eating to perform another action. Gīvāyāmakaṃ is an adverb (bhāvanapuṃsaka) and means stretching the neck to make it long. Alternatively, it can refer to a situation where one has to stretch the neck because of overeating. Catumāsam-pi means throughout the four months of the rainy season. Wealth is called kuṭumba, and one who possesses that wealth is a kuṭumbika (householder). One who is shaven-headed yet lives like such a householder is called a muṇḍakuṭumbika. His livelihood is such; the meaning is that he lives by practicing such a livelihood. This should be understood as a mere indication of the types of storable items shown by the term āmisa.

To show the practice of monks who are free from that, the text says "bhikkhuno pana" (but for a monk) and so on. Therein, it is stated in the Sāratthadīpanī that "a ball of molasses is the size of a ripe palm fruit." Catubhāgamattaṃ means the amount of one kuṭumba. However, because it is said in the Commentary to be "one nāḷī of rice," teachers say that a quarter of that nāḷī is one pattha. And it is said:

"Four kuḍuvas make one pasata; four of those make a pattha.
Four patthas make an āḷhaka; four āḷhakas make a doṇa."
359:
To the question "Why?", the text says "te hi" (for they) and so on. It is allowable to have items brought and stored; how much more so to keep them as they are received? By the words "at a time of discomfort" (aphāsukakāle) and so on, it is shown that the use of rice, etc., stored with a pure mind does not disturb the practice of effacement (sallekha). Referring to the four types of huts such as the formally designated hut (sammutikuṭi), or the five types of huts including the Uposatha hall, etc., which are not residential dwellings, the text says "allowable hut" (kappiyakuṭi) and so on. There is no fault of "storing" (sannidhi) there because storing and cooking inside have been permitted. By the words "tathāgatassa" and so on, the meaning is applied according to the context. Piloti-kakhaṇḍa refers to a piece of worn-out or old cloth.

By the words "stretching the neck," it is shown that there is no fault if a performance naturally comes into one's field of vision. "Even this much" refers to the investigation of the decision and the mention of the basis. "Only for the sake of benefit" means only for the purpose of explaining the meaning of the words. If the meaning of a word cannot be understood without a detailed explanation, then in that case, the detailed explanation is also included within the word-definition (padattha-saṅgaha).

It is called pekkhā (spectacle) because it is to be looked at with curiosity; it is an undertaking according to the rules of the science of actors. Because it is performed by a group of actors for a group of people, it is called "naṭasamajja" (gathering of actors). For samajja means what is performed in a crowd or gathering of people. In the Sārasamāsa, they also say "pekkhāmahaṃ"; in the view of those teachers, the meaning is a festival for seeing a spectacle. Akkhāna (epic/legend) refers to the battles and so on of the two brother-kings named Bharata and of King Rama, which are to be recited by those trained in them. It is not even proper to go there; how much more so to listen to those stories? Intending to mean the sound produced by striking with the hands (pāṇissara), the text says "kaṃsatāḷa." Kaṃsa is a specific type of bronze musical instrument, or a bronze bowl; the meaning is the sound of striking that. Intending the meaning of the sound of clapping the hands, they also call it "pāṇitāḷa" (hand-clapping). The striking of solid musical instruments is called ghanatāḷa; it is the striking of wooden clappers or stone slabs. "By means of a mantra" means by a mantra for spirit possession. "Some" (eke) refers to the authors of the Sārasamāsa and the residents of the Uttaravihāra; wherever "eke" appears hereafter, it should be understood in the same way. They are said to be teachers who propound specific interpretations of the Dīgha Nikāya. The striking of the four-sided ambaṇaka drum refers to a drum made by creating a four-sided trough from heartwood or a staff, etc., covering the four sides with leather, and then striking it. Because that drum has the shape of a measure holding eleven doṇas, it is called "ambaṇaka"; "bimbisaka" is also a name for that same drum. Similarly, it is called kumbha because of its pot-like shape, or it is simply a pot; the reciters of the Khuddaka Nikāya say it is the striking of that pot. Abbhokkiraṇa refers to the making of offerings to deities at the place of performance. For those actors play by making what is called an offering to the deities at the place of dancing; that offering is also called "nandī".
360:
A poetic composition or dance, elaborately created through one's own manifest wisdom, which arouses defilements such as the union of men and women, is called 'Sobhanakara' because it creates beauty (or adornment). In the text 'Sārasamāsa', it is called 'Sobhanagharaka'. It refers to the game of iron balls called 'Caṇḍāla' because it is capable of being fierce. Those called 'Caṇḍāla' are of low caste and are accustomed to eating dog meat; it is also called 'Caṇḍāla' because it is their practice (or implement). The game of soaking hemp fibers with water and striking them against each other is called 'Sāṇadhovanakīḷā'. 'Vaṃsa' refers to a game played with bamboo, hence it is stated as "playing by erecting a bamboo pole."

'Nikhaṇitvā' means having buried or planted firmly in the ground. 'Nakkhattakāle' means at the time of a festival associated with a lunar mansion (constellation). To prove this meaning by the Aṅguttara Nikāya, Dasakanipāta Pāḷi, it was said: "Vuttampicetaṃ," and so forth. Therein, 'tattha' refers to that bone-washing ceremony. 'Indajālena' refers to a magical illusion where, by reciting the bone-washing mantra, others see only the bones and the flesh etc. are made to disappear. Magic is called 'Indajāla' (Indra's net) because it has the power to cover or conceal like the net of Sakka (Indra), similar to terms like 'Indacāpa' (Indra's bow). 'Aṭṭhidhovana' is indeed the game of bone-washing.

'To fight with elephants etc.' refers to riding elephants and the like to fight with others, or fighting against elephants and the like oneself. It means for others to fight with elephants etc., or for oneself to fight them. 'Te' refers to those elephants and so forth. It is the combat of those who strike with their arms, called wrestlers (malla), because they grapple and strike one another. 'Sampahāra' is indeed battle (saṅgāma). It is called 'Balagga' because it is the place where the counting or grouping of the army's strength is done. It refers to the place for counting the forces, such as "so many elephants, so many horses." It is called 'Senābyūha' because the soldiers are stationed there in distinct divisions, or because there is an arraying of the army. It is the place where the fourfold army is deployed according to specific locations for battle, such as "let the elephant troops be on this side, let the cavalry be on this side." That arraying also varies in types, such as the 'Sakaṭabyūha' (wagon array) and others. By the word 'ādi' (etc.), one should include the Cakkabyūha (wheel array), Padumabyūha (lotus array), Daṇḍabyūha (staff array), Bhogabyūha (snake array), Maṇḍalabyūha (circle array), and Asaṃhatabyūha (uncompacted array). Referring to the word-by-word commentary (padabhājana) of the Kaṇḍaviddha training rule, it was stated in the manner of "Three... etc.": "Three elephants constitute the minimum elephant corps (hatthānīka); three horses constitute the minimum cavalry (assānīka); three chariots constitute the minimum chariot corps (rathānīka); four infantrymen holding arrows in their hands constitute the minimum infantry (pattānīka)." That 'anīka' (corps) should also be understood as being described by counting the elephants and so forth, such as "twelve men per elephant, three men per horse, four men per chariot..."
361:
According to the characteristics stated in (Pācittiya 314, Uyayuttasena Sikkhāpada): "A chariot with four men, and infantry consisting of four men holding arrows in their hands," it should be understood by the counting of elephants and so on. By this, the definition of a unit (anīka) stated in the Cammaskhandhaka commentary as "six female elephants and one male elephant make one unit" is rejected.

'Kāraṇa' (cause) is said to be the basis (ṭhāna) for an effect, as in "negligence is... the basis." 'Padāni' are the positions or squares for the dice pieces (sāri) and so on. 'Aṭṭhāpada' refers to having eight squares by convention. It is also read as 'aṭṭhapada'. 'Dasapada' is a gambling game with twenty squares in two rows. 'Aṭṭhapadadasapadesu' refers to playing on eight-square and ten-square boards.

'Ākāseyeva kīḷanaṃ' (playing in the air) refers to playing a gambling game in the air by merely saying, "I have moved this piece to such-and-such a square, and this piece to such-and-such a square." 'Nānāpathamaṇḍala' refers to the circulation of dice pieces through many various paths. 'Pariharitabba' refers to the piece that is suitable to be moved. They are called 'sāriyော' (dice pieces/pawns) because they move (saranti) here and there; they are dice seeds made of any material. 'Tattha' refers to those dice pieces, or to the removing and placing of them. 'Jūtakhali' refers to the gambling circle. There is also a current reading 'jūtaphalake' (gambling board).

'Pāsaka' (die) refers to a plaything showing one to six dots on its six sides. By increasing this, they play by removing or placing the pieces according to what is obtained, such as one dot, etc. It is called 'pāsaka' because it strikes (bādhati) or touches (phusati) in games like Aṭṭhāpada; there are twenty-four types of dice. Referring to this, it is said: "The Buddha declared twenty-four modes: eight types of Mālika, six types of Sāvaṭṭa, four types of Bahula, and two types of Bindusantibhadraka." Therefore, the game here is the game of dice (pāsaka).

'Ghaṭana' means striking; playing by striking with a short stick is called 'ghaṭikā', hence it is said: "with a long stick," and so on. Some say 'ghaṭikā' is playing with a pot (ghaṭa). 'Mañjiṭṭhikā' refers to the decoction cooked from the heartwood of the madder vine (mañjiṭṭhi) which is said to be a league long. 'Sitthodaka' refers to water mixed with boiled beeswax. 'Salākahattha' is a name for a bundle of palm-leaf strips and the like. Some say 'salākahattha' is playing by taking one unmarked stick from many sticks, throwing it back in, and then picking it out again. 'Guḷakīḷā' is playing with a wood-apple or playing with any kind of nuts/balls. 'Paṇṇanāḷikā' is a pipe made of a leaf in the shape of a flute; thus it is said: "blowing it." By the word 'khuddakanaṅgala', it shows the use of the suffix 'ka' in the sense of 'khuddaka' (small). 'Mokkhacikā' is so called because one turns over (acati) while releasing (muñcitvā) the hands and feet; thus it is said: "in the air," and so on.
362:
By the word "Khuddakanaṅgala," it is shown that the suffix "-ka" is used in the sense of smallness. Because it involves turning (tumbling/acrobatics) by releasing the hands and feet, that game is called "Mokkhacikā." Therefore, it is said "ākāse vā" and so on. To show that it is called a wheel (cakka) simply because it rotates all around, it is called "Paribbhamanacakka."

A tube (cup) made of leaves is called "Paṇṇanāḷi." By this word, the synonym of the two words "Pattāḷhaka" is shown in order. Playing by measuring with that leaf-cup is called "Pattāḷhakā." Therefore, it is said "tāyā" and so on. A small chariot is called "Rathaka." This is because the word "-ka" expresses the sense of smallness. This method should be understood for the remaining words as well. Writing a letter in the air or on someone's back and making them know "this letter is such-and-such" is called "Akkharikā." Some also say it is a game of knowing things like finding a lost handful by taking a letter that comes to the mouth of the questioner. The word "vajja" has the meaning of fault/offense, so it is said "yathāvajjaṃ nāma" and so on. Dancing or singing in accordance with the music is also called "Yathāvajja."

One should understand the nature of gambling in games like dice-paths by making an effort with a focus on winning and losing, saying "If I do this, I will win; if I do this, I will lose." The effort that brings winning or losing, such as the success or failure of a task performed with bamboo strips or flute-playing, is mentioned. The word "Yathāvajja" is also used for gambling with cowries/dice by showing gestures similar to a blind person, etc., through the power of winning and losing. All these games do not exceed the meaning of the word "jūta" (gambling) in the sense that they manifest winning and losing, or that those involved in them reach winning and losing through them.

"Pamāṇātikkantāsana" refers to a seat or bedding that exceeds the prescribed size, as it is said, "A couch should be made with legs eight finger-breadths long according to the Sugata's finger-breadth." This is said with reference to its use through the word "anuyuttā viharanti." "Vāḷarūpāni" refers to figures of wild beasts such as lions and tigers. In the Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga, it is said, "A pallanka (couch/throne) is that which is made with figures of wild beasts." In the Sārasamāsa, it is said, "A couch cluttered with unallowable figures is called a pallanka." "Dīghalomako Mahākojavvo" refers to a large black rug with hair longer than four finger-breadths. It is called "Kojavva" because it stays well and extensively on the ground (ku). Because of the statement, "The hair of that rug is said to be more than four finger-breadths," [it continues...]
363:
...it is said to be allowable below [that length]. The terms "Uddalomī" and "Ekantalomī" are merely to show specific distinctions; therefore, if a rug does not fall into these categories, it should be considered allowable. "Vānavicitta" is a covering made beautiful by weaving or stitching in the form of walls, roofs, etc. "Uṇṇāmayattharaṇa" is a covering made of wool. "Setattharaṇa" is a white covering. It is called "Setattharaṇa" because it is used by those desiring coolness; some also say it is "a covering with many soft hairs." "Ghanapupphaka" is a covering complete with floral patterns in every way. In the Sāratthadīpanī, it is said, "Uṇṇāmayattharaṇa is a red covering made of wool." Because it is mostly made with rows of flowers shaped like emblic myrobalan (āmalaka) leaves, it is also called "Āmalakapatta."

"Tiṇṇāṃ tūlānaṃ" refers to the three types of stuffing known as tree cotton, vine cotton, and grass/pod cotton. A covering that has hair/fringe rising upwards on both sides is called "Uddalomī" (formed by changing the 'i' to 'a', dropping the 't', and doubling the 'd'). A covering that has hair/fringe at one end is called "Ekantalomī." "Ubhayattha keci" refers to the authors of the Sārasamāsa and the residents of the Uttaravihāra. In their view, a covering with wool-made flowers rising from one side is called "Uddalomī" according to the method mentioned. A covering with identical wool-made flowers at both ends is called "Ekantalomī"; this is the etymological meaning. In the Vinaya Commentary, however, it is said, "Uddalomī is a woolen covering with hair rising from one side; there is also a reading 'Uddhalomī'. Ekantalomī is a woolen covering with hair rising from both sides." This is merely a difference in name. In terms of meaning, it should be understood that there is no special feature left out in either commentary.

Silk (koseyya) and gold thread (kaṭṭissa) are collectively called "Kaṭṭissāni" by the method of virūpekasesa. A covering made of those silk and gold threads is called "Kaṭṭissa." To show this very meaning, it is said "koseyyakaṭṭissamayapaccattharaṇa," which means a covering woven by inserting gold threads between silk threads. It is said that gold thread is called "Kaṭṭissa" or "Kassaṭa." Therefore, the teacher Dhammapāla Thera said "koseyyakassaṭamaya." Some say "Kaṭṭissa" is a specific type of fiber. "Ratanaparisibbita" means a covering stitched with jewels; some say it is gilded with gold. "Suddhakoseyya" is a silk covering free from being stitched with jewels. The phrase "in the Vinaya" refers to either the Vinaya Commentary or the sequence of the Vinaya teaching. In this Suttanta teaching sequence, it is said, "Except for the stuffed mattress (tūlikā), all coverings such as the gonaka, even those stitched with jewels, are allowable." But when reaching the sequence of the Vinaya teaching...
364:
Because it is established in a place of respect, only a pure silk rug is allowable; it should be understood as a decision that other rugs sewn with jewels, gold thread, or silver thread are not allowable. In the Suttanta teachings, however, even if free from being sewn with jewels, a rug stuffed with cotton (tūlikā) is not allowable; other rugs not stuffed with cotton are allowable. Even if those rugs are sewn with jewels, they are allowable to be brought and spread on couches, benches, etc., as appropriate, in the manner of a floor covering. Others say that because it was taught in the Suttanta according to the capacity of laypeople, it was said, "Except for rugs stuffed with cotton... they are not allowable," for the sake of favoring those laypeople. In some palm-leaf manuscripts, there is the reading "Dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ," which means in the ancient Dīgha Nikāya Commentary. 

"Naccayoggaṃ" refers to a rug suitable for dancing. Because dancing is performed on this rug, it is called "kuttakaṃ"; that kuttaka is specifically a special type of rug with wool on both sides (uddhalomī) or wool on one side (ekantalomī). It is said:
"Rugs with wool on both sides or one side are uddhalomī and ekantalomī; if that very uddhalomī or ekantalomī rug is suitable for sixteen dancing girls to dance upon, it is called a kuttaka rug."

A rug spread on the back of an elephant is called "hatthattharaṃ." The same should be understood for the remaining terms. "Ajinacammehi" means with the skins of black antelopes; those skins are said to be very delicate, therefore they are sewn into two or three layers. Because they are sewn in that way, it is called "ajinappaveṇī"; it is called "paveṇī" because it is made continuous by the power of sewing them layer upon layer. "Kadalimigo" is a deer with the appearance of a cat (a civet-like animal); a noble rug made from the skin of that animal is likewise [not allowable]. The words beginning with "Taṃ kira" show the manner of making it; therefore, teachers say that the pure skin of the kadali deer is allowable. 

Because it covers the upper part, it is called "uttaracchado," meaning a canopy. Since only a red canopy is intended here, it is said "rattavitānena" (with a red canopy). In the phrase "Whatever rug is together with an upper canopy, that rug is called sa-uttaracchada," the remaining reading should be understood; it means it is together with being well-sewn. Among red canopies, red dyed with bark-dye (kāsāva) is allowable; only pure red dyed with safflower (kusumbha), etc., is not allowable. However, rugs of various colors, rugs made ornate by weaving, or rugs made ornate by painting are allowable. Since the bedspread itself is the primary thing, it is said that even a white canopy connected to that bedspread is not allowable. 

"Ubhato" means at both the head and the foot of the couch. Regarding these head-pillows and foot-pillows, the decision should be understood as in the case of the rug with a canopy. The phrase "padumavaṇṇaṃ vā" (or lotus-colored) is said in reference to a pillow that is not excessively red. The phrase "vicitraṃ vā" (or variegated) is said because it is allowable in every way, not because it is unallowable for pillows at both ends. In truth, the word "lohitaka" (red) does not apply to a variegated color. This is because the word "paṭalika" alone includes rugs made ornate with floral designs. 

To establish the previously mentioned meaning "if it is of proper measure" by way of exclusion, it is said, "But a large pillow is rejected." "Mahā-upadhānaṃ" refers to a pillow that exceeds the proper measure. The measure of the head itself is the measure for that pillow. The Blessed One said, "Monks, I allow the making of a pillow the size of the head." What is called "the size of the head" is a pillow that, when measured across the width between two of its three corners, is one span and four finger-breadths. The middle part of the pillow is one fist-cubit in width. In length, it is one and a half or two cubits. That pillow was rejected only because it is not allowable; it was not rejected because it falls under the category of high and luxurious beds. "Two [pillows]" means the head-pillow and the foot-pillow. "Having made a bedspread" means having spread it over the top. This statement is also said in reference only to a sick monk. Therefore, in the Senāsanakkhandhaka Vaṇṇanā, it is said: "For a monk who is not sick, only two pillows—a head-pillow and a foot-pillow—are allowable; for a sick monk, it is allowable to sleep having spread out pillows and placed a bedspread over them."
365:
The Blessed One said, "I allow a pillow the size of a head to be made." The size of a head means that when measuring the width between two of the three corners of the pillow, it is one span and four finger-breadths. The width of the center of that pillow should be a fist-cubit (muṭṭhiratana), and the length should be one and a half cubits or two cubits. Such a pillow is forbidden only because it is unallowable (due to being too large), and not because it falls under the category of high and large beds (uccāsayana mahāsayana). "Both" refers to both the head-pillow and the foot-pillow. "Having made a bedspread" means spreading a bedsheet over it; this is said with reference to a sick (gilāna) monk. Therefore, in the commentary on the Senāsanakkhandhaka, it is stated: "For a monk who is not sick, only two types—the head-pillow and the foot-pillow—are allowable. For a sick monk, however, it is allowable to lie down after spreading pillows and placing a bedspread over them," just as the Blessed One taught in the Vinaya. How did He teach? It is said, "Thus He taught," and so on. In cutting the legs of a chair (āsandi), it should be known that the base should be eight finger-breadths. As for a throne (pallaṅka), removing the attached animal figures and making them so they cannot be reattached is also considered "breaking" (bhedana). "Having unraveled" means untying the tangled knots. "To make a pillow" means making a pillow by putting those unraveled cotton fibers inside.

By the phrase "of children come forth from the mother's womb," only egg-born (aṇḍaja) and womb-born (jalābuja) beings should be taken; because of the reason "having come forth from the mother's womb," the meaning "this body odor is due to sleeping inside the mother's womb for many days" is clear. "They rub" means anointing. "To perfect the form" means to achieve a good appearance. "They massage" means kneading all around.

"Of those children" refers only to children of merit (puññavanta). They are taken because it is appropriate to the context. "Mahāmallānaṃ" refers to great wrestlers who engage in hand-to-hand combat. A "mirror" (ādāsa) is a special utensil made of bronze, iron, etc., for people who are fond of grooming to see the reflection of their own faces. With reference to such a utensil, it was said, "Whatever... is not allowable." In this context, only decorative eye-liner is meant, not medicinal eye-ointment. Since the intention is the practice of grooming, medicinal eye-ointment is not intended here. In the world, the word "mālā" refers only to a bound garland of flowers, according to the expression "mālā, mālyaṃ, pupphadāmaṃ". However, in the Dispensation (Sāsana), it is also established for loose flowers; thus it is said, "whether it be an unbound garland." "Of black moles, pimples, etc." refers to dark-colored boils and sores. "Fine clay" (mattikakakka) is clay powder prepared with medicinal herbs. "They give" means anointing. "Calite" refers to destruction when movement occurs due to transformation. After causing the bad blood, which is the cause of black moles and pimples, to coagulate with mustard powder and removing it, when that bad blood is exhausted, "with face powder" means anointing with scented powder suitable for the face. Anointing the face with face powder and face unguents, such as fine clay, mustard powder, sesame powder, and turmeric powder, is not allowable. Since the meaning can follow in sequence, this is the explanation of the two terms "mukhacuṇṇakaṃ mukhavilepanaṃ". Alternatively, the two terms can be interpreted as synonyms (tulyādhikaraṇa) for face unguent called face powder. "Binding on the hand" refers to an ornament worn on the hand. Since those ornaments include conch-shell rings, etc., it is said, "conch-shell, etc." The conch-shell itself is the shell (kapāla). With the words "others," etc., the meanings of terms such as sikhābandhana (hair-knot ornament) are explained in order. Among those terms, "sikhā" means a crest or a top-knot. "Cīraka" is [something] to make the crest or top-knot firm...
366:
The term "calite" means when it has come to movement, it is destroyed. "Tena" means by mustard powder. "Dose" refers to the defect of the blood which is the cause of blackheads, pimples, etc. "Khādite" means when it is removed by way of elimination. "Sannisinne" means when such bad blood is exhausted. "Mukhacuṇṇakena" means with face-smearing powder. "Cuṇṇenti" means they smear or apply. All face powders and face-smearing perfumes, such as those made of fine clay, mustard powder, sesame powder, and turmeric powder, are unsuitable. Because it should follow the sequence of meaning, this is the explanation of the two terms "mukhacuṇṇaka" and "mukhavilepana." Alternatively, it is an elucidation of the meaning of the two terms as synonyms, meaning face-smearing perfume known as face powder.

"Hatthabandhana" refers to ornaments to be bound on the hand, and regarding them, such as conch-shell bangles, it is said "on the hand," etc. The conch-shell itself is the shell (bangle). By the words "apare" (others), etc., the meanings of terms such as "sikhabandhana" are explained in order. Therein, "sikhā" means the topknot (crest). "Cīraka" is a decorative hairpin inserted to make the topknot firm and beautiful. A string of pearls or a sequence of pearls is called "muttālatā." A staff of four cubits is called "daṇḍa." "Alaṅkatadaṇḍaka" refers to something shorter than that, such as a chariot goad. "Bhesajjanāḷika" is a medicine tube (medicine box). Since it is customary to carry the alms-bowl, etc., only on the left shoulder, it is said "hung on the left side." "Kaṇṇikā" means a pinnacle (bud-shaped ornament), and it refers to a sword whose sheath is surrounded by that pinnacle and jewels. "Pañcavaṇṇasuttasibbita" refers to the three types of umbrellas sewn with threads of five colors: blue, yellow, red, white, and crimson. "Ratanamattāyāmaṃ caturaṅgulavitthataṃ" is stated either by way of practice or by the measurement sufficient to bind on the forehead. By the words "showing the end of the hair," it shows the manner of binding the headband without covering the hairline. "Meghamukhe" means inside the clouds. The word "maṇi" refers to the head-ornament jewel, so it is called "cūḷāmaṇi," meaning a jewel on the topknot. A whisk made from the hair of a yak (camarī) is called "cāmaravālabījanī." Since whisks for mosquitoes, bark whisks, usīra-root whisks, peacock-feather whisks, and palm-leaf fans are allowable, it should be understood that only the (unallowable) yak-tail whisk is taken here.

Because one escapes from the miserable states and from saṃsāra by this means, it is called "niyyāna" (leading out/emancipation). It is the path to heaven and the path to liberation. Because it is worthy of that emancipation, or because it is joined with that emancipation, or because that emancipation is its fruit, it is called "niyyānikā." Alternatively, because it leads out from the defilements of verbal misconduct, it is called "niyyānikā." Here, making the long 'ī' short and adding the letter 'ya'...
367:
...and adding the letter 'ka' (it is called niyyānikā). In fact, the word 'aniya' often expresses the meaning of 'ka'. Here, the abstinence from frivolous talk (samphappalāpa) along with the volition (cetanā) is intended. Because it is the opposite of that 'niyyānikā', frivolous talk is 'aniyyānikā' (not leading out); the state of that is 'aniyyānikatta'; because of that state of not leading out from the miserable states and saṃsāra (it is called aniyyānikatta). 'Tiracchānabhūtā' means being obstructive and hindering, so that one does not see or know the Path, Fruit, and Nirvana. Here, the word 'nāma' in 'so pi nāma' is used in a sense of reproach. 'Kammaṭṭhānabhāve' means in the state of a meditation subject of the Four Truths, because it is connected with impermanence. 'Kāmassādavasena' means by way of the gratification known as sensual pleasure. 'Saha atthena' is 'sātthaka', meaning connected with benefit. The word 'upāhanā' (sandals) is said in connection with talk about vehicles. Because it is well-inserted, it is called 'suniviṭṭha'. Similarly, that which is badly placed is called 'dunniviṭṭha'. By the word 'gāma' (village), the people living in the village are also taken; therefore, it is said "the residents of such-and-such a village," etc.

'Sūrakathā' (talk about heroes) in this context, the word 'sūra' expresses bravery (vīra), as shown by the words "he was a hero." 'Visikhā' refers to a place where roads meet; here, by taking 'visikhā', those living at that junction are also taken, just as in the saying "the whole village has come"; therefore, it is said "the faithful and devoted," etc.

The place of the pot is called the place of water, hence it is called 'udakaṭṭhānakathā' (talk about the water-place). It is also called 'udakatitthakathā' (talk about the water-landing) because it is included in that same water-place. Alternatively, the place where pots are made is 'kumbhaṭṭhāna'. By indicating that place of pots, it shows that pot-carrying slave women are meant, as shown by the words "or talk about pot-slaves (kumbhadāsikathā)." Relatives who have died in the past are called 'pubbapeta'. The three terms 'peta', 'pareta', and 'kālaṅkata' are synonymous. To point out the method mentioned below, the words "therein," etc., are stated.

'Purimapacchimakathāhi vimuttā' means talks that are free from the preceding and succeeding talks mentioned in this sutta. By the words 'nānāsabhāvā', it states that it is a synonym for the nature of 'atta' (self). 'Asukena nāma' refers to Pajāpati, Brahmā, or Viṣṇu. Because the world is described by way of its arising, duration, and constituents, etc., it is called 'lokakkhāyikā' (cosmogony). It shows that this talk is based on the Vitanda treatise known as Lokāyata, as shown by the words "Lokāyata-vitaṇḍa-sallāpakathā." It is called 'Lokāyata' because fools exert themselves in this treatise due to their relish for its views. Or, it is called 'Lokāyata' because the world does not strive or seek benefit through that treatise. Depending on that book, beings do not even [incline] their minds to perform meritorious deeds...
368:
It is called Vitaṇḍa (sophistry) because it expands upon talk that is mutually contradictory or talk that is contrary to heaven and liberation. Alternatively, it is called Vitaṇḍa because in this work, proponents strike at other proponents with the stick of contradictory views. The formation of words should be understood through the method of linguistics (nirutti) in all instances.

In the phrase 'dug by Sāgaradeva', it is also said to be dug by the sons of King Sāgara. It is called Samudra (ocean) because it has a head (muddhā) which is the cause of knowing; here, the letter 'dh' is changed to 'd'. In this word, the term 'sa' expresses the meaning of existence, as in 'with hair, with wings' (salomako sapakkhako), etc. Bhava means growth; it is called bhava because it grows. Vibhava means decline, as it is devoid of that growth. Since the word 'iti' heard before a dvanda compound should be applied to each term, it is said, 'thus bhava, thus abhava'. 'Whatever or that' (yaṃ vā taṃ vā) means 'anything whatsoever', implying an indefinite sense. The teachers show the false and indefinite meaning with the words 'yaṃ' and 'taṃ' along with the alternative (vikappa). Alternatively, bhava means the eternalist view (sassata-diṭṭhi), and abhava means the annihilationist view (uccheda-diṭṭhi). Or bhava means the pleasure of the senses, and abhava means the practice of self-mortification.

Thus, together with these six kinds of talk on bhava and abhava, there are thirty-two kinds of lowly talk (tiracchānakathā). Alternatively, although not explicitly mentioned in the Pāḷi text, talk about forests, mountains, rivers, and islands is included by the word 'iti' and thus called the thirty-two kinds of lowly talk. In the phrase 'iti vā' in the Pāḷi text, the word 'iti' has the meaning of variety (pakāra), and the word 'vā' has the meaning of alternative (vikappa). This means: 'They live devoted to such a variety of, or other such kinds of, useless talk.' Or, the word 'iti' has the meaning of 'and so forth' (ādi), as in 'abstaining from seeing shows of dancing, singing, and music' (naccagīta-vādita-visūkadassanā paṭivirato), etc.; it means they live devoted to other such talk beginning with these.

Taking up a contradiction is called viggaha; those who have such contradictions are called viggāhikā (wranglers), and their talk is thus called viggāhikā kathā. Or it is called viggāhikā kathā because one takes up contradictions by means of that talk. Sārambhakathā is aggressive talk (upārambhakathā) that oppresses others. Sahito means talk that is not contradictory from beginning to end. For that very reason, it is smooth and coherent. To show that such talk is smooth because it is endowed with meaning and reason, it is said, 'it has the meaning of being endowed with benefit and endowed with reason.' The word 'taṃ' (it) stands revolved. It means one knows nothing, like a soldier who has fallen into the hands of the enemy and is powerless, but only defeats oneself. 'Vāda' (argument) and 'dosa' (fault) are synonymous terms. Likewise...
369:
'Go, wander.' 'There and there' means in the various lineages of teachers. 'Solve' (nibbedhehi) means 'resolve and destroy the view I have proposed.'

The work of a messenger is called dūteyya (errand-running); the talk of such a messenger is also the same. Here, the words 'here and there' (idha, amutra) are locative cases used in the sense of the accusative; therefore, it means 'such and such a place.' Since the detailed decision is stated in the Vinaya Commentary, it is stated here briefly as 'but in brief,' etc. 'News of laypeople' means news that is the opposite of what was previously mentioned. 'Of others' means only of laypeople.

'In three ways' means by the three divisions: speaking in the vicinity of the four requisites, depending on postures, and the use of the four requisites. 'They cause amazement' means they cause others to feel amazement and admiration for them, thinking, 'This is an amazing man!' Scholars of linguistics say that the root 'mhi' preceded by 'vi' is used in the sense of joy. The state of joy itself is amazement. 'They talk' means they praise either themselves or the donor so that the donor gives something, showing it by way of praising and uplifting to remove hesitation. Because they have the habit of making signs, they are called nemittika (hinters); this is in the sense of habit by the power of the taddhita suffix, just like 'pāṃsukūlika' (dust-heap-robe-wearer). Alternatively, they are called nemittika because they speak by means of signs or make signs. A 'sign' refers to bodily or verbal action that produces the perception of wanting to give requisites in others. Grinding into fine powder is called nippesa. Because they grind and oppress, it is called nippesa; that very nippesa is called nippesika. Alternatively, because they perform the act of grinding and oppressing, they are called nippesika. Nippesa refers to abusing, disparaging, ridiculing, and backbiting (eating the flesh of another's back) for the sake of gain and honor, like a servant. 'Gain with gain' means seeking gain in one place with gain obtained from another. The three words 'nijigīsanti', 'magganti', and 'pariyesanti' are synonyms meaning 'to seek.' Words such as kuhaka (schemer) are said to be 'names for kuhana (scheming), etc.' because they arise in persons endowed with those qualities, based on scheming, etc. 'And the commentary' (aṭṭhakathañca) refers to the ancient commentaries that explain the meaning of the various Pāḷi texts.

## The Explanation of the Middle Morality is Finished.
370:
## Mahāsīla-vaṇṇanā

Because it occurs based on limbs such as the hands and feet, the entire treatise associated with limbs is called 'Aṅga'. Alternatively, it is called 'Aṅga' by the method of eliding the subsequent word. The same method applies to the word 'Nimitta'; hence the statement beginning with 'hatthapādādīsu' was made. However, some teachers say that 'Aṅga' refers to the deformation of limbs, and it is the knowledge of gain, loss, etc., obtained by observing the deformation of others' limbs (or the treatise that makes this known).

'Nimitta-sattha' (the science of signs) is the treatise that explains the various ways of knowing through signs. To clarify this treatise with an illustrative story, the passage beginning with 'Paṇḍu-rājā' was stated. 'Paṇḍu-rājā' is also referred to simply as 'Dakkhiṇārāmādhipati' (the Lord of Dakkhiṇārāma). It is said that he was the king who built the monastery named Dakkhiṇārāma in the island of Sri Lanka. In some palm-leaf manuscripts, it is written as 'Dakkhiṇamadhurādhipati', meaning the ruler of the city of Southern Madhura. 'Muttāyo' refers to pearls. 'Muṭṭhiyā' refers to a hand gesture (mudrā). 'Gharagolikāyā' refers to a house gecko. That diviner spoke of 'muttā' (pearls) by way of a perception-sign (saññā-nimitta), and 'tisso' (three) by way of a number-sign (saṅkhyā-nimitta).

By the word 'mahantānaṃ', it is shown that a small sign is merely a 'nimitta' (sign), whereas a great sign is called an 'uppāda' (portent); this shows the distinction between signs and portents. 'Uppatitaṃ' refers to 'uppatana' (falling of lightning, etc.). It is called 'uppāda' because it arises while manifesting good or bad results; it is also called 'uppāta'. It is a transformation of the great elements (mahābhūta) that indicates good or bad fortune. Such phenomena, like a falling meteor, merely manifest the result of kamma, just as smoke manifests fire; they do not actually cause that result.

'Idaṃ' refers to a result of such a name. 'Evaṃ' refers to being in such a manner. 'Ādisanti' means they point out. 'Pubbaṇhasamaye' is stated by way of time. 'Idaṃ nāma' is stated by way of the object. When a person dreams of themselves riding a bull, an elephant, or ascending a palace or a mountain, the object is described as "such-and-such a result will occur." 'Supinakaṃ' refers to the treatise on dreams.

Although 'Aṅga' was previously mentioned merely to show the perfection or failure of limbs, here 'Lakkhaṇa' (marks) is used to show special characteristics that produce great power and influence. This is the difference between the two. 'Lakkhaṇa' refers to specific features visible on the major and minor limbs, such as a sword, Sīrivaccha, mace, palace, and so on. Because various results are marked by these major and minor limbs, they are called 'lakkhaṇa'; the treatise is also called 'lakkhaṇa' because it reveals them.

'Āhate' refers to old (cloth). 'Anāhate' refers to new (cloth). In the reading 'Ahate', however, the meaning should be understood as the opposite of what was stated. 'Ito paṭṭhāya' means that when parts of various cloths, which are appropriately designated as belonging to devas, yakkhas, humans, etc., are bitten (by mice) from this or that place, such-and-such results like wealth and prosperity occur. 'Evarūpena dārunā' refers to wood such as Palāsa or Sirīphala; likewise, it refers to a ladle. If ladle-oblations (dabbihoma), etc., also...
371:
Regarding the question of why these such as ladle-offerings (dabbihoma) and others are taught separately even though they are also fire-offerings (aggihoma), the teachers state "of such a nature," and so forth. Dabbihoma and others are taught to show special results through specific implements and structures of fire-offering, while aggihoma is taught in the sense of completing the remaining factors not mentioned. Therefore, it is said "dabbihomādīni," etc.

Kuṇḍaka refers to rice-powder or broken rice. Because it is the product of sesame (tila), it is called tela (sesame oil). Since compound (samāsa) and derivative (taddhita) terms often become generic (sāmañña) in well-known contexts, the term "tilatelādikaṃ" (sesame oil, etc.) is used for the sake of specification. Pakkhipana is for the purpose of throwing into the fire. There is also a variant reading "pakkhipanavijjā," which means the science that is the cause of throwing into the fire. It refers to "blood from the right collarbone, blood from the right knee," and so forth. By showing the distinction between the treatise on limbs (aṅga) and the science of bodily marks (aṅgavijjā) with the word "pubbe" etc., the fault of redundancy (punarutti) is removed.

"Seeing the finger-bone (aṅgulaṭṭhi)" means seeing a bone that is a finger or a bone produced in a finger; it means they make predictions by specifically observing that bone without looking at the skin of the finger. However, the teacher Elder Dhammapāla stated, "aṅgulaṭṭhi refers to the body." In that case, the body itself is understood as aṅgulaṭṭhi because the growth of major and minor limbs is like a vine (laṭṭhi). Kulaputta (son of a good family) refers to both being a kulaputta by birth and a kulaputta by conduct. In the term "disvāpi," the word "api" is used to include the sense of "even without seeing." The treatise of the teacher Abbhi is the Abbheyya treatise; the treatise composed by the teacher Māsurakkha is the Māsurakkha treatise; the treatise used by kings is the Rājasattha treatise. All these are treatises related to the science of statecraft (khattavijjā).

The word siva has the meaning of peace (santi), thus it is called "santikaraṇavijjā" (the science of making peace). It means the science that pacifies dangers and calamities. When the word sivā is shortened (rassa) and called "sivavijjā," it is said to refer to the "siṅgālarutavijjā" (the science of jackal cries), which is the science of knowing good and bad omens by listening to the cries of jackals. "Bhūtavejjamanta" refers to spells for subduing and controlling spirits (bhūta). Bhūrighara refers to a house made underground or a house made of fine clay. In the Sārasamāsa treatise, it is said, "bhūrivijjā is the science of making crops flourish and multiply."

Sappāvhāyanavijjā is the science of summoning snakes. Visavanta means the flowing out or vomiting of poison. Here, the suffix -māna indicates the sense of the suffix -anta. The construction should be: the science by which they cause poison to flow out is called visavijjā (toxicology). There is also a variant reading "visatantra"; in that case, it serves as an illustration of a treatise that analyzes poison. Tantra is another name for a treatise. It refers to the cries (ruta) and movements (gata) of winged creatures (flies, etc.), wingless creatures (house lizards, etc.), two-legged creatures (devas, humans, seagulls, etc.), and four-legged creatures (chameleons, rabbits, jackals, etc.). Thus, in this context, "sakuṇavijjā" (the science of birds) means...
372:
It shows either the elision of the word miga or serves merely as an example. Sakuṇañāṇa is the knowledge of good and bad results by means of birds. One might ask, "Is not the science of crows (vāyasavijjā) included in the science of birds (sakuṇavijjā)?" To this, it is said, "That science of crows is indeed a separate treatise." It should be understood that in this teaching, various statements are made according to the respective treatises that explain those specific meanings.

Reaching the state of maturity should be taken in terms of the physical body (attabhāva) and the duration of life, as shown by the words "now," and so forth. Ādisiṭṭhañāṇa is the knowledge of things that are pointed out or indicated. Sararakkhaṇa is protecting oneself from arrows or protecting the arrow from oneself. By the phrase "encompassing all," it shows the application of the word miga to all birds and beasts. Alternatively, this is a designation by way of eka-sesa (one remains), because the word miga is well-established only for four-legged animals. The treatise for knowing the cries of all birds and beasts is called Migacakka. Just as in the various ways of knowing good and bad omens, the best treatise is called Cakka and so forth, it is said "sabba...pe... vuttaṃ."

The words "sāmino" etc., are statements that cause the distinction between what is praiseworthy and what is not. Lakkhaṇa refers to the treatise that explains the characteristics of those gems. By the method of elimination (pārisesa), weapons other than the sword are called āvudha. By the words "in which clan" etc., it shows that in this context, the cause of such knowledge is the remaining lakkhaṇa. This distinction refers to the distinction from the characteristics (lakkhaṇa) mentioned below. To clarify that meaning, it is said, "herein, this is the matter." Aggim dhamamānaṃ means making the fire blaze with the wind from the mouth. Makkhesi means it destroys. Piḷandhanakaṇṇikāyā refers to an ear-ornament; gehakannikāyā refers to the peak of a house. Thus, it is endowed with the eka-sesa method or generic designation (sāmaññaniddesa). Kacchapalakkhaṇa is the science of tortoise signs. By the phrase "of all four-legged animals," it states that the word miga denotes four-legged creatures.

Asukadivase is stated by way of lunar days (tithi) such as the second, third, etc. Asukanakkhattena is stated by way of the moon's conjunction with constellations such as Assayuja, Bharaṇī, Kattikā, Rohiṇī, and so forth. Vippavutthānaṃ means those who have departed and are away from their own home. Upasaṅkamanaṃ means approaching. Apayānaṃ means departing. Dutiyapadepi refers to the second sentence stated as "bāhirānaṃ raññaṃ...pe... bhavissati." The victory and defeat stated by the two sentences "abbhantarānaṃ raññaṃ jayo" etc., are indeed clear.

Rāhu is the Asura king named Rāhu who rules over the Asuras. Indeed, it is stated in the Asuranikāya of the Mahāsamaya Sutta—
373:
## 
“The hundred sons of Bali the Asura are all named Verocana; having equipped the army of Bali, they approached the noble Rāhu, Lord of Asuras,” so it is stated (in the Dīgha Nikāya, Mahāvagga Pāḷi).

The matter of Rāhu the Lord of Asuras seizing (eclipsing) the moon and the sun should be understood through the Candima Sutta and Suriya Sutta in the Saṃyutta Nikāya. In this context, the word “iti” carries the meaning of “and so forth.” Since it is mentioned as “lunar eclipses and so forth,” solar eclipses and eclipses of constellations (nakkhatta) must also be included by that term. Therefore, it should be understood that Rāhu seizes constellations just as he seizes the moon and the sun. It is precisely because of this seizing of constellations that the second method regarding the seizing of constellations is stated with the words “api ca,” etc.

“Conjunction with Mars and so forth” means that being in conjunction with the planets known as Mars, Mercury, the Sun, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, and Ketu is also considered the seizing of constellations (planetary transit). This is because conjunction is also regarded as “seizing.” In Vedic treatises, conjunction is also called “gahaṇa” (seizing).

“Falling of meteors” refers to the falling of meteoric lights. When atmospheric masses collide with great force, a light similar to the glow of a torch is produced and falls from the sky. This falling is called “falling of meteors.” In the Jyotiṣa treatise, it is also said:
“Meteors are known to be of various kinds: those with great flames, those with small flames, those shining with reddish-brown flames, and those about the height of a man.”

“Turbidity of the quarters” refers to the agitation in the directions. This state is shown by the words “as if cluttered with flames and smoke-flames.” The prominent appearance of many flames and smoke-flames is called “burning of the quarters” (disādāha). Worldly people call this burning of the quarters a “comet” (dhūmaketu). In the Jyotiṣa treatise, it is also said:
“The light that has a flame like a banner and appears to fall from the sky is called Jyoti (comet).”

“Thunder without rain” refers to the rumbling of clouds shaken by the force of the wind without rain. Worldly people call this sound “nighāta” (impact). In the Jyotiṣa treatise, it is also said:
“When a strong wind in the atmosphere, struck by another wind, falls downwards, that wind-born sound is called ‘nighāta’.”

“Udayana” means the rising (of the sun) or the rising of the ascendant (lagna). It is said: “When the sun rises, then the rising of the zodiac signs in succession (lagna) occurs.” The setting of the sun is also [determined] by the measure of the seventh zodiac sign...
374:
## 
Indeed, the setting of the sun (atthaṅgamana) should also be understood by the power of the measure of the seventh zodiac sign from that [rising sign]. Impurity is caused by these four reasons: clouds, smoke, dust, and Rāhu the Asura. Freedom from these four reasons is called “purity” (vodāna). Thus it is also said: “Monks, there are these four stains (upakkilesa) of the sun and moon, by which stains the sun and moon, being defiled, do not burn, do not shine, and do not blaze. What four? Clouds, monks, are a stain of the sun and moon. Smoke... Dust... Rāhu, monks, is a stain of the sun and moon. Monks, by these four stains, the sun and moon do not burn, do not shine, and do not blaze” (Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.50).

“Deva” is a term for rain. Continuous raining is called “vassana.” “Avaggāha” is the poor taking (lack) of the rain-stream. Therefore, it is called “drought” (vassavibandha). “Hatthamuddā” (hand-gestures) refers to making known the desired numbers by the hand. The teacher Dhammapāla Thera says that this is merely counting by the contraction of fingers. However, the teacher Sāriputta Thera shows that “hatthamuddā is counting by placing marks on the finger-joints.” “Gaṇanā” (arithmetic) refers to continuous counting by the method ending in nine, using the principle of remainders. This counting should be understood as continuous counting by the ninefold method, such as “one, two,” etc., like that of rustics and farmers. “Samūhana” is addition (saṅkalana). “Visuṃ uppādana” is producing separately or subtraction (apanayana). “Paṭuppādana” is also read as “saduppādana,” meaning “properly producing” (subtracting). By the word “ādi” (and so forth), terms such as aggregation (vokalana), division (bhāga), and distribution (hāra) are included. Therein, “vokalana” is making a separate group (mixing). “Bhāga” is making portions (division). “Hāra” is distributing or analyzing. “Sā” refers to the aforementioned aggregate counting (piṇဍgaṇanā). In the word “disvā” (having seen), the meaning should be taken as “having counted merely by seeing.”

In this context of “paṭibhānakavi,” the remaining words “(four types of) poets” as taught in the Aṅguttara Nikāya should be understood. It should be connected as “the poetry-making of poets.” By this, it shows the meaning of “poetry made by poets” or “poetry belonging to poets.” The words “by the power of one's own reflection,” etc., show the nature of those poets.
