Indeed, a “poet of reflection” (cintākavi) should be understood as one who creates by reflecting on the subject matter and the connection by himself for a long time. A “poet of tradition” (sutakavi) is one who creates by connecting what has not been heard with what has been heard. A “poet of meaning” (atthakavi) is one who creates by expanding or condensing a certain meaning that he has grasped. A “poet of intuition” (paṭibhānakavi) is one who, having seen a poem or a play created by another, creates another similar work through his own spontaneous intuition (paṭibhāna). “Nti” means (that is) the meaning.
375:
“Tappaṭibhāga” means being similar to what has been seen. In the word “kattabba” (should be done), it is an adjective; or in the word “kariṣṣāmi” (I will do), it is a neuter abstract noun. “By the power of spontaneous intuition” (ṭhānuppattika-paṭibhāna) means by the power of knowledge that arises in accordance with the cause. “For the sake of livelihood” is meant only in the sense of what is attained through the scriptures. The property of poets is called “poetry” (kavya), and that poetry is also called “song” (gīta).

Taking a girl as a possession is called “āvāhana.” Similarly, giving [a girl] is called “vivāhana.” In this context, it is indicated either by the dropping of the subsequent word of that action or by the power of the causal meaning; therefore, it was said, “of this boy,” and so forth. “Iti” means when it is thus, or because it is thus. “Uṭṭhāna” refers to the revenue or interest arising from fields and such. “Iṇa” (debt) is a loan given to another for the sake of increasing wealth. Some say that a debt recovered before the specified time is called “uṭṭhāna,” while a debt recovered when the specified time arrives is called “iṇa,” but this is not appropriate because the meaning is already accomplished by the word “iṇa” itself. It should be connected as a debt or wealth given to others. “Thāvara” refers to permanent or long-lasting property. “Payoga” (investment) is the engagement of goods for the purpose of receiving double or triple [profit] in another region. “Uddhāra” is the taking of profit according to the specified time, whether in that place or elsewhere. Others also say that giving wealth to those without capital, saying, “Trade and return the capital along with this much profit,” is “payoga,” while a temporary loan is “uddhāra.”

“The wealth invested today becomes double or fourfold” means that if goods are invested (loaned) today, they become double the next day, or fourfold this very day. To exist with beauty (subha) is “subhaga”; the act of making it so is “subhagakaraṇa.” Since this is merely the act of making one beloved and pleasing, or making one auspicious, it is said, “making one beloved and pleasing,” and so forth. “Making one auspicious” means making the body beautiful. “Vilīna” refers to the destruction of the fetus after it has been established but before it reaches maturity. Likewise, it is the failure to remain in a mature state. These four terms are synonyms. “Giving medicine” refers to giving medicine that stabilizes the pregnancy. Regarding the phrase “by three causes,” when the fetus is destroyed by wind or by parasites, even if past kamma has not provided the opportunity, kamma can ripen because of those causes (wind or parasites). However, if kamma itself has provided the opportunity, there is no absolute need to depend on wind or parasites; thus, kamma is mentioned as a separate cause. In the Vinaya Commentary (Samantapāsādikā), however, it is stated as “by two other causes,” with the intention that the fetus cannot be destroyed by wind or parasites without the involvement of kamma. “Nibbāpanīya” refers to a cooling or soothing medicine. “Paṭikamma” is the remedy or treatment so that those parasites do not consume [the fetus].
376:
“Bandhakaraṇa” means making the tongue such that it cannot move or be agitated (i.e., making the tongue heavy/stiff). “Parivattanattha” means for the purpose of turning hands raised with weapons etc. to another place, or for the purpose of throwing elsewhere instead of throwing in the place one had intended. “Khipati” also means throwing to another place. “Vinicchayaṭṭhāne” means in the place of judgment (the court). Some also say that “kaṇṇajappana” (whispering in the ear) is the recitation by way of speaking the desired benefit into the ear of a deity. In the phrase “devataṃ otāretvā,” it means invoking a deity through the recitation of incantations. “Jīvikatthāya” means for the purpose of making a living, just as one lives by performing service. “Ādiccapāricariya” (sun-worship) is the service to the sun by standing facing the sun all day long and making offerings with radiant (or red) flowers. By the word “tatheva,” the word “jīvikatthāya” is drawn in. “Sirivhāyaṇa” is a euphonic combination (sandhi) where the ‘a’ is dropped after the ‘ī’; therefore, it is said “siriyā avhāyaṇaṃ” (the invocation of the goddess Siri). By the word “sirena,” the manner of invocation by way of the location is shown. However, in the reading of teachers who drop the ‘a’ after ‘a’ and read it as “siravhāyaṇa,” the meaning is “invoking the desired benefit with the head by reciting incantations.”

“Devaṭṭhāna” refers to a shrine (the abode of a deity). “Upahāra” means an offering or oblation. “Samiddhikāle” means at the time when the requested benefit is fulfilled. “Santipaṭissavakamma” is the making of a promise to perform an offering made by way of entreating a deity. Here, “santi” refers to making an offering by reciting incantations; it means the effort of praying through that offering. “Tassmiṃ” refers to the desired matter which is the result of the promise, as in saying, “If this matter of mine is fulfilled.” “Tassā” refers to that promise (offering) which is called “paṇidhi.” This is because when the offering is made according to the promise, the prayer (vow) is considered fulfilled. “Gahitamantassa” refers to one who has learned the incantations. “Payogakaraṇa” means performing the ritual nearby. The word “iti” is a particle in the sense of cause; by that word, it shows the occurrence of the terms “vassa” and “vossa” in relation to male eunuchs (paṇḍakas) as a cause. One is called “vassa” because he has [male organs] in excess of a [typical] eunuch. One is called “vossa” because, being devoid of male organs, he is despised and lives in a lowly manner. Alternatively, according to the method of nirutti (etymology), one is called “vassa” because he has an excess of the flow of passion (rāga-savana), and one is called “vossa” because he is devoid of the flow of passion. “Vassakaraṇa” is the act performed with appropriate medicine. “Vossakaraṇa,” however, is the act performed by removing the testicles and so forth; therefore, it is said in the Jātaka Commentary, “Vossavaras are harem guards whose testicles have been removed.”
377:
It has been stated (in the Commentary): "Acchandikabhāvamatta" means merely the state of a woman being without desire. "Liṅga" refers to the male organ.

"Vatthubalikammakaraṇa" means performing offerings to deities (bali) at a building site or house. Such acts are performed to ward off dangers and to bring about prosperity. It also includes the purification of the mouth and face of oneself and others through the chanting of mantras. "Tesaṃ" means "of others." "Yoga" refers to the application of medicine. "Vamana" refers to the act of inducing vomiting (cutting off food). "Uddhaṃvirecana" is specifically a form of vomiting, as it is described as "the expelling of faults (dosas) upwards." "Virecana" refers to normal purgation. "Adhovirecana" refers to the cleansing of the lower bowels and bladder through procedures such as suddhavatthi and kasāvavatthi, as it is described as "the expelling of faults downwards."

Furthermore, simple nausea is called "vamana," while the upward expulsion of faults such as bile and phlegm is called "uddhaṃvirecana." Similarly, simple purging is called "virecana," while the downward expulsion of faults is called "adhovirecana." Thus, the distinction between these terms is clear. "Dosānaṃ" means "of the faults" such as bile and so on. The expulsion of phlegm and other substances from the head is called "sirovirecana" (head purgation). "Kaṇṇabandhanattha" is for the purpose of reattaching severed ears. "Vaṇaharaṇattha" is for the purpose of removing or healing wounds. "Akkhitappanatela" is an oil that removes heat from the eyes. When this oil is applied to the eyes, hot vapors are released. Medicine taken through the nose is called "natthu" (snuff).

"Paṭalāni" refers to the films or membranes in the eyes. "Nīharaṇasamattha" means capable of removing. "Khārañjana" is a pungent or saline eye-ointment. According to the method of linguistics (nirutti), "sīta" (cool) is itself called "sacca"; therefore, the ointment that causes this coolness is called "saccañjana." Thus, the teacher said "cooling medicinal eye-ointment."

"Salākavejjakamma" refers to the treatment of eye diseases. Because the eye disease (cataract) resembles a splinter (salāka), its treatment is called "sālākiya" (ophthalmology). This term is used to include other eye treatments not yet mentioned, as it was said, "Treatments such as tappana are also indeed sālākiya arts." Some teachers say salākavejjakamma is the treatment to remove an embedded splinter, but that should be understood as included under the term "sallakattiya" (surgery).

Cutting and extracting an embedded arrow or splinter is called "sallakatta," and the treatment for such extraction is "sallakatta-vejjakamma." One who rears a child (kumāra) is called "kumārabhata," and his state is "komārabhacca" (pediatrics). Alternatively, the child is called "komāra" and rearing is "bhacca"; thus it means the medical treatment that accomplishes the rearing of the child.

Primary medicines capable of calming diseases are called "mūlabhesajja" (root medicines). Or it can mean medicines for root diseases. Indeed, diseases are of two kinds: the root disease (mūlavyādhi) and the consequential disease (anubandhavyādhi) that follows it. Among them, if the root disease is treated, the other usually subsides. Therefore, it was said, "He shows the treatment of the body (kāyatikicchā)," and so on.
378:
In the phrase "He shows," etc., "kāyatikicchata" means treating with medicines that are bodily in nature as the primary factor, or the state of being a healer of bodily diseases. "Khārādīni" refers to alkaline water and the like. "Tadanurūpe vaṇṇe" means in a wound suitable for the subsided root disease. "Tesaṃ" refers to the removal (apanayana) of those root medicines, which means not treating (atikicchana) with those medicines. This is stated by way of the "method of remainder" (pārisesa), as the specialized treatises such as pediatrics (komārabhacca), surgery (sallakatta), and ophthalmology (sālākiya) have already been mentioned. Therefore, the remaining treatises should be understood as included here. All these arts are intended here as being for the sake of livelihood, as it is stated, "They earn a living through wrong livelihood" (D. i. 21). Where "iti vā" appears in various places in the Pāli, "iti" is a particle meaning "manner" (pakāra) and "vā" is a particle meaning "alternative" (vikappana). This means: "in this manner, or in another manner." By this, it should be understood that the various arts, sciences, and branches of knowledge used as means of livelihood by external wanderers are included.

## The Explanation of the Great Section on Virtue is Finished.

## Explanation of Eternalism regarding the Past

Now, wishing to show the connection (anusandhi) in order to explain the section on Emptiness (suññatā), he said "Evaṃ," and so on. There, in the word "vuttavaṇṇassa," the sixth (genitive) case ending is in the sense of "together with" (saha) or "possession" (sāmi). This is because the word anusandhi functions as an action-teaching by way of state and object (bhāvakamma). "Vuttavaṇṇassa by the Saṅgha of monks" refers to the praise spoken in the passage beginning "To whatever extent by that Blessed One," and so on. The connection in the Pāli is: "Monks, the virtues of the Buddha that are evident to you are not only these; there are other non-evident virtues," which is then explained in detail with "There are, monks, other dhammas."

By the passage "These bases for views are thus held," etc., the state of emptiness of a being (satta) is shown in the manner in which views such as Eternalism are wrongly held. By the passage "He does not misapprehend that knowledge," the non-misapprehension of virtue and so on is shown, thereby demonstrating the absence of a permanent essence (niccasāra). Because of non-detachment from those feelings (vedanā), these obstacles of views arise for those outside the Dispensation. By showing the absence of the nature of a "feeler" or "doer" in the delusion (sammoha) and other factors which are the causes of those feelings, the absence of Self and what belongs to Self (atta-attaniya) in all phenomena is shown. Furthermore, by showing Nibbāna without clinging (anupādāparinibbāna), this teaching is primarily intended to make Emptiness (suññatā) clear.
379:
The teaching (desanā) primarily focuses on elucidating emptiness (suññatā); with this intention, it is said, "It strives to manifest emptiness." Pariyatti refers to the lineage of sacred texts (tanti) categorized by various divisions such as the Vinaya, which are determined by the mind. Desanā refers to the elucidation of that lineage of texts determined by the mind, or the designation that is the recitation of the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma, or the teaching by way of conformity (anuloma) and so forth. The distinction between pariyatti and desanā was already established previously; with this meaning in mind, it is said, "both in desanā and in pariyatti."

In the phrase "evamādīsu" (in these and others), the word "ādi" (and so forth) includes truth (sacca), nature (sabhāva), concentration (samādhi), wisdom (paññā), custom (pakati), merit (puñña), offense (āpatti), the knowable (ñeyya), and so forth. Indeed, this word "Dhamma" occurs in the sense of truth (sacca) in such passages as: "Monks, through not understanding the Four Noble Truths..." (A. Ni. 4.1). It occurs in the sense of nature (sabhāva) in: "Wholesome dhammas, unwholesome dhammas..." (Dha. Sa. Tikamātikā 1). It occurs in the sense of concentration (samādhi) in: "Those Blessed Ones possessed such concentration..." (Dī. Ni. 2.13, 94, 145; 3.142; Ma. Ni. 3.167; Saṃ. Ni. 5.378). It occurs in the sense of wisdom (paññā) in: "Truth, Dhamma (wisdom), steadfastness, and generosity; he who has these does not sorrow after passing away" (Saṃ. Ni. 1.246; Su. Ni. 190). It occurs in the sense of custom or nature (pakati) in: "Monks, to beings whose nature is to be born, such a desire arises..." (Ma. Ni. 1.131, 3.373; Paṭi. Ma. 1.33). It occurs in the sense of merit (puñña) in: "The Dhamma well-practiced brings happiness" (Su. Ni. 184; Theragā. 303; Jā. 1.10.102, 15.385). It occurs in the sense of offense (āpatti) in: "The four Pārājika dhammas (offenses)" (Pārā. 233). It occurs in the sense of the knowable (ñeyya) in: "All dhammas in all their aspects come into the range of the knowledge of the Buddha, the Blessed One" (Mahāni. 156; Cūḷani. 85; Paṭi. Ma. 3.5).

"Dhammas arise" means that they are merely phenomena (dhamma) empty of a being or a soul (jīva). To the question, "What is the benefit of the word Dhamma occurring in the sense of virtue?" the text says "tasmā" (therefore) and so forth. "With a mosquito-proboscis-needle" means with a needle called the proboscis of a mosquito, which has a needle-like mouth. The phrase "as if finding no footing" should be connected here. "Except for the Tathāgata" means excluding the Tathāgata. Since the difficulty of penetrating those dhammas (virtues) with wisdom has already been manifested by the word "duddasā" (hard to see), it is simply said, "they find no footing."

Because it can be obtained, it is called "labbhanīya"; that same term is "labbhaneyya." Alternatively, the act of obtaining is called "labbhana," and because it is worthy of that obtaining, it is called "labbhaneyya." That which is not a reachable footing is "alabbhaneyya." Because they stand in this virtue, it is called "patiṭṭhā." Or, the act of standing is "patiṭṭhā." Because there is no reachable footing (standing) in this virtue, it is called "alabbhaneyyapatiṭṭhā." The meaning is this: If someone, without knowing the measure of their own wisdom...
380:
...without knowing the extent of one's own wisdom, if one strives to penetrate those virtues of the Buddha with wisdom, that wisdom of theirs would find no footing, just like the needle-like proboscis of a mosquito in the great ocean. Because of the inability to penetrate them with wisdom, and because it is impossible to see them as "they are of this extent" or "they are of such a nature," it is said, "Because they are deep, they are hard to see (duddasā)." For those who are unable even to see them, there is no question of penetrating and repeatedly understanding them with wisdom; therefore, it is said, "Because they are hard to see, they are hard to understand (duranubodha)."

They are called "nibbutasabbapariḷāha" (extinguished of all fevers) because they arise at the peak of the noble Fruit of Arahatship, which is the subsiding of the fever of all defilements, and because they are suffused with the attainments (samāpatti) in which the fever of all defilements has been extinguished by way of preceding and succeeding states. Because they possess that state of being extinguished, they are "santa" (peaceful). The Path, Fruit, and Nibbāna are called peaceful objects because of the absence of defilements and conditioned formations (saṅkhāra), which are of an unpeaceful nature.

Alternatively, just as there is the infinity of the concept of space (ākāsa) when the nine kasinas (excluding the space kasina) are removed, and the infinity of the consciousness that has that space as its object, the peacefulness (extinction of the fever of defilements) of the dhammas that have the Path, Fruit, and Nibbāna as their objects should be understood by way of the attention (manasikāra) that is always concentrated due to the state of being free from distraction, which has been very well abandoned. Just as archers can pierce a target without fail, the penetration of the virtues of the Buddha according to their true nature without distortion is like a delicious and superior taste. Therefore, it is said, "by way of the sense of causing insatiability." It means having the nature of causing one not to be satiated. The words "sohicca," "titti," and "tappana" are synonyms for satiety. Regarding the meaning of the word "atittikaraṇaṭṭhena," teachers also say it means "by way of the sense of producing a delicious taste" when desired. Since these virtues come into the range of the objects of only the Buddhas in all their aspects, who have attained penetration, they are not the sphere of the intellect that reasons (takka). Therefore, it is said, "Because they are the sphere of supreme knowledge," and so forth.

"Nipuṇa" (subtle) means being proficient through the sharp functioning of knowledge regarding the knowable. Since that proficiency is very evident because of its unimpeded functioning in the object and its ability to grasp subtle knowable things, it is said, "Because they are of a fine and subtle nature." To confirm the restriction "only by the wise," it is said, "Because they are not the sphere of fools."

This is another method according to the commentaries: They are "gambhīra" (deep) because they elucidate deep things to be guided, such as the Vinaya prescriptions. They are "duddasa" (hard to see) because they are difficult to see even after the passing of many incalculable great aeons. Here, seeing should be understood only as seeing with the eye of wisdom. They are "duranubodha" (hard to understand) because the understanding called the sequence of the Dhamma (dhammanvaya) occurs only to a rare few. They are "santa" (peaceful) because they are of a peaceful nature and because they are the consummation of all the virtues of those to be disciplined. They are "paṇīta" (sublime) because they have been brought to a state of excellence by their own conditions. They are "atakkāvacara" (beyond the sphere of reasoning) because they possess the characteristics of truth that have been well-attained and because they are not within the range of the reasoning wisdom of those who speculate. They are subtle.
381:
Because they are to be entered and known not by reasoning but by knowledge, they are called atakkāvacara (beyond the sphere of reasoning). Because they subtly clarify meanings such as the Truths and Dependent Origination, they are called nipuṇa (subtle). Because they are to be known and proclaimed only by the Fully Enlightened One, the foremost wise one in the world, they are called paṇḍitavedanīya (to be experienced by the wise).

Due to the attainment of unobstructed knowledge (anāvaraṇañāṇa), the Blessed One proclaimed his own qualities such as omniscience, saying: "Monks, I am the all-knower; the Tathāgata is endowed with the ten powers," etc. Therefore, it is said: "Having realized it by himself through higher knowledge, he makes it known." By the word 'sayaṃ' (by oneself), it means being one who is not led by others (ananya-neyya); it means not being made to know by others. In the word 'abhiññā', the elision of the letter 'ya' is as in "aññāṇatā āpajjatī," etc.; this is shown by the phrase "with distinguished knowledge." Alternatively, the meaning of the phrase "sayaṃ abhiññā" is "being one who is not led by others," while the meaning of the word "sacchikatvā" is "having personally witnessed." The word 'sayaṃ' should also be connected with the word 'sacchikatvā.' The phrase "with distinguished knowledge" refers to the cause (hetu) or the instrument (karaṇa) of that self-knowing.

In that context, although omniscience is not of a nature to be realized like the Fruits and Nibbāna, when the knowledge of the destruction of taints (āsavakkhayañāṇa) is attained, that omniscience is already attained. Therefore, the witnessing of that omniscience is called realization (sacchikiriyā), and thus it is said: "having witnessed it with distinguished knowledge." Here, the instrumental case is in the sense of cause (hetu); it means the cause for attaining the distinguished knowledge known as the knowledge of the path of Arahantship (arahattamaggañāṇa). Or, if 'distinguished knowledge' refers to reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇāñāṇa), the instrumental sense is also appropriate. Here, 'making known' (pavedana) should be understood because of the accomplishment of the task of teaching the Truths, etc., which have other objects, and because of the declaration: "I am the unique Fully Enlightened One," etc. 'Guṇadhammehi' means by the dhammas known as qualities. 'Yathābhūtaṃ' means exactly as it is.

In the word 'vadamānā', the word 'māna' has the sense of capability (satti). For example: "Monks, when one person is born in the world, he is born." Therefore, it means "one who makes an effort to speak." Such persons are called those who wish to speak. Therefore, it is said...
382:
In the words beginning with "tathāgatassa," although they speak of what remains, they are not to be called those who speak wrongly like those who speak perversely; to show that they speak correctly, the words beginning with "ahāpetvā" (without omitting) are said. By this, it is shown that only speaking without remainder is speaking correctly. By the phrase "they would be able to speak" (vattuṃ sakkuṇeyyuṃ), the sense of capability of the word "they would speak" (vadeyuṃ) is expressed, like the illustration: "He would disentangle this tangle." The construction is: "What are those dhammas that were thus praised by the Blessed One?" To challenge the contradiction between the Pali beginning with "Monks, there are other dhammas" and the statement called "omniscience" (sabbaññutañāṇa), the words beginning with "yadi evaṃ" (if so) are said. In that context, "yadi evaṃ" means "if that statement called omniscience were so." The expression "plural designation" (bahuvacana-niddeso) refers to the Pali beginning with "Monks, there are..." Here, the word 'atthi' is also plural, as in "there is milk, there are cows," etc., because only its status as an indeclinable (nipāta) is desired. Although that omniscience is one by nature, it deserves the use of plural expressions due to association (sampayoga) and object (ārammaṇa); thus he answers with the words: "due to many thoughts... object." "Due to association with many thoughts" means due to association with many consciousnesses. It is called "puthu-ārammaṇa" because it has many objects; because it has such many objects, it means it has all objects.

Alternatively, because it takes many objects as its object, in the sense of "puthu-ārammaṇārammaṇa," the first word 'ārammaṇa' is elided as in "oṭṭhamukho" and "kāmāvacaraṃ," and it is said as "puthu-ārammaṇato." By this, the accomplishment of many functions of knowledge by that knowledge is shown. Indeed, that knowledge accomplishes, as far as possible, the functions of hundreds of thousands of various knowledges, such as: unobstructed knowledge in the three times, knowledge that distinguishes the four modes of birth, knowledge that distinguishes the five destinations, the remaining uncommon knowledges among the six uncommon knowledges, knowledge that clarifies the seven types of noble persons, knowledge that is unshakable in the eight assemblies, knowledge that fully understands the nine abodes of beings, and the knowledge of the ten powers. It should be understood that many dhammas which are the objects of those knowledges are the objects of this omniscience. The words beginning with "tañhi" are the sequential explanation of that. By the words beginning with "yathāha," the Paṭisambhidāmagga Pali is shown as evidence. In that text, 'tattha' means "among the past dhammas." Setting aside the nature of having many objects at a single time, to show it by way of sequential occurrence through many times, it is said: "by way of repeated arising." Indeed, omniscience occurs sequentially in its objects; it does not occur like that (all at once).
383:
It occurs all at once. This is like what outsiders (titthiyas) say: "Omniscience knows everything at once, not sequentially." If it were so (sequential), how could the knowable (ñeyya), which has inconceivable and immeasurable divisions, be penetrated without remainder by a single finite knowledge? Or else, who says that Omniscience is finite? In fact, that knowledge is as infinite as the knowable itself. For it was said by the General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta, in the Paṭisambhidāmagga: "As far as the range of knowledge extends, so far extends the range of the knowable; as far as the range of the knowable extends, so far extends the range of knowledge." If one argues that even if it is infinite, when the knowable—which is divided into many parts by way of birth, nature, direction, place, time, etc.—is grasped sequentially, then penetration without remainder is simply impossible, is it not? This should not be understood in that way. Because whenever the Blessed One wishes to know anything, whether in its entirety or in part, His knowledge occurs through direct perception because of its unimpeded movement in that knowable object. Furthermore, because the Blessed One is free from distraction, He is concentrated at all times. Therefore, it is impossible to prevent the direct perception of the desired knowable object. It has been said: "The knowledge of the Buddha, the Blessed One, is bound to His wish," and so on. If one argues: "Should it not be understood that the Buddha's knowledge occurs in an indistinct manner when penetrating many phenomena, similar to those seeing a patterned cloth from a distance, or like the knowledge of meditators practicing insight (vipassanā) who perceive 'all phenomena are non-self' in an indistinct way?" This should not be so understood, because the Buddha's knowledge has inconceivable power. That is why the Blessed One said: "The range of a Buddha is inconceivable." The conclusion here is: By attaining the unobstructed knowledge (anāvaraṇa-ñāṇa) which is capable of penetrating all phenomena in every aspect and which occurs in connection with His wish, the Blessed One was able to penetrate all phenomena through His mental continuum. Because He has abandoned the obstructions (āvaraṇa) that hide all knowable things, He is called "Sabbaññū" (the All-Knower). He is not called Sabbaññū because He penetrates all phenomena at once (simultaneously in one moment), but rather He is like fire which is called "sabbabhū" (all-consuming) because it is capable of burning all fuel through its continuous process.

Although this meaning has been explained in detail previously, it is explained again here to benefit students through another method, and because this new sub-commentary (ṭīkā) is produced by refining the old sub-commentary. Therefore, one should not look for the fault of repetition in such places. In this praise of the Buddha's qualities, although the Buddha's knowledges such as the Ten Powers (dasabala) are also unique to Him, those knowledges do not fully encompass the Buddha's qualities without remainder because they have limited objects. However, as for Omniscience...
384:
Since Omniscience has an object without remainder (nippadesa-visaya), to take that knowledge is to take all the qualities of the Buddha. Therefore, following the meaning of the Pali, it should be understood that only Omniscience is taken. Indeed, in the Pali, it is shown as: "Those who would speak rightly of the Tathāgata's praise as it truly is," because apart from Omniscience, there is no other knowledge that has an object without remainder, and only through knowledge with an object without remainder is it possible to speak rightly as it truly is.

Regarding the word "aññeva" (only others), the word "eva" is used here to show the sense of conclusion; thus it is said, "'aññeva' is a word of definition here." A word of definition means a word of conclusion, and conclusion is indeed restriction (avadhāraṇa). How? It is said, "aññeva," and so on. By this restriction, it shows the exclusion: "not the avoidance of taking life, etc." This word "eva," being in an indefinite position, can stand in other places as well according to the intended meaning, just like the word "ca"; thus it is said, "gambhīrāva" (only deep), and so on. By the word "iti" and the sense of "ādi" (etc.), it shows the exclusion: "only difficult to see, not easy to see; only difficult to understand, not easy to understand; only peaceful, not distressing; only sublime, not inferior; only beyond the sphere of reasoning, not within the sphere of reasoning; only subtle, not coarse; only to be experienced by the wise, not to be experienced by the foolish." The phrase "by all words" means that the word "eva" should be applied to all words up to the word "paṇḍitavedanīyā."

To strengthen this exclusion by logic, he said "sāvaka-pāramī-ñāṇaṃ," and so on. There, "knowledge of a disciple's perfection" (sāvaka-pāramī-ñāṇa) refers to the knowledge consisting of the three true knowledges (vijjā), the six higher powers (abhiññā), and the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā), which arises from the fulfillment of perfections like giving (dāna) by the disciples. Likewise, it includes the knowledge of enlightenment of Paccekabuddhas (paccekabodhi-ñāṇa). "Tato" (than that) means than the knowledge of a disciple's perfection. "Tattha" (therein) means in the knowledge of a disciple's perfection. "Tatopi" (even than that) means even than the knowledge of enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha mentioned immediately after. By the word "api" or "pi," he expresses praise: "What need is there to speak of it being deeper than the knowledge of a disciple's perfection?" "Tatthāpi" (therein also) means in the knowledge of enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha as well. "Ito pana" (but from this) means but from Omniscience. Therefore, the meaning is that the definition is found only in this Omniscience. "Gambhīratarā" means exceptionally deep among deep things, or especially deep compared to deep things. Or it means "this Dhamma is deep, and that Dhamma is deep, but these qualities of the Buddha are especially deep compared to those Dhammas," thus they are called "gambhīratarā" (more profound). Here, the restriction of meaning is accomplished by the suffix "tara" itself. 

In this context, the construction (yojanā) is as follows: Although the knowledge of a disciple's perfection is deep compared to the lower knowledges of those in training (sekha) and the knowledge of worldlings (puthujjana), it is not so deep compared to the knowledge of enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha. Therefore, it cannot be restricted as "only deep." Likewise...
385:
The knowledge of a Private Buddha (Paccekabodhi-ñāṇa) is also deep when compared to the aforementioned knowledge of a disciple's perfection (Sāvaka-pāramī-ñāṇa). However, when compared to the Omniscient Knowledge (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), it is not deep in that way; therefore, it cannot be definitively stated that "it is only deep" (using the word *eva*). Thus, such a definitive restriction cannot be applied to the knowledge of a disciple's perfection and the knowledge of a Private Buddha. The qualities of Omniscient Knowledge, however, are not deep relative to any other knowledge in the way that the knowledge of a disciple's perfection is (i.e., there is no state of not being deep); thus, the definitive restriction "they are indeed deep" is applicable. Just as this definitive restriction is shown regarding Omniscient Knowledge, likewise, the knowledge of a disciple's perfection is difficult to see. It should be understood that the possibility of definitive restriction exists in such statements as, "The knowledge of a Private Buddha is even more difficult to see than that; therefore, there is no such definitive restriction in those types of knowledge." For this reason, it was said, "Likewise, they are indeed difficult to see... etc... should be understood."

There is also a reading "Pucchāvissajjanaṃ," which means the answer to that question. "Etaṃ" refers to the aforementioned words of the answer. "Evaṃ" refers to the manner of analyzing these views. In this context, this intention should be understood—let it be first accepted that although Omniscient Knowledge is one, it is presented in the plural form as "Monks, there are other dhammas..." etc., for the sake of accomplishing the function of knowledge which has many bases and objects, because it is the means of clarifying the Buddha's qualities without remainder. However, why was the answer to that question initiated not by the method of analysis unique to the Buddha, such as the specific domains of the Truths (Sacca) and Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda), but by the method of analyzing views together with their bases? In that question, just as the analysis of the Truths and Dependent Origination is the domain of Omniscient Knowledge alone and not shared with others, so too, the analysis of all views without remainder is the domain of Omniscient Knowledge; to show this, the passage beginning with "Buddhānañhi" was initiated. In that passage, "ṭhānāni" means causes.

"The roar is great" means that because the meaning to be taught has many varieties and is difficult to understand, the roar of the teaching (desanā-gajjita) proceeding through various methods is great, extensive, and has many divisions. "Knowledge enters into" means that because of the greatness of that roar of teaching, the teaching-knowledge enters into the dhammas to be taught by way of analysis; it means it is as if it stands having entered into those dhammas.

"The greatness of the Buddha's knowledge is manifest" means that because there is both the teaching of such a nature of Dhamma and the penetration (realization) of it, the noble nature of the teaching-knowledge and the penetration-knowledge of the Buddhas becomes manifest. "The teaching is deep" means that among those four types of depth which are deep by nature, the teaching is indeed deep by the power of the Dhamma to be taught. That teaching of the Buddhas, in all matters and at all times, proceeds only through the gateway of the three vehicles (yāna), and thus it is said, "Marked by the three characteristics, connected with emptiness (suññatā)." This means it is marked by the three characteristics and is connected with the state of being empty of self and what belongs to self. In this context also...
386:
According to the statement, "Every verbal action of the Blessed Buddha is preceded by knowledge and follows knowledge," it is true that there is not even a slight part of the Blessed One's teaching that is devoid of knowledge. However, due to having equal exertion and having a practice similar to the lion king, there is the occurrence of equal effort in all places. Nevertheless, by the power of the Dhamma to be taught, the teaching should be understood as specifically entering into knowledge and being exceedingly deep.

When it comes to the laying down of the Vinaya (disciplinary rules), how can the teaching be marked by the three characteristics and connected with emptiness? Is it not that in that laying down of Vinaya, there is only the mere regulation of discipline? It is not only the mere regulation of discipline there. For even in that laying down of Vinaya, the teaching that proceeds in accordance with the inclinations of the assembled audience clarifies the impermanence of conditioned things (saṅkhāra) and manifests the emptiness of all dhammas from self and what belongs to self. Therefore, it was said, "Having taught the Dhamma discourse through various methods," and so on.

"Vinaya-paññatti" means the laying down (making known) of the Vinaya. When the letter 'ña' is changed to 'ṇṇa', there is also the reading "Vinaya-paṇṇatti." "Bhūmantara" refers to the specific stages of dhammas and the specific locations (planes). Because of the derivative meaning "dhammas arise herein," a stage and a location are called "bhūmi." Among those two, the "specific stage" refers to the divisions of dhammas such as mindfulness, etc., into the categories of foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), faculties (indriya), powers (bala), factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), and path factors (magganga), similar to the distinctions of "calf, steer, and bull." The "specific location" refers to the divisions such as the sense-sphere realm (kāmāvacara), etc. The meaning of the term "paṭiccasamuppāda" (mode of conditions) has already been stated below. "Samayantara" refers to specific views, meaning various types of views; or it means another doctrine, specifically an external doctrine. It should be connected with the passage beginning with, "Reaching the laying down of Vinaya, the roar is great." "Tasmā" (therefore) means because the roar is great... because it is connected with emptiness, therefore (tasmā).

"Chejjagāminī" means reaching that which is incurable (Pārājika). "In the matter thus reached" means when reaching such a matter by way of light or heavy offenses, etc., through the aforementioned method. "Where there is the laying down of a training rule (sikkhāpada)" is how it should be connected. "Thāma" is the capacity of knowledge. "Bala" is the nature of courage known as immovability. Alternatively, both words "thāma" and "bala" are merely terms for capacity and should be applied by the power of reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇā-ñāṇa) and teaching-knowledge (desanā-ñāṇa). For teaching-knowledge is preceded by reviewing knowledge. "Esā" (this) points to the laying down of training rules using the masculine gender in consideration of the word to be spoken. It means that this domain known as the laying down of training rules is not the domain of others. "Iti" is used as the cause for the state of being or not being such a domain...
387:
The word 'iti' has the sense of re-specification (paṭiniddesa) or the sense of illustration (nidassana). By this word 'iti', it specifies the method such as, "This is a light training rule (lahuka-sikkhāpada), this is a heavy training rule (garuka-sikkhāpada)." In other places as well, it should be understood in this same manner as far as possible.

Although the Foundations of Mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) and so forth are analyzed in the Suttanta Piṭaka by way of the contemplation of the body (kāyānupassanā) and so forth, they are specifically analyzed in the Abhidhamma by way of the Suttanta-bhājanīya method and so forth; thus it is said, "These four foundations of mindfulness... having analyzed the Abhidhamma Piṭaka." In that statement, "seven contacts" (phassa) is said by way of association with the seven consciousness elements (viññāṇadhātu). Likewise, "seven feelings" (vedanā) and so forth are also stated. In the phrase "what are called supramundane states (lokuttara dhammā)," the word 'iti' here has the sense of 'beginning with' (ādi) or 'variety' (pakāra). By that word 'iti', it encompasses the manner of analysis of the remaining states that appear in the Abhidhamma.

In this text, there are twenty-four Universal Patthanas (samantapaṭṭhāna); therefore, 'catuvīsati-samantapaṭṭhāna' is a Bahubbīhi compound (bāhiratthasamāsa). This term is an adjective for 'Abhidhamma Piṭaka'. Here, without taking the causal method (paccayanaya), the existence of the twenty-four divisions of the Samantapaṭṭhāna is stated by way of the states (dhamma) alone. As the Blessed One said:

"The noble Triad Patthana (tikapaṭṭhāna), the supreme Dyad Patthana (dukapaṭṭhāna),
The Dyad-Triad and the Triad-Dyad,
The Triad-Triad and the Dyad-Dyad,
These six methods in the positive (anuloma) are extremely profound...
Six in the negative (paccaṇīka)... in the positive-negative...
The methods in the negative-positive are extremely profound."

Thus, among the Triad Patthana and others which have twenty-four divisions by way of the states, each Patthana becomes fourfold by way of the positive method and so forth through the causal method; thus there are ninety-six Universal Patthanas. Among those Universal Patthanas, in the positive method of states (dhammānuloma), in the Triad Patthana (tikapaṭṭhāna), in the section on wholesome triads (kusalattika), in the section on dependence (paṭiccavāra), in the positive method of conditions (paccayanuloma), in the root condition (hetumūla), there are forty-nine methods of questioning (pucchānaya) and seven methods of answering (vissajjanānaya) by way of the root condition (hetupaccaya). Because there are such infinitely diverse methods shown, it is called 'infinite methods' (anantanaya).

"By nine modes" means by the nine causal modes such as arising (uppāda). To show those modes in their own nature, it is said "having become an arising" and so forth. In that context, it is called 'arising' (uppādo) because the effect arises from this cause; it is simply the state of being the cause for the production of the effect. When ignorance (avijjā) exists, formations (saṅkhārā) arise; they do not arise when it does not exist. Therefore, ignorance assists by being the cause of arising (uppāda) for the formations. Likewise, it is called 'occurrence' (pavattaṃ) because the effect occurs and is maintained in this cause. It is called 'source' because the effect is measured in this cause...
388:
Nimitta (sign/cause). It is called 'nidāna' (source/origin) because it gives its own effect produced by a cause through this cause. (This definition does not agree with the Commentary). It is called 'āyūhana' (striving/accumulation) because it strives for the production of its own effect produced by a cause through this cause. It is called 'saṃyoga' (yoking/conjunction) because the effect is yoked with its own produced effect in this cause. It is called 'palibodha' (impediment/obstruction) because it arises itself in a continuity and entangles the effect through this cause. It is called 'samudaya' (origin) because the effect arises through this cause when there is a combination of other conditions. It is called 'hetu' (root/cause) because it reaches the state of being a cause. Indeed, when ignorance (avijjā) exists, formations (saṅkhārā) occur and are maintained. When ignorance exists, those formations give their own effect, throw it into the planes of existence (bhava) and so forth, strive for the production of their own effect, yoke with their own effect, entangle the continuity in which they themselves have arisen, arise when there is a combination of other conditions, and reach the state of being the cause of formations. Therefore, ignorance, having become the occurrence of formations... having become the cause, is the cause. In this way, the distinctions of reaching the state of being a cause for formations by ignorance, such as arising and so forth, should be understood. This same method applies to formations and so forth in relation to consciousness (viññāṇa) and so forth.

To prove that meaning by the Paṭisambhidāmagga Pali, it is said "as it was said" and so forth. In that Pali, it is called 'ṭhiti' (stability/standing) because the effect stands by this cause; it is the cause itself. Arising itself is the stability of arising (uppāda-ṭhiti) because it is the cause of standing. The remaining terms should be understood in this same way. However, because it was said, "With the arising of taints (āsava), there is the arising of ignorance (avijjā)," the taints alone are the cause of ignorance. Therefore, it is said, "Both these states are dependently arisen (paccayasamuppannā)." This means that both these states—ignorance and formations—arise only from a cause, not without a cause. Wisdom in grasping conditions (paccaya-pariggaha-paññā) is the wisdom that occurs by way of discerning and grasping the causal modes such as arising for both formations and ignorance. Knowledge of the stability of states (dhamma-ṭṭhiti-ñāṇa) is the knowledge of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda), which is called the stability of states because of the causal nature of dependently arisen states. Indeed, from the statement "twelve factors of dependent origination," the twelve causes alone are called dependent origination. This method is not only for the present, but also for the past and future; and it is found not only in ignorance regarding formations, but also in formations and so forth regarding consciousness and so forth. Thus, to show the analyzed state of the causal modes completely, the Pali beginning with "even in the past duration (atītam-pi addhānaṃ)" was cited. The conditions such as root-condition (hetu-paccaya) shown in the Patthana are indeed taken here by way of causal modes such as arising; therefore, they should also be extracted and applied as appropriate. However, we have not applied them for fear of excessive length; those who desire them should take them from the Visuddhimagga and other texts.
389:
"To each and every phenomenon" refers to the conditioned phenomena (paccayuppanna-dhamma) arising from causes such as volitional formations (saṅkhāra). "By way of such and such a causal state" refers to the causal power (paccayasatti) such as the cause of origination (uppāda), and so on. It is called the "Three Rounds" (tivaṭṭa) because there are three rounds by way of the round of kamma, the round of defilements (kilesa), and the round of results (vipāka). It is called the "Three Periods" (tiyaddha) because there are three periods of time by way of past, present, and future. It is called the "Three Connections" (tisandhi) because there are three connections by way of cause-effect, effect-cause, and cause-effect. In these groups of cause and effect, because ignorance (avijjā) and so on, and consciousness (viññāṇa) and so on, are included, they are called "Groups" (saṅkhepa); they are also cause and result. Alternatively, they are called "Groups" (saṅkhepa) because they are summarized as cause and result. Ignorance and so on, and consciousness and so on, are also synonyms of the word "koṭṭhāsa" (portion/part), where the word "saṅkhepa" denotes a collection or group. It is called the "Four Groups" (catusaṅkhepa) because there are four groups by way of the past causal group, and so on. Although not explicitly mentioned in their own form, because they are shown by taking ignorance, volitional formations, and so on in those respective groups, they are called "Aspects" (ākāra); they are the varieties of the past causes, and so on. Because there are twenty aspects by making five in each of those four groups, it is called the "Twenty Aspects" (vīsatākāra).

Although divided into many types such as kings (khattiya) and so on, eternalists (sassatavādī) are of only four types by way of the cause of their misapprehension, such as the recollection of a hundred thousand births; there are no more or less than that. To show that the delimitation of the extent of the eternalists' views is not within the range of anyone other than the Buddha, He said, "four types of people," and so on. This method applies similarly to the remaining terms. In that context, "four types of people" should be understood as four groups of people, because even within each of those four types, there are many varieties of views. "They" refers to those who hold the sixty-two views. "Depending on this" refers to not properly grasping (not knowing) the nature of specific conditionality (idappaccayatā). In that law of dependent origination, because the continuity (santati) of phenomena connected as cause and effect cannot be broken, even though the distinction exists in the ultimate sense (paramattha), it occurs depending on the "grasping as one" (ekattaggahaṇa) taken without considering the method of diversity (nānatta-naya) connected with the distinction. "They grasp this" means they speak by misapprehending this eternalist view; in this same way, partial-eternalism (ekaccasassatavāda) and so on should also be applied and spoken of as far as possible. "Having analyzed" means having analyzed by way of "depending on ardor," and so on, or having dispelled by way of "Monks, the Tathāgata knows this view," and so on. "Unentangled" (nijjaṭaṃ) means without being entwined. "Unobstructed" (nigumbaṃ) means without being covered or closed. Alternatively, it is called a "tangle" (jaṭā) in the sense of being interwoven above and below like bamboo, etc. It is called a "thicket" (gumba) in the sense of obstructing like kusa grass, etc. Because of the similarity to those, the confused and manifest state of views is called "tangle" and "thicket." By disentangling the tangle of views and by opening the thicket of views, it is made unentangled and unobstructed—this is the meaning.
390:
With the words "Tasmā" (Therefore) and so on, because the teaching arose based on the virtues of the Buddha, the Blessed One, who is skilled in teaching with reference to the knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), shows that He answers through the knowledge of omniscience itself by way of refuting other false views.

The word "santi" is a synonym for the word "atthi" (there are/exist). That word "atthi" is also a synonym for the term "saṃvijjanti." The state of being manifest is the state of being perceivable by knowledge; thus He said "santi," and so on. By showing what is manifest, through this word "santi," the King of Dhamma (Dhammarāja) demonstrates the continuity of the existence of those holding wrong views, the effectiveness of His own teaching in loosening and separating them from that wrong grasp, and its unerring nature. The word "atthi" also has the same meaning as the word "santi." It is a single particle (nipāta) used in the plural sense, as in such passages as "In this body, there are (atthi) hairs," and so on.

The word of address (vocative) refers to the word of address used by the Buddha. Only the Blessed One addresses as "Bhikkhave" or "Bhikkhavo"; the disciples do not address in this way. The disciples, however, address only by connecting with words such as "Āvuso" (friend) or "Āyasmā" (venerable). When "eke" (some) is said, it means "certain ones." Because the word "eka," which expresses number, is fixed in the singular, He said "by way of having entered the homeless life" (pabbajjūpagatabhāvena), etc., to show that they are not recluses or brahmins (samaṇa-brāhmaṇa) by way of having calmed or removed evil. Whether it be so or otherwise, He shows with the words "by the world" (lokena), etc., that here they are intended only by way of conventional designation (sammuti-paññatti).

They are called "Speculators on the Past" (pubbantakappikā) because they speculate on the past by way of eternalism, and so on. Because those people speculate on the past through the speculations of craving and views (taṇhā-diṭṭhi) established previously, and because of the strength of repeated practice and the diversity of their occurrences, they speculate specially and then grasp, misapprehend, and misinterpret through the graspings of craving and views that are established later as adherence. Therefore, it is said, "having speculated and specially speculated on the past, they grasp." Alternatively, the speculation and grasping should be understood respectively by way of craving and clinging (taṇhā-upādāna) established in the earlier and later parts. For clinging arises with craving as a condition.

Among the objects (visaya) such as abundance, praise, blame, excess, association, and constant application, the meaning of "existing" by way of constant application is appropriate here; thus He said "pubbanta-kappo vā," and so on.

"These suffixes such as 'mantu' occur in the sense of abundance, praise, blame, excess, constant application, and association."
It is also said.
391:
## Koṭṭhāsesūti
In this context, the word 'koṭṭhāsesū' should be understood as 'koṭṭhāsādīsū' (in parts, etc.) because the word 'ādi' is elided and it is stated by way of illustration. Indeed, the word 'anta' is found in the sense of a mere expletive, proximity, and a wrong path (vile), etc. This is shown in such passages as: "Friend, first learn the Suttas, or the verses, or the Abhidhamma," and "Having made an opening in the Sutta," etc.—in these, the word 'anta' occurs as a mere expletive. In passages such as "a dwelling near a village" (gāmanta), it occurs in the sense of proximity. In passages such as "the enjoyment of pleasure in sensual desires is one vile path (extreme)" and "Kaccāna, this vile path (extreme) exists," etc., it occurs in the sense of a wrong path (vile).

'Antapūro' means being full of the large and small intestines. In the Mahāhatthipadopama Sutta of the Majjhima Nikāya, it is stated: "That fire [reaches] the boundary of green grass or the boundary of a path [and goes out for lack of fuel]." In that passage, 'sā' refers to the fire element (tejo-dhātu). 'Haritantaṃ' refers to the boundary of green grass and trees. 'Panthantaṃ' refers to the boundary of the path. 'Āgamma anāhārā nibbāyati' (having reached [the boundary], it goes out for lack of fuel) is the remaining meaning. In the Piṇḍiyālopa Sutta, it is stated: "Monks, this living by alms-gathering is the lowest of all forms of livelihood." In that passage, one who seeks (ulati) alms (piṇḍaṃ) is called 'piṇḍola' (an alms-collector); the state of that alms-collector is 'piṇḍolyaṃ', meaning living by alms-gathering.

'Esevā' refers only to the Dhamma of Nibbāna, which is the destruction of all conditions; therefore, it is said, "It is called the destruction of all..." By this, it is shown that Nibbāna, being unconditioned (asaṅkhata) due to the destruction of all conditions, is the other side (the end) of the conditioned suffering of the round (vaṭṭa-dukkha); thus, the meaning of 'the other side' (the end) is appropriate here. 'Sakkāyo' refers to the view of self (sakkāya-diṭṭhi/clinging).

'Kappo' means a pretext (sign/reason). 'Kappakatenāti' means by making one of the three kinds of disfigurement (on a robe). Here, by the word 'ādi', it is shown that the word 'kappa' also occurs in the sense of a great aeon (mahākappa), entirety, sensual defilement, thought, time, designation, similarity, etc. For instance, in passages such as "Monks, there are these four incalculables of an aeon," it occurs in the sense of a great aeon. In passages such as "having illuminated the entire Veḷuvana monastery," it occurs in the sense of entirety. In passages such as "thought is sensuality, lust is sensuality, lustful thought is sensuality," it occurs in the sense of sensual defilement. In passages such as "thinking, pondering, thought," it occurs in the sense of thought. In passages such as "at which time he dwells for a permanent time," it occurs in the sense of time.
392:
...and in the sense of designation in passages such as "The Venerable Kappa desires thus" (Sutta Nipāta 1018); and in the sense of similarity in passages such as "Friends, though we were consulting with a disciple who is like the Teacher, we did not know it" (Majjhima Nikāya 1.260).

To prove the occurrence [of these terms] in craving and wrong view by means of the Mahāniddesa (Mahāniddesa 28), he said "This was also said," etc. There, "uddānato" means in brief. The word "tasmā," etc., is a statement praising the quality of the aforementioned explanation. "Taṇhādiṭṭhivasena" means by the power of craving, known as delighting, which assists through the conditions of decisive support (upanissaya) and co-nascence (sahajāta), and by the power of wrong view, which is a false misapprehension in the form of eternalism, etc. Since the intention here is the construction (imagining) regarding the aggregates that one inhabited in the past, the word "pubba" denotes only past time. It does not denote 'foremost' (predominant), etc., as in "Mind is the forerunner of all things." Since there is no object of construction apart from the aggregates such as form (rūpa), the word "anta" denotes only a part or section (koṭṭhāsa). To show that it does not denote 'internal' (abbhantara), etc., it was said "the past aggregate-section." By the word "kappetvā," it means the ability to complete the act of craving and misapprehending in that past section. "Ṭhitā" means not relinquishing that view. The construction is: "They have a view that follows only the past." The state of 'existing' and 'following' means arising again and again, as shown by the words "by way of arising repeatedly." With "te evaṃ," etc., he comments on the meaning of the Pali "pubbantaṃ ārabbha," etc. There, "ārabbha" means having made [it] an object. For the past aggregate-section is the object (visaya) of that view. Because it is the object, it is the place of origin and the object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya) for that view; thus it was said "having come to, depending on" (āgamma paṭicca). To show the establishing of others [in that view], he said "making other people also fall into the way of wrong view."

## Adhivacanapathānīti
[Adhivacanapadāni in the Commentary] means the grounds for designation by way of mere usage (ruḷhī). Just as the names "Sirivaḍḍhaka," etc., occur among slaves by giving weight to the mere word, so too, designation itself is called 'adhivacana'. And that designation is the path (way) of conventional usage. Alternatively, the word "adhi" means 'above' or 'upon', and "vacana" means 'speech'. Speech [placed] upon the meaning is 'adhivacana'. Designation based on (upādā-paññatti) the aggregates such as form, which are objects of clinging, is meant; therefore, it should be understood as the pathways that clarify designation. It is said that this is a mere designation, namely "self" and "world"; they are not [ultimate realities] like form, feeling, etc.
393:
This is the end of the connection of words. In this term 'adhimuttipathāni', the word 'adhimutti' has the same meaning as the word 'abhivacana' (designation), because the word 'utti' (or 'mutti') is a synonym for 'vacana' (speech/word), as in the Pali passages such as 'niruttipatho' (the path of language). By the phrase 'bhūtaṃ atthaṃ' (the true meaning) and so forth, they are called 'adhimutti' because they resolve upon something beyond the true ultimate reality, or because they resolve by transcending that true ultimate reality. It shows the meaning 'adhimuttipathāni' because it points out those paths of views called 'adhimutti'. Alternatively, they are called 'adhimutti' because they resolve upon things that exceed the ultimate reality, such as eternalism (sassata). Indeed, wrong views arise by superimposing unreal meanings—such as eternalism, primordial nature (pakati), substance (dabba), soul (jīva), and body (kāya)—which exceed the ultimate reality, onto the ultimate phenomena (paramattha-dhamma).

'Abhivadanti' means they speak with clinging and conviction, saying, "Only this is true, everything else is empty." They also speak by way of overcoming others, saying, "This alone is the Dhamma, this is not the Dhamma," and so forth. The present tense is used to show that the act of proclaiming by way of overcoming is still ongoing even now. This is the explanation of the Pali in this sub-commentary (ṭīkā). The connection is that they ask because the desire to speak is the cause. It is called 'diṭṭhi' (view) because it sees wrongly. 'Diṭṭhi' itself is 'diṭṭhigata'. This is because the word 'gata' expresses that very state, as in the Pali terms 'muttagata' and 'saṅkhāragata'. Or, it is called 'diṭṭhigata' because it is merely what is reached by view, as there is no actual destination to be reached. The meaning is that it is merely a grasping by view, and there is no other reality to be understood. Alternatively, 'diṭṭhigata' refers to the variety of views. Indeed, world-renowned teachers accept the words 'vidha', 'yutta', 'gata', and 'pakāra' as having the same meaning. The teacher says, "Taking one of the aggregates such as form (rūpa) as the self and as the world," because the designation (paññatti) occurs based on the specific way of grasping even a single aggregate as 'self' and as 'world'. 'Amara' (immortal), 'nicca' (permanent), and 'dhuva' (stable) are synonyms for 'sassata' (eternal). Alternatively, it is 'amara' because of the absence of death. It is 'nicca' because it exists at all times without arising. It is 'dhuva' because of its sense of firmness and the absence of change. By the phrase 'yathāha' (as he said), the meaning already stated is clarified through the Mahāniddesa Pali and the Paṭisambhidāmagga Pali. In that Pali, it should be understood as being connected with the remaining text 'rūpaṃ gahetvā' (having taken form).

This meaning is stated by the power of the fivefold identity view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi): "One regards form as self; one regards feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as self." Furthermore, by the power of the remaining fifteenfold identity view, such as "self possessing form," the meaning is also obtained that they take four aggregates as 'self' and designate the remaining aggregates as 'the world'. Likewise, it should be understood in this context that they designate by taking one aggregate as 'self' and another aggregate which is one's own requisite as 'the world'; or by taking the aggregates within one's own continuity as 'self' and the aggregates within another's continuity as 'the world'.
394:
In this context, one might ask: "Why is it said below that 'these people have an eternalist view (sassatavāda)'? Do they not intend that the self and the world are eternal, rather than the view itself?" That is true. However, because it is associated with the eternal, the view is also called 'eternal' (sassata) by way of metaphor, just as it is said, "The spears are marching." Alternatively, the word 'iti' is elided here, and it should be understood as "the view *that* [it is] eternal belongs to them." It is also appropriate to say 'sassatavādā' because they speak of it as eternal, proclaiming with clinging, "Only this is true, everything else is empty."

31. 'Ātāpana-bhāvena' means by the state of afflicting, or in the sense of scorching. In this context, the afflicting of defilements is called 'abandoning' (pahāna). 'Padahana-vasena' means by the power of right striving. Right striving (samādahana) means encouraging the mind without letting it fall into the side of laziness. Just as concentration (samādhi) reaches a distinguished stage, the repeated practice of energy (vīriya) is called 'application' (anuyoga). Thus, by these three terms, only energy is meant; therefore, it is said, "Thus, energy is of three types." In order, these three terms show the energy of access (upacāra), the energy of absorption (appanā), and the energy that tames the mind.

'Na pamajjati etenāti appamādo' means it is called heedfulness (appamāda) because one does not forget by means of this mindfulness; it is the non-absence of mindfulness. That heedfulness is indeed the four mental aggregates associated with the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna). It is called 'right attention' (sammāmanasikāra) because one reflects on the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) by the proper method through this wisdom. That right attention is indeed only wisdom (ñāṇa); it is not the attention that reflects on the object, nor the attention that produces the process (vīthi), nor the attention that produces the impulsion (javana). Therefore, it is said, "In sense, it is wisdom." 'Prathama-manasikāra' means causal attention. That very meaning is supported by the phrase 'yasmiñhi' and so forth. There, 'yasmiṃ manasikāre' refers to the attention known as insight-wisdom (vipassanā-ñāṇa), which is the means for reflecting on the meditation subject. By the phrase 'in this place', it is shown that the word 'sammāmanasikāra' has a specific meaning according to the context, just as it does when associated with other words. 

'Vīriyañca' refers to the three types of energy mentioned by the three preceding terms. In this passage 'ātappa... manasikāramanvāya', the practice for attaining the four fine-material sphere absorptions (rūpāvacara-jhāna) together with the purification of virtue (sīlavisuddhi) is stated here. However, because that practice has been explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga, it is said, "This is the summarized meaning." 'Tathājātikaṃ' means 'of such a nature'. By this, it is shown that the fourth fine-material sphere absorption has been tamed and mastered through the fourteen ways of taming the mind. 'Cetosamādhi' means the concentration of the mind; that concentration is specifically the concentration of the fourth fine-material sphere absorption endowed with eight factors. Since the word 'yathā' is an indeclinable in the sense of 'yena' (by which), it is said, "by which concentration."
395:
He is called 'jhānānubhāvasampanna' because he is endowed with the power of jhāna, which consists of the mundane supernormal knowledges (lokiya abhiññā) that are manifest and radiant. The use of the present tense (vattamāna vibhatti) in saying "this person of wrong view speaks thus" should be understood by the wise as intended to show that such speaking occurs at all times due to its uninterrupted nature. Indeed, when a specific time is not delimited, it is a statement of indefinite time.

She is called 'vañjhā' (a barren woman) because she yearns for children; the suffix 'jha' is added, and the letter 'na' is changed to a niggahīta. Alternatively, she is called 'vañjhā' because she kills (destroys) the fruit that is a child; the letter 'gha' along with the suffix is changed to 'jha', and a niggahīta is added. Like that woman, because it does not produce any fruit, it is called 'vañjho' (barren). Therefore, the Teacher said 'vañjhapasu' (barren animal) and so forth. To resolve the latent question of what kind of potential meaning is shown by this word with such a literal meaning, he said 'etena' and so forth. For one who has attained jhāna, the factors of jhāna especially become manifest; moreover, with those jhāna factors as the lead, the remaining associated states also become manifest. With reference to this meaning, it is said 'jhānādīnaṃ'. 'Rūpādijanaka-bhāvaṃ' means the capacity to produce matter and so forth. 'Paṭikkhipati' means he rejects [the idea], saying, "These [states] do not produce any matter at all." If it is asked why: If there were a productive nature in jhāna and so forth, then, like the states of matter etc., and like the states of pleasure etc., they would be known as having the nature of arising because of their dependence on conditions. If there is arising, there must inevitably be cessation; in that case, there would be no room for permanence. Therefore, he rejects that productive nature.

'Ṭhito' means remaining motionless. Alternatively, the word 'kūṭaṭṭha' itself should be understood as being established in the world in the sense of absolute permanence. It is called 'ṭhāyī' because it stands. Because it is a pillar and stands firmly and motionlessly, it is called 'esikaṭṭhāyī'. This word 'esikaṭṭhāyī' has the modifier placed after [the noun]; therefore, the meaning is like a city pillar (indakhīla) that is deeply embedded in the ground and stands motionlessly. Thus, the Teacher said 'yathā' and so forth. Here, by the word 'kūṭaṭṭha', he speaks of the absence of impermanence. By the words 'esikaṭṭhāyī ṭhito', he speaks of the absence of transformation, meaning that just as a pillar does not shake due to the impact of wind and so forth, so too it does not undergo transformation due to any cause. Since transformation is essentially destruction, it is said, "By both [terms], he shows the absence of destruction of the world."

Having shown the view of the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) in the manner stated, he now says 'keci pana' and so forth to show the view of some [teachers] (Kecivāda). 'Muñjato' means from the muñja grass. 'Īsikā' is the stalk (kaḷīra). Regarding that nature of things called the 'self' (atta) which is said to be born: it means that what already existed previously in the form of potential (satti-rūpa) now emerges and becomes manifest in the form of actuality (byatti-rūpa). By this statement 'vijjamānam-eva' (already existing), by showing the existence of the effect within the cause...
396:
He shows the Theory of Manifestation (abhivyatti-vāda) by way of manifest form (vyatti-rūpa). To clarify this statement: just as a rice ear existing within the sheath of the rice plant is the potential form (satti-rūpa), and its emergence is like the manifest form (vyatti-rūpa). If it is asked: "How does that which already exists by way of potential form, but was previously unmanifest, reach manifestation by way of manifest form?" The answer is: "Just as a pot covered by darkness reaches manifestation through light, so too does this [unmanifest thing] reach manifestation by way of manifest form."

In this Theory of Manifestation, the wise should investigate this analogy. In what way is light said to reveal the pot? If it is said that light reveals it by producing the cognition that has the pot as its object, then the Theory of Manifestation fails, because it points to the arising of a cognition that did not previously exist. If it is said that it reveals it by dispelling the darkness that was an obstacle to the cognition of the pot, even then the Theory of Manifestation fails. For if the cognition of the pot [already] existed, how could darkness be an obstacle to it? Just as the manifestation of the pot is untenable, so too the manifestation of the Self (atta) as conceived by those holding [wrong] views is untenable. In the case of the Self conceived by those teachers of [wrong] views, if a cognition that did not previously exist arises due to the meeting of the sense faculties such as the eye and objects such as forms, then by the very word "arising," the Theory of Manifestation fails. This is because it goes beyond mere manifestation and points to the arising of a cognition that did not previously exist. Likewise, Eternalism (sassata-vāda) also fails for that very reason. If it is said that cognition arises by dispelling delusion (moha), which is like darkness and acts as an obstacle to the occurrence of cognition, even so, if the cognition that knows the object [already] exists, how could delusion be an obstacle to it? Thus, the Theory of Manifestation fails. Furthermore, the Theory of Manifestation fails because of the existence of diversity (bheda). The diversity of the manifesting agents—such as the moon, sun, gems, or lamps—does not cause diversity in the objects to be manifested, such as pots. However, diversity of cognition does occur due to the diversity of objects, as cognition arises in accordance with the object. Therefore, manifestation is even more untenable. Moreover, in this Theory of Manifestation, the assumption of "occurrence" (vutti) by way of manifesting what [already] exists is not tenable. This is because the "occurrence," which is called the action of manifesting what exists, and the "possessor of the occurrence" (vuttimanta) are not recognized as being different. Indeed, the action called "occurrence" is not different from the thing that possesses it, just as the nature of touching, etc., is not different from contact (phassa), etc. Therefore, the Theory of Manifestation of certain [teachers], which assumes an "occurrence" called the manifestation of what exists as being non-different from the possessor of that occurrence, is certainly untenable. This is the analysis.

To speak further: some teachers, reading "Īsikaṭṭhāyī ṭhito" (standing like a reed), desire the aforementioned meaning. Taking that meaning as the cause, they also make a connection of the meaning with the words: "Those beings wander and roam, pass away and are reborn." To show that they do not leave the meaning unconnected as in the Commentary, he said "And because..." (yasmā ca), etc. In the phrase "Those beings wander," the meaning is: those very beings who stay in this human world as humans, only they, by approaching the state of devas, etc., reach the world of devas, etc., other than this human world. The intention is that [otherwise] there would be the destruction of kamma that was performed, or the arrival of kamma that was not performed, in another way. In the word "successively" (aparāparaṃ), another intention is "from one birth to another" or "repeatedly in various births." Changing the word "they pass away" (cavanti), he explains the meaning as "they reach such a reckoning." The permanent nature of the Self thus perceived...
397: It means that those who exist in this human world as human beings go to another place from this human world by attaining the state of a deva and so forth. Otherwise, it is intended that the destruction of performed kamma and the arrival of unperformed kamma might occur. 'Aparāpara' means occurring repeatedly, either from one existence to another or from one existence after another. By altering the word 'cavanti', the meaning is explained as 'they come to be reckoned in this way'; because the self (attā) thus conceived is of an eternal nature, there is no passing away (cuti) or rebirth (paṭisandhi). Due to its all-pervading nature, there is also no running on (sandhāvana) or wandering (saṃsaraṇa); however, it is intended that they come to be reckoned in this way and are so designated only because of the specific occurrence of phenomena (dhammas). By this statement, he shows this distorted view: that for the self which has an enduring nature, and for the being possessed of the five aggregates, there is only the arising and passing away of phenomena. As for the words to be spoken here, I shall speak them when clarifying the meaning of the term 'evaṅgatikā' during the investigation of this eternalist view (sassatavāda). Now, in order to show the mere connection of meanings mentioned in the Commentary, the passage beginning with 'Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana' is stated. With the words beginning with 'sandhāvanti', he destroys his own doctrine; the meaning is that the nature of impermanence established by words such as 'running on' is contradictory to the eternalist view previously professed by himself. The words beginning with 'diṭṭhigatikassa' serve to establish that meaning. 'Na nibaddhaṃ' means not permanent. Referring to the words beginning with 'sandhāvanti' and to the eternalist view, it is said, 'whether it is good or bad, it just happens.' Because they occur at all times, they are called 'sassati'; by changing the letter 'ra' to 'sa' and doubling it, the earth, Mount Sineru, the moon, and the sun are like the 'sassati' (eternal things). This is a word expressing a state (bhāva). 'Attā ca loko ca' (the self and the world) is the subject. Alternatively, 'sassatisamaṃ' is the indication of the subject through a change of gender. The meaning is that the self and the world, which are like the eternal earth, Mount Sineru, the moon, and the sun, truly exist. Here, the word 'iti' is a mere expletive (padapūraṇa). Grammarians (those who know sounds) desire the changing of the letter 'i' of the word 'iti' into the letter 'va' when it follows the letter 'e' of the word 'eva'. 'Sassatisamaṃ' also means enduring and having an eternal time; it is stated in the Sub-commentary (Ṭīkā) with the intention that the word 'sassatisama' has the same meaning as the word 'sassata'. Desiring to show the reason, the connection of words should be: 'This person of wrong view speaks, desiring to show the reason for those who designate the self and the world as eternal.' He does not establish the meaning realized by his own view for himself alone; rather, by means of the meaning realized by himself, he also establishes the meaning not realized by himself, and he makes others understand the meaning he desires, but he cannot make others understand the meaning he does not desire.
398:
Wise scholars desire the change of the letter 'i' to 'v' in the word 'iti'. The word 'sassatisamaṃ' also carries the meaning 'eternal, having a time that is never interrupted'. The old sub-commentary (ṭīkā) states that the word 'sassatisama' has the same meaning as the word 'sassata'. Since those who hold the view of eternalism (sassatadiṭṭhi) proclaim the self and the world to be eternal, the phrase should be connected as: 'This person of wrong view speaks thus' to show their reasoning. The benefit realized through one's own view is not accomplished for oneself alone; through the benefit one has realized, one can also bring about a benefit that is not [yet] realized. One can make others know the benefit one has decided upon, but one cannot make others know what has not been decided.

This reasoning is because, among many hundreds of thousands of births, in one birth, the thought arises: 'My self and the world are eternal' due to the possibility of recollection. He who experiences a certain thing is the only one who can recollect it, not another. Just as Dhammarakkhita cannot recollect what was experienced by Buddharakkhita, another person is not capable of recollecting what was experienced by someone else. As it is in these lives, so it was in lives earlier than these. Therefore, falling into the grip of wrong view by way of eternity—thinking 'My self and the world are eternal; just as they are eternal for me, so are they eternal for other beings'—that person of wrong view establishes others in that same view.
