In the Pali, because it is said, 'They proclaim various paths of conviction; he speaks thus,' it should be understood that 'reasoning' (hetu-dassana) is intended here by way of persuading others. 'Etam' refers to the eternal nature of oneself and the world. The phrase 'na kevalaṃ' etc., shows the view arrived at by way of meaning. The word 'ṭhāna' is used in the sense of 'cause', and here that cause is specifically the recollection of past lives (pubbenivāsānussati), as stated by 'idaṃ' etc.

There are three types of causes: the attaining cause (sampāpaka), the producing cause (nibbattaka), and the indicative cause (ñāpaka). Among these, the Noble Path is the attaining cause for Nibbāna; a seed is the producing cause for a sprout; and the state of being produced by conditions (paccayuppannatā) etc., are the indicative causes for impermanence etc. Here too, only the indicative cause is intended. Because the 'to-be-known' meaning is the cause of knowledge that has that meaning as its domain, it is called a cause. Because that knowledge stands depending on that [cause], it is called 'ṭhāna' (ground); and because that knowledge dwells or stands in this cause, it is called 'vatthu' (basis). For this reason, the Blessed One, having pointed it out with the word 'vatthu', explained it with the word 'ṭhāna'.

32-33. The second and third cycles (vāra) have no difference from the first cycle, except for the difference in time; thus the teacher said, 'In the two cycles above, the method is the same.' To show that difference in time in accordance with the Pali, 'kevalañhi' etc., is stated. The meaning is that the remaining second and third cycles are spoken of by way of recollection up to ten aeons of contraction and expansion, and up to forty aeons of contraction and expansion respectively. If so, why is eternalism divided into four? Should it not be divided into only two, like the theory of fortuitous origination (adhiccasamuppattika-vāda), without making a distinction of time? To resolve this objection, it is said: 'For one of dull wisdom...' It is divided into four by making a three-fold distinction of time based on three types of persons (such as those of dull wisdom) who have attained the knowledge of recollecting past lives, together with the reasoner (takki). Is it not the case that, just as there are four divisions by way of reasoners such as those who follow tradition (anussavādi), there should also be many varieties due to the inferiority or superiority of those with dull wisdom who have attained special meditative states? Despite this, why...
399:
Since there can be various types of divisions, there could be many categories. Why, then, are all individuals who have attained special distinctions grouped into only three categories and taught as such? It is because of the desire to show the highest limit. Indeed, among those three groups, those with inferior or medium wisdom can only recollect world-cycles fewer than the stated limit. However, even those with supreme wisdom cannot recollect beyond the stated limit. Therefore, desiring to show the highest limit in those various lives, the Buddha taught by grouping them into only three categories based on the ability to recollect hundreds of thousands of lives, ten world-cycles of contraction and expansion, and forty world-cycles of contraction and expansion. "Beyond that" means they cannot recollect beyond the aforementioned three periods or the forty world-cycles of contraction and expansion. Why? Because of the weakness of their wisdom. It is stated in the Commentaries that their wisdom is weak because they lack the discernment of mentality and materiality (nāmarūpa-pariccheda).

34. The Teacher says "he reasons (takkayati)" to indicate that it is only in the sense of the agent (kattu), as it is also connected to the nature of the first method. Because it is connected to that nature, the second method is also accomplished. In that context, "he reasons" means he speculates; the meaning is that he directs the mind towards various objects in the mode of eternalism and so forth. "Takka" (reasoning) is vitakka (thought/reflection) which is the basis for wrong view, characterized by striking at the object or deciding upon the object. Referring to reasoning through various means, it is said, "having reasoned, having reflected." The phrase "endowed with investigation" is merely an explanation of the meaning. 

As for the derivation (nibbacana), it should be stated in two ways, as in the word "takkī." Investigation is called "vīmaṃsā." That investigation is of two kinds: real wisdom and that which merely resembles wisdom. Here, however, only that which resembles wisdom is taken. In terms of its essence, that pseudo-wisdom is the arising of consciousness accompanied by greed, or improper attention (ayoniso manasikāra) known as wrong conviction. Or, it is the wavering of views which is wrong seeing occurring in the preliminary stage of a view. To show these three meanings, it is said: "weighing, liking, and accepting." In the words "having weighed" and so forth, they should be applied respectively as "weighing with the arising of consciousness accompanied by greed," and so on.

Striking at an object from all sides or repeatedly is called "pariyāhata" (beaten/pondered). Such striking at the object is indeed the speculation of thought (vitakka) upon the object. The Teacher shows that this word is a neuter abstract noun (bhāva-napuṃsaka) by the phrase "having reasoned through various means." "Pariyāyena" (by means) means "by cause." "Of the aforementioned variety" means having the three kinds of divisions mentioned. "Anuvicarita" (pondered) means repeatedly occurring, or repeatedly touched upon by the investigation that follows the scrutiny. Even the function of the mental states following that investigation is spoken of in that way by attributing it to the primary state.

It is called "paṭibhāna" (inspiration/illumination) because it appears clearly. It is called "paṭibhāna" because it arises from the arising of consciousness associated with views, which clarifies the specific mode of concentration as it has been attained. Thus, it is a manifestation, one's own personal inspiration...
400:
...one's own inspiration. Therefore, the Teacher said, "produced merely from one's own inspiration." By the word "matta" (mere/only), he excludes the attainment of distinctions such as the jhānas, paths, and fruits. In describing the period that has not been scrutinized, the explanation of the meaning is appropriate only by way of the present tense; thus, he says, "he speaks thus."

In the Pāli text, the division of the reasoner (takkī), which is stated by way of a general description or by the method of ellipsis (ekasesa) as "he is a reasoner, an investigator," is analyzed by the words "Among them, there are four types," and so on. Hearing again from others is "anussuti" (tradition/hearsay); he who has this tradition is an "anussutika" (traditionalist). One who remembers a birth previously experienced in the past is a "jātissara" (one who remembers past births). Because it is obtained, it is called "lābha" (gain); whatever is obtained by oneself, such as form (rūpa) and so on, or pleasure (sukha) and so on, is just any kind of gain, but not the distinction of jhāna and so forth. Therefore, it is said in the Pāli text: "He speaks this word which is beaten out by reasoning, followed by investigation, and self-generated inspiration." In the Commentary also, it is said: "produced merely from one's own inspiration." The Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla also says: "By the word 'matta', he excludes the attainment of distinctions and so forth" (Dī. Ni. Ṭī. 1.34). He who has those gains is a "lābhī" (one who has gains). Pure reasoning, unmixed with previous views, or reasoning that is pure, is "suddhatakka" (pure reasoning); he who has that pure reasoning is a "suddhatakkika" (pure reasoner).

"Tena hi" is a particle in the sense of exhortation; by that, he exhorts the grasp of the eternalist view in the manner of, "If King Vessantara and the Blessed One are the same." "Lābhitāya" means because of being one who gains form, pleasure, and so forth. "In the future also, it will be thus"—this statement is made referring to the reasoning intended here by way of showing the possibility that it can also happen to a reasoner who has gains (lābhī-takkī). This is because one becomes an eternalist specifically by reasoning about the future portion. The statement "In the past also, it was thus" is merely to show the strong dependence (upanissaya) for reasoning about the future portion. Indeed, that person with wrong view first relies on reasoning following the past portion, thinking, "Just as my self is happy now, so it was in the past," and then, reasoning that "In the future also, it will be thus," he adopts the wrong view. By the words "When this is so, this happens," the fault arises that in impermanent states, "one person acts and another experiences"; and if that were so, there would be the destruction of what was done (by the doer) and the arrival of what was not done (by the experiencer). However, in permanent states, the fault that "one person acts and another experiences" does not arise. Thus, he shows the mode of seeking logic by the reasoner, (thinking) that if it is so, there would be the non-destruction of what was done and the non-arrival of what was not done.

"Takkamatteneva" means merely by pure reasoning. By the word "matta" (mere), he shows the absence of scriptures (āgama) and tradition (anussava) and so forth. If one asks, "Is it not true that even one who attains special distinctions (like jhāna) can be an eternalist?"...
401:
Eternalists, who hold the view that things are permanent, due to the cause of attaining special distinctions such as meditative absorptions (jhāna) and higher knowledge (abhiññā), recollect their own continuity of aggregates and the mental phenomena associated with those aggregates as they were experienced in many hundreds of thousands of births, in ten cycles of world-contraction and expansion (saṃvaṭṭa-vivaṭṭa), and in forty cycles of world-contraction and expansion, thinking, "The self is eternal, the world is eternal." From that recollection, based on the reasoning that it was so in past lives, they reason that it will be so in the future regarding their own future state and the state of all beings, and thus they develop a wrong adherence to eternity.

If this is the case, all Eternalists—whether they are those who reason based on hearsay (anussutika), those who reason based on recollection of past lives (jātissara), or those who reason after attaining meditative absorptions—would fall only into the category of reasoners (takkī), as their views are formed through reasoning based on the objects they have attained. If they were so categorized, there would be no distinction, and this Eternalism would be established as only one type. Furthermore, reasoning in the manner described must necessarily be accepted. Otherwise, would not an Eternalist who has attained special distinctions fall into the category of Partial-eternalism (ekaccasassatika) or the category of Fortuitous-origination (adhiccasamuppannika)? Such a question may be raised.

This should not be understood in that way. For those who have attained special distinctions, the ability to recollect the continuity of aggregates over a very long period is the unique cause (asādhāraṇa-kāraṇa) for adopting the eternalist view. Therefore, the Buddha showed recollection itself as the primary cause (padhāna-kāraṇa), saying, "I recollect many past lives; through this special attainment, I know this." The reasoning of such a person, thinking "Through this special attainment, I know this," is not primary here; because it occurs depending on recollection, that reasoning falls into a secondary status. In the Dispensation (Sāsana) as well as in the world, it is well-known to designate things by their unique primary cause, such as "eye-consciousness" or "barley sprout."

In this way, this teaching clarifies the primary cause. Therefore, although there are many varieties among those who have attained special distinctions, such as those with dull wisdom, and among reasoners, such as those who rely on hearsay or those who are inferior, the Blessed One classified and established Eternalism into four types by grouping other varieties together. Indeed, the Buddha, the King of Dhamma, does not teach the Dhamma with anything left out in this context. If it is asked, "In the case of those who rely on hearsay (anussutika) and others, would not hearsay also become the primary factor?" the answer is no. This is because, in the absence of direct realization through higher knowledge, reasoning alone is the primary factor for them. This meaning has already been stated: "Designation by the unique primary cause is well-known in the Dispensation and in the world."

Alternatively, to show that reasoning without the basis of attaining special distinctions is a separate cause for adopting the eternalist view, the attainment of special distinctions is stated as a separate cause for the eternalist view. Since those who attain such distinctions are of three types—those with dull wisdom, medium wisdom, and sharp wisdom—they are classified into three varieties.
402:
The Blessed One established Eternalism in four ways by taking all reasoners together under the commonality of being reasoners (takkī).

To show the meaning of the word "aññatarena" (by one), it is said "ekena" (by one). With reference to the indefinite meaning of the word "vā" (or) when applied to what is not the primary case, it is said "dvīhi vā tīhi vā" (by two or three). By this word "vā," it is shown that among the four causes, reasoning is a supporting cause in the designation of certain types of Eternalism. The word "bahiddhā" is a particle indicating the subject meaning "outside"; to show this, "bahi" etc., is stated.

Here a question is raised: Are these causes the reason for one's own wrong adherence (abhinivesa), or are they the reason for establishing the view in others (patiṭṭhāpana)? There is a further objection here: If they are primarily the causes for one's own wrong adherence, why are only recollection (anussaraṇa) and reasoning (takkana) taken, and not perverted perception (saññā-vipallāsa) and so on? Indeed, perverted perception, improper attention (ayoniso manasikāra), association with the unworthy (asappurisa-upanissaya), and hearing false Dhamma (asaddhamma-savana) are also bases for views (diṭṭhiṭṭhāna) in the sense that they bring about wrong views. If they are the causes for establishing the view in others, then just as attainment (adhigama) is the cause for recollection, and logic (yutti) is the cause for reasoned inquiry, scripture (āgama) should also be stated as a cause. In either case, since other causes mentioned above are possible, the statement "there is nothing outside of this" would be inappropriate.

It is not inappropriate; it is appropriate. Why? In the aspect of wrong adherence (abhinivesa-pakkha), this person of wrong views first emerges through improper attention due to association with the unworthy and hearing false Dhamma, and thus becomes one with perverted perception (vipallāsa-saññā). Because of not understanding the nature of phenomena like form (rūpa) which break down moment by moment, he oversteps the logic of phenomena (dhamma-yutti), wrongly adopts the method of oneness (ekatta-naya), and through the aforementioned recollection and reasoning, develops the wrong adherence in the aggregates that "the self and the world are eternal." Because these are the proximate causes and the primary causes, and because by taking them other causes are also included, only recollection and reasoning are taken here.

In the aspect of establishing the view in others (patiṭṭhāpana-pakkha), scripture (āgama) also stands only on logic (yutti). This is especially because outsiders who lack scripture are those who grasp through reasoning. Therefore, only recollection and reasoning are taken as the bases for the eternalist view.

Furthermore, the characteristics of ultimate realities (paramattha-dhamma) are of two kinds: individual characteristics (sabhāva-lakkhaṇa) and general characteristics (sāmañña-lakkhaṇa). Among them, the realization of individual characteristics is direct knowledge (paccakkha-ñāṇa), and the realization of general characteristics is inferential knowledge (anumāna-ñāṇa). Scripture (āgama) also brings about only inferential knowledge because it perfects the wisdom resulting from hearing (sutamaya-paññā).
403:
Scripture brings about only inferential knowledge (anumāna-ñāṇa) because it fulfills wisdom based on learning (sutamaya-paññā). One who stands in the contemplation of wisdom by reflecting on the nature of the teachings heard gives rise to wisdom based on reflection (cintāmaya-paññā) and gradually attains direct knowledge (paccakkha-ñāṇa) through cultivation. In this way, scripture also does not transcend the sphere of reasoning (takka). Therefore, it should be understood that scripture is included under the term 'reasoning' (takka). In the Commentary, this scripture is clearly explained by the term 'reasoning based on tradition' (anussuti-takka). Since there is no remaining cause not included in such recollection and reasoning, it should be understood that the statement 'There is no view outside this [dispensation]' is appropriate. Because it is taught, 'They speak of various inclinations,' and 'They designate the self and the world as eternal,' only the grounds (vatthu) that establish wrong views in this context of eternalism are taught here. This is because by teaching the grounds for establishing the view, dogmatic adherence (abhinivesa) is also accomplished. Among many various teachings, when a certain teaching is given, it should be understood that other teachings are also established; only that specific teaching is taught. Between dogmatic adherence and the establishment of a view, even if adherence is taught, the establishment of the view is not necessarily accomplished. This is because establishment is not certain whenever there is adherence. Among those who adhere dogmatically, some establish the view while others do not. But if the establishment of the view is taught, adherence is also accomplished, because adherence is certain when there is establishment. For whoever establishes another in a wrong view also adheres to that view himself.

In the word 'tayidaṃ', the teacher says the syllable 'ta' refers to the statement 'They designate the self and the world as eternal.' 'Tato' means because of knowing in such a manner. Because they are extremely blameworthy and are the cause of many harms, the views themselves are called grounds (ṭhāna); thus they are called 'grounds for views' (diṭṭhiṭṭhāna). Just as it was said, 'Monks, I declare wrong view to be the ultimate fault,' with that meaning in mind, it is said 'Views themselves are the grounds for views.' The cause of views is also called 'grounds for views' (diṭṭhiṭṭhāna) in the sense of giving rise to views. The sentence starting with 'Yathāha' is established by the Paṭisambhidāmagga Pali. Among those causes, the five aggregates are also called 'grounds for views' in the sense of being objects. Is it not taught, 'He regards form as self,' and so on? Ignorance (avijjā) is also called a ground for views because it assists by way of decisive support (upanissaya) and so on. It is taught, 'Monks, an uninstructed worldling who has no regard for the noble ones, who is unskilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones...' and so on. Contact (phassa) is also called a ground for views because it is the means of grasping a wrong view through contact. Likewise, it is taught, 'They experience that feeling, having been touched through the condition of contact.' Perception (saññā) is also called a ground for views because it perceives only the appearance. It is taught, 'The tendencies to proliferation (papañca) which have perception as their source,' and 'Having perceived earth as earth,' and so on. Thought (vitakka) is also called a ground for views because it reflects on the appearance. Therefore, it is taught, 'Having applied thought to views, they speak of two things as true or false,' and 'He is given to thinking, given to investigating.' Unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra) is also called a ground for views because it is a cause associated with unwholesome states. Therefore, it is taught, 'In one who attends unwisely, one of these six views arises: the view "Self exists for me" arises in him as true and established.' A bad friend (pāpamitta) is also called a ground for views in the sense of imitation of what is seen, and so on.
404:
"By reason of contact" means (as stated in the Dīgha Nikāya) "they experience by touching and touching." Perception (saññā) is also a cause of wrong view because it grasps only the appearance. Thus, it has been taught: "From perception as a source, the conceptual proliferations (papañca-saṅkhā) arise," and "Having perceived earth as earth," and so forth. Thought (vitakka) is also a cause because it reflects on appearances. Therefore, it has been taught: "Having formulated thoughts among views, they speak of the dual states of truth and falsehood," and "He is a thinker, an inquirer," and so forth. Improper attention (ayoniso manasikāra) is also a cause because it is the common cause of unwholesome states. Thus, He said: "For one who attends improperly in this way, one of the six views arises. The view 'The self exists for me' arises as true and firm," and so forth. A bad friend (pāpamitta) is also a cause because of following what is seen. It is also taught: "Monks, I do not see any other single external factor that leads to such great harm as this, namely, bad friendship," and so forth. The voice of another (paratoghosa) is also a cause because of hearing a poorly explained Dhamma. Thus, it is taught: "Monks, there are these two conditions for the arising of wrong view. Which two? The voice of another and improper attention," and so forth. Teachings heard or taught by others are called the voice of another.

The Pali passage beginning with "The aggregates are the cause" clarifies that meaning. Therein, 'hetu' (root) is so-called in the sense of producing, and 'paccaya' (condition) in the sense of supporting. 'Upādāya' means having clung to or depending on. There is also a variant reading 'uppādāya', meaning for the sake of arising. It is called 'samuṭṭhāna' (origination) because it originates from this; these are the aggregates and so on. Here, however, the term 'samuṭṭhāna' refers only to the state of being an origin, because the word 'bhāva' (state) is elided and the emphasis is on the state. They are grasped by clinging within one's own continuity. They are made to occur in one's own and others' continuities. The word 'para' has the sense of repetition, so it is said "again and again." 'Pariniṭṭhāpitā' means reaching the end or the peak of clinging wrongly, such as "Only this view of mine is true, other views are empty and false." The phrase 'ārammaṇavasena' (by way of object) refers to the aggregates among the eight grounds for wrong view. The phrase 'pavattanavasena' (by way of occurrence) refers to ignorance, contact, perception, thought, and improper attention. The phrase 'āsevanavasena' (by way of repetition) refers to bad friends and the voice of another. Although they are synonyms by way of their intrinsic meaning, to show how they should be expressed by way of conventional meaning, it is said "the next world of such a nature." This is because a synonym is meaningful only through some specific distinction.
405:
The next world is called 'abhisamparāya' because in this next life, beings, by the power of kamma, are directed toward, reach, and arise in the next world. Just as in the Pali passages such as "Ānanda, thus wholesome virtues lead gradually to the highest (jhāna, magga)," those learned in grammar desire the word 'para' to have the sense of "going" (gati) according to the Curādi group of roots. This is another method besides the commentary's method.

'Evaṅgatikā' means having such a destination, having such an end, or having an end in breaking and destruction through such inquiry. Here, the word 'gati' has the sense of "end" (niṭṭhāna), as in the Pali passages such as "For that Great Man endowed with these marks, there are only two destinations (ends)." The meaning is this: these grounds for wrong view, which are grasped and misapprehended by superimposing a self and a state of permanence—which do not exist in the ultimate sense—upon ultimate reality, are like the babbling of fools. They continue to occur and appear as long as the wise do not inquire into or scrutinize them. However, when scrutinized by the wise, having no stable foundation and being unable to withstand investigation, they break and perish like dewdrops at sunrise or like fireflies.

In that inquiry, the summary is as follows: If the self or the world conceived by the sectarians were permanent, then because of its immutability and its not abandoning its previous form, it would be impossible to effect any distinction. Thus, instructions for the purpose of restraining from harm and practicing for benefit would be useless for an eternalist. Otherwise, how could he even carry out that instruction, given the absence of change? In such a case, for the conceived self, actions such as giving or harming would be impossible, just like for the open sky. Similarly, regarding the experience of pleasure and pain, it would be inconsistent for an eternalist because there is no connection to kamma. Since birth and so on would be impossible, liberation (vimokkha) would not occur. If it is argued, "The mere ultimate reality of that self arises and perishes, and by the power of that arising and perishing, these designations of action and so on occur," even then, it is impossible to conceive that a self which is stable and does not abandon its previous form is a mere ultimate reality. Or else, those states of that self are momentary. Therefore, the states that arise for that self would be either different from the self or not different. If they are different, there is no distinction in the self even when those momentary states arise, by which it is desired that it acts, experiences, passes away, and is reborn. In such a case...
406:
Speculating on ultimate reality (paramattha) would also be useless. Therefore, in that state where ultimate reality exists only for a moment, the aforementioned fault would remain exactly as it is. If [the states] were not different from the self (ananya), then since the self would be non-different from the moments (avatthā) that have arising and passing away, it would possess the nature of arising and passing away just like those moments; so where could there be an opportunity for permanence? Or else, those moments themselves would have to exist with permanence like the self. Therefore, because liberation from the bonds [of kamma] (bandhavimokkha) would be impossible, Eternalism (sassatavāda) is certainly untenable. In this Eternalism, no proponent would be able to state a pure logical proof for the permanence of phenomena. A statement devoid of logic does not please the minds of the wise. That is why we said: "As long as the wise do not cross-examine and investigate, those views continue to circulate and manifest."

In the phrase "sakāraṇaṃ sagatikaṃ" (with cause, with destination), the word "sa" (saha) has the sense of "existing" (vijjamāna), as in "salomako sapakkhako" (one with hair, a bird with wings). It does not have the sense of inherence (samavāya). This is the intended meaning because the wrong view mentioned by the phrase "Monks, the Tathāgata knows that wrong view" is conjoined by the word "ca" (and), and because it was taught that only the cause and destination are known by the phrase "And the Tathāgata knows that [cause and destination]." The meaning is this: Monks, the Tathāgata knows that wrong view which has a cause and a destination. He knows not only that [view], but indeed he knows all that which is called the cause and destination of that view. The meaning of the sentence taught as "Tato... pajānāti" is explained by the method already mentioned, starting with "Tato ca," etc. Since this Brahmajāla Sutta is an analysis of Omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa) specifically, the words "sabbaññutañāṇañca" are spoken according to the context. Alternatively, if Omniscience is mentioned, the knowledge of the destruction of taints (āsavakkhayañāṇa) is included as its basis. Or, because it is inseparable from Omniscience, all the Ten Powers (dasabala), etc., are also included; thus that same statement is made.

"Evaṃvidhaṃ" refers to virtue (sīla), etc., of the various types already mentioned, starting with "sīlañca." In the word "pajānantopi," the word "pi" (or "api") shows that the word "ca" in the phrase "tañca" has the sense of commendation (sambhāvana). By this, it commends [the Buddha], saying that the Tathāgata does not even settle into or cling to the special qualities such as virtue, which are the essence and far superior to that wrong view—so what need is there to mention the baits of the round of rebirth (vaṭṭāmisa)? The word "Ahaṃ" (I) shows the manner of misapprehending and clinging through the power of wrong view (diṭṭhi) and conceit (māna). In the word "pajānāmi," the word "iti" has the sense of "manner" (pakāra) or "illustration" (nidassana). "Mama" (Mine) shows the manner of misapprehending and clinging through the power of craving (taṇhā). "Taṇhādittimānaparāmāsavasena" means through the power of misapprehension known as craving, wrong view, and conceit. Transgressing the nature of ultimate reality and grasping as "I" or "Mine" in a way that is not true is called misapprehension (parāmāsa); these are just craving, etc. Indeed, there is nothing among the five aggregates that should be grasped as "I" or "Mine."
407:
"For that Tathāgata who does not misapprehend or cling, the extinction [of defilements] (nivvuti) is known"—this is how the words are connected. The word "aparāmasato" is a qualifying attribute (visesana) that is internal to the cause of knowing the extinction [of defilements] in detail. In relation to the word "viditā" (known), it is in the possessive case (genitive) with the sense of the agent (kattar). The meaning is: Because of the practice devoid of misapprehension, the extinction—the Unconditioned Element (asaṅkhata-dhātu)—is known or attained by that Tathāgata who is the agent. The word "aparāmasato" here is in the ablative case in the sense of cause.

The phrase "aparāmāsapaccayā" (by reason of non-clinging) is a statement showing the cause of knowing [Nibbāna] individually and in detail. Although the agent was already expressed by the word "assa," the teacher said "sayameva attanāyeva" (by himself, by his own self) to show the specific nature of the agent as "individually by himself." The words "sayaṃ" and "attanā" are adverbial forms (bhāvana-pumsaka). They are also indeclinables (nipāta). Because it is taught as "aparāmasato," in this sutta, only the extinction of misapprehensions (parāmāsa)—namely craving, view, and conceit—is taught. By that teaching, the extinction of other defilements is also accomplished; therefore, the meaning is shown by the phrase "tesaṃ parāmāsakilesānaṃ" (of those defilements called misapprehensions). Alternatively, because it is taught as "aparāmasato," it is understood that in this Brahmajāla Sutta, only the extinction of misapprehensions is taught. However, by teaching [the extinction of] those misapprehensions, the extinction of the remaining defilements is also said to be taught, because they have a single purpose in being abandoned (pahānekaṭṭhatā), etc. Therefore, the extinction of those remaining defilements should also be extracted and shown. Thus it is said, "tesaṃ parāmāsakilesānaṃ." The meaning is: the extinction of the misapprehensions called craving, view, and conceit, as well as the other defilements. This is the "ox and bull" method (go-balīvadda-naya). "Nivvuti" is the Unconditioned Element (asaṅkhata-dhātu), which is the extinction of defilements. The Blessed One reached that Nibbāna at the foot of the Bodhi tree. Therefore, he has known that Nibbāna individually by himself.

"Yathāpaṭipannena" means "by whichever practice." To show that practice, the connection is shown by "tāsaṃyeva... ādimāha." One might ask: "Why does he teach the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) only regarding feelings (vedanā)?" To answer this, he said "yāsu," etc. By this, he shows the beauty of the teaching (desanā-vilāsa). The Blessed One, having attained the beauty of teaching and being skillful in teaching, although there are many teachings on the Four Noble Truths by way of the aggregates (khandha), bases (āyatana), etc., he extracts only feeling as the ground for full understanding (pariññā-bhūmi) to show that those with wrong views fall into the thicket of views through wrong practice regarding feelings. "Idha" means "in this doctrine." The word "ettha" is the same. "Kammaṭṭhānaṃ" refers to the meditation subject of the Four Noble Truths. Among these Four Noble Truths, the five aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandha) taken by taking feeling are the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca). The arising of ignorance (avijjā-samudaya) taken by taking the cause of feelings (samudaya) is the Truth of the Origin (samudaya-sacca). The cessation (atthaṅgama) and the escape (nissaraṇa)...
408:
The five aggregates of clinging, which are grasped by grasping feeling, are the Truth of Suffering. The arising of ignorance, which is grasped by grasping the cause of feelings, is the Truth of the Origin. The Truth of Cessation is understood through the methods of the cessation and the escape from feelings, and the Truth of the Path is understood by the phrase "knowing as it really is." Thus, the Four Noble Truths should be understood. The phrase "knowing as it really is" is a term with the meaning of an analytical explanation; therefore, to show that meaning analytically, the words beginning with "Therein (in that feeling)" are stated. Specifically, the meaning should be shown analytically as appropriate in terms of the characteristics such as "with the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of feeling." Generally, however, it means knowing and penetrating the cause of feeling, etc., by the power of penetrating the object with insight-wisdom (vipassanā-paññā), and by the power of non-deluded penetration with path-wisdom (magga-paññā). 

"In the sense of arising due to conditions" means by the arising of conditions such as ignorance, according to the characteristic stated as "When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises," and by not being eradicated by the Path. For as long as a condition is not eradicated by the Path, it is called a "condition." "Characteristic of production" (nibbattilakkhaṇa) means the characteristic of arising, the meaning of birth (jāti). In the phrase "of the five characteristics," one should not only take the characteristic of the arising of the four conditions but also the characteristic of the condition itself, because they are beneficial to those effects depending on the cause of arising. Therefore, it is described as "by not being eradicated by the Path."

"In the sense of cessation due to the cessation of conditions" means by the cessation of conditions such as ignorance, according to the characteristic stated as "When this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases," and by the eradication by the Noble Path. "Characteristic of change" (vipariṇāmalakkhaṇa) means the characteristic of cessation, the meaning of breaking up (bhaṅga). "Passing away" (vaya) means cessation. "Which" (yaṃ) means because of the cause known as the state of being a condition. "Dependent on feeling" means having obtained the previously arisen feeling which has become a condition such as an object. "Pleasure and joy" (sukha somanassa) means both pleasure and joy. "This" (ayaṃ) refers to the state of being a condition for the pleasure and joy that arise later, as appropriate, following the previous feeling. It is called "gratification" (assāda) because it is to be enjoyed.

Another method: "Which" (yaṃ) refers to pleasure and joy. The word "this" (ayaṃ), although referring to pleasure and joy which are expressed in the neuter gender, is expressed in the masculine gender in consideration of the word "gratification" (assāda). In this alternative explanation, only the arising of pleasure and joy is shown by those things that have the nature of arising, because the power and the possessor of power are not different. Indeed, without pleasure and joy, the arising of that gratification cannot be obtained. Thus, the arising of pleasure and joy dependent on a previous feeling is also called the "gratification" (assāda) of the previous feeling because it is enjoyed.
409:
The summary of the meaning here is: when joy arises based on a previously arisen feeling, either the mode of being enjoyed, which is called the state of being a condition of the previous feeling, or the mode of enjoying that, which is called the arising of joy—this is the gratification (assāda) of the previous feeling. But how does pleasure arise based on feeling? Is it not a tactile object? This is not a fault because it is intended as the occurrence based on mental pleasure (cetasika-sukha) alone. In the occurrence based on an object, the taking of "joy" (somanassa) is merely a qualification, as in "joy is pleasure," just as one might say "the tree is a Sissoo tree." However, bodily pleasure (kāyika-sukha) that arises due to other conditions is also gratification; or this statement should be seen as being said according to what is obtainable.

By the words "that feeling which is impermanent," etc., the power of the feeling which possesses that power is shown. Therein, the meaning is: that feeling is impermanent (anicca) in the sense of non-existence after having been. It is suffering (dukkha) in the sense of being oppressed by arising and passing away. It is subject to change (vipariṇāmadhamma) in the sense of being made to change in two ways: by aging and by death. This state of being impermanent, suffering, and subject to change of all such feelings is the danger (ādīnava) of feeling. It is called ādīnava because the state of being extremely pitiable proceeds from that danger. Alternatively, just as a miserable person is called ādīnava in the sense of proceeding in extreme wretchedness, this danger is also called so because it has such a nature. Indeed, the power and the possessor of power are not different, because one cannot exist without the other.

In this context, by the word "impermanent" (aniccā), the danger of neutral feeling (upekkhā-vedanā) is shown by way of the suffering of formations (saṅkhāra-dukkhatā), or the danger of all feelings is shown. By the word "suffering" (dukkhā), the danger of painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā) is shown by way of the suffering of pain (dukkha-dukkhatā). By the word "subject to change" (vipariṇāmadhammā), the danger of pleasant feeling (sukha-vedanā) is shown by way of the suffering due to change (vipariṇāma-dukkhatā). Or, without distinction, all three terms should be applied to all three types of feelings. 

"The removal of desire and lust" (chandarāga-vinaya) means the destruction or removal of lust known as desire. According to the saying, "The gender and case-ending change according to the power of the meaning," it should be connected as "the abandonment of whatever desire and lust." These two terms are merely synonymous. Since the Path is mentioned by the phrase "knowing as it really is," the connection in sequence by way of the Path and Nibbāna is also appropriate. The word "vedanāya" (from feeling) is in the ablative case (nissakka). "Escape" (nissaraṇa) means renunciation (nekkhamma) (from feeling). For as long as one does not abandon the desire and lust bound to feeling, so long is this person attached to feeling. But when he abandons that desire and lust, then this person is escaped from and dissociated from feeling. Therefore, the abandonment of desire and lust is called the escape (nissaraṇa) from feeling.
410:
By speaking of the escape from those feelings, the statement regarding the escape from the five aggregates of clinging is already established, because the mental and physical phenomena that arise together with feelings and serve as their support and object are already included. However, the teaching proceeds by taking feeling as the primary head; the reason for prioritizing feeling has already been stated below. This meaning should also be clarified through the power of the method of the Mode of Characteristics (Lakkhaṇa-hāra). For the Venerable Mahākaccāyana Thera said this:
“When one phenomenon is mentioned, whatever other phenomena have the same characteristic are all [considered] mentioned; that mode is called the Mode of Characteristics.” (Netti. 485).

Because the remaining types of clinging have clinging to sensual pleasures (kāmupādāna) as their root, and because when clinging to sensual pleasures is abandoned, the remaining types of clinging no longer exist, it is said: “one without clinging due to the absence of desire and lust.” By this, the meaning of the phrase “anupādā-vimutto” (liberated through non-clinging) is shown in brief. The intended meaning is this: one is without clinging due to the absence of desire and lust, and because of being without clinging, one is called “anupādā-vimutta” (one liberated without clinging). To expand upon or to complete that meaning, the words beginning with “yasmiṃ” are spoken. In that context, “yasmiṃ upādāne” refers to clinging to sensual pleasures (kāmupādāna), which is the root of the remaining types of clinging. “Tassa” refers to that clinging to sensual pleasures. “Anupādiyitvā” means without grasping (without clinging) through the power of desire and lust. By this word “anupādiyitvā,” it is shown that in the term “anupādā-vimutto,” the letter “ya” is elided, either as a compound (samāsa) or as a sentence (byāsa).

The words beginning with “ime kho” are a concluding statement indicating that the phenomena inquired about have been fully answered. To show that the very knowledge mentioned as “pajānāti” (he knows) is indicated by the word “ima,” He said the words beginning with “ye te.” The construction (yojanā) is to be understood as follows: those phenomena of Omniscient Knowledge (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) about which [the wanderers] inquired, those phenomena of Omniscient Knowledge with which they might praise [the Tathāgata], those He knows; thus, these phenomena of Omniscient Knowledge indicated in this way are profound... and to be experienced by the wise. The words beginning with “evaṃ” show the summarized meaning. In that context, although by the words, “Monks, the Tathāgata is liberated through non-clinging,” He shows the attainment of the supreme Path and Fruit of Arahatship, and by the words beginning with “and the origin of feelings,” He shows the meditation on the Four Noble Truths. Nevertheless, because He has thoroughly penetrated that Dhamma-element (dhammadhātu) which is Omniscient Knowledge, He is able to analyze this speculative view together with its cause and its destination in detail. The King of Dhamma, the Buddha, wishing to make that very Omniscient Knowledge more evident through its proximate cause, the preliminary practice, and its ground of arising, shows it in this way; thus it is said, “tadeva niyyātitaṃ” (that very [knowledge] has been delivered). It means it is concluded, it is finished.
411:
The meaning is: in between the words of the teaching asked and answered, the Buddha analyzed the sixty-two views by way of showing the manner in which that Omniscient Knowledge, the quality of the Buddha, knows them.

## The Līnatthappakāsanā sub-commentary on the explanation of the First Recitation Section is finished.

## Explanation of the Doctrine of Partial Eternalism (Ekaccasassatavāda)

To clarify the derivative (taddhita) term ‘ekaccasassatikā’ by means of a compound (samāsa) term, it is said ‘ekaccasassatavādā.’ Because they hold the view that some things among beings and conditioned formations are eternal, that doctrine is called the Doctrine of Partial Eternalism (Ekaccasassatavāda). Those who hold this view are called ‘ekaccasassatikā’ by way of the derivative, and ‘ekaccasassatavādā’ by way of the compound. This method also applies to the term ‘ekacca-asassatika’ (partial non-eternalists). If it is asked: “When ‘ekaccasassatikā’ is said, is it not already established by implication that others are ‘ekacca-asassatika’?” It is true that it is established by meaning, but it is not yet established by word. Therefore, it is spoken in that way to make it more evident by word. The Lord of Dhamma, the Buddha, does not teach the Dhamma in this discourse leaving any remainder.

Those who hold the doctrine that “The Lord Issara (Viṣṇu) is eternal, but other beings are non-eternal” are those who take some beings to be eternal, like the Theists (Issara-vāda). Likewise are those who hold that “Brahmā is eternal, but others are non-eternal.” Those who hold that “Atoms (paramāṇu) are eternal, but composites such as diatomic molecules (dviaṇuka) etc. are non-eternal” (see Vaisheshika Philosophy, Chapter 7, Section 1) are those who take some conditioned formations to be eternal, like the followers of Kāṇāda. Likewise are those who hold that “The eye etc. are non-eternal, but consciousness (viññāṇa) is eternal” (see Nyāya and Vaisheshika Philosophy).

‘In this’ (idha) means in this term ‘ekaccasassatikā’ or in this teaching. ‘Are taken’ (gahitā) means are spoken, or are well-taken by the knowledge of the teaching as things to be taught, because they are indeed taught in that way. To expand: in this Brahmajāla Sutta, the first three doctrines are taught in relation to beings, and the fourth doctrine is taught in relation to conditioned formations.

This statement ‘saṅkhārekaccasassatikā’ (partial eternalism regarding formations) is spoken by way of showing the true nature of those phenomena which are grasped by them as being eternal; it is not spoken by way of showing the view of one who holds that [only] some are eternal. In his view, the phenomenon he considers eternal is only the Unconditioned (asaṅkhata). That is why it is said in the Pali: “That which is called mind... etc... will remain.” For one who does not admit that a certain nature is conditioned by causes, if he is not insane, he would not be able to admit that such a nature is eternal, permanent, etc. By this text ‘saṅkhārekaccasassatikā,’ the inappropriateness of the Sevenfold Predication (Sattabhaṅga-vāda), which posits that “natures endowed with arising, vanishing, and permanence might be partly eternal, partly non-eternal, or partly indescribable as eternal or non-eternal,” is made evident.
412:
"It may be that it should not be said [as permanent or impermanent]," etc. (Dī. Ni. Ṭī. 1.38). By this and other statements, the unsuitability of the Sattabhaṅgavāda (Sevenfold Predication) that has arisen has been clearly demonstrated.

To explain this unsuitability: If a phenomenon is said to "exist" in a certain nature, and that same phenomenon is said "not to exist" in that same nature, it would be Anekantavāda (the doctrine of non-absolutism/indefinite view). If it is said in another nature, it would not be Anekantavāda. In this doctrine, it is not appropriate to speak of connections with locations and so forth, because that fact is well-known throughout the world and there is no dispute about it.

Some teachers say: "Just as when a gold pot is made into a crown, the state of being a pot perishes and the state of being a crown arises, but the state of being gold remains; likewise, among all natures, some phenomena perish, some arise, but the nature itself remains." These teachers should be asked: "What is that gold which remains in both the pot and the crown? If it is matter (rūpa) etc., that matter is impermanent like sound. If it is merely a collection of matter etc. (a concept/paññatti), then the states of existence, non-existence, or permanence cannot be found in that collection." Therefore, Anekantavāda is not possible. The fault regarding the different or non-different occurrence of phenomena (dhamma) and the possessor of phenomena (dhammī) has already been mentioned in the investigation of Sassatavāda (Eternalism). Therefore, that fault should be understood according to the method already stated.

Furthermore, since the self (attā) and the world (loka) are admitted to exist in the ultimate sense (paramattha), they do not have a nature that is permanent, impermanent, or indescribable. For example, matter is one of the types such as permanent etc., or like a lamp etc. Indeed, in matter etc., which have the nature of arising and passing away, it is impossible to know a nature that is indescribable as permanent or impermanent. The matter of the soul (jīva) would also be one of the types such as permanent etc. Thus, like the perishing of a being, the impossibility of other perishable phenomena would occur. Therefore, the unsuitability of Sattabhaṅgavāda should be understood (Dī. Ni. Ṭī. 1.38).

"Some phenomena are eternal, some are non-eternal." In this view, is not the decision on the impermanence of the eye etc. the realization of the true nature? If so, why is it a wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi) for those who hold this? Or who says "The decision on the impermanence of the eye etc. is a wrong view"? The answer: Only the decision that some phenomena are eternal among impermanent phenomena is taken as wrong view here. Because it occurs within such a single doctrine, the realization of the impermanence of the eye etc. is corrupted by being mixed [with the view of permanence], like a lump of butter mixed with poison. Therefore, because that knowledge cannot perform its function, it does not deserve to be placed in the category of right view (sammādiṭṭhi). Or, even if decided by the nature of impermanence...
413:
The eye and so forth are grasped by those with wrong views only as having a pre-conceived nature of a soul (jīva). Therefore, it is impossible to prevent the realization of those eyes etc. from being a wrong view. That is why it is said in the Pāli: "The eye is... the body is... this is the self," and so forth. In this way, the objection that "the Vibhajjavāda (Doctrine of Analysis) which proceeds by way of the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu) and the conditioned element (saṅkhata-dhātu) as 'some phenomena are eternal, some are non-eternal' would also be Ekaccasassatavāda (Partial Eternalism)" is groundless. This is because it is a practice according to the undistorted nature of phenomena. By the method mentioned, because it is not mixed with Ekaccasassatavāda and because it does not pre-conceive the nature of a soul, this is indeed a practice according to the undistorted nature of phenomena.

Here, the objector says: In the former Sassatavāda as well, grasping impermanent phenomena as "eternal" is specifically a wrong view. Grasping eternal things as "eternal" is not a wrong view because it is grasping according to the true nature. If so, this doctrine should not be called another doctrine (a wrong view). Just as in this view, in the former view also, the grasp of permanence can occur only in some phenomena. (The answer:) Because the division occurs in the phenomena to be grasped by way of imagining "only some phenomena are eternal, some are non-eternal" only among impermanent phenomena, this doctrine is shown as another doctrine.

Another question: Since a part is included in the whole, would not this partial grasp of eternalism (sappadesasassataggāha) merge into the former complete grasp of eternalism (nippadesasassataggāha)? Even so, it should not be said so, because the two doctrines occur by way of the specific objects of the proponent. For some people with wrong views are convinced that "all phenomena are eternal," while others are convinced that "some are eternal, some are non-eternal." The two doctrines are clearly distinct by the inclusion of all formations (saṅkhāra) without remainder and the inclusion of only a part.

Furthermore, it should not be said so because of the conviction in the continuity of the aggregates (khandha) as a manifold collection or a single collection. For the four types of eternalists, by way of specific births, become convinced of eternity through higher knowledge (abhiññā) or through tradition in the mass of mental phenomena dependent on various types of physical bodies, because they grasp the destruction of the physical body. Thus it is said: "Having passed away from there, he was reborn in that place," and "They pass away, they are reborn," and so forth. But the partial eternalist who has attained a specific distinction [in jhāna] develops conviction by grasping the aspect of permanence in the continuity of phenomena where destruction is not discerned by wisdom. This is because that conviction has as its object the continuity of aggregates included in a single life. Therefore, in the three doctrines, "He [recollects] his past lives..."
414:
"He remembers, beyond that he does not remember"—only this much is stated. The distinction in the wrong preoccupation of "permanence" held by both types of individuals—the Eternalists (Sassatavādī) and the Partial-Eternalists (Ekaccasassatavādī)—is very clear because it has the phenomena of form and formless as its objects.

Because of the destruction again after the passing of the three incalculable aeons (asaṅkhyeyyakappa) known as the "staying during contraction" (saṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyī), "expansion" (vivaṭṭa), and "staying during expansion" (vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyī), and because the word addhā is a synonym for time, it is preached thus; intending this, he said "of the long" (dīghassa), etc. To occur by passing is called accaya. Because roots have many meanings and because they can express specific meanings through the power of prefixes (upasagga), the word vaṭṭa combined with the prefix saṃ expresses destruction; intending this, it is said "it perishes" (vinassati). Alternatively, the root vatu occurs only in the sense of "going." Because it is combined with the prefix saṃ which clarifies the sense of "exhaustion," the meaning of "destruction" is obtained through connection with the meaning of that prefix saṃ; this is shown by the word "it perishes" (vinassati). "It occurs by way of exhaustion" is the literal meaning; in this word saṃvaṭṭa, the letter 'ta' is changed to 'ṭa'. From the falling of the great rain that causes destruction until not even a formation (saṅkhāra) as minute as an atom remains, the world is said to be "contracting" (saṃvaṭṭati). In the Pāḷi, "world" (loka) refers to the physical world (bhājanalo-ka) such as the earth, etc. Since the world of beings (sattaloka) remaining from that physical world occurs for the most part, it is said "for the most part" (yebhuyyena) with reference to that world of beings; this is shown by the word "who" (ye), etc.

"In the higher Brahma worlds" (upari-brahmalokesu) means in the planes above the Radiant (Ābhassara) plane. In this context, the destruction of the aeon by fire is intended; therefore, it is preached in the Pāḷi: "They become denizens of the Radiant realm" (ābhassara-saṃvattanikā honti). If it is asked why only destruction by fire is mentioned, it is because destruction by fire occurs most frequently.

This is the regulation of the frequency:
"Seven times it perishes by fire,
Every eighth time by water,
When sixty-four times are complete,
It shall perish once by the noble wind."

In the phrase "or in the formless realms" (āruppesu vā), the word vā has the sense of alternative, specifying that it also occurs in other world systems apart from the world systems that are currently perishing. It cannot be known that all beings in the lower realms are reborn in the fine-material and formless realms at that time, because it is impossible for beings with very long lifespans in the lower realms to be reborn in the human world, and without being reborn in the human world, their rebirth in those higher realms at that time is impossible. Even a person with fixed wrong view (niyata-micchādiṭṭhi) is not released from hell when the aeon perishes; it is said in the Commentaries that they are reborn only in the outer world systems (the world systems that do not perish). Although all beings have the nature of being born through the mind of meritorious and non-meritorious volitional formations, yet without external causes, by the mind alone...
415:
...being born, only the beings of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) are called "mind-made" (manomaya). To show that others who are created by external causes are not called "mind-made," he said: "Because they are born of the mind, they are mind-made."

If it is asked—if that is so, would not the spontaneously reborn (opapātika) beings of the sensuous sphere (kāmāvacara) also be "mind-made"?—it is not so. To show that the term "mind-made" is used only for beings born of the extraordinary mind which is the higher mind (adhicitta), he specified it with the word "jhāna" and said "by the jhāna-mind."

If it is asked—if so, would not the beings of the formless sphere (arūpāvacara) also be "mind-made"?—it is not so, because in that formless realm, there is no doubt that they must be produced by external causes, and thus it is not possible to make an emphasis (avadhāraṇa) that "they are born only of the mind." This term "mind-made" is well-established in the world for the beings of the fine-material sphere. Thus, the proponents of the Vedas imagine the self (attā) in five ways: made of food (annamaya), made of drink (pānamaya), made of mind (manomaya), made of bliss (ānandamaya), and made of consciousness (viññāṇamaya). In the doctrine of annihilation (ucchedavāda), it will also be said: "divine, having form, mind-made."

To show that those beings of the fine-material sphere, through the power of jhāna, have joy as their food, are self-luminous, and move through the air, he said: "Joy is their (food)," etc. It means they have their own radiance. Alternatively, it is also appropriate to say "abiding in beauty" (subhaṭṭhāyī) because they have a beautiful assembly (place of abiding). The word "especially" is said with reference to the Radiant (Ābhassara) Brahmas. The Brahmas of Limited Radiance (Parittābhā) and Immeasurable Radiance (Appamāṇābhā) abide for two and four aeons respectively. "Eight aeons" refers to the eight great aeons (mahākappa) which are the collection of four incalculable aeons.

40. Although the word vaṭṭa expresses destruction, because it is combined with the prefix vi which has the sense of negation, it indicates the meaning of staying (arising); to show this, he said "it stays." Alternatively, because roots have various meanings, it means "it arises" or "it increases." In fact, from the falling of the great world-forming rain, through the successive arising of the water that supports the earth, the wind that supports that water, etc., until the appearance of the moon and the sun, that period is called "the world expands" (loko vivaṭṭati).

"By nature" (pakatiyā) means by its own nature, and it should be connected with the word "empty" (suñña). He stated the reason for such emptiness as "because of the absence of beings who have been born." It means because other beings have not yet been born earlier. Therefore, he intends to show that this mansion is not empty in the way that some mansions are empty because the beings born there have departed.

Another way—the first performance of one's own kamma is called pakati. It should be connected as "beings born because of that (pakati)." By that phrase, he intends to show that just as this being is born first by the power of his own kamma, there are no other beings born earlier than him or at the same time.
416:
Furthermore, it shows that this mansion is empty because there are no beings born there. In this context, the Brahmapārisajja Brahmas, Brahmapurohita Brahmas, and Mahābrahmas are called Brahmakāyika. Because it is the dwelling place of those Brahmas, the plane is also called 'Brahmakāyika'. In the reading 'Brahmakāyikabhūmi', it means the plane belonging to the Brahmas. One who acts by oneself is called the 'agent' (kattā). One who commands others is called the 'instigator' (kāretā). In the manner stated in the 'Discussion on the Knowledge of Recollecting Past Lives' (Pubbenivāsañāṇakathā) in the Visuddhimagga, this text shows the sequence of arising, as well as the cause in the state of being produced by temperature (utu) which has kamma as its condition. This plane is called 'kammapaccaya' (kamma-conditioned) because kamma is the cause by way of strong dependence (upanissaya). Alternatively, it is called 'kammapaccaya' because it is a co-nascent cause of the kamma that produces results for the beings born in that plane. It is called 'utusamuṭṭhāna' (temperature-originated) because temperature is the cause of its arising. There is also a reading 'kammapaccayautusamuṭṭhāna' by way of a compound (samāsa). The cause that exists together with kamma is called 'kammapaccaya'; that very cause is temperature, and because that temperature is the cause of the arising of this plane, it is called 'kammapaccayautusamuṭṭhāna'. 'Ratanabhūmi' (gem-like plane) refers to the plane that has become like a gem due to the power of extraordinary meritorious kamma. It means not only the plane itself but also its surroundings; thus, it says 'pakati' and so on. 'Pakatinibbattaṭṭhāna' means the place where former beings were born in previous aeons (kappas). 'Ettha' (herein) refers to the Brahmakāyika plane called the Brahma mansion. These two types of support (ādhāra) exist by way of the general (sāmañña) and the specific (visesa).

Since it might be asked why those staying in the superior plane of the second jhāna are reborn in the inferior plane of the first jhāna, the text says 'atha sattānaṃ' and so forth. It means they develop the first jhāna by the power of attachment (nikanti-taṇhā). It is connected as: "craving that is attached by its very nature arises." 'Vasitaṭṭhāna' refers to the place where one has lived before. 'Descending from there' means they move away or go from the second jhāna plane to the first jhāna plane by way of rebirth. 'Appāyuka' (short-lived) means having a short lifespan due to the sequence of results appropriate for the noble meritorious kamma that was performed. 'Tassa devalokassa' means 'in that celestial world', or it is an indication of connection by way of dependence. 'Āyuppamāṇeneva' means only by the maximum extent of the lifespan. 'Paritta' means 'small' or 'limited'. 'Antarāva cavanti' means that, like a measure of rice placed in a king's granary, they pass away even in the interval before the full lifespan of that celestial world is reached, due to the exhaustion of merit according to the measure of their own kamma.

If it is asked, "What is this maximum lifespan (paramāyu), and how is that lifespan delimited?", I shall say: "Of the sequence of the results (vipāka) in the various specific existences of those various beings..."
417:
The determination of the duration of existence (lifespan) is generally a fixed limit in various realms (gati-nikāya), etc., just like the specific differences in bodily parts, color, shape, and size, by the power of the aspiration for a previously accomplished existence. For womb-born beings, beings of the sensual sphere (kāmāvacara) devas, and beings of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), it is also supported by causes such as the parents' semen and blood, climate (utu), and nutriment (āhāra). This lifespan is called 'āyu' by way of causal metaphor (karaṇūpacāra) because it is the cause of life, and it is called 'paramāyu' (maximum lifespan) by way of the supreme limit.

For, although the physical and mental life faculties (jīvitindriya) that occur for the purpose of maintaining the physical and mental phenomena born together with them last only for a moment according to their own nature, they do not merely protect them as a cause for their momentary existence; rather, they also serve as the cause for the non-interruption of the sequence until the moment of dissolution (bhanga).

Therefore, this lifespan is indeed a cause. That lifespan is generally a fixed duration for devas and hell-beings (nerayika), but for the inhabitants of Uttarakuru, it is an absolutely fixed duration. For the remaining humans, hungry ghosts (petas), and animals, the lifespan is of an unfixed duration, being long or short depending on the causes such as the parents' semen and blood produced in a continuity associated with kamma during times when kamma leading to long life is abundant, and depending on causes such as climate and nutriment produced by the regular or irregular revolutions of the moon and sun, which have that kamma as their root. In that unfixed duration, just as the determination of the specific color, shape, etc., in various realms is accomplished by the power of the aspiration for a previously accomplished existence, and is established from the beginning through observation and tradition (dassanānussava), so too, the determination of the fixed lifespan from the beginning should be understood by the power of the aspiration for existence. This aspiration is carried out by being immersed through craving in that maximum lifespan, having obtained through observation and tradition the duration of existence which is generally of equal measure for beings born in those various births (upapatti).

Because kamma is capable of producing color, shape, etc., dependent on various births, but is not capable of producing results (vipāka) beyond the limit in births that have a fixed lifespan, it is said: "They pass away only at the end of their lifespan." Because the manner in which the groups of clinging (upādinnaka-kkhandha) are to be maintained by supporting and protecting causes is, in essence, for one with a maximum lifespan, not exceeding the aforementioned limit, staying longer is not possible even if there is remaining kamma. Therefore, it is said: "They are unable to remain by the power of their own merit." From the words "Passing away from the Ābhassara body due to the exhaustion of life or the exhaustion of merit," it should be understood that for the Brahmakāyika Brahmās, like the kāmāvacara devas, there is generally a fixed lifespan. For this reason, it is said in the commentaries: "They pass away from the deva world." Devas pass away from the deva world due to four causes: exhaustion of life, exhaustion of merit, exhaustion of food, and anger. In the phrase "for an aeon or half an aeon," an incalculable aeon (asankheyya-kappa) is intended. That incalculable aeon is simply a period of such a nature. The word "vā" (or) has the meaning of considering one-third of an aeon, or less or more than that.

41. "Anabhirati" (dissatisfaction) is simply the desire to meet other devas and Brahmās, described as discontent due to living alone. Because it is stated in the Pāli text that they lived alone in that mansion for a long time, the teacher said the words beginning with "aparas māpi". To show this meaning, the teacher shows the distinction (vyatireka) with the words beginning with "yā puri", asking, "Is it not possible that weariness (ukkaṇṭhitā) could also occur?" through the method of objection and resolution. Mental fatigue due to separation from a loved object or not obtaining a loved object is called "ukkaṇṭhitā" (weariness/longing). That ukkaṇṭhitā...
418:
Just like the devas of the sense sphere, the lifespan of the Brahmas of the Brahma-kāyika realm should mostly be understood as having a fixed limit. For this reason, it is stated in the Commentaries (Dhammapada Commentary, Appamāda-vagga) that deities pass away from the deva realms due to four causes: the exhaustion of lifespan, the exhaustion of merit, the exhaustion of nutriment, and through anger. In the phrase 'for an aeon or for half an aeon', an incalculable aeon (asankheyya-kappa) is intended, and that incalculable aeon is simply a duration of such a nature. The word 'vā' (or), however, has the sense of specifying either a third of an aeon, or less or more than that.

41. 'Anabhirati' (dissatisfaction) is simply the desire to meet others, described as discontentment due to living alone. In this context, because it is taught in the Pali as 'due to having lived alone for a long time', the phrase 'aparassāpi' and so forth is stated. Having thus shown the sequence of meaning, the author shows the negative aspect (vyatireka) by way of resolving the objection: 'Might there not also be ukkaṇṭhitā (longing/distress)?' with the words 'yā panā' and so forth. 'Ukkaṇṭhitā' is the mental distress caused by separation from a beloved object or by not obtaining a beloved object. In terms of its ultimate nature, that ukkaṇṭhitā is simply the arising of a state of mind accompanied by displeasure (domanassa); therefore, it is said to be 'associated with aversion (paṭigha)'. That ukkaṇṭhitā does not exist in the Brahma world because it has been abandoned by the power of jhāna. In this context, 'paritassanā' (agitation/trembling) is simply the trembling or quivering of the mind in its preceding state, described as craving (taṇhā) and views (diṭṭhi). Indeed, that paritassanā arises due to the aforementioned dissatisfaction in one who has remained in the bliss of jhāna for a long time, and it is also the cause for the grasping of 'I' and 'mine'. Therefore, it will be said later: 'Trembling due to craving does not occur, nor does trembling due to views'.

In extracting the meaning, is it not stated by citing this very Pali: 'O friends, the longing that other beings might also come to this state of existence is called taṇhā-tassanā (trembling through craving)'? That is true; however, because of the desire to show taṇhā-tassanā as a separate illustration from diṭṭhi-tassanā (trembling through views), taṇhā-tassanā alone was extracted and stated therefrom. There is no fault here, as it was not stated because diṭṭhi-tassanā is unobtainable. Now, having extracted the meanings expressed by similar terms, the author says 'sā panesā' and so forth to clarify the intended meaning in this context. The mental alarm described as aversion (paṭigha) is 'tāsa-tassanā' (trembling through fear). The same should be understood accordingly in other instances.

'Dependent on birth, fear arises' and so forth is the Vibhaṅga Pali. The commentary on that is as follows: 'Fear dependent on birth' means fear arisen with birth as a condition. 'Bhayānaka' (fearful) is a designation of the mode of fear. 'Chambhitatta' (stupefaction/stiffening) is the trembling of the limbs due to fear, specifically the quivering of the heart-flesh. 'Lomahaṃsa' (horripilation) is the bristling of the body hairs, their standing upright like ivory pegs on a wall. By these two terms, fear is shown by way of its function, and then it is shown by way of its nature as 'the alarm of the mind'. In the Sub-commentary (Ṭīkā), however, it is said that 'bhayānaka' is a powerful fear caused by a terrifying object, and the resulting rigidity of the body is called 'chambhitatta'. By this very term, a slight fear is shown in this context. Thus, the meaning should be understood in all respects. In the phrase 'paritassita-vipphanditam-eva', the commentary explains that it is only the quivering through the agitation described as views or described as craving. It should be understood that by this phrase, diṭṭhi-tassanā alone is highlighted, excluding taṇhā-tassanā.
419:
It is stated (in the Dīgha Nikāya Ṭīkā 1, 41): 'chambhitattaṃ'. By this term 'chambhitattaṃ' alone, a minor fear (khuddaka-bhaya) is shown in this context of 'bhayaṃ'. In this usage, this 'tassanā' (trembling) has this meaning in all instances. Regarding the phrase 'paritassita-vipphanditam-eva', the commentary will state the meaning: 'It is only the quivering, the moving, the trembling through the agitation described as views and described as craving'. By that forthcoming statement, it is understood that although it is obtainable, diṭṭhi-tassanā (trembling through views) alone is extracted, excluding taṇhā-tassanā (trembling through craving).

In the Sīhopama Sutta Pali beginning with 'tepi', 'tepi' means even the long-lived devas. 'Bhayaṃ' (fear) is the knowledge of fear (bhaya-ñāṇa) that arises by way of fearing all conditioned things at the conclusion of frequent practice of the contemplation of dissolution (bhaṅgānupassanā). 'Saṃvegaṃ' (spiritual urgency) is the knowledge accompanied by moral dread (ottappa), or simply moral dread itself. 'Santāsaṃ' (alarm/terror) is the knowledge of being alarmed by conditioned things through the contemplation of danger (ādīnavānupassanā) and the contemplation of revulsion (nibbidānupassanā). 'Upapatti-vasena' means simply by way of rebirth (paṭisandhi).

'Sahabyataṃ' (companionship) literally means the state of being a companion, because the word 'sahabya' functions in the sense of a companion (sahāya). Indeed, such a person 'sahabyāyati'—meaning they proceed together, or they cover up faults—thus they are called 'sahabya'; the state of that sahabya is 'sahabyatā'. However, since the state of being a companion is just 'sahabhāva' (being together), the word 'sahabhāvaṃ' is used to show the meaning according to the intention. Alternatively, the word 'saha' has the sense of union (samavāya) along with its means (sādhana), like the word 'adhi' in the term 'adhikicca'. Therefore, the state of one who exists together as one is 'sahabyaṃ', just like the word 'dāsabyaṃ' (servitude). That 'sahabyaṃ' itself becomes 'sahabyatā' by adding the suffix 'tā' in the same sense. Intending this very meaning, the Buddha said 'sahabhāvaṃ'. Furthermore, one who proceeds together is 'sahava'; the state of that sahava is 'sahabyaṃ', just as 'the state of a hero (vīra) is vīriya'. That 'sahabyaṃ' itself is 'sahabyatā'; thus it is stated in the Vimānavatthu Commentary. Therefore, it should be noted that it is stated this way to show that meaning.

In the phrase 'having overpowered these beings', the remaining words should be understood. Here, 'overpowering' (abhibhavanā) is simply the self-conception: 'I stand overpowering those beings' either by a base nature or by the status of being the chief. Therefore, it is said: 'I am the chief'. By the word 'aññadatthū' (surely/certainly), which expresses the absence of obstacles in vision, and by the word 'daso' (seer), which expresses the absence of failure to grasp specific details in vision, he claims the state of unobstructed vision. Therefore, it is said that the meaning is 'I see all'. Indeed, when there is no failure to grasp (aggahaṇa) the specific details of what is to be seen, which are the parts, the partless nature (nippadesatā) of what is to be grasped is understood. It is just like the word 'dikkhito' (consecrated).
420:
In the word "does not give" (na dadāti), because of not taking a specific gift which is a part, it is understood that the monk does not give everything, implying the completeness of the gift to be taken without remainder. In such cases, it should be understood in the same way. He is called "Vasavattī" because he brings others under his will. Since it is associated with the word "Ahaṃ" (I), in all instances, the meaning is construed in connection with the first person (amha). There is a connection that he is also the creator of the world which is the vessel for beings. The words beginning with "Earth" (pathavī) are an explanation of the intention by way of the vessel world (bhājanaloka). "Sajita" means created or analyzed. Therefore, it is said, "You are called a Khattiya," and so on. He is called "Ciṇṇavasitāya" because he has well-practiced the five masteries (vasībhāva).

In that context, among the beings that have come to be (bhūta) and are to be (bhabya), "antovatthimhi" means inside the mother's womb. "Paṭhamacittakkhaṇe" means at the moment of the rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhicitta). "Dutiyato" means starting from the moment of the first life-continuum consciousness (bhavaṅgacitta). "Paṭhamairiyāpathe" means in whatever posture one takes rebirth-linking, it occurs in that posture. Thus, the meaning of the word "bhūta" is shown by way of the past, and the meaning of the word "bhabya" is shown by way of the present. However, in the Ṭīkā, the meaning of the word "bhabya" is also stated by way of the future. For they are called "bhūta" because they "have been." They are called "bhabya" because they "are being" and "will be." This is because the suffix 'ṇya', like the suffixes 'tabba' and 'anīya', also occurs in the sense of the agent (kattar).

One might ask: "After saying 'Lord, Doer, Creator,' what is the purpose of saying again 'I have created these beings'?" It means that he makes this claim because he now wishes to establish it by way of a cause. Let us raise an objection: Since that Brahmā is a worldling (puthujjana) and has unstable vision, he abandons the knowledge of the ownership of kamma (kammassakatā-ñāṇa) practiced in previous lives. Through the power of psychic transformation (vikubbana-iddhi), he has a perverted view regarding the creation of beings which is connected to the mere arising of a thought. Does he not then fall into the view of a creator (issarakutta-diṭṭhi), saying "I have created these beings," and remain fixed there by way of obsession? He does not remain there by way of establishing others. If so, why is it said that he makes the claim because he wishes to establish it by way of a cause?

It should not be viewed in this way. Since it will be stated later that for the Brahmās who arise afterwards, such a wrong obsession occurs as "It is thus," his obsession arose only by way of the sequence of establishing others, and not by mere obsession alone. Therefore, it should be understood that it was said in this way. For that very reason, it is said, "For what reason is that?" and so on. In the Pali, "manaso paṇidhi" means the longing of the mind; thus it means the mere arising of a thought.

This kind of state is called "itthabhāva." Since in this context that kind is intended only as the state of a Brahmā (brahmabhāva), it is called "brahmabhāva." This kind is called "ittham."
421:
The definition is "itthatta" because it is the state of that (kind). "Kevala" means pure, unmixed with the knowledge of the ownership of kamma. "Maññanāmatteneva" means by mere imagining of a view, and not by way of overestimation (adhimāna). Just as a crooked pin fits into a crooked hole, those with crooked views incline and go to the feet of that very Brahmā; the meaning is that they become his partisans.

Now, do not devas, immediately after rebirth, have the reflection: "Having passed away from such a destination (gati), I am reborn here because of such a kamma"? If so, why would such an imagining occur to those Brahmās? Such reflection occurs only to those whose inclinations (āsayas) were well-established in the knowledge of the ownership of kamma in previous lives. And that reflection occurs only for the most part. However, these Brahmās were those who had a fixed obsession by way of the view of a creator (issarakutta-diṭṭhi) even in previous lives, and thus they imagined in this very way. Therefore, it was said in the Pali, "By him we [were created]," and so on.
