He is called "Īsa" because he overcomes and dominates. Great power (īsa) is called "Mahesa." Because he has well-established great power and is called "Mahesa" by others, he is "Mahesakkha." One who is "Mahesakkha" to an even greater degree than other Mahesakkha Brahmās is "Mahesakkhatara"—this is the word-meaning. That state of being Mahesakkhatara is understood through the cause, which is the perfection of sovereignty and retinue; therefore it is said, "One who has greater fame by way of sovereignty and retinue."

Asking "What is that cause?", he said "So tato" and so on. By that, he shows that the very coming to this human world, as stated in "itthattaṃ āgacchati," is the cause. "Idheva āgacchati" means he comes to this very human world by way of rebirth-linking. "Etaṃ" refers to the statement "Monks, this situation (ṭhāna) exists." In the Pali, in the phrase "yaṃ aññataro satto," "yaṃ" is a mere particle (nipāta), or it is a particle in the sense of cause, or it is a nominative case (paccatta) used in the sense of reason (hetu), meaning "by which reason," or it is a term referring to the action. In the phrase "itthattaṃ āgacchati," it means that this cause, known as the coming to this state, exists. This is also the case in the words: "he goes forth, he touches concentration of mind, he recollects past lives." For these words, "Monks, this situation exists, that a certain being," should be applied individually to the words "goes forth" and so on. It is called "agāra" (house) because one does not go (away from it). "Āgāriya" refers to what is beneficial for the house, such as farming and cattle-rearing. Since that does not exist here in this Dispensation, it is called "anāgāriya" (homelessness/going forth). Therefore, he said "from the house" and so on. It is said that the word "vaja" distinguished by the prefix "pa" is in the sense of approaching, thus "upagacchati" (he approaches).
422:
'Para' means 'later', or 'excessive', or 'another' in the sense of the aggregates lived in the past. Even though it is said 'he does not remember', this meaning is implied by the phrase 'for the sake of remembering' and so forth. 'Apassanto' means being unable to see due to the cause of not seeing with the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa). Indeed, just like the word 'māna' (the suffix -māna), here the word 'anta' (the suffix -anta) has the meaning of 'ability'. 'Sadābhāvato' means because of being constantly manifest. In the phrase 'jarāvasenāpi', the word 'pi' includes the sense of 'by the power of death' as well.

'Khiḍḍāpadosino' is a word formation by the power of the agent (kattar). 'Khiḍḍāpadosikā', however, is formed by the power of the suffix 'ka' used in the sense of 'self-nature' (sakattha). To show the meaning without regarding the word, it is said 'khiḍḍāya' and so forth. Alternatively, while it should be said 'khiḍḍāpadosakā', it is said as 'khiḍḍāpadosikā' due to the arrival of the vowel 'i'. Or, 'padosa' means corruption; corruption due to play is 'khiḍḍāpadosa'; those deities have that corruption due to play, therefore they are called 'khiḍḍāpadosikā'. By the statement "they also write the Pali as 'padūsikā'", it shows the scribal error of other sects (nikāyas) besides the Mahāvihāravāsī. In fact, this commentary (aṭṭhakathā) proceeded by the power of the tradition (vācanāmagga) of the Great Elders belonging to the Mahāvihāravāsī sect. Alternatively, that word shows a scribal error when it was recorded on palm leaves. That word 'padūsikā' should be taken only according to the corrected mark in the commentary for the purpose of purifying the meaning of the word; therefore, it says "sā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ natthi" (that word is not in the commentary).

Exceeding the time for eating is called 'ativela'; that word 'ativelaṃ' is an adverb (bhāvanapuṃsaka). Therefore, it says 'aticiraṃ' (for a very long time). It means exceeding the time of consuming food. The word 'ratidhamma' should be joined with the words 'hassa' and 'khiḍḍā' respectively as "the nature of delighting in laughter and play." Laughter is 'hassa', meaning the laughter of playful deities. Play is 'khiḍḍā', meaning physical and vocal play. To show that they have fully reached the state of delighting in that play by the power of repeated practice, it says 'hassaratidhammañceva' and so forth. Deities who have play are called 'keḷino'; their laughter is likewise. Here, the happiness arising from being associated with play and laughter is called 'keḷihassasukha'. The happiness arising from being associated with the remaining physical and vocal play is called 'kāyikavācasikakīḷāsukha'.

The phrase 'te kira' and so forth is an explanation in detail. Here, the word 'kira' only illuminates the detail; it does not indicate hearsay or dislike, etc. This is because it is stated thus in the Pali and the Commentaries. 'Sirivibhavena' means by the glory of physical beauty and so forth, and by the accomplishment of retinue and so forth. 'Nakkhattaṃ' means a festival. Indeed, because it is mostly performed in conjunction with a constellation, it is called 'nakkhatta' whether it is aligned with a constellation or not. Regarding the word 'āhāraṃ', there are questions: "What is the food of the deities? What is their mealtime?" For all deities of the sense-sphere, ambrosia (sudhā) alone is the food.
423:
The food of the deities is called "Sudhā" (ambrosia) because it sustains happiness by destroying twelve kinds of evil states. That divine ambrosia is white, like a conch shell, incomparable in appearance, pure, fragrant, and pleasant in nature. Referring to this, it is said in the Sudhābhojana Jātaka: "Like a conch shell, bright white, incomparable in appearance, pure, fragrant, pleasant, and wonderful; which deity placed in my hands this divine ambrosia, which my eyes have certainly never seen before?" It is also said: "When this divine ambrosia is consumed, it removes twelve evils: hunger, thirst, discontent, distress and fatigue, anger, malice, quarreling, slandering, cold, heat, and laziness; this is the best of all tastes."

That divine ambrosia is increasingly more refined for deities in higher and higher realms than for those in lower realms; they consume that food daily according to the days determined for their respective realms. Some teachers say: "Those deities eat an amount of divine ambrosia the size of a 'biḷārapada' (a weight unit); just by placing that food on the tongue, it permeates the entire body up to the tips of the hair and nails; it is capable of sustaining them for seven days according to the days counted for their respective realms." In the view of these teachers, the word 'biḷārapada' denotes a specific number/weight called 'suvaṇṇa'. In terms of size, it is about the size of an udumbara (fig) fruit, which is also called 'kabaḷaggaha' (a mouthful) that can be held in the palm. In the Madhukosa text, it is said: "Pāṇi, akkha, picu, suvaṇṇaka, udumbara, biḷārapadaka, and pāṇitala are all the same weight (one tola); that very pāṇitala is called kabaḷaggaha (a mouthful)."

The phrase "even though they are constantly eating and drinking" is said as a supposition; it should not be determined as "constantly" in this way because eating and drinking are not constant. The digestive fire (tejodhātu) born of kamma is strong because it arises from great merit and because it must digest the great, heavy, and refined divine ambrosia. However, the physical body (karajakāya) is weak because it is delicate. For that very reason, the Blessed One said to Sakka, the king of deities, who was unable to stand on the natural ground in the Indasāla Cave, "Assume a gross body." The weakness of the digestive fire born of kamma and the strength of the physical body in humans should be understood as the opposite of what was said. Here, 'karajakāya' refers to the body; that which arises in that body...
424:
“Although there is constant eating and drinking,” this statement is made by way of reasoning. In reality, it cannot be said to occur invariably in this manner. Such eating and drinking occur according to the state of the fire element born of kamma (kammaja-tejo). Why is the kammaja-tejo powerful? It is because it arises due to noble merit and because it is capable of digesting the noble, heavy, yet subtle divine food (sudhā-bhojana) of the devas. Furthermore, because it is delicate and tender, the physical body (karaja-kāya) is weak. For this very reason, the Blessed One said to Sakka, the King of Devas, who was unable to stand on the natural ground in the Indasāla Cave, “Create a gross (coarse) body.” Among humans, however, it should be understood that the opposite of what was stated applies: the kammaja-tejo is weak and the karaja-kāya is strong.

In the term “karaja-kāya,” the body is called “karaja.” The “dust” (raja) of passion that arises in that body is called “kara.” What is that karaja? It is the semen and blood of the parents. Because it is the result of the dust of passion, of which it is said, “Passion is called dust (raja), but mere particles of earth (reṇu) are not called dust,” the body is designated as “karaja” by using the word “ka” (representing the body) and applying the name of the cause to the effect. Teachers say that the body produced from that karaja, known as semen and blood, is the “karaja-kāya.” Therefore, the body is said to be produced from the semen and blood of the parents.

In the Sub-commentary to the Mahā-assapura Sutta, however, it is said: “It is called ‘kara’ because it is cast into the womb; it is the source (semen). Because it is born from that source, it is called ‘karaja,’ meaning it is produced from the semen and blood of the parents. Other teachers say it is called ‘karaja’ because it is born from the hand (kara) through the power of the mother and others establishing it well. In both cases, ‘karaja-kāya’ refers to the matter of four-fold origin (catu-santati-rūpa).” It is also said: “It is called ‘kara’ because it brings forth children; it is semen and blood. Because it is born from that semen and blood, it is called ‘karaja.’” Similarly, even though the bodies of devas and others are not produced from the semen and blood of parents, they are still called “karaja-kāya” by conventional usage, just like the terms “putrid body” (pūti-kāya) or “old jackal” (jara-siṅgāla). “Tesaṃ” means of those humans. “Accha-yāgu” refers to clear gruel without dregs. “Vatthu” refers to the karaja-kāya. “Ekaṃ āhāra-velaṃ” means for just one day; however, according to some teachers, it means seven days.

Having thus shown the meaning through both direct (anvaya) and indirect (vyatireka) methods, and wishing to clarify the meaning further by way of a simile, he said “yathā nāma,” etc. “Tatta-pāsāṇe” means on a very hot stone. Water lilies other than the red and white lotuses (paduma) are called “uppala.” “Akathāyaṃ” means in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā. “Avisesena” means speaking generally as “devānaṃ” without making a distinction. This is because the kammaja-tejo of devas is strong and the karaja-kāya is tender, or because of the commonality of the cause known as the strength and tenderness of the kammaja-tejo and karaja-kāya. Since this cause is the same for all devas, it means all devas should be included. They are called “kabaḷīkārāhārūpajīvīno” because they live depending on the divine food (sudhā-bhojana) which is taken in morsels. “Keci” refers to the teachers residing at the Abhayagiri Monastery. The passage, “These devas are called khiḍḍāpadosikā merely by being corrupted through play,” should be read immediately after the phrase, “It should be understood that they alone pass away,” because it is connected to that context. The connection here is: if all devas of the sense sphere who act in this way were to pass away, then why did the Blessed One preach using the specific name “khiḍḍāpadosikā”? This was said as an investigation. By this, he shows the meaning: “Although all devas pass away in this manner, based on the nature of being destroyed by play...”
425:
“...they are so called by a specific name.” If some teachers should say, “This passage is one that establishes the view of certain teachers (keci-vāda),” that statement is incorrect because of the intervention of another word “iti” and because that “iti” does not exist at the end of the sentence. However, those who wish to include that passage within the “keci-vāda” should connect it by inserting the word “iti” at the end of the sentence.

47-48. In the word “manopadosino,” the formation of the word should be understood by way of the agent (kattar). In the word “manopadosikā,” the formation should be understood by way of the suffix “ka” in the sense of the word itself (sakattha). To show merely the meaning, he said “manenā,” etc. Alternatively, while it should be said “manopadosakā,” it is said as “manopadosikā” due to the arrival of the letter “i.” “Manenā” means with a mind corrupted because of being oppressed by envy (issā). Another method: destruction caused by the mind through the power of envy is called “manopadosa”; because that nature of destruction exists in those devas, they are called “manopadosikā.” Because of the Pali statement, “They, with minds corrupted towards each other, with weary bodies and weary minds, pass away from that body,” he said, “These are the devas of the Realm of the Four Great Kings (Cātumahārājikā).” These devas are called “manopadosikā” merely by being corrupted through the mind. “Tesu kirā,” etc., is the detailed explanation. The phrase “enters the street by chariot” is merely an illustration (upalakkhaṇa), as it is possible to travel to other places by vehicles other than a chariot. “Etaṃ” refers to one’s own prosperity and wealth. “Like a swollen person” means as if uplifted by joy (pīti) which is the cause. “As if breaking” means as if being broken by that joy, or as if being destroyed by joy acting as the agent. Angry people are very easy to recognize; therefore, the meaning is “knowing the state of his anger.”

“The one who is not angry protects” means that if the other person does not get angry, the anger of the angry person has no fuel (anupādāna) and, having arisen only once without repeated cultivation (āsevana), it is unable to cause one to pass away; it is extinguished like a fire that reaches the edge of water. Therefore, the one who is not angry protects the other from passing away. However, if both get angry, the anger—which has a sharp occurrence through the power of mutual increase and has the function of burning its own support—arises and completely burns the heart-base (hadaya-vatthu), thereby destroying the extremely subtle physical body (karaja-kāya). Consequently, the entire individual existence (attabhāva) vanishes. To show that meaning, he said “ubhosu panā,” etc. And so it is said in the Pali: “They, with minds corrupted towards each other, with weary bodies and weary minds, pass away from that body.” In the phrase, “The anger of one is the cause for the other, and the anger of that person is also the cause for the other,” the causal state should be understood only for the excessive increase of anger, not for the act of passing away. It is only by one’s own anger, which has the function of burning its own support and burns the heart-base, that the truly subtle...
426:
It is indeed due to the passing away and shifting of the extremely subtle physical body (karajakāya). In the phrase "kandantānaṃyeva orodhānaṃ" (while the harem ladies were just weeping), the genitive case is used in the sense of disregard (anādara). Here, "natural law" (dhammatā) means the state of passing away instantly due to the extreme delicacy of those deities' physical bodies and the power of the anger that arises; this is the natural law (dhamma-niyāma) and inherent nature of the mental and material phenomena occurring in those deities.

49-52. "Seeing the destruction of the eye and so forth" means seeing the transformation when opposing conditions meet, and because they eventually reach a state of invisibility, the destruction of material phenomena is visible due to its grossness. It means becoming a condition by providing the conditioning force through the power of the proximity condition (anantara-paccaya) and so on. Therefore, it should be connected with "not seeing." Even though it is very powerful, it is not seen for this reason. The word "more powerful" is said with reference to the extremely rapid dissolution of the mind (citta). For this reason, while one material form (rūpa) lasts, sixteen moments of mind dissolve. In the statement "one does not see the dissolution of the mind," the mind that dissolves moment by moment does so only by serving as a proximity condition for the subsequent mind. Therefore, as if concealing the non-existence (abhāva) of the preceding mind, the aspect of existence (bhāva-pakkha) is more dominant and evident due to the arising of the subsequent mind, while the aspect of non-existence (abhāva-pakkha) is not evident. It should be understood that the phrase "cittaṃ pana" and so forth is stated to show this reason. This meaning should be understood through the simile of a firebrand circle (alātacakka). Because the logician (takkī) finds it difficult to comprehend the method of diversity (nānatta-naya) and wrongly grasps the method of unity (ekatta-naya), he develops the wrong obsession: "This consciousness always proceeds in this manner; this is my self, which is eternal." Therefore, that matter is explained with a simile starting with "so taṃ apassanto."

## Description of the Doctrine of Finitude and Infinitude (Antānantavāda-vaṇṇanā)

A doctrine that co-exists with finitude (anta) and infinitude (ananta) is called Antānantavāda, similar to saying "the spears are moving." Alternatively, a doctrine based on finitude and infinitude is called Antānantavāda, similar to saying "the beds are crying out." To show that those who hold such doctrines are called Antānantika, the term "Antānantavādā" is used. By the aforementioned methods, those who hold a doctrine that co-exists with, is based on, or proceeds within finitude and infinitude are called Antānantavāda. Now, wishing to analyze the meaning in accordance with the upcoming text such as "This world is finite," the phrase "antaṃ vā" and so forth is stated. Reaching a limit or conclusion is called anta.
427:
A limit is called anta, and by the negation of that limit, it is called ananta (infinite). The four—finite, infinite, both finite and infinite, and neither finite nor infinite—are expressed simply as "antānanta" through the method of general designation (sāmaññaniddesa) or the method of ellipsis (ekasesa), as in the Pali passages like "nāmarūpapaccayā saḷāyatanaṃ." Here, since the fourth term has the same meaning as the third term, the fourfold meaning is understood by the term "antānanta" itself through the two aforementioned methods.

To whom does this finitude and infinitude belong? It is the finitude and infinitude of the "self" which has reached the designation of "world" (loka), which is regarded as "self" by those with wrong views who seek liberation from saṃsāra. Therefore, it is said in the Pali: "They describe the finitude and infinitude of the world." What is this "self"? It is the kasiṇa sign (kasiṇa-nimitta) which is the object of jhāna. This person with wrong views dwells perceiving the world in that sign, either as limited or unlimited, by way of expanding the counterpart sign (paṭibhāga-nimitta) up to the edge of the universe or according to tradition. Therefore, the commentary will say: "Taking that [sign] as the world." Some teachers, however, say that jhāna and its associated states are taken here as "self" and "world," but that does not agree with the commentary.

Here, an objection is raised: It is appropriate for the first three theorists to be called Antānantika because their doctrines proceed based on the finite, the infinite, and both. But how can the last logician's doctrine be called Antānantika when it proceeds by negating both? It is precisely because it proceeds by negating both. Even the doctrine that negates finitude and infinitude is concerned with the subject of finitude and infinitude because it proceeds with reference to them. Intending this very meaning, it is said in the commentary: "Doctrines that proceed based on the finite, or the infinite, or both, or neither." 

Alternatively, just as in the third doctrine, a single world can be both finite and infinite by way of spatial division, so too in this logician's doctrine, both can exist in a single world by way of temporal division; thus, both are stated through mutual negation, and both negations are relative negations (pariyudāsa-paṭisedha). How? By negating the finite, the infinite is stated; and by negating the infinite, the finite is stated. This is because two negations indicate the original meaning. Thus, since both, known as finitude and infinitude, are stated by way of negation, it is appropriate for the last doctrine concerning that subject to be Antānantika.

If that is so, would it not fall under the third doctrine since it is an Antānantika doctrine? No, because temporal division is intended. Unlike the third theorist who is Antānantika by way of spatial division...
428:
The last reasoner (takkīvādī) is also a finitist-and-infinitist (antānantika) by virtue of the difference in time. How so? Because he hears from the Great Sages (mahesī) who have attained the distinction of direct vision that 'this self, called the world, is infinite,' he therefore [assumes] 'it is not finite.' Because he hears from those same Great Sages that 'at times this [self] is finite,' he therefore [assumes] 'it is not infinite.' This reasoner, because he existed before the expansion of the counterpart signs (paṭibhāganimitta), and because the state of expansion can be obtained in both ways, remains merely in what is heard (anussava) without being able to personally realize the conceived self. By virtue of the time of expansion, he rejects [the view] 'it is not finite'; by virtue of the time of non-expansion, he rejects [the view] 'it is not infinite.' It is not a rejection because of the absolute non-existence of finitude and infinitude, as in the case of 'neither-perception-nor-non-perception' (nevasaññānāsaññā). Just like the one who reasons based on tradition (anussutika-takkī), it should be applied as far as possible to those who reason based on recollection of past births (jātissara-takkī), etc.

Some teachers, however, explain the occurrence of the fourth doctrine through reasoning thus: 'If this self were finite, then activities such as rebirth in a distant place and recollection would not be possible. If it were infinite, then while staying here, one would experience pleasure and pain in the celestial realms, hells, and so forth. If it were both finite and infinite, then it would be associated with the faults of both. Therefore, the self is a matter that is undeclared (abyākaraṇīya) as either finite or infinite.' If this person were a finitist-and-infinitist in the manner already stated, why was the rejection of the first three doctrines mentioned in such words as: 'Those recluses and brahmins who say "This world is finite and bounded," their word is false' (D. i, 57)? It is because the first three doctrines have characteristics that differ from the manner intended by him. For that reason alone, such a rejection was stated, not because of the absence of his being a finitist-and-infinitist, nor because of a rejection by words of a view that is without limit. This point should certainly be understood in this way. Otherwise, this fourth doctrine would fall into the side of endless equivocation (amarāvikkhepa). Indeed, there is no mode of the self that is free from both finitude and infinitude, and the reasoner is one who follows the path of logic. By virtue of the difference in time, it is not that both are unsuitable in a single world; they are indeed suitable. Let the finitist-and-infinitist nature of the last two doctrines be appropriate, as their doctrine has both as its object by virtue of finitude and infinitude. But how is the finitist-and-infinitist nature of the first two doctrines individually appropriate?
429:
If it is asked: 'Can their doctrine be [called antānantika] since it focuses on only one [aspect] at a time?' It is said: It is possible because a term used for a whole is also applied metaphorically (upacāra) to its parts. Indeed, the term 'antānantika' (finitist-and-infinitist), which is applied to the group of finitists and infinitists, is well-known among them and thus applies individually to the finitists and infinitists who are its parts. For example, the name 'eight liberations' (aṭṭha-vimokkha) is applied to each of the formless jhānas, and as one speaks of the 'inclinations of beings' (sattāsaya) in the world. Or else, this conventional usage is made by virtue of the reasoning that occurred in the period before fixed attachment (abhinivesa). Before those of such views attained such mental concentration (cetosamādhi), the state of being a finitist-and-infinitist became well-known by virtue of the reasoning that relied on both modes: 'Is this world finite, or is it infinite?' Later, even though they obtain a distinction [in concentration] and adopt only one of those doctrines of finitude or infinitude, they are still referred to by the previously established usage (ruḷhī). For example, the name 'being' (satta) is applicable in such phrases as 'all beings are subject to death,' and as the term 'frog,' etc., is applicable even when it has gone to another existence.

54-60. To show the occurrence of finitude and infinitude by virtue of reaching or not reaching the edge of the universe in the downward, upward, and across directions during the expansion of the counterpart sign, the passage beginning with 'paṭibhāganimittaṃ' is stated. 'Nti' refers to the counterpart sign. In the phrase 'without expanding it upwards or downwards, but expanding it across,' the words 'making the edge of the universe the limit' should be applied and understood according to the context. 'In the manner already stated' means in the same manner stated under Eternalism (sassatavāda), both by way of the term, such as 'he reasons, therefore he is a reasoner (takkī),' and by way of the meaning, such as 'the four types of reasoners.' 'Following what was previously seen' means by repeatedly recollecting the finitude, etc., previously perceived by the consciousness that constitutes seeing. By doing so, the inclusion of those who reason based on tradition (anussuti-takkī) and pure reasoners (suddha-takkī) is also accomplished here. Or else, by the word 'seen' (diṭṭha), it should be understood that hearing and so forth are also included, as in the passage 'seeing the spectacles of dancing, singing, and music.' Since these doctrines arise only by virtue of grasping at the permanent existence of the desired self through such [views] as 'it is finite,' they should be understood as being included in Eternalism (sassatadiṭṭhi). For this reason, [the teacher] will say: 'There are only seven types of Annihilationism (ucchedadiṭṭhi); the remaining views are Eternalism.'
430:
## Explanation of the Doctrine of Amarāvikkhepa

"Does not die" (na marati) means that because there is no definitive conclusion such as "it is exactly like this," it does not cease; it is simply non-exclusive (not certain). "Pariyantarahita" means endless, not reaching a conclusion. "Vividha" (various) refers to the various ways [of equivocation] such as "it is not like this to me," and so forth. "Khepa" is the rejection of others' views with one's own view. What is this Amarāvikkhepa? It is the arising of consciousness (cittuppāda) dominated by wrong view (diṭṭhi) that occurs in such a manner and gives rise to such speech. They are called "Amarāvikkhepī" because they reject in various ways with endless views or speech, or because they remove [views] in various ways. They are also appropriately called "Amarāvikkhepika."

Saying "one kind" (ekā) instead of just "a kind of fish" shows that this is a specific type of fish. It runs here and there because it does not stay fixed in a single nature. Just as it runs so as not to be caught, the rejection of the amarā fish is like that. Because it is similar to the rejection of the amarā fish, it is called "Amarāvikkhepa." This is because it is compared with the meaning of the word vikkhepa (wavering/tossing) by way of its emerging and submerging. This meaning is also stated by the teacher Sāriputta Thera in the Sāratthadīpanī-ṭīkā. Some teachers say Amarāvikkhepa means rejection like the amarā fish. Alternatively, they are Amarāvikkhepī because they reject like the amarā fish; they are the same as Amarāvikkhepika.

Because the equivocationist (vikkhepavādī) lacks the wisdom to penetrate the specific nature of superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma) and indeterminate states (abyākatadhamma), the meaning of the terms wholesome (kusala) and unwholesome (akusala) is stated only by way of the courses of wholesome and unwholesome action (kamma-patha). Vighāta means oppression or bodily suffering. Because it is spoken of as the cause of distress (domanassa) through the "arising of remorse," the teacher says "suffering would occur." The term "musāvāde" is the locative case used in the sense of cause, or the locative in the sense of the ablative. It means because of the cause of lying, or out of shame (hiri) and fear (ottappa) regarding lying. 

To the possible question of what kind of Amarāvikkhepa one reaches, it says "Apariyantavikkhepa" (endless equivocation). By that, it excludes the second method called equivocation similar to the amarā fish. In the two methods mentioned, this meaning is shown by the first method. To show equivocation similar to the amarā fish by the second method, the text will say "When asked, 'Is this wholesome?'" and so forth.

"It is not like this to me" means "I do not have the view that it is like this" regarding what you asked. This should be understood accordingly in all sections. "Aniyamitavikkhepa" (unregulated equivocation) refers to [equivocation] regarding eternalism and so forth...
431:
Not standing even in one variety of view but rejecting specifically with words of view or causing extensive wavering is called vikkhepakaraṇa. When asked by another proponent about any variety of view, rejecting that view by tossing it aside or wavering is "rejection-equivocation" (paṭik္khepa-vikkhepa). Alternatively, in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), only the showing of endless equivocation is done with "It is not like this to me—unregulated equivocation," and "When asked, 'Is this wholesome or unwholesome?'" and so forth. Because it is the doctrine of endless equivocation, by not confirming and by rejecting the doctrines of eternalism, partial-eternalism, annihilationism, and traditional reasoning (takki) with "It is not like this to me," it simply rejects those various doctrines. Having shown them as "Amarāvikkhepī," because they have a doctrine that does not stand firm, to show that they do not stand in any side of a view, it says "He himself does not explain this...". Now, by not explaining wholesome states and so forth, that very lack of standing is clearly shown with "When asked, 'Is this wholesome?'" and so forth. Therefore, it is said, "He does not stand even in one side of a view." "Is it your view that 'it is not that it is not'?" is the meaning of "Kiṃ no no ti te laddhi." "I do not have the view that 'it is not that it is not'" is the meaning of "No no ti pi me no."

63. To show the connection by way of lust (rāga) and so forth regarding one's own state of being wise, it says "Even though not knowing," and so forth. "Sahasa" means quickly, without reflecting with wisdom. "Bhadramukha" is a form of address used by the wise, meaning "one with a beautiful face." "Tattha" is the locative case used in the sense of "in that explanation" or "in that cause." Although the terms chanda (desire) and rāga (lust) have the same meaning, because they are joined by the word "vā" (or), it is appropriate that they have different meanings according to the go-balīvadda (cow-bull) method. Thus, "Chanda is weak lust; rāga is strong lust." The same applies to dosa (anger) and paṭigha (resentment). In "Ettakampi nāma," the word "api" is used in the sense of inclusion, and "nāma" in the sense of reproach. It means "Not only do I not know what is beyond this, but I do not even know this much; what then to say of knowing what is beyond?"

The connection by way of lust and so forth regarding respect and honor given by others: "Even though I do not truly know wholesome and unwholesome, if I were to explain wholesome as 'wholesome' and unwholesome as 'unwholesome,' and because of such explanation those people were to pay me respect and honor saying 'Oh, how wise this person is!', then desire (chanda) or lust (rāga) would arise in me." The same should be applied inversely for anger and resentment. "That would be my clinging (upādāna), that would be my distress (vighāta)"—this should be connected according to the Abhidhamma method as appropriate to the terms and meanings. In Abhidhamma, only craving (taṇhā) and wrong view (diṭṭhi) are taught as clinging (upādāna). Now, the teacher shows the connection without distinction according to the Suttanta method with "In both cases, or..." and so forth. In the Suttanta, it is taught: "Because of anger (kodha), they are oppressed by clinging and reach exhaustion," and so forth. Although the term "ubhayattha" (in both) is stated by meaning, it is not stated by word. This is because all four terms—lust, anger, resentment [and desire]—express the combination of the two meanings. "Ggahanaṃ" means a grasping that does not let go. Anger also does not let go of the object because it occurs by way of malice and so forth. Although the nature of greed as clinging is clear, the word "ggahana" is used to show the nature of other states as clinging. "Vihananaṃ, vihiṃsanaṃ, vibādhanaṃ" mean oppression and affliction. Lust also oppresses the person who depends on it by way of burning. Based on the specific showing of lust and anger as clinging, that meaning is completed. It should be connected as: "He takes the object because he wishes to destroy it." Because of such taking and oppressing, it is called clinging and distress.
432:
In the Abhidhamma, only craving (taṇhā) and views (diṭṭhi) are taught as 'clinging' (upādāna). Now, the general application according to the Suttanta method is shown starting with 'ubhayattha vā'. In the Suttanta, anger (dosa) is also taught as 'clinging'. This is as taught in passages such as 'kodhupādānavinibandhā vighātaṃ āpajjanti' (beings bound by the clinging of anger fall into distress). This statement 'ubhayattha' is made only in terms of meaning, not in terms of the word itself. This is because the four words—rāga, dosa, and paṭigha—express both meanings. Firm grasping (daḷhaggahaṇa) means holding on without letting go. Aversion (paṭigha) also does not let go of the object because it occurs by way of grudges (upanāha) and the like. Since only greed (lobha) is well-known as clinging, this word 'gahaṇa' is used to show that anger (dosa) is also a form of clinging. Vihanana means harming, oppressing, or afflicting. Lust (rāga) also harms the person it relies on because it occurs with agitation by way of burning (pariḷāha). Starting with 'rāgo hi', the completion of that meaning is shown by highlighting the specific nature of lust and anger as clinging. It should be connected as: 'it takes the object with the desire to destroy it'. Because of such taking and harming, it is called 'iti'.

Wisdom is called 'paṇḍā' either because it knows ultimate realities (paramattha) or because it arrives at the true nature of things. The meaning that those who possess such wisdom are called 'paṇḍita' is shown starting with 'paṇḍiccena'. The state of being a wise person is 'paṇḍicca' (wisdom). The very wisdom with which a person is endowed to be called a 'paṇḍita' is 'paṇḍicca'. By this term, wisdom based on learning (sutamaya-paññā) and wisdom based on reflection (cintāmaya-paññā) are meant, as these are its domains. The wisdom of one who has attained meditative attainments is called wisdom based on mental development (bhāvanāmaya-paññā). By the word 'nipuṇā', natural wisdom known as rebirth-linking wisdom (paṭisandhi-paññā) produced by kamma is intended; therefore, it is said 'saṇhasukhumabuddhino' (those of subtle and fine intellect). 'Atthantara' means various meanings or the meaning itself. By the phrase 'viññātaprappavāda', it is shown that the word 'kata' expresses being endowed with knowledge, as in 'katavijjo'. By the phrase 'katavādaparicaya', it shows the state of having well-practiced doctrines, as in 'katasippo'. Between these two, the use of the word 'ca' with the sense of conjunction should be understood as a general designation (sāmaññaniddesa) or a residual elision (ekasesa).

They are called 'vālavadhīrūpa' because they have the habit like archers who shoot the tip of a hair; this is stated by the words 'vālavadhidhanuggahasadisā'. The meaning is that they are like archers who can hit the tip of a single hair that has been split a hundred times. Only such an archer is intended by 'vālavadhī'. The word 'maññe' is used to illustrate a simile, hence 'bhindantā viya' (as if piercing through). 'Paññāgatena' means by way of the varieties of wisdom or by wisdom itself. Questioning a doctrine is called 'samanuyuñjanā'. Investigating the reasons for that doctrine is 'samanugāhanā', as shown by 'kiṃ kusalaṃ' and so on. 'Samanubhāsanā' is also just questioning (samanuyuñjanā) by way of admonition. In the word 'sampāyanti', the teacher said 'sampāyanti' to show the change of the letter 'da' to 'ya' and the potential sense of the word 'eyya'.

65-66. A person who has dull wisdom is called 'mandapañña' (dull-witted). Therefore, the commentator said, 'apaññassevetaṃ nāmaṃ' (this is indeed a name for one without wisdom).
433:
He said, "samanuyuñjeyyuṃ". In the term "na sampāyeyya", the expression "na sampādeyya" etc. is stated to show the substitution of the letter 'ya' for the letter 'da', and the sense of capability in the word "eyya".

65-66. One whose wisdom is not sharp is 'mandapañña' (dull-witted); therefore, it is said, "this is indeed a name for one without wisdom". Although it should be said as "mohamūha", it is stated as "momūha" by dropping the letter 'ha'; this indicates an intensive meaning because of the redundant sense of the two synonyms. Thus, the commentator said "atisammūḷha" (extremely confused) as the definition. Indeed, when a purpose is already accomplished, a further effort is either for the sake of certainty or to make known a special meaning. Just as one has come by kamma in the past, so one comes here in the same way; thus, one is called "tathāgata" (a sentient being).

In this context, although the first three types of persons are indeed dull due to their lack of understanding of the nature of wholesome and other states, they are distinct because they are aware of their own lack of understanding. The last person, however, is called "manda-momūha" (dull and extremely confused) because of the absence of such awareness. One might ask: Does the last person not also have awareness of his own lack of understanding, given the statement: "If I thought 'there is an afterlife', I would answer you 'there is an afterlife', but I do not think so"? Although such awareness exists, he does not have the sense of fear or disgust regarding lying about unknown things as the previous persons do; rather, he is simply one who is greatly deluded, and thus he is described so. Alternatively, by saying "I do not think so", he merely presents the question to evade it; it does not show an awareness of his own lack of understanding. Therefore, he specifically is called "manda-momūha". It is for this reason that, regarding Sañjaya Belaṭṭhaputta who spoke in such a way, it was said: "Among these recluses and brahmins, this one is the most foolish and most confused."

Among those questions, "Is there an afterlife?" is a question asked from the perspective of Eternalism (sassata-diṭṭhi) or from the perspective of Right View (sammā-diṭṭhi). If a person of wrong view asks, it is from Eternalism; if a person of right view asks, it is from Right View—the meaning is valid in both ways. "There is no afterlife" is asked from the perspective of Nihilism (natthika-diṭṭhi) or Right View. "There both is and is not an afterlife" is asked from the perspective of Annihilationism (uccheda-diṭṭhi) or Right View. "There neither is nor is not an afterlife" is asked either by prioritizing evasion—since no other mode is possible once the three aforementioned modes are rejected—or from the perspective of Right View.
434:
The questioning is done either with confusion as the precursor or by the power of right view. In the remaining three tetrads, the meaning should be understood according to the method already stated. Just as with the triad of meritorious formations (puññasaṅkhāra), the meaning encompassed in the first tetrad by the triad of bodily formations (kāyasaṅkhāra) is also encompassed in the remaining three tetrads by the method of challenging the misconception of a being (sattaparāmāsa) and the fruitfulness of merit and so forth. Here, it should be understood that the method of challenge is stated by the third tetrad because of the fruitfulness of kamma such as merit, and by the remaining three tetrads because of the misconception of a being.

The eel-wriggler (amarāvikkhepika), because of his dislike for eternalism (sassatadiṭṭhi) and other such views, resorts only to wriggling in all matters by saying, "It is not thus for me," and so forth. In that context, the phrase "It is not thus for me" and so forth shows the manner of wriggling by way of negating the points questioned in various doctrines. Why is only the rejection by the proponent of wriggling (vikkhepavādī) stated in all doctrines? Would it not be appropriate to accept the side of wriggling by saying "It is just so," since he does not abide in any side? No, it is not so, because he is utterly confused in that regard, and because the doctrine of wriggling proceeds only by way of rejection. Indeed, when Sañjaya Belaṭṭhaputta was asked by King Ajātasattu about the visible fruits of recluseship (sāmaññaphala), he answered evasively, starting with the negation of the existence of the world beyond and so forth.

Here, an objector says: Do not all these eel-wrigglers merely resort to wriggling when asked various questions because they do not truly understand states such as the wholesome (kusala) or the existence of the world beyond? If so, how can such a person be considered one of wrong view? It is not appropriate to call someone a holder of wrong view merely because they resort to wriggling due to not knowing the meaning of the question, like someone who does not wish to speak. The reply is: One is not called a holder of wrong view merely by resorting to wriggling in response to a question, but rather by the power of wrong adherence (micchābhinivesa). A person who has wrongly adhered through the adherence to eternalism, because of dull intelligence, does not penetrate the truth of states such as the wholesome or the existence of the world beyond. Because he is unable to make others understand what he himself does not know, and because of the fear of lying (musāvāda), he resorts to wriggling. Thus, the commentator will say later: "Among those views, only seven are views of annihilationism (ucchedadiṭṭhi); the rest are views of eternalism (sassatadiṭṭhi)." Alternatively, because of not knowing and not believing in merit, demerit, and their results, he develops a preference and inclination, thinking that resorting to wriggling in questions concerning those matters is best. This view that arises in one who thus wrongly adheres should be understood as a distinct view, like the sevenfold division of views (sattabhangadiṭṭhi). And so it is said:
435:
“It has been said (in the Commentary): ‘The view and the speech of one with wrong view have no limit or boundary.’ The statement that ‘these four individuals also belong to the doctrines of speculators about the past (Pubbantakappika) because they hold views following the sequence of phenomena that occurred previously’ is said only by way of including this doctrine of eel-wriggling (Amarāvikkhepavāda) within Eternalism (Sassatadiṭṭhi). Why is this eel-wriggling doctrine included in Eternalism? Because it is not contemplated by way of annihilation (uccheda). Since there are many differing views in the world, there is no one who knows things as they truly are. The contemplation of phenomena with other words such as ‘it is only thus’ has existed in the world from time immemorial. Therefore, because a hint of eternity (sassata) can be found in this eel-wriggling doctrine, it should be understood as being included in Eternalism.

## Description of the Doctrine of Fortuitous Origination (Adhiccasamuppannavāda-vaṇṇanā)

‘Adhicca’ means bypassing any desired cause (i.e., causeless). The view that focuses on the manner of the causeless arising of the aggregates, which are designated as ‘self’ and ‘world,’ arising for someone without prior knowledge (or cause), is called ‘Adhiccasamuppanna’ (Fortuitously Originated). It is called so because it occurs depending on that manner of causeless arising, or because it occurs together with that manner, similar to the metaphor: ‘The beds are crying out, the spears are walking’ (metonymy). Or, in the phrase ‘Adhiccasamuppanna-dassana,’ the final word ‘dassana’ is elided, and it is called ‘Adhiccasamuppanna,’ just as ‘rūpabhava’ is called ‘rūpa.’ With this meaning in mind, it is said ‘Adhiccasamuppanna,’ etc. ‘Akāraṇasamuppanna’ means arising spontaneously, excluding a cause.

68-73. In this term ‘Asaññasattā,’ the word ‘Asaññā’ is the meaning. ‘Desanāsīsa’ means the head or principal part of the teaching. Because it is taken as the primary focus, the Blessed One taught this discourse by making perception (saññā) the main theme. To show that although other mental phenomena (nāma-dhamma) exist in that realm of non-percipient beings, they are taught without being made the primary focus, He said ‘the non-arising of consciousness,’ etc. Just as the Blessed One, when teaching the supramundane Dhamma (lokuttara-dhamma), teaches by making concentration (samādhi) or wisdom (paññā) the main theme, so too when teaching the mundane Dhamma (lokiya-dhamma), He teaches by making consciousness (citta) or perception (saññā) the main theme. In teaching thus, there are suttas such as: ‘At whatever time one develops supramundane jhāna,’ ‘Right concentration with five factors, right concentration with fivefold knowledge,’ ‘Having seen with wisdom, his taints are exhausted,’ and likewise, ‘At whatever time a wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere arises,’ ‘Monk, what consciousness do you have?’, ‘Phenomena have mind as their forerunner,’ ‘Monks, there are (beings with diverse bodies and diverse perceptions),’ etc.”
436:
"There are beings with diverse bodies and diverse perceptions," "The sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception," and so forth, are the discourses that serve as evidence for this meaning. Wrong view is called tittha. It is called tittha because [beings] mostly wander in that wrong view, or because fools cross (wander) in this view. That very tittha is called titthāyatana because it is the place of origin or the place of residence for many disadvantages and for heretics (titthiyas). "In that titthāyatana" means in the views of other heretics outside the Dispensation (Sāsana). Heretics perceive liberation (vimutti) in a specific kind of rebirth. Being those who see the disadvantages and advantages in the detachment and non-detachment from perception, they produce the attainment of non-perception (asaññasamāpatti) and are reborn in the realm of non-percipient beings (asaññasatta), which is a ground devoid of opportunity [to attain the Path]. Those within the Dispensation are not reborn there. Therefore, it is said, "A certain person, having gone forth in the view of heretics..." "Having performed preliminary work (parikamma) on the air kasiṇa (vāyokasiṇa)" means having produced the three jhānas starting from the first in the fourth of the primary element kasiṇas, and being one who has achieved mastery (vasī) in the third jhāna, emerging from that third jhāna and performing preliminary work to attain the fourth jhāna. For this reason, it is said, "Having produced the fourth jhāna."

Why is the preliminary work mentioned only for the air kasiṇa here? To answer: Just as in specific kasiṇas that are counterparts to form, the specific immaterial attainment (arūpasamāpatti)—known as the meditation on detachment from form—is realized by the dissolving of form; likewise, in the specific air kasiṇa which is a counterpart to the immaterial because of its indistinct form, the specific fine-material attainment (rūpasamāpatti)—known as the meditation on detachment from the immaterial—is attained by the dissolving of the immaterial. Therefore, in this fine-material attainment, by seeing the disadvantages in the occurrence of the immaterial through such methods as "Perception is a disease, perception is a boil," and "Woe to the mind, that mind is loathsome," and by determining the peaceful and sublime state in the absence of that immaterial, the fine-material attainment is conditioned. The meditation on detachment from form consists of the immaterial attainments along with access concentration (upacāra), specifically the first immaterial jhāna. If that is so, should it not also be said, "In the limited-space kasiṇa (paricchinnākāsakasiṇa) as well"? For in that kasiṇa too, the nature of being a counterpart to the immaterial is found. According to the view of some teachers, it should indeed be said so, but it is not mentioned in the Commentaries because the ancient teachers did not accept it. Just as the meditation on detachment from form arises in a specific object that is a counterpart to the things to be detached from, being weary of the mere nature of things to be detached from, so too there is no contradiction in saying the same for the meditation on detachment from the immaterial. However, because that attainment is to be practiced only by heretics, and because they practice that jhāna only as a sign of a portion of the object, that reason...
437:
It should be understood that the ancient teachers mentioned the preliminary work for the meditation on detachment from the immaterial only in the fourth primary element kasiṇa, which is the air kasiṇa. To say a bit more: as in the color kasiṇas (vaṇṇakasiṇa), in the first three primary element kasiṇas as well, only the reflection similar to color occurs as the conceptual object (paññatti-ārammaṇa) of the jhāna, in accordance with worldly usage. By doing so, the statement in the Visuddhimagga comparing the earth kasiṇa (paṭhavīkasiṇa) to the disk of a mirror or the disk of the moon is also fulfilled. But in the fourth primary element kasiṇa (air kasiṇa), only the reflection of the element itself becomes the object of the jhāna; therefore, it is appropriate that only the air kasiṇa has a nature similar to the immaterial (arūpa). Thus, it should be understood that the preliminary work is mentioned only for the air kasiṇa.

To the question "How does one see?", [the text] says "While the mind exists (citte sati)," etc. "Peaceful" (santo) means extinguished; this means it is Nibbāna in the present life. "Having passed away" (kālaṃ katvā) means having died. Or it also means having completed the lifespan produced by supporting conditions in the human world. "Is reborn among the non-percipient beings" (asaññasattesu nibbattati) means one is reborn by way of material rebirth only, in the group of beings called non-percipient. Or, because that realm exists in other world-systems (cakkavāḷa) as well, the use of the plural (asaññasattesu) should be understood as referring to the various types. "Right here" (idheva) means only in the five-constituent existence (pañcavokāra-bhava). "There" (tattha) means in the non-percipient existence.

If only the material aggregate (rūpakkhandha) appears in the non-percipient realm, how does matter occur there without the support of the immaterial (mind)? Should not the arising of the material aggregate occur only with the support of the immaterial? For such an occurrence of matter is not seen here in this five-constituent realm. This inquiry is applicable elsewhere too. "How does the immaterial occur in the immaterial realm (arūpa-dhātu) without the support of matter?" This statement is of the same nature as the objection regarding the non-percipient realm. Why? Because such an occurrence is not seen here [in this realm]. "How does matter occur in the fine-material realm (rūpa-dhātu) without solid food (kabaḷīkārāhāra)?" This too is of the same nature. Why? Simply because it is not seen here. Thus, since such occurrences are seen in other realms, what is the use of this objection here by pointing to others?

Furthermore, just as when craving that is not detached from matter is the cause for the arising of a certain mental continuum, that mental continuum occurs depending on matter because it arises together with matter, the cause being regardful of matter; and just as when craving that is detached from matter is the cause for the arising of a certain mental continuum, that mental continuum occurs without matter because the cause is regardless of matter; so too, when craving that is detached from the immaterial is the cause for the arising of a certain material continuum, that material continuum occurs without the immaterial because the cause is regardless of the immaterial. Thus, just as there is the occurrence of both matter and the immaterial in the five-constituent realm due to the absence of the power of meditation, so too in the four-constituent realm due to the power of meditation...
438:
Just as in the Formless realm (arūpa-bhūmi) only mentality (nāma) is manifest, so too in the Non-percipient realm (asaññasatta-bhūmi), by the power of meditation (bhāvanā), it should be understood that only matter (rūpa) is manifest.

Considering the objection (codanā): "How does a mere continuity of matter, devoid of present causes, persist for a long time in that Non-percipient realm? Or for how long does it persist?", the teacher said, "Yathā nāma," and so on. By these words, he shows that it is not only the traditional scripture (āgama) mentioned here and elsewhere that makes this meaning known, but rather that the following reasoning (yutti) is also appropriate in this context. "Jiyāvegukkhitto" means like an arrow shot by the force of a bowstring. "Jhāna-vega" (the force of jhāna) refers to the power of jhāna, which is the ability to produce a result. "Tattakameva kālaṃ" (for that much time) means for a maximum of five hundred great aeons (mahākappa). "Tiṭṭhanti" (they remain) means they remain in the very posture in which they were born, like a painted figure. "Jhāna-vege" refers to the force of the fourth or fifth jhāna-kamma, which is encompassed by the non-percipient attainment (asañña-samāpatti). "Antaradhāyati" means it vanishes due to the cessation of causes; it does not continue to occur. "Idha" (here) means in this sense-sphere realm (kāmāvacara-bhava), because those non-percipient beings cannot be reborn in any other realm. "Paṭisandhi-saññā" (rebirth-perception) refers to the arising of rebirth-consciousness itself, spoken of by way of perception (saññā).

If it is asked: "How can consciousness arise here in this sense realm from a consciousness that has been ceased for a long time, across many hundreds of aeons? Indeed, it is never seen that eye-consciousness arises when the eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda) has ceased." This objection should not be taken as absolute. For even though the mind has ceased, because no mind of a similar class arises in the interval, it remains merely as a proximity condition (samanantara-paccaya), not as a seed (bīja). Kamma alone is called the seed. Therefore, from kamma which acts as the seed, and through conditions such as the object (ārammaṇa), the rebirth-consciousness in the sense element (kāma-dhātu) certainly arises for those who have passed away from the Non-percipient realm. Thus it is said, "Rebirth-perception arises in this realm."

In this context, an analogy is given: Just as trees that are fixed to bloom at a certain time according to the law of seasons (utu-niyāma) may bloom at an irregular time if an incision or splitting (vekkha) is made by force, so too, while the phenomena of matter and mentality are occurring inseparably in the five-constituent existence (pañcavokāra-bhava), if the 'splitting' called the meditation on the dispassion for matter and mentality is performed, then in accordance with the force of that attainment-splitting, the occurrence of aggregates devoid of matter in the Formless realm, and the occurrence of aggregates devoid of mentality in the Non-percipient realm, should be understood to arise respectively. 

Why is it said again here, "Because of the arising of perception, those devas fall from that body," thus stating the arising of perception as the cause of their falling? Or what meaning is shown by the word "saññuppādā"? In response to this objection, he said "Yasmā pana," and so on. It is stated as a signaling cause (ñāpaka-hetu) because their falling can be known by the arising of rebirth-perception here in this sense realm. Or, the word "saññuppādā" is simply to show the manifestation of their falling.
439:
The meaning is that it shows the state of their falling becoming manifest. For "saññuppādā" means they fall because of the arising of perception as the cause; or the connection is: those devas are ones who have an arisen perception (uppāda-saññā). "Santabhāvāya" means for the sake of Nibbāna, the state of peace. Is it not the case that the theory of fortuitous origination held by one who has attained jhāna (lābhī-adhiccasamuppannika-vāda) could have many varieties, just like the eternalist theory held by one who has attained jhāna (lābhī-sassata-vāda), occurring by way of reaching the Non-percipient realm after a hundred thousand births or ten world-contraction cycles, or within that interval? That is indeed true. However, it should be understood that the theory of fortuitous origination held by one who has attained jhāna is shown as a single method by way of reaching the Non-percipient realm which is immediate and near. Alternatively, because the theory of fortuitous origination is included within the eternalist view (sassata-diṭṭhi), the Blessed One showed the theory of fortuitous origination held by one who has attained jhāna without detailed classification, in order to show this distinction: that all methods of teaching that come in the eternalist theory should also be taken in the theory of fortuitous origination as applicable. And its inclusion in the eternalist view must necessarily be desired, because the inclinations of beings in the side of defilement (saṃkilesa) are only of two kinds: by way of eternalism and annihilationism; and among those, this theory does not fall into the side of annihilation (uccheda).

For this reason, it is said in the Commentary, when extracting the meaning of the word "āsaya" (inclination): "The eternalist and annihilationist views." Likewise, it will be said later: "Among the views, only seven are annihilationist views; the rest are eternalist views" (DA. 1.97, 98).

Is it not improper to include the theory of fortuitous origination in the eternalist view? For it proceeds by way of "Formerly I did not exist," etc., thus grasping the manifestation of a being that did not exist before. The eternalist view, however, grasps the perpetual existence of the self and the world, proceeding as "It exists as something eternal." It is not improper; it is proper. This is because it is subsumed under the eternalist grasp due to not seeing the future end (anāgata-koṭi). For although this theory proceeds by way of reflecting on the past end of the self and the world, saying, "That 'I' having not existed before, has now evolved into a manifest state," yet from the present moment onwards, it does not see any limit in the future. Especially, eternalism is produced by not seeing a limit in the present and future times, as it is said: "It will remain just so, as something eternal." If this were the case, then the inclusion of this theory and the eternalist theories among the "speculators about the past" (pubbantakappika) would be improper, because they proceed by way of reflecting on the future time. It is indeed proper, because their origin (samudāgama) belongs to the past portion. For their origin is counted among the knowledges of past lives (pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa) which belong to the past portion, or among the reasonings (takka) developed based on hearsay similar to that knowledge. In this manner, the commentator has also explained.
440:
Even so, from the present moment onwards, those individuals do not see the end limit of the future in certain existences. Specifically, it is Eternalism (sassata-vāda) developed through not seeing the end limit in the present and future. The Blessed One said in the Brahmajāla Sutta of the Sīlakkhandhavagga Pāḷi: 'It will remain just so, similar to Eternalism.' If this is the case, one might object that it is inappropriate to include these doctrines of fortuitous origination (adhiccasamuppannika-vāda) and Eternalism among the pubbantakappika (speculating about the past) views, because they arise from a wrong assessment of the future. However, it is indeed appropriate to include these views among the pubbantakappika views. This is because their origin (samudāgama) lies in the past portion. It should be understood that the origin of these views is encompassed by the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa) belonging to the past portion, or by reasonings developed through hearsay and the like which resemble that knowledge. The commentator has also explained it in this way.

Alternatively, the Lord of Dhamma, who possesses unobstructed knowledge and vision regarding all objects, having personally realized through higher knowledge the wrong path (agati) and the right path (gati) without remainder as they truly are, has made these views known in detail. Therefore, however many views the Blessed One has taught, and in whatever manner He has taught them, all those views should be accepted with conviction just as they were taught. In this matter, one should not engage in logical investigation, because it is the domain of a Buddha (Buddha-visaya). The Buddha-visaya of the Buddhas is inconceivable (acinteyya). Thus, it will be said in the Commentary: 'In that matter, one should not search for a cause exclusively.'

## The Explanation of the Second Recitation Section is Finished.

## Explanation of the Speculations about the Future (Aparantakappika-vāda)

Just as in 'knowledge of the future' (aparante ñāṇaṃ) and 'those who hold views about the future' (aparantānudiṭṭhino), the word 'aparanta' refers to the future portion in due order; thus it was said: 'known as the future portion.' In the same manner as explained in 'speculating about the past' (pubbantaṃ kappetvā), the meaning in 'speculating about the future' (aparantaṃ kappetvā) should also be understood. Here, I shall mention only the distinctive points.

## Explanation of the Doctrine of Conscious Survival (Saññī-vāda)

'Uddhamāghātanā' means 'above death' (uddhamāghātanaṃ); the meaning is the self existing after death. The doctrine that has arisen as 'uddhamāghātanaṃ' is called 'uddhamāghātana' by way of association (sahacaraṇa) or by way of derivative (taddhita); or it is a description with the final word elided (antalopa-niddesa). Because that doctrine belongs to them, they are called 'uddhamāghātanikā'. To show the meaning of what is thus established by the word, it was said: 'they say the self exists above death.' The meaning is the state of self (attabhāva) existing above or after death. For those holders of views say: 'After death, the self is unchanging.' By the phrase 'that belongs to them' (so etesaṃ), the sense of possession (assatthi-taddhita) is shown, just as in 'He is called Buddha because he has enlightenment (buddhamassa atthīti buddho)'. This is another method from the Commentary: the doctrine that has arisen as 'saññī' is called 'saññī' by way of association and so on. Because they have the doctrine of conscious survival, they are called 'saññī-vādā' by way of compound (samāsa). The meaning is that for those teachers of views, only the doctrine of conscious survival exists as their doctrine.
441:
76-77. In the phrase 'the self having form' (rūpī attā), why is the kasiṇa form called 'self'? Should not the self be distinct from form? If it is said, 'the self has form,' then just like perception (saññā), form is also merely a property of the self (attaniya). In the phrase 'the self having perception' (saññī attā), perception itself is not the self; rather, in the sense that 'this self has perception,' it is merely a property of the self. Thus it was said: 'Taking the perception that has arisen in that kasiṇa form as the perception of this self.'

This statement should not be understood as: 'He is called rūpī (having form) because form belongs to this self.' Rather, it should be understood as: 'He is called rūpī because he has the nature of being affected (ruppana-sīla).' Here, 'being affected' (ruppana) means reaching a distinction by way of the time of expansion or non-expansion of the kasiṇa form, because it is similar to ultimate form (paramattha-rūpa). That distinction cannot be said 'not to exist,' because special characteristics such as being minute or vast are clearly present.

If it is argued: 'If he is called rūpī because he has the nature of being affected, then since that which has the nature of being affected is subject to destruction, it is inappropriate to include this view under Eternalism (sassata-diṭṭhi)'; it is indeed appropriate, because he intends the unchanging nature of the self imagined after the breaking up of the body. Thus it was said: 'It is healthy after death.' Alternatively, even if it is said 'He is called rūpī because form belongs to this self,' there is no fault, because we see descriptions where a distinction is made through imagination even where no distinction exists, such as 'the body of a stone statue.'

Furthermore, just as we see the whole described by way of its parts (for example, 'contemplating the body in the body'), or 'form' (rūpa) is the act of being affected, the nature of form; because this self has that nature of form, it is called 'rūpī'. This is like in the phrase 'states having form' (rūpino dhammā). In this way, because the self has the nature of form, saying 'the self having form' is consistent with logic; thus it was said: 'the kasiṇa form is the self.' The phrase 'taking' should be connected with that statement. 'In that' means in the kasiṇa form. 'To this one' means to the imagined self. The meaning is: just as the Ājīvakas and others designate [the self] by mere reasoning. The Ājīvakas are mere reasoners (takkika), not attainers [of jhānas]. Because they hold the doctrine of fatalism (niyata-vāda) and thus reject the fruit of kamma, they do not attain meditative absorptions (jhāna-samāpatti). Thus, in the 'black birth' (kaṇhābhijāti) and so on, some Ājīvakas claim that a dark form and the like is the 'self.' The former method shows the view of those who have attained [jhānas], while the latter method shows the view of the reasoners. In such matters, it should be understood in this way.

The word 'disease' (roga) is a synonym for destruction (bhanga), because destruction also has the nature of being painful. In this way, it is appropriate for the word 'healthy' (aroga) to be a synonym for permanence (nicca). Therefore, it is said: 'it is permanent.' Alternatively, the word 'disease' (roga) is a synonym for illness. When 'healthy' (aroga) is said, the holder of the view claims permanence because of the unchanging nature, taking freedom from disease as the primary sense; thus it is said: 'it is permanent.'
442:
The conceptual space obtained by removing the kasiṇa, the first immaterial consciousness, the concept of nothingness, and the base of nothingness are called the signs of the immaterial attainments (arūpa-samāpatti-nimitta) as appropriate. Just as the bitter taste of the same extent as the neem leaf exists in the leaf, the Nigaṇṭhas, by mere reasoning that the immaterial (arūpī) self of the same extent as the body exists in the body, designate that 'the immaterial self has perception.' Thus, the Teacher said, 'like the Nigaṇṭhas and others.'

The third view is the belief that 'the self is both material and immaterial.' 'By way of grasping a mixture' means it occurs by taking the aforementioned signs of the material and immaterial attainments together as a single 'self,' and taking the perception occurring therein as its 'perception.' Indeed, this person of wrong view, having attained material and immaterial attainments, grasps their signs as 'self' in terms of both materiality and immateriality, and generates the misinterpretation that 'it is both material and immaterial,' like a non-proponent of truth (athetavādī). Or else, by mere reasoning, by way of grasping a mixture of material and immaterial phenomena, he stands firm in the misinterpretation that 'the self is called both material and immaterial.' The fourth view is the belief that 'the self is neither material nor immaterial.' 'By way of grasping through reasoning alone' means that, like phenomena that have reached a subtle state with remaining formations (saṅkhāra), because of reaching an extremely subtle state and being unable to accomplish their own functions—like a combination of a stool, a wall, hands, feet, etc.—it is not material; and because of not transcending the nature of materiality, it is not immaterial. This occurs through such a grasp of reasoning.

This is a method not found in the Commentaries (aṭṭhakathāmuttaka). In this view of 'neither material nor immaterial,' the meaning should be understood by way of mutual exclusion, as in the fourth view of the Finite and Infinite (antānantika). Although this view has the same meaning as the third view, the distinction between the third and fourth views here should be understood by way of the difference in time and object, just as there is a distinction by way of the difference in place and time in that Finite and Infinite view. Indeed, the occurrence of the third view here is by way of the difference in time, because the material and immaterial signs do not appear together. The occurrence of the fourth view is by way of the difference in object, because of the state of being a collection of material and immaterial phenomena. The second tetrad should be understood by the method stated in the Finite and Infinite view, because the literal meaning is the same in every way. Whatever needs to be said here has already been said by us with the words 'amati gacchati bhāvo osānamettha,' etc. However, the distinction is clear: there it occurred by way of speculating about the past (pubbantakappanā), while here it occurs by way of speculating about the future (aparantakappanā). And although the view 'the self has diverse perceptions' (nānattasaññī) is also obtainable by way of one who has attained [meditative states], because of the possibility of diverse perceptions by way of a person of wrong view who has obtained the eight attainments. Even though it is so...
443:
Because perception appears in only one mode in the attainment, the state of having a single perception (ekattasaññitā) is highly appropriate by way of the person who has attained it. Therefore, it is said, 'one who has perception of oneness (ekattasaññī) by way of the attainer.' Or else, the meaning should be understood by way of one who has obtained a single attainment. Although diverse perceptions are possible due to the diversity of attainments, since coarse diverse perceptions occur only in the many external objects, it is said, 'one who has diverse perceptions (nānattasaññī) by way of the non-attainer,' in order to show the state of having diverse perceptions by way of a reasoner (takkī). 'By way of a limited kasiṇa' means by way of a small kasiṇa because it has not been expanded. Here, the word 'kasiṇa' indicates the object of perception. The limitedness of perception occurs by way of the object. By this, it is shown that although there are phenomena distinct from perception, he says, 'perception itself is the self.' In the case of 'by way of an immeasurable kasiṇa' (vipulakasiṇavasena), it should be understood in this same way. By doing so, although the first and second views of the Finite and Infinite tetrad in both the Finite and Infinite view and here in this Perception view are the same in literal meaning, the distinction between those two views and these two views is established by their nature. Otherwise, in the views of the described types, although there might be a distinction in some views by the mere difference of speculating about the past and future, there would be no distinction at all in others. 

This, however, is a method not found in the Commentaries. By way of the belief that 'the self is the size of a thumb, the self is the size of an atom,' etc., it is both limited and has perception; thus it is called 'one of limited perception' (parittasaññī), like Kapila, Kaṇāda, and others. By way of claiming the all-pervading nature of one's self, it is both immeasurable and has perception; thus it is called 'one of immeasurable perception' (appamāṇasaññī). 

Because the knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings according to their kamma (yathākammūpaga-ñāṇa) is an accessory to the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu), although the beings' possession of happiness, etc., is seen by the yathākammūpaga-ñāṇa produced by the power of the divine eye, it is said to be seen by the divine eye itself. Therefore, it is said, 'by the divine eye' (dibbeṇa cakkhunā), etc. Referring to the fourfold and fivefold methods, it is said, 'in the planes of the third and fourth jhānas' (tika-catukka-jhānabhūmiyaṃ). Indeed, among the five-constituent jhāna planes which are the sphere of those of wrong view, excluding the Vehapphala plane, the remaining planes are the places of fruition for the third jhāna in the fourfold method and the fourth jhāna in the fivefold method as appropriate; thus they are called the planes of the third and fourth jhānas. The Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa), however, are not within their sphere. 'Nibbattamānaṃ' means a being that is arising. Is it not the case that since the views occurring as 'the self is exclusively happy,' etc., are views about the future (aparantadiṭṭhi), the use of the present term 'seeing the one being reborn' (nibbattamānaṃ disvā) would be inappropriate? For these views have the future as their object. [The answer is:] It is appropriate, [referring to] the self's state of being exclusively happy, etc., in the future...
444:
Because it is intended to see the manifestation in the present by imagining oneself as being absolutely happy, etc., in the future. Therefore, the teacher said, "Seeing a being as it is arising, one takes it as 'absolutely happy'." In this view, based on seeing the occurrence of phenomena accompanied mostly by happiness, etc., in various planes, they take it as "absolutely happy," etc.; thus, it should be understood that only the plane appropriate to that view is meant. Just as a specific meaning can be obtained through connection with another word, a specific meaning can also be obtained through the context (*pakarana*), etc. In phrases such as "absolutely happy," the term "absolute" (*ekanta*) is mostly used to refer merely to the occurrence [of that state]. This is because they take it in this way by seeing such a mere occurrence. Alternatively, like the blind men looking at an elephant, those with wrong views cling to and speak of only what they see. The Blessed One said in the Udāna: "Monks, wanderers of other sects are blind and sightless; they have no eye of wisdom," and so on. Therefore, there is no need to search for logic here. To substantiate the meaning of "seeing with the divine eye," the commentator said "*Visesato hi*," etc.

## Explanation of the Doctrines of Non-percipient and Neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient

78-83. The objection "If so, is there no distinction?" is resolved by the words "*Kevalañhi*," etc. It should be connected as the views of those who hold [the self to be] "non-percipient" (*asaññī*) and "neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient" (*nevasaññīnāsaññī*). "Cause" (*kāraṇa*) refers to a specific cause or the cause for the arising of the wrong view. Although it is possible to search for some cause, it was said "a cause should not be sought absolutely" to show that the doctrines of those with wrong views should be disregarded. Why? Because, as stated in "*Diṭṭhigatikassa*," etc., they are not worthy of investigation; thus, it shows the cause that should not be sought. The meaning is this: In the doctrine of non-perception (*asaññīvāda*), the first doctrine arises by way of beings born in the non-percipient plane; the second doctrine, called "non-percipient," arises by taking perception itself as "self" according to the method "one regards perception as self," because there is no other perception apart from that perception; similarly, the third doctrine arises by taking material phenomena together with perception, or all material and immaterial phenomena, as "self"; and the fourth doctrine arises by way of speculative reasoning.

In the second tetrad as well, because the *kasiṇa* form has the nature of non-cognition, it is designated as "non-percipient," and four variations arise according to the method stated in the doctrine of finitude and infinity (*antānantikavāda*). In the doctrine of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the first doctrine arises by acknowledging the existence of subtle perception because a distinct function of perception cannot be performed during the death and rebirth of a being in the plane of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, or in all objects. The second doctrine, etc., arise by way of subtle perception and by acknowledging the nature of cognition, according to the method stated in the doctrine of non-perception. Thus, although it is possible to search for a cause in some way, it should be understood that the cause should not be sought with great effort because the doctrines of those with wrong views are not worthy of investigation. But...
445:
The first doctrine arises by way of acknowledging the existence of subtle perception, which is unable to perform a distinct function of perception during the death and rebirth of a being in the plane of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, or in all objects. The second doctrine, etc., arise by way of subtle perception and by acknowledging the nature of cognition, according to the method already stated in the doctrine of non-perception. Thus, although it is possible to search for a cause in some way, one should not search for the root cause of those wrong views with great effort because they cannot withstand investigation.
