It is clear that these doctrines of perception, non-perception, and neither-perception-nor-non-perception are included in the view of eternalism (*sassatadiṭṭhi*) because of the statement "After death, one is free from disease (the self exists)."

## Explanation of the Doctrine of Annihilationism

Since destruction cannot occur to what does not exist, in order to show that annihilation (*uccheda*) has existence as its cause, it is stated in the Pali as "*sato*" using the word "*santa*," which expresses existence. To show that only a being (*satta*) associated with such existence, which is the object of those with wrong views, is intended here, it is stated in the Pali as "*sattassa*." By the word "*sattassa*," this meaning is shown: although ultimate realities (*paramattha-dhamma*) that arise by way of cause and effect and belong to a single continuity (*santāna*) are distinct from those belonging to a different continuity, in reality, the phenomena that are cause and effect are different in nature from one another. Just as the wrong adoption of the method of diversity (*nānatta-naya*) by deciding on an absolute difference—as if they were phenomena belonging to different continuities—is the cause for clinging to the view of annihilation, so too, although the difference in nature of the phenomena that are cause and effect is evident, taking them as absolutely non-different by the method of unity (*ekatta-naya*) because they belong to a single continuity is also the cause (for clinging to the notion of a "being").

Indeed, because of the inability to analyze the compact mass (*ghana*) in the aggregates (*khandha*) that arise by way of the continuity, the grasping of them as a "being" occurs. Based on that grasping of a "being" as existing, the doctrine of annihilation (*ucchedavāda*) arises. Here, "annihilation" (*uccheda*) is intended as the immediate destruction by way of successive cessation. The commentator used the term "*upaccheda*" because of the assumption that this self still exists until it reaches the point of being cut off. The prefix "*u-*" is a synonym for "*upa-*" and has the meaning of "approaching." Here, "approaching" means being immediate by way of arising successively and ceasing without interruption. Alternatively, only the destruction without further arising, by way of not reappearing, is called annihilation. For that very reason, by taking it according to the stated method, it is called "*upaccheda*." The prefixes "*u-*" and "*upa-*" here express the meaning of "the part beyond." The part that occurs after cessation is also called "the part beyond" (*uparibhāga*) here.
446: The word 'upa' in this context of the view of annihilation (uccheda-diṭṭhi) has the meaning of 'beyond'. The state following cessation is also called 'beyond' in this context of annihilationism. 'Vināsa' (destruction) is specifically called ruin due to the power of non-continuity or non-increase. This destruction is called 'adassana' (non-seeing) because it transcends the visual range of both the fleshly eye (maṃsa-cakkhu) and the wisdom eye (paññā-cakkhu). In the world, the word 'nāsa' is well-known in the sense of non-seeing, as in the passage 'dve cāpare vaṇṇavikāranāsā' and so forth. 'Bhāva-vigama' means the departure from nature (sabhāvāpagama). Here, the word 'bhāva' denotes nature (sabhāva) in the sense of existing according to the Dhamma. That which is cut off by way of destruction without continuity or increase is called 'vibhava' (departure from existence) because it is unable to remain in its own nature. By the word 'tattha' and so forth, the arising of the doctrine of annihilation is shown merely as an illustration according to the text. Therefore, the teacher will say, 'having distinguished it thus and otherwise.' 'Tattha' occurs in the statement, 'They describe the cutting off, the destruction, the annihilation of a persistent being.' 'Lābhī' refers to one who has attained the knowledge of the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu-ñāṇa). In this context of those who speculate about the future (aparantakappika), one who has attained other supernormal powers besides the divine eye, or one who has no supernormal powers at all, is simply called 'alābhī' (one who has not attained). 'Cuti' (passing away) refers to the death of both trainees (sekha) and worldlings (puthujjana). This same method applies to the phrase 'cutimattam-eva' (merely passing away). 'Upapattiṃ apassanto' (not seeing rebirth) means not seeing due to not looking, even though the ability to see exists. 'Na upapātaṃ' means being unable to see rebirth either due to a lack of previous practice or due to not performing the preliminary preparations (parikamma). Thus, the distinction between the two methods is clear. The view of annihilation is taken up by way of nihilism (natthika-vāda), thinking, 'Who knows the next world? It is simply unknown,' which should be connected with the rest of the text. The meaning is that one holds this view because of not understanding that 'there is another world beyond this' due to the great delusion of nihilism. It is also said 'or through greed for sensual pleasures' (kāmasukhagiddhatāya vါ) because one might hold this view out of extreme attachment to sensual happiness, like a king who holds his own daughter's hand, thinking, 'This range of the senses is all there is.' Regarding the leaves fallen from the stalk, it is said 'they do not grow again,' referring to the fact that they cannot be reattached to the stalk. 'Evam-eva sattā' (even so are beings) means that just as a yellow leaf that has fallen from its bond does not reattach, similarly, all beings are without rebirth, ending in death; they reach a death without rebirth, having no further existence. His doctrine is that beings are like water bubbles because they do not arise again. 'Tathā' (thus) refers to the method indicated by 'the attainer remembering' and so forth. 'Aññathā' (otherwise) means it can also occur by another method, since reasoning (takkana) can have many forms. Even for one who has attained jhāna, these views can arise through reasoning merely by not seeing rebirth beyond death; thus the word 'vikkappetvā-va' (only after distinguishing) is used. Truly, it should be connected as: it arises having reasoned in that way, and it arises having reasoned in another way. Even for one who has attained...
447: It is stated by the word 'only after distinguishing' (vikkappetvā-va) that these views arise through reasoning based merely on the non-seeing of rebirth beyond passing away. The connection is that they arise having distinguished in that way, and they arise having distinguished in another way. Therein, by the words 'two persons' and so forth, this meaning is shown by demonstrating the different ways of grasping the view of annihilation. Just as the doctrines of the eel-wrigglers (amarāvikkhepika-vāda) are taught solely by way of those who have not attained jhāna, and just as in the fourth tetrad of the doctrine of percipient rebirth after death (uddhamāghātanika-saññīvāda), the doctrines of percipient rebirth are taught solely by way of those who have attained jhāna, these annihilationist views are not like that. These annihilationist views, however, are taught by way of both those who have attained and those who have not attained, like the doctrines of eternalism (sassatavāda) and partial-eternalism (ekaccasassatavāda). If that is so, why is the teaching here not given separately by way of the attainer and the reasoner, as in the eternalist doctrines, but is instead given in a manner different from the teachings on eternalism and so forth? It is said to be because of the attainment of elegance in teaching (desanā-vilāsa-patti). The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, have attained elegance in teaching; they teach the Dhamma in various ways according to the inclinations of those to be led (veneyyajjhāsaya), and not otherwise. If there were an inclination of those to be led in this group of views that required such a teaching, the Blessed One would have spoken in that very way. How? 'Here, monks, some recluse or brahmin, by means of ardor... [as before]... when the mind is concentrated, he directs his mind to the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings. With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees the death-thought of an Arahant, or of many other beings, but he does not see rebirth beyond that. He says: "Since, sirs, this self, which has form, is composed of the four great elements, and is born of mother and father, is cut off and destroyed at the breakup of the body and does not exist after death,"' and so forth—thus he would have taught by separating the attainer of distinction and the reasoner. However, since the inclination of those to be led that would require such a teaching does not exist here, it should be understood that this teaching was given through the elegance of teaching according to the inclinations of those to be led, in a manner different from the teachings on eternalism and so forth. Alternatively, unlike in eternalism and partial-eternalism, in this doctrine of annihilation, the doctrine of the attainer is not different in form from the doctrine of the reasoner; rather, because they are of the same nature, they have the same form. To manifest this distinction, this doctrine of annihilation was taught by the Blessed One as having a distinct form from the previous doctrines. This is because in this doctrine of annihilation, the obsession of a reasoner based on hearsay and so forth can occur just like the realization of one who has attained. Furthermore, these views were [not] taught by the Blessed One [as something to occur] in the future...
448:
The Blessed One did not teach these wrong views by way of predicting that they would occur in the future, nor did he teach them by way of mere conjecture that they might be so. In fact, in whatever way those with wrong views perceive that "This alone is the truth, everything else is vain," in that very way he has declared these wrong views, having defined them according to how they actually are through his omniscience. By such declaration, the Buddha-Dhammas, which are profound and so forth and are not the domain of ordinary worldlings, become manifest. Also, by the proclamation of these wrong views, the Tathāgatas are rightly praised.

Another way—just as the annihilationists who see higher and higher existences establish their own views by rejecting the views of those who see other existences, in that very manner this teaching was given. Therefore, the variation in the occurrence of this teaching from previous teachings should not be questioned. If one were to act in this way and divide annihilationism into four according to the divisions of the formless realm (arūpa-bhava), then one should also speak of it as being divided into many according to the divisions of the sense realm (kāma-bhava) and the fine-material realm (rūpa-bhava). If this were the case, there would result more types of annihilationism than the sevenfold division taught by the Blessed One. Or else, if one were to speak without dividing the formless realm as one does the sense and fine-material realms, then there would result fewer types of annihilationism than the sevenfold division taught by the Blessed One. Such objections are entirely groundless. This is because the teaching proceeds according to the inclinations of those with wrong views.

"Mātāpitūnaṃ etaṃ" means that because of the connection with those parents, it is the property of the parents. "Sukka-soṇitaṃ" means the father's semen and the mother's blood, or the blood known as semen of both. The word "mātāpettike" is in the locative case (sattamī) in the sense of cause (nimitta). "Iti" refers to these three words. By saying "rūpakāya-sīsena" (by way of the material body) instead of "rūpakāya-vasena," it indicates their grasping of the immaterial (arūpa) as "self" (attā). To show the meaning "in this manner," he said "evameke." Here, the word "evaṃ" has the meaning of "in this manner." "Eke" means some or others.

Because humans were mentioned previously and because other beings are not possible, the word "kāmāvacaro" in this context means being included among the six sense-sphere deities. Here, "kabaḷīkāro" refers to the divine nutriment (sudhāhāra) already mentioned.
449:
Regarding the phrase "jhānamayena nibbattoti" (produced by jhāna), everything that should be said has already been stated below. A major part is called an "aṅga" (limb), and a part that occurs separately within that limb is called a "paccaṅga" (minor limb). Thus, it is endowed with all major and minor limbs. "Tesaṃ" refers to the eye-faculty and ear-faculty. "Itaresaṃ" refers to the nose, tongue, and body faculties. The appearance of those faculties should also be understood as having a male form. For it is said in the commentaries: "Even though both genders are absent there, the Brahmas in that realm have only a male appearance, not a female appearance."

88-92. The word "ākāsānañcāyatana" here refers only to the realm of existence (bhava), hence he said "ākāsānañcāyatana-bhava." Here, an objector says: In the first three views, it is appropriate to say "with the breaking up of the body" (kāyassa bhedā) because those views proceed based on the self (attā) included in the five-constituent existence (pañcavokāra-bhava). But in the four views starting from the fourth, which proceed by depending on the self included in the four-constituent existence (catuvokāra-bhava), why is it said "with the breaking up of the body"? For formless beings do not have a body, do they? That is true. However, the person with wrong views applies the term "kāya" (body) metaphorically even to the immaterial self, using the same terminology used for the material self. In the world, a term used for one thing is seen to be applied metaphorically to another, such as "rabbit's horn" or "sky-flower." Just as those with wrong views designate their views, the Blessed One also teaches in that same way. Furthermore, because it is a mental body (nāma-kāya), the designation "kāya" should be understood as referring to the immaterial self which is a collection of states such as contact (phassa). Even in the sense of a group, it is called "kāya," as in "elephant corps" (hatthi-kāya) or "cavalry" (assa-kāya).

Among these, let the status of being "speculators about the future" (aparantakappika) for the second and subsequent views—which establish the absolute cessation of existence starting from the sense-sphere deity's self—be appropriate, because those views concern the future. But how can the status of being "speculators about the future" be appropriate for the first view, which establishes the cessation of the present human self? For that view concerns the present. For the second view and others, it is appropriate to be "speculators about the future" because they recognize the annihilation of the self that has arisen in a higher existence in the future, relative to the self included in the preceding views. Thus it was said: "But, sirs, this self is not yet completely annihilated by this much," and so forth. What is said there—"Sirs, there is another self"—is said in consideration of a specific lower self such as the human self, not because it is different in every way. But for the first view, regarding the self that has arisen in a higher existence in the future...
450:
Is it argued that being an Aparantakappika (one who speculates about the future) is inappropriate because there is no knowledge of the cessation of existence in the future beyond that, and because in the statement 'Friends, there is another self,' it is not apprehended as another self? It is not that it is inappropriate; indeed, it is appropriate. Although it is included within this present world, the proponent of the first view intends only the being that will exist in the future. This is because the proponent of the first view also intends the annihilation after death of the self that is included in this present world, by way of the future. Therefore, there is no contradiction in his being an Aparantakappika.

## Explanation of the Doctrine of Nibbāna in the Present Life
It is called 'diṭṭha' (seen) because it is to be seen by wisdom. It is 'dhamma' because it is seen and because it is a phenomenon in the sense of its own nature; thus it is 'diṭṭhadhamma' (the present life). The meaning is the nature obtained by wisdom that sees truly. Since that diṭṭhadhamma is only the object present before the senses such as the eye, it is said, 'It is called the immediate phenomenon (paccakkha-dhamma).' In that diṭṭhadhamma, although a certain personality (attabhāva) is not an object of the senses, it is to be understood that it is so stated because it is very prominent, like an object of the senses. For this very reason, it is said, 'It is a designation for the personality obtained in various existences.' The meaning is a term or a name that denotes the personality to be obtained according to one's kamma in various existences. Here, Nibbāna is merely the allaying of suffering (dukkhavūpasamana); it is not the supreme fruit (arahatta-phala), nor is it the unconditioned element (asaṅkhatadhātu), because those are not within the scope of such theorists. Therefore, it is called 'the allaying of suffering.' It is also appropriate to call them 'Diṭṭhadhammanibbānavādā' because they hold a doctrine concerning the allaying of suffering (Nibbāna) in the present life.

They are called 'kāma' (sensual pleasures) because they are desirable. Those sensual pleasures are called 'guṇa' (cords/qualities) because they are a collection of many parts and because they bind beings. Aiming at this meaning, it is said, 'By way of pleasing forms, etc.' Here, the word 'ādi' (etc.) includes up to tangible objects. It is called 'sammā ṭhapita' (well-established) because it is well-applied. Since 'placing' (ṭhapanā) here means 'attachment,' it is said 'attached.' To show the meaning that one causes one's respective senses to roam among those various cords of sensual pleasure and causes them to take the object, it is said 'in those cords of sensual pleasure,' and so on. For this very reason, it is said, 'It leads them here and there.' Alternatively, the word 'cara' distinguished by the prefix 'pari' is used in the sense of sporting; thus it is said 'palalati,' etc. 'Palalati' means he sports in various ways or performs graceful dalliance. By the words 'And here,' etc., it is shown that they designate the Nibbāna of the present life only for those possessing supreme cords of sensual pleasure. The sensual pleasures of the Great King Mandhātu and the deity Vasavatti are shown as examples of supremacy. Why? It is said, 'Of such a nature,' and so on.
451:
The word 'Aññathābhāvā' is a term in the ablative case (pañcamī) in the sense of cause. 'Vuttanayena' means by the method taught in the Sutta passages. By this word 'vuttanayena,' the manner of the arising of sorrow and so on is shown. Sorrow (soka) is the inner brooding and grieving of one who is affected by the five kinds of ruin (vyasana), namely: ruin of relatives, ruin of wealth, ruin of health, ruin of virtue, and ruin of view. Because it has the characteristic of inner grieving, sorrow is said to be 'that which has the characteristic of inner grieving.' Lamentation (parideva) is the intense wailing arising from that sorrow which is the root cause. Because it has the characteristic of intense wailing based on that sorrow, lamentation is said to be 'that which has the characteristic of intense wailing based on sorrow.'

Bodily suffering (kāyadukkha) is the oppression of the body-consciousness associated with pain, which is based on the body-sensitivity (kāyapasāda). This expression is a 'description with its constituents' (sasam-bhāra-kathana), just as when it is said, 'He shoots with a bow,' it is the arrow that shoots, not the bow. Alternatively, it is also appropriate to say 'oppression of the material body' because it arises following an undesirable object which is the support for that body-sensitivity and body-consciousness. Mental grief (domanassa) is the distress of the mind associated with aversion (paṭigha). The meaning that it has the characteristic of mental distress should be applied to all terms in this manner.

Despair (upāyāsa) is the intense tribulation arising from internal sorrow in one who is affected by the ruin of relatives and so on, but is unable even to lament. Since that despair is simply a state of lack of clarity of mind, it is said to be 'visāda-lakkhaṇo' (having the characteristic of dejection/lack of clarity). The words 'sādana,' 'pasādana,' and 'sāda' denote clarity (pasannatā). A word without a prefix can convey the same meaning as one with a prefix, as in the word 'gotrabhū.' This should be understood in all cases. Departure from that clarity is 'visāda' (dejection/lack of clarity).

'Vitakkana' is 'vitakkita.' In terms of meaning, 'vitakkita' is simply 'vitakka' (initial application). Likewise, in the word 'vicārita,' it is simply 'vicāra' (sustained application). Therefore, it is said, 'Vitakka which proceeds by way of directing the mind onto the object,' and so on. By the word 'etena' (by this), it refers to vitakka and vicāra, indicating either the instrument (karaṇa) or the cause (hetu). By this word 'etena,' this meaning is illuminated: because vitakka and vicāra are by nature disturbing, the jhāna associated with them is as if oppressed by them. Therefore, it is said, 'It appears as if it were with thorns.' The state of grossness is indeed the proceeding together with the thorns called vitakka and vicāra. To be with thorns is the same as being with oppression. In the world, that which has thorns is called harsh and gross.

'Pītigata' is simply 'pīti' (rapture). Just as in words like 'diṭṭhigata,' the word 'gata' denotes that very state. It is the nature of the commentators (Aṭṭhakathā and Ṭīkā teachers) to explain the meaning by setting aside redundant words and words in apposition. Such explanations are seen in various commentaries.
452:
"Yo pana" refers to a person of such a nature, whether dark, fair, and so forth. "Nibbānadhātu" is said to be merely the cooling of the eleven fires, such as birth, aging, and death. When that elated joy, which acts as a cause, arises, the mind is said to be "uplifted" (ubbilāvita). Since the suffix "-ta," expressing a state, occurs in the sense of a cause, that upliftment itself is called "the state of being uplifted" (ubbilāvitattta). Thus, because the upliftment of the mind occurs only when joy arises, that state of upliftment is said to be "made by joy." Therefore, the Commentator said, "causing the state of elation" (ubbilabhāvakaraṇa).

Reflection (manasikāra) is called "attention" (ābhoga). Bringing the object to mind in proper sequence or repeatedly is called "concentration" (samannāhāra). This is the method stated in the Old Sub-commentary: the state of the mind's reflection, the state of being inclined towards the object, is called "attention" (ābhoga). Indeed, through happiness (sukha), the mind inclines towards the object. It is not like the mind turning away from happiness through suffering (dukkha), nor is it like the mind neither inclining nor turning away through equanimity (upekkhā), which is neither-suffering-nor-happiness.

In this doctrine of Nibbāna in the present life (diṭṭhadhammanibbānavāda), just as a person oppressed by hunger and thirst has an increased longing for delicious food, so too does the longing for sensual pleasures increase specifically for one who is secluded from them. Just as one who has eaten delicious food to their fill has no desire to consume more, so too one who has accumulated and enjoyed the sublime taste of sensual pleasures as much as desired has no further desire to consume them. One who is not greedy for sense objects is spontaneously released from those objects that are otherwise difficult to abandon, like a leech. Thus, the first proponent declared the subsiding of the suffering of saṃsāra through satisfaction with sensual pleasures, reflecting in an unwise manner. The second and subsequent proponents declared the cessation of the suffering of saṃsāra through satisfaction with the happiness of the first Jhāna and so forth, because they saw the danger in sensual pleasures and the peaceful nature of the happiness of the first Jhāna and so forth. In this doctrine of Nibbāna in the present life, one should also apply the reasoning (vicāra) mentioned in the doctrine of annihilationism as far as possible. The distinction here is that five views can be found even within a single individual existence (attabhāva).

In the first view, if the self is endowed with sensual pleasures, then that self is said to have reached Nibbāna in the present life. In the second and subsequent views, if that same self included in the first view is endowed with the first Jhāna and so forth, then it is said to have reached Nibbāna in the present life. Therefore, unlike in the doctrine of annihilationism, the Buddha did not include the word "another" as in "another self" in the Pali text of this doctrine of Nibbāna in the present life. Why is the doctrine of Nibbāna in the present life, which designates the self as ultimate Nibbāna, included only in eternalism (sassatadiṭṭhi) and not in annihilationism (ucchedadiṭṭhi)? It is because it demonstrates that the self, purified by liberation from the bonds of Kamma obtained through being endowed with those specific types of happiness, remains in its original nature. Those sectarians hold the view that the self, having become pure through liberation from the bonds of Kamma thus obtained and having reached Nibbāna in the present life, remains in its original nature. That is why in the Pali: "To this extent..."
453:
"To this extent, dear sirs, this self has reached supreme Nibbāna in the present life"—thus their doctrine is shown with the implication of an eternal nature.

With the words "To this extent" and so forth, the meaning of the Pali is summarized. Therein, the word "of which" (yāsaṃ) is an indefinite expression referring to the aforementioned views. The statement "these sixty-two views" is a definite (niyama) expression. Or, it is an expression that does not regard the definite, as in the passage "referring to which it was said." "The rest" refers to the fifty-five views. Among them, the fact that the doctrines of finitude and infinity (antānantikavāda) and so forth are included in eternalism (sassatadiṭṭhi) has already been explained in the respective commentaries. What is the reason here that only the past (pubbanta) and the future (aparanta) are shown as the objects of wrong views, and not both of them together? Impossibility is the reason here. It is not possible to speculate a view in the middle, which is free from both, as one can in the past and the future, because the interval between the two is of such short duration. If the present existence is considered the middle between the two, then the nature of that present, which is fit for speculating a view, is already included within the past and the future; so how could it be that both are not shown together? Alternatively, because it has a beginning and an end, the middle is also called "past and future" (pubbantāparanta). That middle should also be understood as having been taught separately from the past and future by the Blessed One when He said above: "speculators on the past, speculators on the future, and speculators on both the past and the future." In the Commentary as well, it should be understood as included by the general designation "all those are speculators on the past and future," or by the method of ellipsis (ekasesa). Otherwise, if the summarized statement does not include everything without remainder, it would lead to being purposeless. Who are those "speculators on the past and future"? They should be understood as those who cling to both the past and the future, such as those who, being speculators on finitude and infinity, also hold the doctrine of Nibbāna in the present life.

## 100-104.
"Now" and so forth, the distinction between the two concluding statements is shown. Therein, "in one" (ekajjhaṃ) is an indeclinable in the sense of making a heap or group. Grammarians say "ekajjhaṃ" because it makes things in one way; it is a neuter abstract noun (bhāvanapuṃsaka) acting as an adverb. The word "iti" has the meaning of "this" (idaṃ); the meaning is that He asked and answered in this manner. "Inclination" (ajjhāsaya) refers to the inclination of views by way of eternalism and annihilationism. Through both of these, beings have a two-fold inclination regarding the side of defilement. Thus it is said:

Eternalist view and annihilationist view,
And also conformable patience (khanti),
And whatever knowledge is in accordance with reality—
These are called 'inclinations' (āsaya).

(This should also be seen in the Mahāဋီကာ of the Visuddhimagga, etc.)
454:
The Blessed One, regarding that inclination (āsaya), even though it is divided into many various types through the arising of specific things to be known that are truly infinite, for infinite beings in infinite world systems, He desired to show it by delimiting it with His Omniscient Knowledge (Sabbaññutañāṇa) through the power of grouping them into sixty-two divisions, such as 'Four persons are eternalists' (Sassatavāda). Thus, the teacher said, 'As if weighing with a scale,' meaning He is like one holding a scale which is the means of comparison. Likewise, he will say later, 'Being caught within the net,' and so forth. Furthermore, by this phrase, 'As if taking sand from the foot of Mount Sineru,' he shows that no knowledge other than Omniscient Knowledge is capable of delivering this discourse, because it is a statement of supreme profundity.

In this Brahmajāla Sutta, because it is said: 'All these [recluses and brahmins] speak with these sixty-two grounds, or with one or another of them; there is nothing outside of this,' and because there is no one with wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi) who is free from the three groups such as those who speculate about the past (pubbantakappika), the various types of wrong views such as Akiriyavāda (doctrine of non-action), Ahetukavāda (doctrine of non-causality), and Natthikavāda (nihilism) mentioned in other suttas like the Sāmaññaphala Sutta, as well as views such as Issaravāda (theism), Pakativāda, Pajāpativāda, Purisakālavāda, Sabhāvaniyati-vāda, Yadicchāvāda, etc., though they appear outside [the Sīlakkhandhavagga Pali], they should be understood as being included within these sixty-two views by way of being grouped together. How is this to be understood? Firstly, Akiriyavāda is included in Sassatavāda because it shows the absence of action with words like 'The self is barren, standing like a mountain peak.' Similarly, Pakudha's doctrine (Pakudhavāda) which proceeds in the manner of 'These seven bodies...' and Ahetukavāda which proceeds in the manner of 'There is no cause, no condition for the defilement of beings' are included in Adhiccasamuppannavāda (the doctrine of fortuitous origination). Natthikavāda which proceeds in the manner of 'There is no other world' is included in Ucchedavāda (annihilationism). Indeed, in that Natthikavāda, it is said: 'With the breakup of the body, he is cut off,' and so forth. By the first 'ādi' (etc.), doctrines such as Nigaṇṭhavāda are included.

Although in the Sāmaññaphala Sutta Pali, the fourfold restraint (cātuyāmasaṃvara) appears as the doctrine of Nāṭaputta, yet because of the wavering nature of the view that exceeds the seven practices, Nāṭaputta's doctrine, like Sañjaya's doctrine, is included in Amarāvikkhepavāda (eel-wriggling). Views such as 'The soul is the same as the body' or 'The soul is one thing, the body another,' and such other types of doctrines [are included in] 'The self is percipient...'
455:
...and healthy after death,' and such other doctrines. Views such as 'The Tathāgata exists after death' and 'There are spontaneously born beings' are included in Sassatavāda. Views such as 'The Tathāgata does not exist after death' and 'There are no spontaneously born beings' are included in Ucchedavāda. Views such as 'The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death' and 'There both are and are not spontaneously born beings' are included in Ekaccasassatavāda (partial eternalism). Views such as 'The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death' and 'There neither are nor are not spontaneously born beings' are included in Amarāvikkhepavāda. Issaravāda, Pakativāda, Pajāpativāda, Purisavāda, and Kālavāda are included in Ekaccasassatavāda. Kaṇādavāda, Sabhāvavāda, Niyati-vāda, and Yadicchāvāda are included in Adhiccasamuppannavāda. In this way, wrong views seen in other suttas and in the external systems of other sectarians (aññatitthiya) should be understood as being included within these sixty-two views. If these views were explained according to the methods found in various Pali texts and commentaries, the book would become too voluminous, and it would be like descending into a place that is not a landing-place (atittha); therefore, we do not elaborate. In investigating the meaning of this Pali, our responsibility is only to clarify the meanings that are not clear in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā).

Regarding the phrase 'Thus this discourse comes by way of Yathānusandhi,' he said 'Tayo hi' (For there are three...) and so forth to analyze the connections (anusandhi) of the sutta. The extraction of a specific point is for the purpose of excluding other meanings. In that context, the act of connecting is *anusandhi*, meaning simply a connection. This *anusandhi* is also called *samuṭṭhāna* (origination) in the sense of being the cause of the discourse. Questions (pucchā) and so forth are the external causes of the discourse because the discourse proceeds in accordance with them. That connection is also a cause because it depends on the question. The internal causes are Great Compassion (Mahākaruṇā), the knowledge of teaching (desanāñāṇa), and so on. This meaning will be made clear later. A connection made by a question is called *Pucchānusandhi*. Because the sutta is taught by making the question the connection, the sequence of the sutta is said to be made by the question. It is also appropriate to say *Pucchānusandhi* is the connection known as the question. By the connection dependent on the question, the question itself, which is its basis, is also taken. Alternatively, *anusandhi* is that which connects; *Pucchānusandhi* is that which has the connection known as the question; it refers to various parts of the sutta. Or, *Pucchānusandhi* is that which is connected by a question; it is simply the part of the sutta originating from that question, taught by making the question the verbal connection. The same method applies to *Ajjhāsayānusandhi* (connection by inclination). *Anusandhi* is that which is connected. Whatever the connection is, or that which is in accordance with the connection, is *Yathānusandhi*.

Without connection to a question or inclination, it is the part of the sutta that follows, proceeding by way of a doctrine that is either similar to or opposite to the doctrine taught at the beginning.
456:
In truth, that commentator shows that the analysis is according to the Pali text as stated in the commentary, starting with "By which Dhamma... as it appears in the Kakacūpama Sutta," by using the word "Tattha" and so forth. In that Pali, they recite: "When this was said, Nanda the cowherd said this to the Blessed One." Such a reading is not good (incorrect) because it is not found that way in the Sutta. It should only be recited as: "When this was said in the Nandagopālaka Sutta, [someone] said this to the Blessed One," because in that Sutta, the meaning "A certain monk said this to the Blessed One" is appropriate. This Sutta is a sutta recited in the Saḷāyatana Vagga of the noble Saṃyutta Nikāya. When [the Buddha] preached to the clansmen who had gone forth out of faith, using the simile of a log floating in the Ganges, Nanda the cowherd thought, "I shall fulfill this practice," and having received the going forth and higher ordination from the Blessed One, he practiced accordingly and soon attained Arahantship. Therefore, it is known as the "Nandagopālaka Sutta." However, the words "Venerable Sir, how is it?" and so forth were spoken only by a certain monk. For it is said there: "When this was said, a certain monk said this to the Blessed One: 'Venerable Sir, what is "this bank"?' and so forth."

The meaning in that Pali is— "When this was said" means when [the Buddha] preached to the clansmen who had gone forth out of faith, using the simile of a log floating in the Ganges, saying: "Monks, if a log does not ground on this bank," and so forth. "Said this to the Blessed One" means speaking the words "Venerable Sir, how is it?" and so forth due to skill in the sequence of the discourse (anusandhi). Indeed, the Blessed One, reflecting, "In this assembly, there is one skilled in the sequence who is sitting here; he will ask me a question," concluded the teaching with just that much. "This bank" means the shore that is on this side. Likewise, "the further bank" should be understood. "Sinking in the middle" means diving and sinking in the midst of the water. "Grounding on a bank" means being cast up on a bank rising in the middle of the water. "Seized by humans" means being connected with humans or being caught by humans. Likewise, "seized by non-humans" should be understood. "Caught in a whirlpool" means being caught by an eddy of water. "Rotten within" means being internally rotten due to the rotting of virtues such as morality, even if the kidneys, heart, and so forth are not rotten.

The sutta starting with "Then to a certain monk" is the Mahāpuṇṇama Sutta found in the Uparipaṇṇāsa of the noble Majjhima Nikāya. The meaning in that Pali is— "Thus it is heard"—here the word "kira" is used in the sense of dissatisfaction; by that word, he shows his own state of dissatisfaction with the emptiness of self as taught by the Blessed One. "Bho" is a vocative word addressing the Dhamma; it means "O natural phenomena." If form is non-self... if consciousness is non-self. Thus...
457:
In the word "Sati", the construction (yojanā) should be made along with the remaining text. "Anattakatāni" means [deeds] not done by a self, or done by the aggregates which are non-self. "What self will the kamma touch?" means what kind of individual existence (attabhāva) will it touch? The meaning is: since there is no self and the aggregates are momentary, what self will those kammas touch with their result? Who will experience the fruit of kamma? The connection is: "Having known the thought in that monk's mind with his own mind"—that is, with the mind associated with the knowledge of encompassing others' minds (cetopariyañāṇa) or associated with the knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa).

"Avidvā" means a person without wisdom because of being unskilled in the Dhamma of the Noble Ones due to a lack of hearing (learning) and so forth. Indeed, "Vidvā" is a designation for the wise, meaning "one who knows" (vidati). "Avijjāgato" means one who has arrived at ignorance; the meaning is one whose ignorance is unabandoned because of not being disciplined in the Dhamma of the Noble Ones. "With a mind dominated by craving" means with a mind accompanied by the clinging to the doctrine of self (attavādupādāna) arising from the dominance of craving, thinking: "If there is no such thing as 'I', then who experiences the fruit of the kamma done by me? But if that [self] exists, there could be the enjoyment of the fruit of kamma." "Atidhavitabbaṃ" means it should be overstepped or overreached. The meaning is this: although formations (saṅkhārā) are momentary, because the result arises in the same continuity (santāna) where the kamma was performed, even though the connection between kamma and its fruit is established within a mere heap of phenomena, one might wrongly grasp the method of unity (ekattanaya) and think: "There must be a single person who is the doer and the experiencer; otherwise, there would be no connection between kamma and its fruit." Thus, one might think that the Teacher's instruction, which reveals emptiness of self and what belongs to self, should be overstepped. Now, to clarify the state of not overstepping, he said "Taṃ kiṃ maññatha" and so forth.

"Upper teaching" means the teaching delivered above the lower teaching which illuminates the origin of the teaching. This statement "The six higher knowledges (abhiññā) appear above" is a demonstration of the sequence (yathānusandhi) by way of illuminating the corresponding Dhamma, among the two kinds of sequences—illuminating corresponding Dhamma and opposing Dhamma—relative to the Dhamma that is the origin of the teaching. All the remaining words [show the sequence] by way of illuminating the opposing Dhamma. These suttas are mentioned only in the Mūlapaṇṇāsaka of the noble Majjhima Nikāya. "By defilement" means by the power of defilement, as in "Greed is a defilement of the mind" and so forth. "By quarreling" means by way of dispute. "By intolerance" means by way of anger. "Simile of the saw" means the simile of a tool with a row of sharp teeth. In the phrase "here also", the word "pi" is used in the sense of expectation (apekkha), as in "This also is a Pārājika" and so forth, or in the sense of combination (sampinḍana). By that word "pi", by way of illuminating the opposing Dhamma in the Vattha Sutta and so forth...
458:
In this Brahmajāla Sutta as well, the word 'pi' (also) performs the function of referring back or combining, as in 'ayampi pārājiko' (this also is a defeat), and so forth. Just as in the Vattha Sutta and others, the connection (anusandhi) occurs by way of showing the opposite quality, so too in this Brahmajāla Sutta, the connection is established by referring back or combining. This statement is true; this teaching, which arose by the power of wrong views that proclaim a permanent essence and so on, is concluded by revealing the emptiness of such permanent essence and so on. By the words beginning with 'tena', the quality of the aforementioned commentary (saṃvaṇṇanā) is shown.

## Commentary on the Section on Agitation and Vacillation

105-117. 'Mariyādavibhāgadassanatthaṃ' means for the purpose of showing the demarcation and distinction without confusion between the misapprehension through craving and views of those with wrong views and the knowledge and vision of the Tathāgatas, as well as between wrong views such as eternalism and right view (sammādiṭṭhi). For those with wrong views, there is only misapprehension through craving and views; there is no knowing and seeing according to reality as there is for the Tathāgatas. This teaching shows the demarcation and distinction by explaining that the experience of this wrong view is merely the agitation of craving and views, and it lacks the stability found in the experience of right view of a Stream-enterer (sotāpanna). Therefore, it will be said later: 'By whatever gratification in views ... that is feeling,' and 'By what is called view ... it shows.' Because it is said 'tadapī' (that also), the words beginning with 'yena' are spoken to show the meaning that they proclaim while being joyful with such gratification in views. In this context, the word 'ta' (that) refers only to the meaning already understood by implication. 'Diṭṭhi-assādena' means by the gratification which is the cause of the view. 'Diṭṭhi-sukhena' and so forth are merely synonyms for that term. The connection is that the experience of that wrong view by those recluses and brahmins who neither know nor see is an experience associated with craving.

It is also stated without specification as 'the nature of true things.' This is because one does not fall into or cling to wrong views merely by not knowing the nature of conditioned things (saṅkhata-dhamma). A general statement stands for a specific meaning. Therefore, a specific construction (yojanā) should be made here: 'The basis of this view, "the self and the world are eternal," is thus grasped, thus misapprehended, has such a destination, and such a future state'—for those who do not know or see this according to reality... or, 'In whichever feeling this wrong view is clung to because craving has not been abandoned, for those who do not know or see the arising and passing away, etc., of that feeling according to reality...' By such a specific construction, it becomes clear that this teaching shows how the Tathāgatas, who are endowed with unobstructed knowledge (anāvaraṇa-ñāṇa) and the Universal Eye (samantacakkhu), have knowing and seeing according to reality in this matter of doctrines, whereas those with wrong views do not have such knowing and seeing, but rather only misapprehension through craving and views. Thus, this teaching has arisen for the purpose of showing the demarcation and distinction.
459:
'Vedayita' (feeling) refers to the experience of that gratification in views, spoken of by way of the gratification and happiness in views that arise through the proclamation of the wrong view: 'The self and the world are eternal.' 'Taṇhāgatānaṃ' (gone to craving) means those who have approached craving or those in whom craving has arisen; this very meaning is explained by the method of the commentary (vutti) as 'kevalaṃ ... vedayitaṃ' (entirely ... feeling). By the phrase 'tañca kho panetaṃ', it reflects only on the aforementioned feeling. By that phrase, it is shown that the connection should be made by first concluding, 'That feeling is also only the feeling of those with wrong views who have approached craving,' and then again, 'That feeling is also only agitation and vacillation (or agitation and vacillation in views).'

Because of the reason 'it does not yet reach that feeling,' the teacher said, 'It is not stable like the vision of a Stream-enterer,' in order to show the demarcation by way of the lower limit. 'Dassana' (vision) means the happiness associated with non-perverted seeing, or the happiness of the Path and Fruit (magga-phala-sukha). If one asks from where this meaning is derived, it is answered that it is derived from the power of the word 'eva' (only). Because it is said 'paritassitavipphanditameva' (only agitation and vacillation), it does not remain in a single state without vacillation like the happiness of the Path and Fruit; rather, that view, which is the bait of the round (vaṭṭāmisa), is indeed vacillation because it is oppressed by being constantly pierced by the arrows of views and craving. That is why the teacher said 'paritassitena' and so forth. This is the method, including the connection of terms, that is independent of the literal commentary in this matter of the experience of happiness in views.

Having thus analyzed the sixty-two wrong views by way of specific causes, the Buddha now begins the teaching starting with 'tatra bhikkhave' to show them by way of general causes. Indeed, for all those with wrong views, feeling (vedanā), ignorance (avijjā), and craving (taṇhā) are the non-distinct general causes. In that teaching starting with 'tatra bhikkhave', 'tadapī' refers to the threefold feeling, such as happiness, which is the cause for proclaiming 'the self and the world are eternal.' That feeling also arises for those with wrong views who do not know or see it according to reality as the arrow of suffering (dukkha-salla) and as impermanent (anicca) in due order, or generally as the arising, passing away, gratification, danger, and escape. For that very reason, because the longing for happiness and so forth arises, and because they have approached craving, it is only the vacillation of view (diṭṭhicalana) through the agitation of craving of those who have approached craving. If one asks, 'If there is no self, who experiences the feeling?', it should be said that it is merely the occurrence of the wavering of wrong view through the doors of body and speech. However, the intention is that there is no such thing as a permanent entity to be proclaimed by wrong view. This same method should be understood for the partial-eternalism views and others.

## Commentary on the Section on Contact as Condition

'Paramparapaccayadassanatthaṃ' means for the purpose of showing the sequence of conditions; that is, there is a root cause of the view, there is a cause for that root cause, and again a cause for that cause. Thus, it means to show the succession of conditions. Indeed, the craving through whose longing those wrong views arise has feeling (vedanā) as its condition, and feeling has contact (phassa) as its condition. Thus, this teaching clearly shows the sequence of conditions.
460:
These views arise because of the longing called craving (taṇhā). For that longing through craving, feeling (vedayita) is the cause. For feeling, contact (phassa) is the cause. In this way, this teaching clarifies the succession of causes.

If it is asked, 'What is the purpose of showing the succession of causes?' It is to make known a specific distinction in meaning. By showing this, just as the things to be made known (paññāpanadhamma) called 'views' and their causal factors arise only through their respective causes and not without causes, so too the things that are to be made known (paññāpetabbadhamma) such as form (rūpa) and feeling (vedanā) do not arise without causes. It is made known that in these things, there is no permanent self (atta) or world (loka). The meaning is that the feeling, which is agitated by craving and views, being the cause of craving which is the cause of views, arises due to the cause of contact.

'Tassa paccayassa' means the cause called contact. 'Diṭṭhivedayite' means in the feeling which is the cause of views, when it is produced by its own causes headed by contact. This word is in the locative case (sattamī vibhatti). 'Balavabhāvadassanatthaṃ' is for the purpose of showing the state of being a powerful cause. This is because feeling can arise without physical bases such as the eye or without certain associated states, but it can never arise without contact. Therefore, contact is the powerful cause of feeling.

It is not only for feeling alone, but also for the remaining associated states. This is because even if the object is present, if the arising of consciousness (cittuppāda) is devoid of the mode of touching (phusanākāra), the object-condition (ārammaṇapaccaya) for that arising of consciousness cannot occur. Therefore, contact is the specific cause (visesapaccaya) of all associated states. Thus, when the Blessed One analyzed the arising of consciousness in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī, He first extracted contact alone, saying 'contact occurs.' For feeling, however, it is only the foundational cause (adhiṭṭhānapaccaya) which is the predominant basis. Because it is said 'they will experience,' the word 'tadapi' follows here, and thus He said 'that feeling.' Alternatively, because the word 'vā' (or), which has a clear meaning, can be used at will, or is elided, or is redundant, it is not used here. In such places, it should be understood in this way.

There is a summary verse here:
'Due to the four reasons: being easily understood, following [from context], elision, and being redundant, the word is not used in some places.'

By showing that contact is a powerful cause with the words 'Yathā hi' etc., He completes that meaning. In that sentence, 'patato' means for a falling house. 'Thūṇā' is a name for the wooden pillar that supports the house.
461:
## Diṭṭhigatikādhiṭṭhānavvaṭṭakathāvaṇṇanā

In the Pali of this section, although the word 'vedayita' (feeling) is not present, the teacher said, 'It encompasses all views and feelings,' intending that feeling is the primary factor here, because it is included in all three cycles (vāra) below and because it will be said above, 'Touching and touching, they experience.' The word 'encompasses' (sampiṇḍeti) is said in reference to the meaning of the word 'pi' found in various doctrines such as 'ye pi te.' Since those recluses and brahmins who hold the doctrine of eternalism... and all of them experience by touching and touching through the six bases of contact, they are encompassed by the power of the verb 'experiencing' (vedayita-kiriyā); thus it is simply an encompassing of feeling. All sentences have the verb as the primary element.

The phrase 'through the six bases of contact' is said for the purpose of including contact above. Here, 'including' means showing that feeling has contact as its cause. By the words 'Touching and touching, they experience through the six bases of contact,' it is shown that the experiencing of the six objects through the six internal bases is certainly caused by the six types of contact. Therefore, it is said, 'All those,' and so on.

'Kamboja' is the name of a country. 'Dakkhiṇāpatha' is the same. By the word 'sañjātitthāne' (place of birth), the word 'sañjāti' shows the locative sense (adhikaraṇa) as 'they are born in this place.' The word 'samosaraṇa' is the same. The word 'āyatana' also carries both meanings. 'Āyatana' refers to a great junction where roads meet. 'Naṃ' refers to that great banyan tree. This is a term from the Saddhānisaṃsa Sutta in the Pañcakanipāta of the Aṅguttara Nikāya. In that Sutta, the detailed explanation is given: 'Bhikkhus, just as a great banyan tree at a crossroads on fertile ground is a refuge for birds from all around.' 'Sati satiāyatane' means if the cause called mindfulness is present, one reaches the state of being a witness in various fields of higher knowledge (abhiññā).

In this word 'āyatana,' the cause is called 'āyatana' because the results arise depending on that cause, or because it produces its own result called 'āya.' 'Sammanti' means they are calmed or they produce relief. The word 'āyatana' here does not signify a different meaning as in other places, but is said to be 'merely a designation' (paññattimatta). It means merely a designation in such and such a way. A collection of trees is called a 'forest' (arañña) merely by designation, and that forest itself is called 'araññāyatana.' In the phrase 'atthatthayepi' (also in the three meanings), the word 'pi' encompasses the meanings of source (ākara), dwelling (nivāsa), and foundation (adhiṭṭhāna). 'Hiraññāyatanaṃ' (source of gold)...
462:
In terms such as *suvaṇṇāyatana* (gold mine), the word *āyatana* is used in the sense of a source (*ākara*). In terms such as *issarāyatana* and *vāsudevāyatana*, it is used in the sense of an abode (*nivāsa*). In terms such as *kammāyatana* (place of work) and *sippāyatana* (place of craft), it is used in the sense of a foundation (*adhiṭṭhāna*) or a support (*nissaya*).

In this context, *āyatana* has the meanings of source (*ākara*), abode (*nivāsa*), and foundation (*adhiṭṭhāna*) respectively. In the bases such as the eye (*cakkhu*), states such as contact (*phassa*) are diffused; these bases are also their abode and foundation by way of being a support condition (*nissaya-paccaya*). Therefore, all three of these meanings are appropriate here. To show how they are appropriate, it is said, "*Cakkhādīsu hi*," and so on. These five states beginning with contact—contact (*phassa*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saññā*), volition (*cetanā*), and consciousness (*citta*)—are mentioned by way of synecdoche (*upalakkhaṇa*) or by way of prominence. This is because they also serve as the bases for other associated states (*sampayutta-dhamma*).

Indeed, the Blessed One, when analyzing the arising of consciousness (*cittuppāda*), first analyzed these very states, saying: "There is contact, feeling, perception, volition, and consciousness." They are said to "arise" (*sañjāyanti*) because they occur right there, depending on the eye and other bases and taking them as objects. They are said to "converge" (*samosaranti*) because they gather there by way of the physical base (*vatthu*), door (*dvāra*), and object (*ārammaṇa*). Furthermore, those bases are their cause (*kāraṇa*), for in the absence of the bases, these states do not exist. The teacher Ācariya Ānanda Thera stated that these aforementioned meanings, such as the place of arising (*sañjātidessa*), occur in those contexts through conventional usage (*ruḷhī*).

This is the meaning that arises through the explanation of the word's derivation: it is called *āyatana* because of exerting (*āyatanato*), because of extending the *āyas* (mental states) (*āyānaṃ tananato*), and because of leading the long suffering of *saṃsāra* (*āyatassa ca nayanato*). In the doors such as the eye, the mental states (consciousness and mental factors) that have those respective doors and objects exert themselves, strive, and struggle through their respective functions such as experiencing. Those bases extend the states that are *āyas*, and they also bring about the long suffering of *saṃsāra*. In this way, the word *iti* in the sense of "and so forth" includes the Pali passage beginning with "Dependent on the ear..." (*sotaṃ paṭicca*).

In that Pali passage, "of the three" (*tiṇṇāṃ*) refers to the three: the object, the faculty, and consciousness—such as the eye-sensitivity, the visible object, and eye-consciousness. Because they are taken as a meeting of these three, it is said, "Contact is the conjunction" (*phasso saṅgati*). Indeed, that contact is said to have "conjunction as its manifestation" (*sannipāta-paccupaṭṭhāna*). It should be connected by presenting it in this manner. By this, the following meaning is shown: although associated states such as perception exist in this sutta which says, "Dependent on the eye... contact," the teaching is given with contact as the head (*phassa-sīsena*) to show that it is the primary cause of feeling. Similarly, here too, beginning with contact in "With contact as condition, feeling..."
463:
...making it the starting point to show the sequence of conditions through the connection with the subsequent rebirth, the teaching was given with contact as the head (*phassa-sīsena*), saying "by the six bases of contact" and "touching, touching." In the term *phassāyatanādīni*, the word *ādi* includes the phrase "touching, touching" (*phussa phussā*).

By the words beginning with "*Kiñcāpi*," a slight objection based on the literal word is shown, and by the words beginning with "*Tathāpi*," that objection is resolved according to the meaning. The bases do not touch because material forms (*rūpa*) do not take objects. Contact is a mental state (*arūpa-dhamma*); although it is distinct and does not physically adhere to an object in one part, it occurs in the manner of touching and thus is as if it touches. Therefore, it is said, "Contact alone touches this or that object." For this very reason, contact is said to have "the characteristic of touching" and "the function of impingement."

In the phrase "they touch by the six bases of contact," although the bases do not have the function of touching, attributing the function of touching to them by metaphorical usage based on contact is called "depositing in contact" (*phasse upanikkhipana*). This is like the example, "The beds cry out" (meaning the people on them). "Having deposited" (*upanikkhipitvā*) means entering it into contact by way of attributing the function of touching. It means attributing the metaphorical designation of contact (*phassūpacāra*) by making the bases share the same course as contact. A metaphor (*upacāra*) is merely a conventional expression; the actual meaning is not established by that metaphor alone, because the base is not of the nature of contact. To show that only the nature of contact, which fulfills the meaning, should be taken as the meaning, the words beginning with "*Tasmā*" are said.

As the teachers of the Commentaries have said as evidence:
"The Lord, the Great Sage, seeker of the world's welfare,
Declared the meaning alone as the refuge,
Not the phrasing (the letter)."

With reference to the six kinds of feeling in brief, from that born of eye-contact to that born of mind-contact, by way of the six contacts which are its conditions, it is said, "Feeling produced by the six bases of contact." In detail, however:
"These feelings are sixfold by way of contact, threefold by way of mental exploration,
twofold by way of support, and increased threefold by way of time."
According to the method stated in the 'One Hundred and Eightfold Exposition,' there are one hundred and eight varieties.

In this context, the residents of the Mahāvihāra, just as with consciousness, name-and-form, and the six bases, also desire only the resultant (*vipāka*) states for contact and feeling, showing them as included in one's own continuum even though they are condition and conditionally arisen. Other teachers, however, desire all [types of contact and feeling], because if the state of being a condition exists, it cannot be excluded regardless of how it occurs. That feeling of the aforementioned varieties is referred to by the word "*sā*" (that). Regarding the term "*rūpatanhādibhedāya*"...
464:
Just as one is called 'the son of a wealthy man' or 'the son of a brahmin' by way of the father's name, so too craving is spoken of by way of the name of the object, ranging from craving for forms (rūpa-taṇhā) to craving for mental objects (dhamma-taṇhā), which are sixfold in brief. In detail, however: 'Craving for forms and so forth are threefold by way of craving for sensual pleasures and so forth; again, they are twofold by way of continuity, and should be multiplied by the divisions of time.' Thus, it is of one hundred and eight varieties.

'Upanissayakoṭiyā' means by way of making the decisive support condition (upanissaya-paccaya) the primary factor. Why is only the decisive support condition extracted here? Do not pleasant feeling and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling assist craving through four conditions: as a mere object (ārammaṇa), as object-predominance (ārammaṇādhipati), as object-decisive support (ārammaṇūpanissaya), and as natural decisive support (pakatūpanissaya)? And does not painful feeling assist through two conditions: as a mere object and as natural decisive support? That is true; however, because all those conditions are included within the decisive support condition itself, only this one condition, decisive support, is extracted. It is quite fitting for object-decisive support to be included in decisive support because it is a general type of decisive support. But how can mere object and object-predominance be included in that decisive support? Since those two are also general types of objects, they are encompassed by object-decisive support, and being thus combined in object-decisive support, they are included within decisive support itself. Intending this meaning, the text does not say 'upanissayena' but says 'upanissayakoṭiyā'. When the required meaning is already established, further effort is for the sake of making it certain or for making known a specific distinction of meaning. This should be understood in such cases.

'Catubbidhassa' refers to the fourfold clinging, from sense-desire clinging (kāmupādāna) to clinging to the doctrine of self (attavādupādāna). Is it not the case that craving itself is sense-desire clinging? How then can that very craving be a condition for that sense-desire clinging? It is true; however, because the subsequent craving becomes firm and strong through the decisive support condition of the preceding craving, the preceding craving alone becomes a condition for the subsequent craving. Indeed, the firmness and strength of craving itself is called 'sense-desire clinging' (kāmupādāna), because the prefix 'upa-' is used in the sense of firmness, as in words like 'kāmupādāna', 'upāyāsa' (despair), and 'upakaṭṭha' (near). Furthermore, weak craving is just craving, while strong craving is sense-desire clinging. Alternatively, the longing for an object not yet attained is craving, like thieves stretching out their hands in the dark; the seizing of an object already attained is sense-desire clinging, like thieves taking the goods that have come into their hands. Craving is the opposite of fewness of wishes (appicchatā); sense-desire clinging is the opposite of contentment (santuṭṭhitā). Craving is the root of the suffering of seeking; sense-desire clinging is the root of the suffering of guarding. This distinction between craving and clinging was shown by the Elder Dhammapāla according to the views of some (keci-vāda), because only the former method was stated as the school's own view (sakavāda) in the Visuddhimagga.
465:
For clinging that is not conascent with craving, the meaning should be taken as 'by way of decisive support' (upanissaya-koṭi), and for clinging that is conascent with craving, as 'by way of conascence' (sahajāta-koṭi), as applicable. Among those two, non-conascent and conascent clinging, craving that is not conascent with clinging but has ceased in the immediately preceding moment assists through six conditions: proximity (anantara), contiguity (samanantara), decisive support of proximity (anantarūpanissaya), absence (natthi), disappearance (vigata), and repetition (āsevana). Craving that has become an object, however, assists through three conditions: object (ārammaṇa), object-predominance (ārammaṇādhipati), and object-decisive support (ārammaṇūpanissaya). All those conditions are also encompassed within decisive support by the method already mentioned, and thus it is said 'by way of decisive support'. Because one enjoys and experiences forms and so forth through craving and thus falls into the use of sensual pleasures, craving assists sense-desire clinging by way of decisive support. Similarly, one who is confused about the varieties of forms and so forth adopts wrong views such as 'there is no result of giving', or one who desires to be liberated from saṃsāra wrongly adheres to a path that is not the path of purification as being the path of purification, or one adopts the view of self (sakkāya-diṭṭhi) which is the grasping of 'I' and 'mine' in the five aggregates. Therefore, it should be understood that craving assists the remaining three types of clinging by way of decisive support. Conascent craving, however, assists conascent clinging in seven ways: by way of conascence (sahajāta), mutuality (aññamañña), support (nissaya), association (sampayutta), presence (atthi), non-disappearance (avigata), and root (hetu). All these are also encompassed within the conascence condition alone, and thus it is said 'by way of conascence'.

## The word 'bhavassa' refers to both kamma-process existence (kamma-bhava) and rebirth-process existence (upapatti-bhava).

Among those two, all kamma leading to existence, described as volition (cetanā) and so forth, is called kamma-process existence. The ninefold division, such as sense-sphere existence (kāma-bhava) and so forth, is called rebirth-process existence. Among those two, the four types of clinging assist rebirth-process existence and kamma-process existence (which is the cause of rebirth-process existence) by way of natural decisive support (pakatūpanissaya), because they are the cause of those existences and because they have come to be their associates. At the time of making kamma an object, however, clinging conascent with kamma assists rebirth-process existence by way of the object condition (ārammaṇa). For conascent kamma-process existence, conascent clinging assists in many ways: by way of conascence, mutuality, support, association, presence, and non-disappearance, as well as by way of root (hetu) and path (magga). For non-conascent kamma-process existence that is in proximity, non-conascent clinging assists by way of proximity, contiguity, decisive support of proximity, absence, disappearance, and repetition. For the other rebirth-process existence that is not in proximity, it assists by way of natural decisive support, and at times of comprehension (sammasana) and so forth, it assists by way of object and so forth. Among those conditions, those such as proximity are included in the decisive support condition, and those such as conascence are included in the conascence condition, and thus it is said 'tathā' (likewise). Or else, that word 'hi' has the sense of conveying the nature of assisting, or it has the sense of drawing in the meaning already stated above. By that word 'tathā', the meaning 'by way of decisive support and by way of conascence' is shown.
466:
In the phrase "With existence as condition, birth arises," "existence" (bhava) refers to kamma-existence (kammabhava). It is this kamma-existence alone that is the condition for birth, not rebirth-existence (upapattibhava). Rebirth-existence is indeed birth itself, and that birth is the first arising of the five aggregates. Therefore, it is said: "In this context, birth should be understood as the five aggregates along with their transformations." By saying this, the objection—"Is not birth itself existence? How then can it be the condition for birth?"—is refuted. If one asks, "How is it known that kamma-existence is the condition for birth?" [the answer is]: because even when external conditions are equal, differences such as inferiority and superiority are seen due to the power of kamma. As the Blessed One said: "Kamma distinguishes beings, that is, into the inferior and the superior."

"With transformations" (savikārā) means being together with the transformations of arising, and nothing else. Those aggregates are, in essence, rebirth-existence itself. That [rebirth-existence] is not suitable to be its own cause, just as in the case where craving is the condition for clinging to sense pleasures, there is no distinction of prior and posterior. Therefore, to show the meaning that kamma-existence alone conditions birth, which is called rebirth-existence, by way of kamma-condition and natural decisive support condition, it is said: "Including kamma-condition within decisive support, it conditions by way of the category of decisive support."

When birth exists, aging and death occur; for the fool oppressed by aging and death, etc., sorrow and so forth arise; they do not arise when birth is absent. Therefore, meaning that birth conditions aging and death by way of decisive support, it is said: "Birth... condition." Because the definitive analysis of the meaning in detail has not yet been made, and because the investigation of conditions is presented primarily through conascent decisive support, and because the arrangement of the factors (aṅga) has not been touched upon, it is said: "This is the summary here," and so forth. Since the investigation of dependent origination is a vast subject, the objection "Where can this complete investigation be obtained?" is removed by the words "In detail," and so forth. By the words "But here, of this," and so forth, it is shown that in the Pāḷi text as well, the discourse on dependent origination is taught only in part. In that context, "here" (idha) means in this Brahmajāla Sutta. "Of this" (assa) means of dependent origination. "Only for the sake of the purpose" (payojanamattameva) means only a portion for the sake of the purpose, by way of feeling (vedanā) which is the cause of views (diṭṭhi). The word "mattam-eva" is a synonymous expression in the sense of limitation (avadhāraṇa). Just as in the passage, "Now, at this time, life is short, only a hundred years," it is purposeful by way of making the mutual meaning understood. Or, the word "matta" means measure (pamāṇa); it is only the measure called the purpose, and nothing beyond that. Some also say: "The word 'matta' is for limitation, and the word 'eva' is for determination (sanniṭṭhāna)." This should be understood thus in all places. And here there is a verse:
467:
"The combination of the two words 'mattam-eva' has a single meaning. The word 'matta' is used in the sense of measure. Alternatively, the word 'matta' is used in the sense of limitation, and the other word 'eva' is used in the sense of determination," so say the teachers.

Since dependent origination is taught only in part in this Brahmajāla Sutta Pāḷi, the commentator says "The Blessed One indeed" (bhagavā hi), etc., to show the reason for such a partial teaching along with an illustration. By that passage, this intention is shown: "When teaching the discourse on the round of suffering (vaṭṭa), the Blessed One teaches by making either ignorance, craving, or views the starting point. Among those, in this Sutta, wishing to teach by making views the starting point, and because feeling is a powerful cause for views, He taught dependent origination only in part, having feeling as its root."

These Suttas are taught in the Book of Tens of the Aṅguttara Nikāya. In that Pāḷi text, "The first point is not discerned" means that it cannot be said that ignorance arose during the time of such-and-such a Buddha or Universal Monarch, and not before that. Thus, the first point or limit of ignorance is not discerned even by my unimpeded omniscient knowledge, because such a limit does not exist. This is the meaning.

Because of this absence of a limit, this ignorance is certainly said [to have no discernible beginning]. However, although it is said to have no limit in terms of time, the phrase "conditioned by this" (idappaccayā) means that ignorance arises due to this condition called the five hindrances (nīvaraṇa). Thus, by way of the law of phenomena (dhamma-niyāma), the point (beginning) of ignorance is discerned. For it is said in that same Book of Tens: "What is the nutriment for ignorance? It should be said: the five hindrances." In the Sub-commentary (Ṭīkā), however, it says "conditioned by the taints" (āsavapaccayā), but that statement does not agree with the illustrative Sutta.

In the term "idappaccayo," this condition is expressed by the change of the letter 'm' to 'd'. Grammarians, however, say that because such usage is seen, the word "ida" itself is the original form (prakati). That is incorrect, because various usages are seen due to phonetic transformation (vaṇṇa-vikāra) and so forth. For just as although "amū" is the form, "asū" is seen due to phonetic transformation, and although "imesu" is the form, "esu" is seen; so too here, phonetic transformation is found in compounds just as in sentences, as in "jānipati" and "tudampati." What more is there to say here? The word spoken by the Venerable Mahākaccāyana Thera, who possessed the analytical knowledges, should be taken as the standard.

"Craving for existence" (bhavataṇhā) means craving that has become a fetter to existence. "Conditioned by this" (idappaccayā) means due to this condition of ignorance. For has it not been said: "What is the nutriment for craving for existence? It should be said: ignorance"? "View of existence" (bhavadiṭṭhi) means the eternalist view (sassatadiṭṭhi). "Conditioned by this" (idappaccayā) means in this context...
468:
It should be understood that the meaning is simply "with feeling as condition" (vedanāpaccayā). One might ask: "Should not only the views be discussed? What is the purpose of teaching Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda)?" To address this, the phrase beginning with "Tena" is said. The meaning is this: The discourse on Dependent Origination in forward order is called the discourse on the round (vaṭṭakatha). By teaching this, the Blessed One shows that "as long as these holders of wrong views do not abandon this false vision, they will remain submerged in the round of existence through this succession of causes." "Ito" means from the beginning of this existence. "Ettha" means in these beginnings of existence. The same method applies to the remaining two terms. By these words, he shows the endless occurrence of successive births. "Vipannaṭṭhā" means those who have reached destruction in various ways.

## Explanation of the Discourse on the Cessation of the Round, etc.

"Diṭṭhigatikādhiṭṭhāna" means that which is the basis for the false grasp and vision of those with wrong views; it is said to be person-based (puggalādhiṭṭhāna) by way of those with wrong views. This teaching is a person-based discourse on the Dhamma. "Yuttayogabhikkhuadhiṭṭhāna" means that which is the basis for monks devoted to meditation; it is said to be person-based by way of the monks. "Vivaṭṭa" means the departure from the round (vaṭṭa). By the words beginning with "Yehi", it is shown that the Blessed One, being skilled in teaching, took the same sense bases of contact (phassāyatana) mentioned below—which are the cause of feeling (vedanā), which in turn is the cause of the wrong views of those with views—and taught them here. The phrase "Vedanākammaṭṭhāna" is said in reference to this Pali text: "the origin of feelings" (vedanānaṃ samudayaṃ), etc. Because there is only a slight difference, he said "Yathā pana", etc.

... refers to the cause taught as "with the origin of contact, with the cessation of contact" (phassasamudayā phassanirodhā). In the words "with the origin of nutriment" (āhārasamudayā), etc., edible food (kabaḷīkārāhāra) should be understood. Since it is stated in the Paṭṭhāna that "edible food is a condition for this body by way of nutriment-condition," it indeed serves as a supporting condition even for the eye-base (cakkhu), etc., which are produced by kamma. In the words "with the origin of name-and-form" (nāmarūpasamudayā), etc., only the three mental aggregates starting with feeling are called "name" (nāma). According to the teaching "with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases" (nāmarūpapaccayā saḷāyatanaṃ), should it not be said "with the origin of name-and-form, with the cessation of name-and-form" for all six sense bases of contact? Why, then, is it said "with the origin of nutriment, with the cessation of nutriment" for the eye-base, etc.? While that is generally true, it should be understood that it is said here specifically to show that this is also possible for the eye-base, etc.

By knowing the higher truth, the knowing of the wrong view is also accomplished; thus, although it does not appear directly in the Pali, the commentator says "he also knows the view" (diṭṭhiñca jānāti). Virtue, concentration, and wisdom (sīla, samādhi, paññā) are a mixture of mundane and supramundane. Here, "liberation" (vimutti) refers to the attainments of fruition (phalasamāpatti) occurring in the lower three fruits. "As far as..."
469:
Because of the separate mention of the fruit of Arahantship (it is the separate mention of the highest fruit). In this context, there is knowing distinctly through direct perception (paccakkha) and inference (anumāna). Therefore, it is said: "A monk who is learned (bahussuta) and a bearer of the scriptures (ganthadhara) knows," and so forth. Or it should be applied as appropriate.

In the phrase "desanā pana," the word "pana" has the sense of dissatisfaction (aruci). By this word, this meaning is shown: even if non-returners (anāgāmīs) and others know according to reality, the teaching is concluded with the pinnacle of Arahantship by virtue of the Arahant's superior and special knowledge. Just as a golden house is finished with a jeweled pinnacle, this teaching is finished with the pinnacle of Arahantship. In this Pāḷi, by the words "Yato kho... pajānāti," the good conduct of the Saṅgha is shown along with the emancipating nature (niyyānika) of the Dhamma. Therefore, in the Commentary, it is fully stated: "Who knows thus? The Arahant knows, down to the one who has begun insight (āraddhavipassaka)," thus showing the Bhikkhu Saṅgha.
