Therefore, the statement mentioned below, "Show also by virtue of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha," should be understood as being shown according to the literal meaning of the Pāḷi.

## Vivaṭṭakathāvaṇṇanā

To make known the complete perfection of the teaching, it should be understood that it is shown that "there is no holder of wrong views who is outside the net of the teaching." The interior of the net is called "antojāla." Even if they are not placed inside the net by way of their physical substance, they are called "antojālīkata" (made to be within the net) because they are placed there by way of the views dependent on them. Or, they are called "antojāla" because they stand within the net. Although they do not stand within the net by way of physical substance, they are called "antojālīkata" because they are made to stand within the net by way of their views. In the word "antojālī," the suffix "ī" is in the sense of "becoming what it was not" (abhūtatabbhāva). Or, grammarians say that the final vowel is changed to "ī", as in "dhavalīkāra" and "kabaḷīkāra." To show this meaning, the words beginning with "imassa" are said.

When those who have sunk or entered emerge, it means "they emerge" (ummujjanti). In the word "ummujjamānā," the suffix "māna" has the sense of characterizing one state by another (bhāvenabhāvalakkhaṇa). This is because the state of emerging again is characterized by the state of emerging that has not yet been abandoned. In words like "osīdantā," the suffix "anta" is likewise used. Even though sinking is not explicitly mentioned alongside emerging, it is shown by words like "osīdantā" (sinking). Therein, sinking downwards (osīdana) refers to falling into the planes of misery. Rising upwards (uddhamuggamana) refers to rebirth in prosperous existences. Likewise, it should be applied respectively by way of the sense-sphere realm and the sublime realm, by way of the shrinking and overrunning of views, and by way of views about the past (pubbantānudiṭṭhi) and views about the future (aparantānudiṭṭhi). "Pariyāpanna" means being included within. Because of being connected with that net of teaching, this state is described as "they are bound by this teaching." By the words "Na hettha" and so forth, the meaning arrived at in the aforementioned Pāḷi is shown.

Now, the comparison is stated with the words "Kevaṭṭa viya" and so forth. A fisherman is called "kevaṭṭa" because he frequents the water. In the Pāḷi, the apprentice of the master fisherman is also mentioned. However, because that apprentice merely follows the teacher, he is called "kevaṭṭantevāsī." The phrase "dasasahassilokadhātu" (ten-thousandfold world system) is said with reference to the field of birth (jātikhetta). This is because the Four Noble Truths can be penetrated in that birth-field, and because by taking the field of birth, the field of authority (āṇākhetta) and the field of range (visayakhetta) are also included. In truth, even in the field of authority and the field of range other than the field of birth, those with wrong views who enter within this net of teaching are indeed called "antojālīkata." "Oḷārika" means coarse because it is prominent. "Tassa" refers to the shallow water.

This shows the meaning that by including the views, the persons are also included. To show that He Himself does not enter the net, being skilled in the teaching, He wishes to show that He does not enter into existences and so forth, which are the places of emerging and sinking for the aforementioned holders of wrong views, and thus He leads beings to the desired destination.
470:
## Comparison of Similes

Now, the teacher provides the comparison of similes with the words beginning with "Like a fisherman." One is called a fisherman (kevaṭṭa) because he moves about or frequents the water (ke). Although the fisherman's apprentice is also mentioned in the Pāḷi, he is only a follower of the fisherman, which is why it is stated in this way. "The ten-thousandfold world system" refers to the field of birth (jātikhetta). This is because the penetration of the Four Noble Truths is possible only within that field of birth, and by taking the field of birth, the other fields—the field of authority (āṇākhetta) and the field of range (visayakhetta)—are also included. Those with wrong views (micchādiṭṭhi) in other fields are also included within the net of this teaching. "Oḷārika" (coarse) refers to being gross due to being evident. "Tassa" (of that) refers to a small amount of water.

137. By the phrase "by including all views" (vāda-saṅgahaṇa), the inclusion of persons (puggala-saṅgahaṇa) is shown. Being skilled in teaching (desanā-kusalatā), the Buddha says "Attano..." (of himself) and so forth to show his own non-involvement (anavarodha) in the states of existence where those with wrong views emerge and sink. They are called "nayanti" (they lead) because they carry beings to a desired place; since such leading is by the power of pulling, it is said "by the neck" and so forth. By the phrase "because of being like a lead (netti)," a metaphorical usage or a derivative (taddhita) of comparison is shown. The phrase "Sā hi" and so forth clarifies the state of similarity. In the word "gīvāya" (by the neck), it should be understood as a reference to "many people." In the word "neti" (leads), it should be connected as an object, because the root "nī" is bitransitive, and in the usage of verbs, the genitive case (sāmivibhatti) often manifests the meaning of the agent or the object. "Assa" (of him) should be connected as: "by this Blessed One, that conduit to existence (bhavanetti) has been cut." Furthermore, the meaning of sufficiency (sāmatthiya) is stated as "because there is no more rebirth." When the exhaustion of life is mentioned, it implies no more rebirth, because that very absence of rebirth is the primary cause for not seeing the Buddha. In the word "na dakkhanti" (they will not see), the formation of the word by the power of the future tense is shown by the word "na dakkhiဿnti," as in the Pāḷi passages: "Where a disciple will know, will see, or will realize such a thing." What is meant? It means "they will reach the state of being non-designatable" (apaṇṇattika-bhāva). "The state of being non-designatable" refers to the state where there is no longer any designation for the existing aggregates (the state where no mental or physical phenomena remain). As for past designation, the designation "Tathāgata" remains until the disappearance of the Dispensation (sāsana); beyond that, it will continue to exist during the appearance of other Buddhas, just as the designations of the Buddha Vipassī and others exist now. Therefore, it will be said later: "It will be a mere conventional expression (vohāramatta)." In this word "apaṇṇattika," grammarians state that the word "paññā" is substituted by "paṇṇa."

"Kāya" (body) refers to the physical form (attabhāva), which is a collection of material and immaterial phenomena (rūpārūpa-dhamma). Only when the body is taken as a collection of phenomena does its similarity to a mango tree, and the similarity of its parts—such as the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha), the eye-base (cakkhāyatana), and the eye-element (cakkhudhātu)—
471:
to a ripe mango fruit become appropriate. "Taṃ" refers to the body. Just as there are three sizes of ripe mangoes—clusters of five, twelve, or eighteen—so too a mango cluster (piṇḍī) is of three kinds. It is called "piṇḍī" because there is a cluster of mangoes at the stalk, and it is also called a bunch (thavaka). "Tadanvayāni" refers to those that follow the stalk. Therefore, it is said, "they follow that very stalk."

"Maṇḍūka-kaṇṭaka-visa-samphassaṃ" refers to contact with the venomous spine of a toad, or with other venom. Or, it means contact with the venom existing in the spine of a toad. Here, "maṇḍūka" refers to a creature that has a spine and moves in the water. Some call this creature a "stone-turtle" (pāsāṇa-kacchapa) [stingray], and say it refers to the spine located at the tip of its tail. Others say it is a single venomous fish-spine. The word "kira" is a particle used in the sense of hearsay (anussavana). In this simile, just as when the stalk is cut, the ripe mangoes attached to the stalk are severed from the mango tree, so too when the cord of craving, which is the conduit to existence (bhavanetti), is cut, the aggregates and so forth attached to that craving are severed from the continuity of existence. Only this much is the simile directly appearing in the Pāḷi; the remaining meanings should be understood as being obtained through the sense of the text.

"Buddhabala" refers to the power of knowledge (ñāṇa-bala) of the Buddhas. In the phrase "kathita-suttassa nāma," the word "nāma" is a particle used in the sense of praise (sambhāvana). Thus, it praises the quality of the Sutta in the manner: "A Sutta endowed with such qualities has been preached." The word "handa" is a particle used in the sense of relinquishment or exhortation (vossagga). Therefore, he makes a relinquishment, saying: "I will now have the name of the Sutta taken; I will not make it long."

"Dhamma-pariyāya" refers to the Pāḷi text known as the Dhamma teaching. "Idhattha" means the benefit in the present life. "Parattha" means the benefit in the future life, or both. The meaning of the preached Pāḷi text is also appropriate, because in the word "Dhamma-jāla," the Pāḷi Dhamma is taken. "Iha" means in this Dispensation (sāsana). The word "naṃ" is a mere particle, as in "na naṃ suto samaṇo gotamo" and so forth. "Nti dhammā" refers to the Pāḷi Dhammas. Because it encompasses all meanings, it is called the Net of Meanings (Attha-jāla). The same applies to the terms Dhamma-jāla, Brahma-jāla, and Diṭṭhi-jāla. Because one conquers the battle by this teaching, it is called the Victory in Battle (Saṅgāma-vijaya). Here, "battle" (saṅgāma) refers to encountering and fighting the five Māras; thus it is said, "even the Māra who is a son of a god (devaputta-māra)..." and so forth. The connection of meanings should be understood thus: it is "Attha-jāla" due to the perfection of meaning; "Dhamma-jāla" due to the perfection of phrasing and the description of faultless states such as virtue (sīla); "Brahma-jāla" because it analyzes the Path, Fruit, and Nibbāna, which are supreme (brahma); "Diṭṭhi-jāla" because it analyzes Right View by explaining Emptiness (suññatā) through the exclusion of wrong views; and it is the "Unsurpassed Victory in Battle" (Anuttara-saṅgāma-vijaya) because it is the means to crush the doctrines of the heretics.
472:
"Nidānāvasānato" means from the end of the introduction expressed by the words, "Then the Blessed One arrived." This is a statement indicating a limit or boundary. Alternatively, "Nidānāvasānato" means starting from the words, "Monks, others might speak in dispraise of me," etc., because they were spoken at the end of the introduction, thus being the conclusion of the introduction. This is a statement indicating an inclusive boundary. This phrase is spoken in connection with the verb "spoke" (avoca). Since it is said, "having a beautiful beginning through the introduction," the introduction, like the conclusion, is also included within the Sutta. The two terms "alabbha... gambhīraṃ" are adjectives for Omniscient Knowledge (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa).

Just as others become hostile because of practicing what is harmful to themselves—as the Buddha, the King of Dhamma, said in the Dhammapada and Udāna: "Whatever harm a thief may do to a thief, or an enemy to an enemy, a wrongly directed mind can do one even greater harm than that"—these monks are not like those with such minds. Rather, they are called "those of their own mind" (sakamana) because they practice for their own benefit. The fact that they have their own minds because their minds are seized by joy is shown by the words "gone to the Buddha" (buddhagatāya), etc.

Another method from the Commentary: "Attamanā" means those with perfected minds, meaning those whose mental intentions are fulfilled by this teaching. "Desanāvilāsa" is the grace of the teaching, and that is indeed the Omniscient Knowledge that accomplishes the task of teaching. He is called "karavīkarutamañjū" because he has a voice as sweet and melodious as the call of the karavīka bird. Water that is prepared with all medicinal ingredients and calms the distress of body and mind is called "amata" (nectar) because it leads to long life. He is said to be "amatābhis ekasadisena" because he is like an anointing with that nectar. He is called "brahmassaro" because he has a voice endowed with eight factors like the voice of Brahmā. The word "abhinandati" is said to "also come in the sense of craving" because it falls under the meaning of desire. Since roots have many meanings, "abhinandanti" means they approach or they associate with, as indicated by the phrase "upagamane pi."

Similarly, "abhinandanti" means accepting with joy, as indicated by "sampaṭicchane pi." The meaning already expressed by "abhinanditvā" is revealed by this word "anumoditvā" (having rejoiced), and with this in mind, it is said "anumodane pi."
473:
To show this very meaning by way of verse composition, he said "well spoken" (subhāsitaṃ), etc. In that verse, it is called "subhāsita" because it is well spoken in terms of sound, and "sulapita" because it is well uttered in terms of meaning. Alternatively, it is "subhāsita" by revealing virtue (sīla), and "sulapita" by revealing emptiness (suññatā). Or, it is "subhāsita" by analyzing views (diṭṭhi), and "sulapita" by analyzing the Omniscient Knowledge that penetrates those views. In this way, it should also be applied according to the distinctions shown here in this Brahmajāla Sutta, such as the prohibition of praise from dispraise. "Tādino" refers to the Blessed One who is "Such" (tādī) due to five reasons, such as equanimity toward the desirable and undesirable. The detail of this term is stated in the Mahāniddesa: "Such in the desirable and undesirable, Such because of having crossed over, Such because of having given up," etc.; that detail will also become clear in the later commentary.

Because it was spoken by way of answering a question asked with the desire to teach, occurring in various places such as "And what is that, monks?", this Sutta is called a Veyyākaraṇa (Exposition). Byākaraṇa is indeed Veyyākaraṇa. However, a Sutta proceeding by way of question and answer is called Geyya (Mixed Prose and Verse) if it is accompanied by verses. If it is without verses and lacks other factors of the [nine] angas, it is called Veyyākaraṇa. Thus, because a Sutta proceeding by way of question and answer also shares traits with Geyya, and because the state of being without verses—lacking other factors—is unique to it, he said, "Because it is without verses, this is a Veyyākaraṇa," showing the absence of verses as the reason for being a Veyyākaraṇa, without considering its nature of question and answer.

The objection "Why?" is cleared (answered) by the words "For it is said, bhaññamāne (while being spoken)." This word "bhaññamāne" is a "word connected to both" (ubhaya-sambandha-pada) because it connects to what precedes and what follows. This is what is meant: because it is spoken in the present tense as "bhaññamāne," it should be understood that the earth shook not only at the conclusion of the Sutta, but also at the sixty-two grounds of views. If it is argued that the meaning "it shook while this entire Sutta was being spoken" is the only one possible, and the meaning "it shook at the end of each of those views" is not possible—this inquiry is invalid as it is an interrogation based on mere possibility. This meaning is stated not just as a mere possibility, but according to the manner of the shaking during the time of the teaching as handed down by the lineage of teachers. Indeed, it was in that manner that this meaning was included in the Council (Saṅgīti), and it was stated by the author of the Compendium (Saṅgaha) according to that Council method; this should be the conclusion. Otherwise, the discussion of this matter, which is beyond the scope of logic, by means of logic would be inappropriate. In such matters, the meaning of "due to the disturbance of elements" (dhātukkhobhena), etc., should be taken from the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta Vaṇṇanā.
474:
## Aparesupīti

In the phrase 'aparesupīti', the word 'pi' includes the contemplation of the Perfections (pāramī). It is stated in the Buddhavaṃsa: 'When contemplating these qualities (dhammā) together with their nature, function, and characteristics, the earth of the ten-thousandfold world system trembled by the power of those qualities.'

Similarly, the establishment and disappearance of the Dispensation (sāsana), etc., should be included. Regarding the establishment of the Dispensation: first, when the Blessed One accepted the Veluvana Monastery; when the Elder Mahā Mahinda accepted the Mahāmeghavana Park; when the Elder Mahā Ariṭṭha recited the Vinaya Piṭaka, and so forth—at such times, this great earth trembled as if dancing with joy, thinking, 'The roots of the Dispensation have been firmly planted.' Regarding the disappearance of the Dispensation: it is like the trembling when the Dispensation of the Buddha Kassapa disappeared, as if reaching a state of sorrow (domanassa), thinking, 'Alas, such a True Dhamma (saddhamma) has vanished!' This is stated in the Apadāna: 'Then this whole earth, which is normally unmoving, moved; and the ocean, as if filled with grief, roared a pitiful sound.'

'Bodhimandūpasaṅkamane' refers to the time of first approaching the Bodhi-mandala on the full moon day of Visākha. 'Paṃsukūlaggahaṇe' refers to the time of taking the rag-robe (paṃsukūla) made of hemp, which had been discarded in a cemetery after being worn by a slave girl named Puṇṇā; [the Buddha] shook off about a gallon (tumba) of maggots and took it while remaining within the noble lineage of the Ariyas (ariyavaṃsa). 'Paṃsukūladhovane' refers to the washing of that very rag-robe. The Kāḷakārāma Sutta is found in the Catukka Nipāta of the Aṅguttara Nikāya. The Gotamaka Sutta is also found in the Tika Nipāta of that same Aṅguttara Nikāya. 'Vīriyabalena' means by the power of the energy (vīriya) that was the cause for renouncing the glory of a Universal Monarch during the Great Renunciation. Regarding the approach to the Bodhi-mandala: 'Let only skin, sinews, and bones remain; let the flesh and blood in the body dry up completely'—it should be understood that the meaning is by the power of the fourfold energy thus described. 'Acchariyavegābhihatā' means struck by the power of a wondrous action. Regarding the washing of the rag-robe, teachers say the earth moved due to the power of the Blessed One's merit. Regarding the taking of the rag-robe, it seems appropriate to say 'struck by the momentum of a wondrous act'; that trembling of the earth occasionally...
475:
...occurs, and thus it is called 'untimely trembling' (akālakampana). In the Vessantara Jātaka, however, it is called akālakampana because it trembled many times due to the power of merit from fulfilling the Perfections. 'Sakkhibhāvena' (as a witness) is said because it acts like a witness, corresponding to the matter spoken of when providing evidence, as at the time of the victory over Māra. 'Sādhukāradānena' (by giving applause) is said according to the context of the text, as at the time of the preaching of the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta and the time of the Councils (Saṅgīti), etc.

By showing the trembling of the earth with various meanings through the words 'Na kevalaṃ,' etc., only the great majesty of this Sutta is demonstrated. In that passage, 'Jotivana' refers to the Nanda Grove. It is stated in the Vinaya Commentary (Vinaya-saṃvaṇṇanā) that it is called Jotivana because it is the place where the light (joti) of the Dispensation, known as the light of knowledge, appeared. 'Dhamma' refers to teachings such as the Anamatagga Sutta. 'Pācīna-ambalaṭṭhika' refers to the place marked by a young mango tree in the eastern direction.

The word 'Evaṃ' points to the trembling of the earth at the times the Blessed One preached, and so forth. 'Anekaso' means in many ways. It should be construed as: 'Of that noble Brahmajāla Sutta preached by the Self-Enlightened One (Sayam-bhū).' 'Idha' means in this Dispensation. 'Yoniso' means 'let them practice with proper means,' such as abandoning wrong view and undertaking right view. This concludes the explanation of the difficult meanings (Līnatthavibhāvanā) of the Commentary in this context.

## Pakaraṇanayavaṇṇanā

After this, the Teacher Dhammapāla provided various explanations of the meanings through Samuṭṭhāna (origin), Hāra (modes of conveyance), and so on. We should not neglect that explanation, for it is a purification of the meaning of this [Brahmajāla] Sutta. Therefore, we shall also speak of it for the increase of knowledge of the listeners.

This is the explanation of the meaning of the Pali according to the method of the treatise (pakaraṇanaya). Pakaraṇanaya is the method of explanation in the Sinhalese language. It is also stated in the Abhidhamma-mūlaṭīkā: 'They also say it is the method of connection used by Dhamma-preachers in the Netti and Peṭakopadesa treatises.' Since this teaching is easy to perform and easy to understand if the Samuṭṭhāna (origin), Payojana (purpose), Bhājana (vessel/recipient), and Piṇḍattha (summary meaning) are first determined—
476:
The origin (samuṭṭhāna), the purpose (payojana),
the vessel (bhājana), and the collective meaning (piṇḍattha);
the wise person, having extracted these,
should then speak of the methods (hāras) and so forth.

In that verse, the 'origin' (samuṭṭhāna) refers to the causal occasion of the teaching. That origin is of two kinds: general (sādhāraṇa) and specific (asādhāraṇa). Likewise, the general origin is of two kinds: internal (ajjhattika) and external (bāhira). Among these, the general internal origin is the Great Compassion (mahākaruṇā) of the Blessed One. Motivated by that Great Compassion, the mind of the Lord of the World arose to teach the Dhamma to those to be guided (veneyya). With reference to the arising of such a mind, it was said: "Out of compassion for beings, he surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye," and so forth. Here, the inclusion of the Great Compassion in its three stages should be understood, as it arises for the purpose of rescuing beings from the great flood of saṃsāra by giving them the hand of the teaching of the True Dhamma. Just like the Great Compassion, Omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa), the Knowledge of the Ten Powers (dasabalañāṇa), and so forth are also called the general internal origin of the teaching. Knowing all knowable things, the manner in which they should be taught, and the inclinations (āsaya) and underlying tendencies (anusaya) of beings as they really are, the Blessed One, through his skill in what is possible and impossible (ṭhānāṭṭhāna) and so forth, set forth the teaching with various methods in accordance with the inclinations of those to be guided.

The general external origin is the request (ajjhesanā) of Sahampati Brahmā, who was accompanied by ten thousand Great Brahmās. In response to that request, the Lord of the Dhamma, having dispelled the hesitation (appossukkata) born from reflecting on the profundity of the Dhamma, became motivated to teach the Dhamma.

The specific origin is also of two kinds: internal and external. Among these, the internal specific origin consists of both the Great Compassion and the knowledge of teaching through which this particular Sutta was set forth. For while they are general in their common state, they become specific in their particular state of Great Compassion and so forth. The external specific origin is stated in the Commentary as the speaking of praise and blame (vaṇṇāvaṇṇa). Furthermore, it is the state of not falling into resentment or delight in beings regarding blame and praise. In that regard, the seeing of the absence of fault (anādīnava) is indeed the external specific origin. Likewise, the lack of understanding by beings regarding the sequence of practice in the face of blame and praise, the manifold virtue (sīla) such as the minor section (khuddaka) which is the object of praise, the Omniscience, the standing point of views such as eternalism (sassata-diṭṭhi), the unimpeded conduct in matters beyond that, and the Tathāgata's non-inclusion in any state of existence—all these are also called the external specific origin.

The purpose (payojana) is also of two kinds: general and specific. Among these, the general purpose is Nibbāna without clinging (anupādā-parinibbāna), because all the teachings of the Blessed One have the taste of liberation (vimuttirasa).
477:
Therefore, the Blessed One said: "This talk is for the purpose of Nibbāna; this consultation is for the purpose of Nibbāna," and so forth. Furthermore, the specific purpose should be understood as the inverse of the external origin. For the removal of resentment (āghāta) and the attainment of delight and so forth in beings to be guided, which are the results of this teaching regarding blame and praise, act as the cause that brings about this teaching. Indeed, a result is said to bring about its cause through the power (satti) that produces that result, because a cause can only attain its status as a cause when the result exists. Alternatively, the teacher Sāriputta Thera stated that the aforementioned result motivates the Blessed One in this teaching. Since the result to be achieved by the teaching is desired, that result is said to motivate the teacher of the discourse. Moreover, the destruction of various wrong livelihoods such as scheming (kuhana) and talking (lapana), the untangling of the net of sixty-two views, the clarification of dependent origination (paccayākāra) through the lens of views, the explanation of the meditation on the Four Truths by way of the six sense bases (phassāyatana), the total exhaustion of all views, and the demonstration of one's own Nibbāna without clinging are also the purposes (payojana).

The vessel (bhājana) refers to the foundation of the teaching. Those beings to be guided who have minds characterized by delight or opposition due to praise and blame, who are devoted to various wrong livelihoods such as scheming, who are submerged in the mire of views such as eternalism, who do not fulfill the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha) and so forth, and who do not know the special qualities and knowledge of the Buddha—these beings are the 'vessel' (bhājana) of this teaching.

The collective meaning (piṇḍattha) is the meaning gathered as appropriate through the words found here, through the collection, and through the words of the Sutta. In detail, it is: the exhortation to the perception of a recluse (samaṇasaññā) in accordance with one's own profession, shown by the words on not harboring resentment and so forth; likewise, the undertaking of patience (khanti) and gentleness (soracca); the devotion to the meditation on the divine abodes (brahmavihāra); the balancing of faith and wisdom; the foundation of mindfulness and clear comprehension; the accomplishment of the power of the meditation on reflection (paṭisaṅkhāna-bhāvanā-bala); the abandoning of the underlying tendencies (anusaya) that arise as outbursts; the practice for the welfare of both oneself and others; and being unstained by worldly conditions (lokadhamma).

Also included are: the purification of virtue (sīlavisuddhi) shown by the words on refraining from taking life and so forth; the fulfillment of shame and moral dread (hiri-ottappa) through that virtue; being endowed with loving-kindness and compassion; the abandoning of transgression (vītikkama); abandoning by substitution (tadaṅgapahāna); the abandoning of the defilements of misconduct; the accomplishment of the three abstinences (virati); the achievement of being dear, pleasant, respected, and venerable to companions; the attainment of gain, honor, and fame; being the foundation for serenity and insight (samatha-vipassanā); the thinning of unwholesome roots; the planting of wholesome roots; the removal of harm for both; confidence in assemblies; living in heedfulness (appamāda); being difficult to be destroyed by others; and being endowed with freedom from remorse (avippaṭisāra) and so forth.
478:
By the words beginning with "Gambhīrā", the following are shown: the manifestation of the profound Dhamma, the state of being without a foothold, the difficulty of appearing even in an incalculable number of aeons, the inability to be penetrated and realized even by subtle knowledge, the difficulty of attainment even through inferential knowledge known as the sequence of the Dhamma (dhammanvaya), the subsiding of all distress, the manifestation of the peaceful Dhamma, having a beautiful conclusion, the state of being insatiable, reaching the state of pre-eminence, being the domain of knowledge according to reality, having a subtle nature, and the manifestation of great wisdom.

By the terms indicating views (diṭṭhi), He shows briefly the recoil and the overrunning in eternalism and annihilationism, the bond of both views, the description of wrong attention, the manifestation of the practice called the wrong path, the making known of grasping through perverted views, the grasping through wrong contact, the establishment of views following the past and the future, the analysis of views of existence and non-existence, the occurrence of craving and ignorance, the description of the views of finitude and infinitude, the entry into the two extremes, and the specific analysis of taints (āsava), floods (ogha), yokes (yoga), defilements (kilesa), ties (gantha), fetters (saṃyojana), and clingings (upādāna).

Likewise, by the words "vedanānaṃ samudayaṃ" etc., He shows the accomplishment of the understanding and penetration of the Four Noble Truths, abandonment by suppression and by eradication, the disappearance of craving and ignorance, the grasping of the cause for the endurance of the True Dhamma, the attainment of learning (āgama) and realization (adhigama), the practice for the welfare of both self and others, the grasping of the three kinds of wisdom, the proper establishment of mindfulness and clear comprehension, the balanced union of faith and wisdom, the application of balanced energy, and the fulfillment of serenity and insight.

By the words "ajānataṃ apassataṃ", He shows the existence of ignorance. Likewise, by the words "taṇhāgatānaṃ paritassitavipphanditaṃ", He shows the existence of craving. By both of these, He shows the existence of the two: hindrances and fetters, the non-interruption of the round of saṃsāra without a perceivable beginning, the bringing forward of the past and the linking with the future, the analysis of causes by way of past and present time, the non-transcendence of ignorance and craving for each other and their mutual assistance, and the description of the opposites of liberation by wisdom and liberation of mind.

By the words "tadapī phassapaccayā", He shows that the designation of eternalism etc. is dependent on conditions. By that same phrase, He shows the prohibition of the permanence of phenomena, the establishment of their impermanence, the rejection of a "doer" (kāraka) etc. in the ultimate sense, the description of such natural law (dhammatā), the revelation of emptiness (suññatā), and the manifestation of the characteristics of conditions as being capable yet effortless.
479:
By the word "Ucchinnabhavanettiko" etc., the Blessed One's attainment of abandonment (pahānasampatti), the mastery in knowledge and liberation (vijjā-vimutti-vasībhāva) or the mastery in entering the fruition of arahantship liberated from defilements through wisdom, the completion of the three trainings, the analysis of the two elements of Nibbāna, the fulfillment of the four resolutions (adhiṭṭhāna), and the state of not being included in the realms of existence and modes of birth etc., are shown.

By the entire sutta passage, the Blessed One's state of being "such" (tādibhāva) towards desirable and undesirable objects, the establishment of others in that state of suchness, the description of the two dhammas that are the beginning of wholesome dhammas, the instruction on the three trainings, the accomplishment of the four types of persons such as those who torment themselves (attantapa), the analysis of the four types of kamma such as dark and bright with their results, the description of the objects of the four immeasurables (appamaññā), the realization according to reality of the group of five beginning with the origin and passing away (of feelings), the manifestation of the six dhammas of conciliation (sāraṇīya-dhamma), and the establishment in the ten dhammas that make for protection (nāthakara-dhamma)—these meanings, collected as appropriate, are called the "summary meaning" (piṇḍattha).

## The Exposition of the Sixteen Haras
## The Exposition of the Desanā-hāra

Now, I shall set forth the Haras etc. by way of the methods stated in the Nettippakaraṇa and the Peṭakopadesa. In setting forth those Haras etc., among the five aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandha) taken as the basis for views such as "self" and "world", and by way of feelings, contact, and the sense bases etc., the five aggregates of clinging excluding craving are the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca). Craving is the Truth of the Origin (samudaya-sacca). That Truth of the Origin is indeed taken in its specific form in the Pali by the words "paritassanā", "taṇhāgatānaṃ", and "vedanāpaccayā taṇhā", and by the term "samudaya". This is first the Suttanta method.

In the Abhidhamma, according to the method found in the Vibhaṅga, the defilements (dhamma-kilesa) taken by the words showing all mundane wholesome and unwholesome dhammas in brief—such as the teaching of "āghāta" (resentment) and "ānanda" (joy), the terms "ātappamanvāya" etc., the mention of "cittapadosa" (corruption of mind), the terms for all types of views, the taking of the wholesome and unwholesome, the taking of existence (bhava), the taking of sorrow (soka) etc., the taking of views (diṭṭhi), and the taking of "samudaya" in various Pali passages—are the Truth of the Origin (samudaya-sacca). The non-occurrence of both [Suffering and Origin] is the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-sacca). That Truth of Cessation should be understood as being taken in the Pali by the synonymous terms "atthangama" (passing away) and "nissaraṇa" (escape) of feelings in various passages, by the mention of the word "nibbuti" (extinction) for each, and by the mention of "anupādā-vimutti" (liberation without clinging). The practice which is the cause for knowing the Truth of Cessation is the Truth of the Path (magga-sacca). That Truth of the Path should also be understood as being taken in the Pali by the description of the penetration according to reality of the origin etc. of feelings in various passages, by the method of knowing according to reality the origin etc. of the six sense bases, and by the mention of the cutting off of the "cord of existence" (bhavanetti/craving).
480:
Among those Four Noble Truths, gratification (assāda) is shown by the Truth of the Origin (samudaya-sacca); danger (ādīnava) by the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca); and escape (nissaraṇa) by the Truth of the Path (magga-sacca) and the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-sacca). Thus, it is shown by the power of the Four Noble Truths. In this Mode of Conveying a Teaching (Desanā-hāra), gratification and so forth should be understood by encompassing them through the power of gratification, danger, and escape as they directly appear in the Pāḷi text. The attainment of the Tādi quality and so forth by the veneyya beings (those to be guided) is called the 'fruit' (phala). The reason is that the specific benefit mentioned above, which is to be achieved through the teaching, is called the 'fruit'; this is the meaning intended. For that purpose, the Blessed One taught this Brahmajāla Sutta. The 'means' (upāya) refers to the cause for attaining various benefits, such as the non-commission of malice and so forth, the fact that the result of malice and so forth occurs only within one's own mental continuum, and the honest admission and clarification of the true nature regarding blame and praise. The statement that 'those who desire their own welfare should well-guard their minds from malice and so forth,' citing the prohibition of committing malice and so forth as a reason, is called the 'command' (āṇatti) of the Blessed One, the King of Dhamma who is worthy of issuing commands. Thus, the Mode (hāra) characterized by the demonstration of the six dhammas—gratification, danger, escape, fruit, means, and command—is called the Mode of Conveying a Teaching (Desanā-hāra). It is also stated in the Netti:

"Gratification, danger, escape, fruit, means,
And the command of the Blessed One, is the Desanā-hāra for practitioners."

## Commentary on the Mode of Investigation (Vicaya-hāra)

Even though there is no conceptualizing (of a self), He said "My" (mama) by way of conventional usage and self-reference. The word "vā" (or) is taken in the sense of alternative (vikappana) because there is no fixed rule. He addressed them as "Monks" (bhikkhave) because they are endowed with qualities such as virtue and for the purpose of making them attentive. He said "others" (pare) because they are different and because they are antagonistic. He said "dispraise" (avaṇṇa) because it is the opposite of praise and because it is not worthy of being spoken. He said "might speak" (bhāseyyuṃ) by way of making it clear and by way of elaboration. He said "of the Dhamma" (dhammassa) because it has the nature of bearing (one to happy states and Nibbāna) and because it is the opposite of non-Dhamma (adhamma). He said "of the Saṅgha" (saṅghassa) because they are united by view and virtue, and because they destroy the defilements. He said "therein" (tatra) to point back to what has been said and because of its proximity to the preceding words. He said "you" (tumhehi) because they were present and because they were many. He said "malice" (āghāta) because it destroys the mind and because it strikes against the object. He said "displeasure" (appaccaya) because of the state of shrinking from the object, the state of not facing it, and the state of being dissatisfied. He said "of the mind" (cetaso) because it thinks of the object and because it is the support (for mental factors). He said "resentment" (anabhiraddhi) because it does not accomplish one's welfare and because it repeatedly accomplishes harm. Because it is not appropriate to the cause, and in the Dispensation of the Teacher...
481:
Because those established in the Dispensation (Sāsana) cannot do so (get angry), He said "it should not be done" (na karaṇီyā). Thus, by demonstrating the occurrence in each intended sense, and also by way of meaning:

The word "maman" is a pronoun indicating the genitive sense (sāmi). The word "vā" is a particle indicating the sense of alternative (vikappa). The word "bhikkhave" is a noun indicating the vocative sense (ālapaṇa). The word "pare" is a noun indicating the agent sense (kattar). The word "avaṇṇaṃ" is a noun indicating the object sense (kamma). The word "bhāseyyuṃ" is a finite verb (ākhyāta) indicating the action sense (kiriyā). The words "dhammassa" and "saṅghassa" are nouns indicating the genitive sense (sāmi). The word "tatra" is a pronoun indicating the locative sense (ādhāra). The word "tumhehi" is a pronoun indicating the agent sense (kattar). The word "na" is a particle indicating the negative sense (paṭisedha). The words "āghāto", "appaccayo", and "anabhiraddhi" are nouns indicating the object sense (kamma). The word "cetaso" is a noun indicating the genitive sense (sāmi). The word "karaṇīyā" is a noun indicating the action sense (kiriyā).

Thus, the investigation by way of the distinction of each word and by way of syllables is called the Investigation of Words (Pada-vicaya). We have not elaborated further because of the fear of being too extensive, and because wise people can understand this meaning by following the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) and the Sub-commentary (Ṭīkā) that explains its hidden meanings.

"If you were to be angry or displeased therein, would you be able to know whether what others said was well-spoken or ill-spoken?"—this sentence is a Question for Consent (Anumati-pucchā). The investigation of questions in all cases as appropriate—such as those based on beings, those based on many things, those having ultimate reality as their domain, or those having the present as their domain—is called the Investigation of Questions (Pucchā-vicaya). "No, Bhante"—this answer is a categorical explanation (ekāṃsa-vyākaraṇa). The investigation of all answers as appropriate—such as being exhaustive, being with a further part (sa-uttara), or being mundane—is called the Investigation of Answers (Vissajjanā-vicaya).

This first teaching, "Monks, if others should speak dispraise of Me... resentment of mind should not be done," is consistent with this second teaching, "Monks... by such anger, there would be an obstacle only for you." Why? Because the first teaching prohibits the corruption of the mind, and the second teaching shows the danger in that corruption of the mind. Likewise, this second teaching is consistent with this third teaching, "Monks... would you be able to know whether what others said was well-spoken or ill-spoken?" Why? Because the second teaching shows the danger, and the third teaching shows the inability even to merely note the meaning of the words. Likewise, this third teaching is consistent with this fourth teaching, "Monks... this point does not exist in us." Why? Because the third teaching completely prohibits the corruption of the mind, and the fourth teaching shows the manner in which one should practice in the face of dispraise. The investigation by connecting the preceding words with the following words in this manner is called the Investigation of Sequence (Pubbāpara-vicaya). The investigation of gratification (assāda-vicaya) and so forth are just as previously stated. The only distinction here is the mere demonstration of their characteristics.
482:
The question, "Would you be able to know the well-spoken and poorly-spoken words of others?" and the answer, "No, Bhante," are consistent. This is because an angry person cannot understand the meaning of what is well-spoken or poorly-spoken, whether it be the words of a Buddha, a Paccekabuddha, a Noble Disciple, parents, or even enemies. The question, "Monks, what is that trifling... praise of the Tathāgata that one might speak?" and the answer beginning with "Having abandoned the destruction of life, he abstains from the destruction of life," are consistent. The Blessed One is endowed with supreme virtues such as abstinence from the destruction of life; however, when compared to Concentration and Wisdom, these are merely trifling, minor, and mere virtue. The question, "Monks, what are those dhammas that are deep and difficult to see?" and the answer beginning with "Monks, there are some recluses and brahmins who are speculators about the past," are consistent. Because the qualities of Omniscience have a foundation that cannot be reached by the knowledge of others besides the Tathāgata, they are deep, difficult to see, difficult to understand, peaceful, sublime, beyond the sphere of reasoning, subtle, and to be experienced by the wise. In this way, investigating the suitability of the answer to the question is called 'Anugīti-vicaya' (Investigation of the Subsequent Recital) here, as there is no summary verse. This is the Vicaya-hāra (The Mode of Investigation), characterized by the investigation of the eleven dhammas such as the phrasing of questions. It is said: "That which is questioned and that which is answered..." (Netti. 4.2).

## Commentary on Yutti-hāra (The Mode of Construing)

The use of the genitive case (sāmivibhatta) to show possession in "mama" (my) is appropriate according to natural linguistics (sabhāva-nirutti). Such usage is observed, and the word "avaṇṇa" (dispraise) depends on that word "mama". Showing the meaning of choice in "vā" (or) is also appropriate. This is because particles (nipāta) have various meanings, and there is no fixed rule for a single meaning here. The use of the address "bhikkhave" (O monks) is also appropriate. This usage is found only in the sense of a vocative (ālapaṇa), and the teacher must consider the listeners. Thus, by way of syllables and so on—

It is appropriate to say that not harboring resentment in every way leads to the state of being 'Tādi' (steadfast). This is because of the nature of remaining equal towards pleasant and unpleasant objects. It is appropriate to say that for the person in whose mental stream resentment and so on have arisen, the dangers caused by that resentment lead only to the obstruction of that person's success. This is because kamma does not pass over into other mental streams. Resentment and so on, which arise by overwhelming the mind, also serve as obstacles in noting well-spoken and poorly-spoken words...
483:
...It is appropriate [to say they] lead to inability [to note well], because anger and greed have the nature of blind darkness. It is appropriate to say that abstinence from misconduct such as the destruction of life leads to the joy and praise of all beings, because the great fame resulting from the perfection of virtue spreads up to the highest heaven. It is appropriate to say that praising the Tathāgata through special qualities such as depth, even if it is only partial, serves to encompass the entire quality of Omniscience, because it is not shared with others. It is appropriate to say that the adherence to Eternalism and so on—which are accompanied by improper attention (ayoniso manasikāra) suitable to those views and involve speculating on what has been attained—leads to entering [those views], because the net of speculation has not been uprooted by the Path.

It is appropriate to say that because of not understanding feeling (vedanā) and so on, craving increases with feeling as a condition, because there is the continual contemplation of gratification (assādānupassanā). Even when there is feeling (when there is the lust for what is felt), the clinging to 'self' and 'what belongs to self' and the clinging to the view of Eternalism and so on in that which is felt are 'agitated' (vipariphandati) because the causes are present. For with craving as condition, clinging (upādāna) arises. It is appropriate to say that for those who proffer views such as Eternalism and for those who experience the feeling corresponding to that proffering, contact (phassa) is the cause, because without the meeting of the object, the sense-base, and consciousness, that contact cannot occur.

It is appropriate to say that the non-interruption of the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) has the six sense-bases of contact as its cause, because ignorance and craving have not been abandoned therein. It is appropriate to say that knowing the arising and passing away of the six sense-bases of contact stands beyond the perception of all those who hold views, because it is the state of penetrating the Four Noble Truths. It is appropriate to say that only by these sixty-two views are all those who hold views included within the net of the teaching, because doctrines of non-action (akiriya-vāda), theism (issara-vāda), and so on are included within them; and this has been explained below.

It is appropriate to say that the physical body (rūpakāya) of the Tathāgata has cut the cord of existence (bhavanetti) because of the fulfillment of the Blessed One's aspiration (abhinīhāra) and because of having truly developed the seven factors of enlightenment while established in the four foundations of mindfulness. It is appropriate to say that after the breaking up of the body, the Tathāgata who has attained Parinibbāna will not be seen, because when Nibbāna without remainder of substrata (anupādisesa-nibbāna) is reached, nothing of form and so on remains. In this way, by way of meaning, the mode characterized by demonstrating the appropriateness of the phrasing and meaning in a Sutta is called Yutti-hāra (The Mode of Construing). As it is said: "The ground of all modes..." (Netti. 4.3).

## Commentary on Padaṭṭhāna-hāra (The Mode of Proximate Cause)

Dispraising one worthy of praise, praising improperly, and having words that should not be accepted are the proximate causes (padaṭṭhāna) of failure. Praising one worthy of praise, praising properly, and having words that are trustworthy are the proximate causes of success. Likewise, resentment and so on are the proximate causes of suffering such as hell. Not harboring resentment and so on is the proximate cause of all success such as heavenly attainment. Abstinence from the destruction of life and so on is [the proximate cause] of the Noble...
484:
Abstaining from taking life and so forth is the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) of the aggregate of pure virtue. The aggregate of pure virtue is the proximate cause of the aggregate of pure concentration. The aggregate of pure concentration is the proximate cause of the aggregate of pure wisdom. The Blessed One's knowledge of the modes of penetration, endowed with distinctions such as profundity and so forth, is the proximate cause of the knowledge of teaching (desanā-ñāṇa). The knowledge of teaching is the proximate cause for the escape of those to be guided from the entire suffering of the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa-dukkha). Because all wrong views are the clinging to views (diṭṭhupādāna), that view is the proximate cause, as appropriate, for the ninefold existence (bhava). Existence is the proximate cause of birth (jāti). Birth is the proximate cause of aging, death, sorrow, and so forth. The penetration of the arising and passing away of feelings as they really are is the sequential realization (anubodha) and the penetration (paṭivedha) of the Four Noble Truths. Between those two, sequential realization is the proximate cause of penetration. Penetration is the proximate cause of the four fruits of recluseship (sāmaññaphala).

By the phrase 'not knowing, not seeing,' ignorance (avijjā) should be understood. Therein, ignorance is the proximate cause of volitional formations (saṅkhāra); volitional formations are the proximate cause of consciousness (viññāṇa). Starting with 'feeling is the proximate cause of craving (taṇhā),' it should be understood by connecting it according to the method found in the Pali text. In the phrase 'the agitation and trembling of those who have reached craving,' craving is the proximate cause of clinging (upādāna). In the phrase 'that [view] also arises from contact as a condition,' the designation of the eternalist view and so forth is the proximate cause of the wrong conviction of others. Wrong conviction is the proximate cause of hearing the false Dhamma and so forth, due to turning away from hearing the true Dhamma, associating with good people, wise attention, and practice in accordance with the Dhamma.

In the phrases such as 'apart from contact,' contact is the proximate cause of feeling. The six bases of contact are the proximate cause of contact and of the entire suffering of the round. Knowing the origin and so forth of the six bases of contact as they really are is the proximate cause of disenchantment (nibbidā); disenchantment is the proximate cause of dispassion (virāga), and so on, it should be led up to final Nibbāna without clinging. The Blessed One's absolute cutting off of the cord of craving that leads to existence is the proximate cause of omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), and likewise, it is the proximate cause of final Nibbāna without clinging. Thus, the determination of the proximate causes of the states mentioned in the Sutta, and the proximate causes of those proximate causes as far as possible, is called the Mode of Proximate Cause (Padaṭṭhāna-hāra). For it is said: 'The Victor teaches the Dhamma, and what is the proximate cause of that Dhamma,' and so forth.

## Explanation of the Mode of Characteristic (Lakkhaṇa-hāra-vaṇṇanā)

By taking 'resentment' (āghāta) and so forth, anger (kodha), enmity (upanāha), contempt (makkha), domineering (palāsa), envy (issā), avarice (macchariya), turbulence (sārambha), and disparaging (vambhana) are included, because they are comprised within the arising of the mind of aversion (paṭigha-cittuppāda) and thus have the same characteristic. By taking 'joy' (ānanda) and so forth, covetousness (abhijjhā), unrighteous greed (visama-lobha), conceit (māna), arrogance (atimāna), intoxication (mada), and heedlessness (pamāda) are included, because they are comprised within the arising of the mind of greed (lobha-cittuppāda) and thus have the same characteristic.
485:
Likewise, by taking resentment, the remaining ties (gantha) and hindrances (nīvaraṇa) are included, because they have the same characteristic as the characteristic of the tie of the body and the hindrances. By taking joy (greed), contact and so forth are included, because they have the same characteristic as the characteristic of the aggregate of volitional formations (saṅkhārakkhandha). By taking virtue (sīla), the training in higher mind (adhicitta-sikkhā) and the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññā-sikkhā) are included, because they have the same characteristic as the characteristic of training (sikkhā). By taking view (diṭṭhi), the remaining clingings (upādāna) are included, because they have the same characteristic as the characteristic of clinging. In the word 'of feelings' (vedanānaṃ), by taking feeling, the remaining aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandha) are included, because they have the same characteristic as the characteristic of the aggregates of clinging. Likewise, by taking feeling comprised within the mental-base (dhammāyatana) and the mental-element (dhammadhātu), all bases and elements that are subject to comprehension (as impermanent, etc.) are included, because they have the same characteristic as the characteristic of bases (āyatana) and the characteristic of elements (dhātu). In the phrase 'for those not knowing, not seeing,' by taking ignorance, the roots (hetu), taints (āsava), floods (ogha), bonds (yoga), hindrances (nīvaraṇa), and so forth are included, because they have the same characteristic as the characteristic of roots and so forth. Likewise, in the phrase 'the agitation and trembling of those who have reached craving,' by taking craving, [others] are also included. In the phrase 'that also arises from contact as a condition,' by taking contact, perception (saññā), volitional formations (saṅkhāra), and consciousness (viññāṇa) are included, because they have the same characteristic as the state of being a cause for perversion (vipallāsa) and as the characteristic of the aggregates (khandha). By taking the six bases of contact, the remaining aggregates, bases, elements, faculties (indriya), and so forth are included, because they have the same characteristic as the state of being the sign for the arising of contact and as the state of being subject to comprehension. By taking the 'conduit to existence' (bhavanetti), the defiling states (saṃkilesa-dhamma) such as ignorance and so forth are included, because they have the same characteristic as the state of being the cause of the round. What has been said thus is the Mode of Characteristic (Lakkhaṇa-hāra), which has the characteristic of determining states not explicitly mentioned in the Sutta by way of having the same characteristic as those mentioned in the Sutta. Thus it was said [by the Elder Mahākaccāyana]: 'When one state is mentioned, those states which have the same characteristic,' and so forth.

## Explanation of the Mode of Fourfold Array (Catubyūha-hāra-vaṇṇanā)

The word 'mama' (mine) is not a word explained by way of its derivative meaning (nirutti); the phrase 'tathā vā' (or likewise) is the same. They are called 'bhikkhus' because they have the habit of begging. They are called 'parā' because they reach a state of opposition; however, in other contexts, this word 'parā' is not explained by its derivative meaning. In this way, the derivative meaning (nirutti) should be understood. Since that nirutti is easily understood through the power of the commentaries on the introductory words such as 'evaṃ' and the Pali words such as 'mama,' and through the power of the sub-commentaries that clarify the hidden meanings of those commentaries, I shall not elaborate further for fear of excessive length.

There are those beings to be guided who have minds shaken by blame and praise, who do not abstain from wrong livelihood, who are wrongly obsessed with false views such as eternalism, who are not established in the aggregates of Dhamma such as virtue, and who turn away from tasting the essence of the qualities of the Fully Enlightened Buddha. By what means can they be freed from the aforementioned faults and, through right practice, perform the welfare of both the present and the future rounds of rebirth...
486:
The intention of the Blessed One in this Brahmajāla Sutta is that beings to be guided (veneyya) should be those who strive for both types of welfare. The persons thus intended and the matters shown in the context of the teaching constitute the origin (nidāna) of this teaching.

The connection of sequence (anusandhi) is of six kinds: connection of words (padasandhi), connection of meanings (padatthasandhi), connection of expositions (niddesasandhi), connection of delivery (nikkhepasandhi), connection of discourses (suttasandhi), and connection of teachings (desanāsandhi). Among these six, the connection of one word with another, such as connecting the word 'mama' (my) with 'avaṇṇaṃ' (dispraise), is called padasandhi. The connection of the meaning of one word with the meaning of another, such as connecting the meaning of the Blessed One referred to as 'mama' with the unvirtuous words of dispraise ('avaṇṇaṃ') spoken by others, is called padatthasandhi. The teaching beginning with 'Monks, if others should speak in dispraise of me...' arose by way of connection with the words of dispraise spoken by the wanderer Suppiya. The teaching beginning with 'Monks, if others should speak in praise of me...' arose by way of connection with the words of praise spoken by the youth Brahmadatta. The teaching beginning with 'Monks, there are other dhammas, deep and difficult to see...' arose by way of connection with the words of praise spoken by the monks. Thus, the connection of a sutta having various sequences with those respective sequences, and the connection of a sutta having a single sequence with its preceding and following parts, is called niddesasandhi. Nikkhepasandhi, however, has been analyzed in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) only by way of the four methods of delivering a sutta. Suttasandhi has also been analyzed in the Commentary by way of the three types of sutta connections, and we have explained it previously. The comparison and connection of one teaching with other teachings is called desanāsandhi. That desanāsandhi should be understood as follows: The teaching, 'Monks, if others should speak in dispraise of me... you should not harbor resentment in your hearts,' correlates with this teaching: 'Monks, even if bandits were to sever you limb from limb with a two-handled saw, if anyone were to harbor an ill-will in his mind, he would not be a follower of my teaching.' The teaching, 'That would be a hindrance only to you,' correlates with this teaching: 'Young man, beings are owners of their kamma, heirs to their kamma, born of their kamma, related to their kamma, and have kamma as their refuge; kamma distinguishes beings as inferior or superior.' The teaching, 'Would you be able to know?' correlates with this teaching: 'The angry person does not know the benefit, the angry person does not see the Dhamma; when anger overcomes a man, there is then blind darkness.' The teaching, 'Monks, if others should speak in praise of me... you should not harbor joy in your hearts,' correlates with this teaching: 'Monks, you should abandon even the [good] dhammas, how much more so...
487:
"...how much more so unwholesome states (adhamma),' and with this teaching: 'Monks, I will teach you the Dhamma compared to a raft for the purpose of crossing over, not for the purpose of grasping.' The teaching, 'Even so, if you... that attachment would be a hindrance only to you,' correlates with this:

'The greedy person does not know the benefit, the greedy person does not see the Dhamma; when greed overcomes a man, there is then blind darkness which makes one blind of wisdom,' and with this teaching:

'Beings who are blind with sensual desire, covered by the net of craving, obstructed by the roof of craving, and bound by the bond of negligence, follow after old age and death, just as fish entering the mouth of a trap follow after death, or as a suckling calf follows its mother.'

The teaching, 'This virtue is only a trifle,' correlates with this teaching: 'Quite secluded from sensual pleasures... he enters and dwells in the first jhāna. Brahmin, this sacrifice of the first jhāna is less difficult to perform and requires less preparation than previous sacrifices, yet it is of greater fruit and greater advantage.' This is because by stating that the first jhāna has greater fruit and advantage than virtue, it shows that virtue has less fruit and advantage compared to jhāna.

The teaching beginning with 'Having abandoned the taking of life' correlates with the teaching beginning with 'Friends, the recluse Gotama is indeed virtuous, possessed of the noble virtue.' The teaching beginning with 'There are other dhammas that are deep' correlates with the teaching beginning with 'This Dhamma attained by me is deep, difficult to see, and difficult to understand.' This is because the depth of knowledge is known through the penetration of the Dhamma which is endowed with special qualities such as depth.

The teaching beginning with 'Monks, there are some recluses and brahmins who are speculators about the past' correlates with the teaching: 'Monks, there are some recluses and brahmins who are speculators about the past... some declare: "The self and the world are eternal; only this is true, anything else is futile." Some declare in various ways: "The self and the world are non-eternal; both eternal and non-eternal; neither eternal nor non-eternal; finite; infinite; both finite and infinite; neither finite nor infinite; only this is true, anything else is futile."'
488:
Likewise, the teaching beginning with, "Monks, there are some recluses and brahmins who speculate about the future," corresponds with the teaching: "Monks, some recluses and brahmins speculate about the future... they declare that after death the self is healthy, percipient. Some declare that after death the self is healthy, non-percipient; both percipient and non-percipient; or neither percipient nor non-percipient. Some prescribe the annihilation, destruction, and non-existence of a truly existing being; or some declare Nibbāna (extinguishment) in the present life."

The teaching beginning with, "The cause of feelings... the Blessed One," corresponds with the teaching: "This conditioned state is gross; however, there is the cessation of formations. Knowing that 'this cessation exists,' the Blessed One, seeing the escape from that conditioned state, stands having transcended that conditioned state."

This teaching, "That knowledge of theirs... is merely a vibration," corresponds with the teaching: "Apart from faith, apart from preference, apart from oral tradition, apart from reasoned reflection, and apart from acceptance of a view after pondering it, the possibility does not exist that this knowledge will be pure and bright by itself. Monks, when there is no pure and bright knowledge by itself, those venerable recluses and brahmins merely purify whatever knowledge has arisen in that view; that mere arising of knowledge is said to be the clinging (upādāna) of those venerable recluses and brahmins."

This teaching, "That view is also conditioned by contact (phassa)," corresponds with the teaching: "Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact; conditioned by contact, feeling arises; conditioned by feeling, craving arises; conditioned by craving, clinging arises." And also with: "Friends, these things are rooted in desire (chanda), originate in attention (manasikāra), meet in contact (phassa), and converge in feeling (vedanā)."

The teaching beginning with, "Monks, when a monk [understands] the six bases of contact," corresponds with the teaching: "Monks, when a monk does not regard feeling as self, nor regard perception, nor formations, nor consciousness as self; not so regarding, he does not cling to anything in the world; not clinging, he is not agitated; not being agitated, he attains Nibbāna (extinguishment from defilements) by himself."

The teaching beginning with, "All these are trapped within the net of these sixty-two grounds," corresponds with the teaching: "Monks, those who... declare [views], all of them declare these five aggregates (khandha) or one of these aggregates."

This teaching, "Due to the breaking up of the body... gods and humans," [corresponds with the teaching: "Upasīva, just as a flame blown by a gust of wind goes out and cannot be designated as 'having gone to such a place,' so the sage (muni), liberated from the group of mental factors (nāmakāya), goes out and cannot be designated."]

This concludes the explanation of the Catubyūha-hāra, which has the characteristic of clarifying the four meanings of the Netti: linguistic analysis (nirutti), intention (adhippāya), source (nidāna), and the sequence of context (pubbāparānusandhi).
489:
"Upasīva, just as a flame blown by a gust of wind goes out and cannot be designated (as having gone to such a place), so the sage (muni), liberated from the group of mental factors (nāmakāya), goes out and cannot be designated," (so the Blessed One said). It corresponds with such teachings. This is called the Catubyūha-hāra, characterized by the clarification of the four: Nirutti, Adhippāya, Nidāna, and Pubbāparānusandhi. Regarding this, it has also been said: "Niruttama-adhippāyo..."

## Explanation of the Āvatta-hāra

By teaching the non-doing of malice (āghāta) and so forth, patience (khanti) and gentleness (soracca) arise. Among them, through patience, there is the inclusion of faith (saddhā), wisdom (paññā), and the enduring of suffering caused by the wrongs of others. Likewise, through gentleness, virtue (sīla) is included. By taking faith and so forth, all the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma) such as the faculty of faith (saddhindriya) revolve. By taking virtue, all the beneficial qualities of virtue such as non-remorse (avippaṭisāra) revolve. By teaching the avoidance of killing (pāṇātipāta) and so forth, there is the abiding in diligence (appamāda-vihāra). Through that abiding in diligence, the entire holy life (brahmacariya) of the Dispensation revolves. 

By taking the Dhamma endowed with special qualities such as profundity, there is the praise of the Great Enlightenment (Mahābodhi). The knowledge of the destruction of taints (āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa) which has unobstructed knowledge (anāvaraṇa-ñāṇa) as its proximate cause, and the unobstructed knowledge which has the knowledge of the destruction of taints as its proximate cause, is called the Great Enlightenment. Through that Great Enlightenment, all the Buddha's qualities such as the Ten Powers (Dasabala) revolve. By taking views such as eternalism (sassata), craving (taṇhā) and ignorance (avijjā) are included. Through that craving and ignorance, the beginningless cycle of rebirth (saṃsāra-vaṭṭa) revolves. By penetrating the origin (samudaya) and so forth of feelings as they really are, there is the purification of the Blessed One's three kinds of full understanding (pariññā). Through that purification of the three kinds of full understanding, with the perfection of wisdom (paññā-pāramī) as the lead, all the perfections (pāramīs) revolve.

In the phrase "to those who do not know, do not see," by taking ignorance (avijjā), unwise attention (ayoniso-manasikāra) is included. Through that unwise attention, the nine things rooted in unwise attention revolve. In the phrase "the agitation and vibration of those who have reached craving," by taking craving (taṇhā), the nine things rooted in craving revolve. The statement "that view is also conditioned by contact" shows that the prescription of views such as eternalism is dependent on conditions. By showing that it is dependent on conditions, the three characteristics (tilakkhaṇa) such as impermanence (aniccata) revolve. By knowing the six bases of contact as they really are, the achievement of liberation (vimutti) is pointed out. By pointing out that achievement of liberation, the seven purifications (visuddhi) revolve. By the text "the Tathāgata's body has the cord of craving for existence cut," the abandonment of craving is stated. By that abandonment of craving, the Blessed One's abandonment of all defilements (saṃkilesa) revolves. Thus, of the things taken in the teaching...
490:
The mode characterized by revolving by way of similar and dissimilar states is called the Mode of Revolving (Āvatta-hāra). Regarding this, it is said: "In one proximate cause, one seeks the remaining proximate causes," and so on (Netti. 4.7).

## Explanation of the Mode of Classification (Vibhatti-hāra-vaṇṇanā)

States such as malice (āghāta) are unwholesome states; the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) of these unwholesome states is unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra) and so on. Those states by which the non-doing and non-occurrence of malice etc. are effected are wholesome states such as non-ill-will (abyāpāda); the proximate cause of these wholesome states is wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) and so on. Among these, malice etc. belong only to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), while non-ill-will etc. belong to the four planes (catubhūmaka). Likewise, abstinence from killing (pāṇātipāta) etc. is either wholesome or indeterminate (abyākata); the proximate cause of that abstinence is shame (hiri), fear of wrongdoing (ottappa), and so on.

Among those wholesome and indeterminate states, some wholesome states belong to the sense-sphere, while some are supramundane (lokuttara). Indeterminate states are supramundane only. The states taught as "Monks, there are other states that are deep," etc., are some wholesome and some indeterminate. Among them, the proximate cause of the wholesome states is insight leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī-vipassanā). The proximate cause of the indeterminate states is the path-states (magga-dhamma), insight (vipassanā), or adverting (āvajjana). Among those, the wholesome states are supramundane only, while the indeterminate states are some sense-sphere and some supramundane. All wrong views (diṭṭhi) are unwholesome only and belong to the sense-sphere only. Generally, the proximate cause of these views is unwise attention in wrong conviction (micchābhinivesa).

Specifically, because of the lack of analysis and differentiation of the continuity and compactness of mind and matter, wrong adherence to the method of unity (ekatta-naya), when combined with reasoning and recollection of past births, is the proximate cause of the eternalist view (sassata-diṭṭhi). Because of the failure to grasp the connection by way of cause and effect, wrong adherence to the method of diversity (nānatta-naya), when combined with attention appropriate to that [wrong view], is the proximate cause of the annihilationist view (uccheda-diṭṭhi). In this way, the proximate causes of the remaining views should also be stated as they arise.

In the word "vedanānaṃ" (of feelings), feeling is sometimes wholesome, sometimes unwholesome, and sometimes indeterminate. It may belong to the sense-sphere, the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), or the immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara). The proximate cause of these feelings is contact (phassa). There is path-knowledge (magga-ñāṇa) which penetrates the true nature and the origin etc. of feelings, and there is fruit-knowledge (phala-ñāṇa) which is liberation without clinging. The classification of states etc. for these path and fruit knowledges should be understood according to the method taught in "there are other states that are deep." In sentences such as "for those who do not know and do not see," ignorance (avijjā) and craving (taṇhā) are unwholesome states and sense-sphere states. Among these, the proximate cause of ignorance is the taints (āsava), or simply unwise attention. The proximate cause of craving is seeing gratification (assāda) in things that are conducive to fetters (saṃyojaniya). That state also...
491:
“In the phrase ‘Phassapaccayā’ (conditioned by contact), the classification of contact into phenomena, etc., should be understood just as in the case of feeling (vedanā). In this manner, the classification of the sense bases of contact (phassāyatana), etc., into phenomena, etc., should be applied accordingly. This mode of conveying (hāra) characterized by classification in terms of shared and unshared qualities, proximate causes (padaṭṭhāna), and planes (bhūmi) regarding defiled phenomena and purified phenomena is called the Mode of Conveying a Formulation (Vibhatti-hāra). Thus it is said (in the Netti): ‘This mode classifies the phenomena, the proximate cause, and the plane,’ etc.

## Description of the Mode of Conveying a Reversal (Parivattana-hāra-vaṇṇanā)

Not committing malice (āghāta), etc., develops patience (khanti) and gentleness (soracca), and through the accomplishment of the power of development (bhāvanā) by reflecting with wisdom, it brings about the practice for the benefit of both oneself and others. However, if malice, etc., are allowed to occur, they produce ugliness, painful sleep, loss of wealth, ill-repute, and difficulty for others to approach, bringing great suffering in hell and so forth. Abstaining from taking life (pāṇātipāta), etc., brings about a sequence of benefits such as freedom from remorse. Taking life, etc., however, brings about a sequence of harms such as remorse. Knowledge endowed with special qualities like depth brings about special qualities such as clear-vision (vijjā) and direct knowledge (abhiññā) for those who are to be tamed, because of the realization of all knowable things according to their true nature. Similarly, knowledge lacking special qualities like depth does not bring about the aforementioned special qualities because it has a common nature regarding knowable things.

All these views, being Eternalism or Annihilationism as the case may be, stand at the two extremes and cannot transcend the shore of identity (sakkāya) because they are not leading out of suffering (aniyyānika). Right view (sammādiṭṭhi), however, together with its requisites, being the Middle Way (majjhimapaṭipadā), transcends the shore of identity and reaches the further shore because it leads out of suffering (niyyānika). The penetration of the origin, etc., of feelings as they truly are brings about liberation through non-clinging because it is the path. The non-penetration of the origin, etc., of feelings as they truly are brings about imprisonment within the prison of saṃsāra because feelings are the condition for volitional formations (saṅkhāra). Delusion (sammoha) which conceals the nature of experience brings about delight in that experience; however, realization according to reality brings about penetration and dispassion (virāga) therein. Craving (taṇhā) accompanied by unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra) in the adherence to wrong views spreads a vast net of views. The first path (the path of stream-entry), which completely cuts off the aforementioned craving, withdraws that net of views. Contact (phassa) is the condition for the designation of Eternalism, etc., because in the absence of contact, such designations do not exist. For those bound by the fetters of views, the non-cessation of the sense bases of contact, etc., leading to the non-cessation of contact, etc., is indeed the non-recession from the suffering of the round of rebirths (saṃsāra). The full understanding (pariññā) of the sense bases of contact, etc., according to reality transcends all views and visions; however, for them, in that manner...”
492:
Not fully knowing the sense bases of contact (*phassāyatana*) and so forth, one cannot transcend wrong views (*diṭṭhi*). Cutting the cord of existence (*bhavanetti*), which is craving, leads to the non-arising of selfhood in the future. If the cord of existence is not cut by the Path (*magga*), the succession of existence (*bhavappabandha*) continues to revolve in the future. This is what is called the Mode of Conversion (*Parivattana-hāra*), characterized by the revolving of the states indicated in the Sutta through their opposites. What did the Blessed One say? He said the words beginning with: "When the wholesome and unwholesome states have been indicated, developed, and abandoned..."

## Vevacana-hāra-vaṇṇanā
The words "*mamaṃ*, *mama*, *me*" are synonymous terms for each other. The words "*vā*, *yadi ca*" are synonymous terms. The words "*bhikkhave*, *samaṇā*, *tapassino*" are synonymous terms. The three words "*pare*, *aññe*, *paṭiviruddhā*" are synonymous terms. The words "*avaṇṇaṃ*, *akittiṃ*, *nindaṃ*" are synonymous terms. The words "*bhāseyyuṃ*, *bhaṇeyyuṃ*, *katheyyuṃ*" are synonymous terms. The words "*dhammassa*, *vinayassa*, *satthusāsanassa*" are synonymous terms. The words "*saṅghassa*, *samūhassa*, *gaṇassa*" are synonymous terms. The words "*tatra*, *tattha*, *tesu*" are synonymous terms. The three words "*tumhehi*, *vo*, *bhavantehi*" are synonymous terms. The three words "*āghāto*, *doso*, *byāpādo*" are synonymous terms. The three words "*appaccayo*, *domanassaṃ*, *cetasika-dukkhaṃ*" are synonymous terms. The three words "*cetaso*, *cittassa*, *manaso*" are synonymous terms. The three words "*anabhiraddhi*, *byāpatti*, *manopadoso*" are synonymous terms. The group of four, "*na*, *no*, *a*, *mā*", are synonymous terms. The three words "*karaṇīyā*, *uppādetabbā*, *pavattetabbā*" are synonymous terms. In this manner, synonyms (*vevacana*) should be stated for all terms. This is what is called the Mode of Synonyms (*Vevacana-hāra*), characterized by the application of various synonymous terms for each respective meaning. Thus it is said: "Many are the synonyms mentioned in the Sutta for a single state," and so forth.

## Paññatti-hāra-vaṇṇanā
Malice (*āghāta*) is designated in ten ways according to the grounds for malice (*āghātavatthu*), or in nineteen ways. Displeasure (*appaccaya*) is designated in six ways by way of mental exploration (*upavicāra*). Joy (*ānanda*) is designated in nine ways through synonyms such as rapture (*pīti*) and so forth. Rapture (*pīti*) is designated in five ways, both generally and by way of minor rapture (*khuddikā-pīti*) and so forth. Happiness (*somanassa*) is designated in six ways by way of mental exploration (*upavicāra*). Virtue (*sīla*) is designated in many ways by way of avoidance (*vāritta*) and performance (*cāritta*). Omniscience (*sabbaññuta-ñāṇa*), which is endowed with special qualities such as profundity, is designated in four ways or twelve ways by way of the arising of consciousness, and in many ways according to the variety of objects.
