View (*diṭṭhi*) is designated in sixty-two ways by way of eternalism (*sassata-diṭṭhi*) and so forth, and in many ways by way of the divisions included within those sixty-two views. Feeling (*vedanā*) is designated in six ways, one hundred and eight ways, and in many ways. Its origin (*samudaya*) is designated in five ways. Likewise, its passing away (*atthangama*) is also designated in five ways. Gratification (*assāda*) is designated in two ways. Danger (*ādīnava*) is designated in three ways. Liberation (*nissaraṇa*)...
493:
Liberation without grasping (*anupādā-vimutti*) exists in one way, four ways, or two ways. Ignorance (*avijjā*), spoken of as "for those who do not know and do not see," has four or eight types according to the division of objects. Craving (*taṇhā*), spoken of as "for those who have reached craving," has six, one hundred and eight, or many types. Contact (*phassa*) is designated in six ways by way of its support. Clinging (*upādāna*) is in four ways. Existence (*bhava*) is in two ways and many types. Birth (*jāti*) is in six ways by way of synonyms. Likewise, aging (*jarā*) is in seven ways, death (*maraṇa*) in eight and nine ways, sorrow (*soka*) in five ways, lamentation (*parideva*) in six ways, suffering (*dukkha*) in four ways, and similarly, grief (*domanassa*) in four ways, and despair (*upāyāsa*) in four ways. This is the designation of divisions (*pabheda-paññatti*) and the designation of groups (*samūha-paññatti*).

The designation "origin arises" is called the designation of source (*pabhava-paññatti*). The designation "one knows as it really is" is the designation of full understanding of suffering (*dukkha-pariññā-paññatti*), the designation of abandonment of the origin (*samudaya-pahāna-paññatti*), the designation of realization of cessation (*nirodha-sacchikiriyā-paññatti*), and the designation of development of the path (*magga-bhāvanā-paññatti*). Phrases such as "caught within the net" are the designation of inclusion (*sangaha-paññatti*) of all views. Phrases such as "the cord of existence is cut" are the two kinds of designation of final liberation (*parinibbāna-paññatti*). In this way, the divisions of designation should be analyzed by way of the designation of source, designation of full understanding, and so forth, for malice (*āghāta*) and others. Likewise, "*āghāta*" is the synonymous designation (*vevacana-paññatti*) for ill-will (*byāpāda*), and "*appaccaya*" is the synonymous designation for grief (*domanassa*), and so forth. This is what is called the Mode of Designation (*Paññatti-hāra*), characterized by the explanation of the ways in which a single state is designated by many designations. Therefore, it is said: "The Blessed One teaches a single state through various designations," and so forth.

## Otaraṇa-hāra-vaṇṇanā
By taking malice (*āghāta*), the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*) is included; likewise, by taking dissatisfaction (*anabhiraddhi*), the aggregate of mental formations is included. By taking displeasure (*appaccaya*), the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*) is included. This is called descending (*otaraṇa*) by way of the aggregates (*khandha*). Likewise, by taking malice and so forth, the mind-base (*dhammāyatana*), the mind-element (*dhammadhātu*), the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*), or the truth of the origin (*samudayasacca*) is taken. This is called descending by way of the bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), and truths (*sacca*). Likewise, ignorance (*avijjā*) co-nascent with malice and so forth is a condition by way of root (*hetu*), co-nascence (*sahajāta*), mutuality (*aññamañña*), support (*nissaya*), association (*sampayutta*), presence (*atthi*), and non-disappearance (*avigata*) conditions. However, ignorance that is not co-nascent but ceased in the preceding moment is a condition by way of proximity (*anantara*), contiguity (*samanantara*), decisive support of proximity (*anantarūpanissaya*), absence (*natthi*), disappearance (*vigata*), and repetition (*āsevana*) conditions. Ignorance that is not immediate is a condition only by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*). For craving (*taṇhā*), clinging (*upādāna*), and so forth, their status as conditions for contact (*phassa*) and others—both for those states co-nascent with them and those not co-nascent—should be stated as appropriate. Herein, some states are by way of predominance (*adhipati*), some by way of kamma, some by way of nutriment (*āhāra*), some by way of faculty (*indriya*), and some by way of jhāna...
494:
It should also be understood that some phenomena assist by way of the path-condition (magga-paccaya); thus, this is the entry (otaraṇa) by way of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda). In this same manner, the entry by way of the aggregates (khandha) and so on for individuals such as Ānanda should be clearly demonstrated.

Similarly, virtue (sīla) consists of the volition of abstinence (virati-cetanā) from killing and so on, and mental factors such as non-ill will (abyāpāda), as well as the volitions themselves regarding killing and so on. Because these virtues, along with the phenomena that assist them such as shame (lajja) and compassion and so on, are included within the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha) and the mental-object base (dhammāyatana), the entry by way of the aggregates and so on should be clearly demonstrated in the same manner as before. This same method should be noted in the grasping of knowledge (ñāṇa), view (diṭṭhi), feeling (vedanā), ignorance (avijjā), craving (taṇhā), and so on. However, in the grasping of escape (nissaraṇa) and liberation through non-clinging (anupādā-vimutti), the entry by way of the elements (dhātu) should be clearly demonstrated even by way of the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu). Similarly, by the passage 'Of feelings... liberated through non-clinging,' the Buddha's five aggregates of Dhamma (pañca-dhammakkhandha) such as virtue and so on, and the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma) such as the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) and so on, are revealed; thus, the entry by way of those aggregates of Dhamma and so on should also be understood. By the passage 'That too is conditioned by contact,' because it shows the nature of being dependent on causes for the designation of eternalism (sassata) and so on, the entry by way of impermanence (anicca) should be understood. Similarly, because of such a nature, the entry by way of dependent origination should also be understood. Due to the nature of suffering (dukkha) and non-self (anatta) in impermanence, the entry by way of the desireless (appaṇihita) and the entry by way of emptiness (suññatā) should be understood. This same method applies to the remaining terms. This method, which has the characteristic of entering into the meaning of the Sutta by way of dependent origination and so on, is called the Method of Entry (Otaraṇa-hāra). Indeed, it was said: 'That which is dependent origination, the faculties, the aggregates, the elements, and the bases...' and so on.

## The Explanation of the Method of Cleansing (Sodhana-hāra-vaṇṇanā)

'Monks, others might speak in dispraise of me' is the initiative (ārambha). 'Or they might speak in dispraise of the Dhamma, or they might speak in dispraise of the Saṅgha' is the cleansing of terms (pada-suddhi), but not the cleansing of the initiative (ārambha-suddhi). 'In that case, you should not harbor resentment, or dissatisfaction, or displeasure of mind' is both the cleansing of terms and the cleansing of the initiative. This same method applies to the second method and so on. Similarly, the statement 'This is a matter of little importance' and so on is the initiative. The statement 'What is it?' and so on is the question (pucchā). The statement 'Having abandoned the killing of living beings' and so on is the cleansing of terms, but it is neither the cleansing of the initiative nor the cleansing of the question. The statement 'This indeed' and so on is the cleansing of the question, the cleansing of terms, and the cleansing of the initiative.

Similarly, the statement 'Monks, there are' and so on is the initiative. The statement 'And what are they?' and so on is the question. The statement 'Monks, there are' and so on is the initiative. 'Based on what?' and so on follow.
495:
It is the initiative-question (ārambha-pucchā). The statement 'As one concentrated' and so on is the cleansing of terms (pada-suddhi), but not the cleansing of the initiative (ārambha-suddhi), nor the cleansing of the question (pucchā-suddhi). The statement 'These indeed' and so on is the cleansing of terms, the cleansing of the question, and the cleansing of the initiative. In this manner, the initiative and so on should be understood in all instances. This method, which has the characteristic of investigating the cleansed or uncleansed state of the terms and initiatives, is called the Method of Cleansing (Sodhana-hāra). It was also said: 'When a question is answered, this initiative is asked in the verse' and so on.

## The Explanation of the Method of Terms of Expression (Adhiṭṭhāna-hāra-vaṇṇanā)

The word 'dispraise' (avaṇṇa) is the term of expression (adhiṭṭhāna) in a general sense. Without differentiating that phenomenon, the statement 'of me' (mamaṃ vā) is the specific statement (visesa-vacana). This same method should be understood in the parts 'of the Dhamma' or 'of the Saṅgha'. Similarly, the word 'virtue' (sīla) is the term of expression in a general sense. Without differentiating that phenomenon, the statement 'abstaining from killing living beings' and so on is the specific statement. The statement 'other phenomena' and so on is the term of expression in a general sense. Without differentiating that phenomenon, the statement 'This, monks, the Tathāgata understands' and so on is the specific statement. Similarly, 'speculators about the past' (pubbantakappika) and so on is the term of expression in a general sense. Without differentiating that phenomenon, the statement 'eternalists' (sassata-vāda) and so on is the specific statement. In this manner, the general and specific aspects should be extracted as they were taught in all words and sentences. This method, which has the characteristic of extracting the general and specific aspects as they were taught by not differentiating the phenomena appearing in the Sutta, is called the Method of Terms of Expression (Adhiṭṭhāna-hāra). Therefore, it was said: 'Phenomena in their unity, and those also which are indicated in their diversity' and so on.

## The Explanation of the Method of Requisites (Parikkhāra-hāra-vaṇṇanā)

Regarding resentment (āghāta) and so on, the nineteen grounds for resentment (āghāta-vatthu) such as 'He has done me harm' and so on are the cause (hetu). For individuals such as Ānanda, the affection for the object (ārammaṇābhisineha) is the cause. For virtue (sīla), the causes are shame and fear of wrongdoing (hiri-ottappa), fewness of wishes (appicchatā), and so on. The cause of the Dhamma described as 'profound' (gambhīra) and so on is all the perfections (pāramī), especially the perfection of wisdom (paññā-pāramī). For views (diṭṭhi), the causes in a general sense are associating with the unworthy (asappurisa-upanissaya), hearing the false Dhamma (asaddhamma-savana), and the occurrence of inappropriate attention (ayoniso-manasikāra) through wrong conviction. Specifically, however, the cause of eternalist views (sassata-vāda) and so on is the ability to recollect past lives (atīta-jāti-anussaraṇa) and so on. For feelings (vedanā), the causes are ignorance (avijjā), craving (taṇhā), kamma, and so on, as well as contact (phassa). For the fruition of liberation from defilements without clinging through craving, conceit, and views, the cause is the Noble Path (ariya-magga). For delusion (moha), the cause is inappropriate attention (ayoniso-manasikāra). For craving (taṇhā), the cause is the repeated contemplation of gratification (assādānupassanā) in phenomena that are objects of the fetters (saṃyojaniya). For contact (phassa), the causes are the six sense bases (saḷāyatana). For the six sense bases...
496:
Mentality-materiality (nāmarūpa) is the cause. The development of purification (visuddhibhāvanā) which is the absolute cutting off of the conduit to existence (bhavanetti/craving) is the cause. Thus, the mode (hāra) characterized by investigating and explaining the causal condition (hetu-paccaya) known as equipment (parikkhāra) is called the Mode of Conveying Equipment (Parikkhāra-hāra). Accordingly, it was said (by the Venerable Mahākaccāyana in the Netti-pāḷi): "Whatever states produce whatever state through a succession of conditions," and so forth.

## Samāropana-hāra-vaṇṇanā

By the teaching on the non-doing of malice (āghāta) and so forth, the fulfillment of patience (khanti-sampadā) is shown. By the words beginning with "This is but a trifle," the fulfillment of gentleness (soracca-sampadā) is shown. By the words beginning with "There is, O monks," the fulfillment of knowledge (ñāṇa-sampadā) is shown. By the words "To that person who does not misapprehend, the quenching of defilements (nibbāna) is known within himself," and "Having known feelings... as they really are, he is liberated without clinging," the fulfillment of concentration (samādhi-sampadā) along with the fulfillment of mastery in knowledge and liberation (vijjā-vimutti-vasībhāva-sampadā) are shown.

Among those fulfillments, the fulfillment of patience is the proximate cause (padatṭhāna) for the fulfillment of gentleness, because it accomplishes the power of reflection (paṭisaṅkhāna-bala). The fulfillment of gentleness, in essence, is virtue (sīla) itself. Virtue is the proximate cause for the fulfillment of concentration. Concentration is the proximate cause for the fulfillment of knowledge. This method of presentation is called the Conveying of Proximate Causes (Padatṭhāna-samāropanā).

The mention of abstaining from killing (pāṇātipāta) and so forth is the demonstration of the classification of virtue by way of synonyms (pariyāya). The demonstration of the classification of views such as eternalism (sassata-vāda) and so forth is the synonymous expression of view (diṭṭhi). This method of presentation is called the Conveying of Synonyms (Vevacana-samāropanā).

Through virtue, the abandonment of transgression (vītikkama), temporary abandonment (tadaṅga), and the abandonment of the defilement of misconduct (duccarita) are accomplished. Through concentration, the abandonment of obsession (pariyuṭṭhāna), abandonment by suppression (vikkhambhana), and the abandonment of the defilement of craving (taṇhā) are accomplished. Through wisdom, the abandonment of the defilement of views (diṭṭhi), abandonment by cutting off (samuccheda), and the abandonment of latent tendencies (anusaya) are accomplished. This method of presentation is called the Conveying of Abandonment (Pahāna-samāropanā).

Through the groups of states such as virtue and so forth, the fulfillment of the development of serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā) is reached because of the accomplishment of the three kinds of abandonment. This method of presentation is called the Conveying of Development (Bhāvanā-samāropanā). Thus, the mode characterized by investigating the states that appear in the Suttas through proximate cause, synonym, abandonment, and development is called the Mode of Conveying Terms (Samāropana-hāra). It was said: "Whatever states have whatever roots, and whatever states are declared by the Sage to have the same meaning," and so forth. This concludes the application of the sixteen modes (hāra).

## Soḷasahara-vaṇṇanā Niṭṭhitā.
497:
## Pañcavidha-naya-vaṇṇanā

## Nandiyāvaṭṭa-naya-vaṇṇanā

By the teaching on the non-doing of malice (āghāta) and so forth, the reduction of craving (taṇhā) and ignorance (avijjā) is shown. Indeed, when there is affection and delusion regarding the self and what belongs to the self (attā/attaniya), malice arises with the thought, "This person has done me harm," and so forth; it does not arise when these are absent. Likewise, by such words as "He abstains from killing living beings," and by such words as "The quenching of defilements is known within himself, he is liberated without clinging, he understands the six bases of contact... as they really are," the absolute abandonment of craving and ignorance is shown.

Furthermore, the basis (adhiṭṭhāna) of that craving and ignorance—which are shown in their own nature by such terms as "speculators on the past" (pubbantakappika) and by such terms as "of one who does not know, who does not see"—are the states of materiality (rūpa) and immateriality (arūpa). Serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā) are their respective opposites. The liberation of mind (ceto-vimutti) and liberation by wisdom (paññā-vimutti) are their fruits. Therein, craving (or craving and ignorance) is the Truth of the Origin (samudaya-sacca). The states of materiality and immateriality, which are the basis for them, are the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca). Their non-occurrence is the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-sacca). Serenity and insight, which are the understanding of cessation, are the Truth of the Path (magga-sacca). In this way, the application of the Four Noble Truths should be understood.

In this method, by the inclusion of craving, the entire unwholesome side is to be brought in by way of deceit (māyā), fraud (sāṭheyya), pride (māna), arrogance (atimāna), intoxication (mada), negligence (pamaada), evil desire (pāpicchatā), evil friendship (pāpamittatā), lack of shame (ahirika), and lack of dread (anottappa). Likewise, by the inclusion of ignorance, [the unwholesome side is brought in] by way of improper attention (ayoniso manasikāra), anger (kodha), resentment (upanāha), contempt (makkha), domineering (paḷāsa), envy (issā), avarice (macchariya), spite (sārambha), difficult speech (dovacassatā), the view of existence (bhava-diṭṭhi), and the view of non-existence (vibhava-diṭṭhi).

Conversely, by way of non-deceit (amāyā), non-fraud (asāṭheyya), and so forth, and by way of proper attention and so forth, the entire wholesome side is to be brought in. Likewise, it is to be brought in by way of the faculty of faith (saddhindriya) and so forth which belong to the side of serenity, and by way of the perception of impermanence (anicca-saññā) and so forth which belong to the side of insight. Thus, the Way of the Turning of the Cycle of Joy (Nandiyāvaṭṭa-naya) is characterized by guiding the meaning of a Sutta through the application of the Four Noble Truths, using craving and ignorance for the side of defilement (saṃkilesa) and serenity and insight for the side of purification (vodāna). For it was said: "He who guides both craving and ignorance by serenity and insight," and so forth.

## Tipukkhalanaya-vaṇṇanā

By the teaching on the non-doing of malice and so forth, the accomplishment of non-hatred (adosa/loving-kindness) is established. Likewise, it is established by the teaching on abstaining from killing and harsh speech. Furthermore, by the teaching on the non-doing of joy (ānanda) and so forth...
498:
Non-greed is established also by the teaching of refraining from unchaste conduct. However, by the teaching of refraining from taking what is not given and so forth, both [non-greed and non-hatred] are established. Non-delusion is established by the words, "Monks, the Tathāgata understands this," and so forth. Thus, by the three unwholesome roots taken, and by the teaching of not committing malice and so forth, which are the opposites of those unwholesome roots, the three wholesome roots are indeed established. Between these two, the wholesome and unwholesome roots, the entire unwholesome side should be elaborated by means of the three unwholesome roots through the threefold misconduct, defilements, stains, unevenness, unwholesome perceptions, thoughts, and mental proliferation (papañca), and so forth. Similarly, the entire wholesome side should be clarified by means of the three wholesome roots through the threefold good conduct, purification (vodāna), evenness, wholesome perceptions, wholesome thoughts, wisdom, the true Dhamma, concentration, the doors to liberation, and liberation, and so forth.

In this method, the connection to the Truths is as follows: Greed is called the Truth of the Origin, or all wholesome and unwholesome roots are called the Truth of the Origin. The aggregates of clinging that arise because of those roots and serve as their basis and object are called the Truth of Suffering. The non-occurrence of that Truth of Suffering and Truth of the Origin is called the Truth of Cessation. Liberation and so forth, which understand the Truth of Cessation, are called the Truth of the Path. This is the ground of the Tipukkhala Method, which has the characteristic of leading the side of defilement by unwholesome roots and the side of purification by wholesome roots through connection with the Four Noble Truths. Thus it is said: "He who leads the unwholesome along with their roots, and leads the wholesome by the wholesome roots," and so forth (in the Nettippakaraṇa).

## Sīhavikkīḷita-naya-vaṇṇanā

Mindfulness is established by the teaching of not committing malice, delight, and so forth. Energy is established by the teaching of refraining from wrong livelihood. Through energy, one dispels thoughts of sensual desire, ill will, and cruelty; and virtue consisting in purity of livelihood (ājīva-pārisuddhi-sīla) is also accomplished through energy. Mindfulness is established by the teaching of refraining from taking life and so forth. Through mindfulness, one sees the blameworthy unwholesome and the blameless wholesome. Having noted the faults and benefits in those states, one abandons the blameworthy and undertakes and practices the blameless. Therefore, that mindfulness is said to have "the mode of delivering [one] from saṃsāra." Concentration and wisdom are established by the words, "Monks, the Tathāgata understands this," and so forth. One who has wisdom penetrates and knows according to reality; one who is concentrated also knows according to reality.

Similarly, the perversion (vipallāsa) of perceiving "permanence" in the impermanent (anicca) by saying "it is permanent, it is stable," and so forth, is established. The perversion of perceiving "pleasure" in suffering (dukkha) by saying "after death one is free from disease, the self is purely happy, one attains Nibbāna in this very life," and so forth, is established. The perversion of perceiving "beauty" in the foul (asubha) by saying "one is endowed with the five cords of sensual pleasure," and so forth, is established.
499:
By the word "samappito" and so forth, there is the perversion of "beauty" (subha) in the foul (asubha). By all the words expressing views, there is the perversion of "self" (atta) in the non-self (anatta). Thus, the four perversions are established here. By way of opposition to those perversions, the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) are also indeed established.

In those foundations of mindfulness and so forth, four types of persons are indicated by the four faculties (indriya) already mentioned. How are they indicated? A person of craving temperament is of two kinds: one with dull faculties and one with sharp faculties. Similarly, a person of view temperament is also of two kinds. Among those four persons, the first, who is of craving temperament and has dull faculties, has the perverted view of "beauty" in the foul; by the power of mindfulness, having noted the nature of the body according to reality, he enters into the certainty of the Path, which is of an unperverted nature. The second, who is of craving temperament and has sharp faculties, has the perverted view of "pleasure" in what is not pleasure (painful feeling); by the power of energy called restraint by energy, as taught in the words "he does not tolerate an arisen thought of sensual desire" and so forth, he destroys that perversion. The third, who is of view temperament and has dull faculties, has the perverted view of "permanence" in the impermanent; by the power of concentration, because of being well-concentrated, he penetrates and knows according to reality the momentary nature of conditioned things (saṅkhāra). The fourth, who is of view temperament and has sharp faculties, has the perverted view of "self" in the non-self, which is merely a heap of states such as contact (phassa), because of the complexity of continuity, mass, function, and object; by the attention to emptiness (suññata-manasikāra) which has four aspects, he destroys that wrong adherence.

In this Sīhavikkīḷita Method, the entire unwholesome side should be led by means of the four perversions through the four taints (āsava), floods (ogha), bonds (yoga), ties (gantha), wrong courses (agati), arisings of craving, clingings (upādāna), and the non-comprehension of the seven stations of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti), and so forth. Similarly, the entire side of purification (vodāna) should be led by means of the four foundations of mindfulness through the four meditative abidings (jhāna-vihāra), determinations, states partaking of happiness, immeasurables, right efforts, bases of power (iddhipāda), and so forth.

Here, the connection to the Truths is: the Truth of the Origin is extracted by means of the perception of beauty and the perception of pleasure, or by the four perversions. The five aggregates of clinging, which are the basis and object of those perversions, are called the Truth of Suffering. The non-occurrence of that Origin and Suffering is called the Truth of Cessation. The foundations of mindfulness and so forth, which understand the Truth of Cessation, are called the Truth of the Path. What has been said is the scope of the Sīhavikkīḷita Method, which has the characteristic of leading the side of defilement (saṃkilesa) by perversions and the side of purification (vodāna) by the faculty of faith and so forth, based on the connection with the Four Noble Truths. It is as taught: "He who leads the defilements by the perversions, and the true Dhamma by the faculties," and so forth.

## Disālocana-naya and Aṅkusa-naya-vaṇṇanā

Thus, because of the completion of the three methods of meaning (attha-naya), the two methods of phrasing (vohāra-naya) are also indeed completed. This is true: the thorough surveying of the states that occur by the power of the three methods of meaning is itself the Disālocana Method (Method of Surveying the Directions). The thorough leading of those states is itself the Aṅkusa Method (Method of the Hook). Therefore, it should be understood that by the power of the method of thoroughly surveying the states which are the "directions" of the methods of meaning in the manner already mentioned, these two methods—Disālocana and Aṅkusa—are also connected. Therefore, the words "Those who are skilled in the wholesome and unwholesome in the expositions (veyyākaraṇa)" and so forth were taught. This is the connection of the five methods.
500:
In the manner already stated, it should be understood that the two methods—disā-ālocana (viewing the directions) and aṅkusa (the hook), which serve as the 'directions' for the methods of meaning (atthanaya)—should also be applied. Therefore, it is said: "In the expositions (veyyākaraṇa), those which are wholesome and unwholesome..." and so forth. This is the application of the five methods.

## The explanation of the fivefold methods is finished.

## Explanation of the Sāsanapaṭṭhāna

In the sixteenfold Sāsanapaṭṭhāna, this Brahmajāla Sutta is a discourse partaking of defilement (saṃkilesabhāgiya), partaking of impressions (vāsanābhāgiya), and partaking of the adept (asekkhabhāgiya), because it analyzes defilements such as craving and views, meritorious actions such as virtue, and the aggregates of the adept (asekkha-kkhandha) such as the virtue of the adept. Alternatively, it is partaking of defilement, partaking of impressions, partaking of penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya), and partaking of the adept, because it analyzes the aforementioned meanings and the aggregates of virtue of the trainee (sekha-sīlakkhandha), and so forth. In the twenty-eightfold Sāsanapaṭṭhāna, it is so because it analyzes meanings such as the mundane and supramundane, person-centric (sattādhiṭṭhāna) and Dhamma-centric (dhammādhiṭṭhāna), knowledge and the knowable, vision and development, one's own words and others' words, answerable and unanswerable, action and result, wholesome and unwholesome, allowed and forbidden, and existence (bhava). This is the application of the Sāsanapaṭṭhāna.

## The explanation of the Pakaraṇanaya is finished.

Thus is the Līnatthavibhāvanā (Clarification of the Hidden Meanings), an explanation of the Brahmajāla Sutta titled Sādhuvilāsinī (also known as Līnatthappakāsanī). It is part of the Sumangalavilāsinī, the Commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya, which elucidates meanings that are extremely subtle, profound, and difficult to comprehend, and which generates the power of pure and extensive wisdom. It was composed by the Great Elder named Ñāṇābhivaṃsa Dhammasenāpati, who held the title of Mahādhammarājādhirājaguru. He was endowed with qualities such as uprightness, gentleness, grace, faith, mindfulness, stability, wisdom, patience, and energy. He possessed an unhindered and fearless intellectual vision regarding the three Pitakas along with their commentaries, and he had penetrated the dense forest of various doctrines, both his own and those of others. He was a great leader of the community (mahāgaṇi) and a master of great grammar.

## The explanation of the Brahmajāla Sutta is finished.
